It's top-down nature and cutesy graphics give you an aura of simplicity. but RwR delivers in providing deep tactical gameplay with opportunities to go Rambo if you so choose.
Fighting through huge urban engagements, trench wars, vehicular warfare, going mad on an LMG/MG.
RwR is well worth its buy in price and can easily be enjoyed in the sandbox single player mode, with friends doing the sandbox mode in coop, or in a server in PvE or PvP.
The AI puts up a good challenge and behaves realistically, trying to flank your position, retreating behind cover when surpressed with MG fire, and bringing in further waves of reinforcements in areas under attack.
The game also has seen mods in the early access period bringing you from laser blasters, modern warfare, and to WW1 and I'm sure those will be carried on going forth.
Highly recommend.
It takes a little getting into, but soon enough it will get under your skin and you'll spend hours conquering maps and feel like a kid playing army-men again.

The game has potential, but in its current state (as of 8/14/15), it has a VERY long way to go, even for Early Access. I'm a huge supporter of early access games. I own probably about 50-60 ea games. This by far, ranks as being one of the most incomplete. It seems more like a pre-alpha.
1) The graphics seem fine/good for this type of game, although many have complained that the cartoony graphics break the immersion of a business sim, making it feel more like a BigFish Games flash game. I can understand that criticism.
2) The concept (oil business) is unique and is a refreshing change for the genre.
3) It's educational (you'll learn about the various practices and buildings necessary in the oil industry.
1) The tutorial, which apparently was recently redone, is amazingly inadequate IMO. There are only about 5-6 steps in the tutorial, and each only tell you to build a specific buildilng. There are additional help pages, but in game that has several moving balls like this, the tutorial should do more to engage the player. The game is fairly sophisticated yet the player is thrown in to figure everything out for themselves. You either have to experiment or get what little information exists through manual help pages.
Here's the thing with that...and is why it's my #1 gripe here:  I enjoy figuring things out on my own. It creates a sense of discovery and accomplishment. But figuring out GAME MECHANICS is not the same thing as figuring out BEST PRACTICES or world/game exploration.
You are supposed to be a businessman in the oil industry. Which means you should already know and understand key concepts and processes, and industry strategy. Obviously, us as gamers do not have this knowledge. THAT is where tutorials come into play. The catch the player up to speed with the mechanics of the game (basic setup practices) and key understandings to be successful. THEN, the game ought to challenge the player to use what they learn to be successful or overcome obstacles.
. Instead, it forces the player to not only learn the basics of the industry themselves, but also the basics of the game mechanics, which breaks the immersion and creates an almost hair-pulling experience, especially compared to so many other involved games that have a proper tutorial.
2) The animations are too simplistic nor are they relevant. They don't tell you anything about the flow of the process nor are they relevant in as far as how buildings interact with one another. There are no construction animations. You place the building and it looks 100% constructed, but are told it isn't. You have to wait. See #4.
3) There are no intuitive capacity indicators for your buildings. No way to easily tell when buildings are getting filled up, which tells the player how the efficient the processes are working.
4) The sense of time is horrible. It takes "5 hours" to build most if not all buildings. But there is no clock, no sense of time whatsoever. You can however speed things up with a FF button which is nice, but it doesn't do anything to help with the lack of sense of time. I know a building is being constructed, but I don't see how long it takes to construct via the expected construction bar (or similar) animation that practically EVERY other builder game in existence has.
5) The price point is always going to be subjective. Obviously what is worth it to one player may not be to another. So instead, I'd argue that the price point is NOT comparable to OTHER early access games for what you get. There are several other early access games at or around the same price point (many even less) that are more fleshed out, more intuitive, more immersive, etc.
Most likely, I'll be requesting a refund. The game has potential, it just has a very long way to go and ought to consider itself a pre-alpha IMHO.

Alright, i've considered to write a review for Ori and the blind forest for a while now, but usually just end up playing it through again.... Now that i have 76 hours in a game with about 14 hours of gameplay (Pluss 10 in the defintive edition...), i guess it's about time.
I'll start with visuals and estetics. The game is beatuful. The forests are dense, mysterious and just feel right. It switches from vivid and wonderfull to looming and dark in the different locations in the world, and it just fits. It never seases to amaze me just how alive the forests sometimes feel. Almost any area and spot in the game is worthy of being a new screensaver. This is what the game is known for, and it shouldn't be a suprise that it gets full marks here.
The music is brilliant and accompanies the scenery perfectly. Wether you are listening to deep chello-tones for the dark and looming forests or the adventorous flute for the bright and beautilful mountains, the music just fits. Again i'd give it full marks here. Also the emotional tracks for the cutscenes easily got a spot in my spotify playlists.
The gameplay is smooth, and i wasn't left wanting. I'm not very used to 2D platformers so some might feel otherwise, but for me the skills you get were varied and appropriate. It also made a nice learning curve to start simple, and later letting you do awesome cominations.
The story for the game is good. Not great or bad, but good. It's deeper than it originally seems, and suprisingly deep for a game where only one character has dialogue (That little glowing orb, Sein, and there is also naration). It's delivered in a nice manner and at a proper pace. The characters are more relatable than expected (Spesifically Kuro), and it's a nice story for the game. The feels are also real in this one. Some of the cutscenes were completely heartbreaking for me, and i rarely feel this from games.
Ok. Time to mention the things that aren't just wonderfull. Every game has flaws, and they exist here too. For me, the ginzo tree part was a far too large escalation in difficulty compared to the previous parts. I've also noted that many of the negative reviews will come from people struggling to get through this part in the game. It probably took me about a hundred tries to make it. This is fixed in the definitive edition, with the addition of difficulty settings, but something to be wary of here. If you are new to platformers then persistence might be nececary for this part. Some areas become blocked when you are done, and anything you miss will stay missed... This is also fixed in the definitve edition.
All in all: Great game, but get the definitve edition...

The game offers to play in different regions in-game, where you choose to place your firm down. You have test drilling, pump, Refinery, Logistics, Storage, Maintain, and Safety to work with. You will also have health for your buildings and machines, and a overview for what is needed to get more barrels pr.day to sell.
The game currently d.13-08-2015, offers multiplayer which is in progress. The game is alot more fun playing agens people and fighting agens the best barrels pr.day or moste money in the current "free mode", that can take forever finish, but gives a good laugh if you play with the right people!  - They are working on content for this which i see as a really good thing.
If you like building up a firm, taking care of machines, safety, and maintain what you have while selling barrels of oils on the markedet to keep your income stable with a interesting oil firm feeling and exploring in regions, then this game is for you.

This is, surprisingly enough from all the negative reviews, a fun platformer. Now, first thing, if you don't like PewDiePie, why are you even here? A lot of the dislike for the game seems to come from one of 3 things, 2 of which are reasonable.
1. Bad experience with bugs and glitches. I have yet to encounter any myself, but a player should always be wary of such.
2. Dislike of the quality. Completely understandable. The voice acting is not that great, and the platforming is rather simple. Don't expect Super Mario or Shovel Knight from this gam (not that the others were, or anything). This seems to be a rather simple game specially crafted for fans of Felix and his friends.
3. This is the unreasonable one. Some people seem to have purchased this game with the intention of giving it a negative review because they don't like the man whose name is plastered on the title screen. They feel the need to insult their peers for enjoying PewDIePie's content, as it's not suited to them. If you're one of those people, there is NO NEED to temporarily spend your money, but instead just do it in a comment section or something for virtually free.
Through my small amount of gameplay so far, I'd say that only if you're a fan of Felix and co. then go right on ahead and buy. If not, maybe take a small dip and see if you'll enjoy it for the simple game that it is. Hey, maybe you'll find a new source of entertainment from the content creators included. Or the duck. You can always like ducks.  And if you hate him for whatever reason, I beg that you spend your time and money doing something more worthwhile, like charity or children. Please?
Personally, as an on and off fan, I'd recommend buying this during a sale. Thanks for taking the time to read this! Bye!

Assassin's Creed 1 is definitely a great game. If you do have some time to play, try playing it first through Black Flag, you certainly will understand a whole lot of things. For me, it's a great game, and you could totally see how much the game has changed over the years.
a/ The story plot: is nice, the way the game alternates and lets you pause between the Memory Blocks (which is pieces of the story of Altair), is great.
b/ The combat: is simple, but effective. It was a little bit too boring at first, but once you get the ability to Counter Kill, things start getting much better. But you will have to be patient til' that part, believe me.
c/ The missions: are nice, but to be honest, as mentioned by a lot of articles and reviews, they are repetitive in general. Every city you enter, you will have to go check out every viewpoint, rescue every cititzen in "harassing" trouble, do some interrogation, meeting your Hashassin guild mates to do some jobs for them, eavesdropping people talking, pickpocketing; you will even have to do some "Flag finding running" too. Doing all that and you'll be able to access the "Assassinating your target" part.
d/ The stealth gameplay: is nice, but since this is the first game, compared to the sequels, you won't feel much of the stealth mechanism, most of the time you will have to do some combat, against 7-8 guys all at the same time (you will start noticing this after getting that Counter Kill ability).
e/ One of the things I like about this game, is the fact that it doesn't require you to collect all additional "flags" to unlock the ending. Not at all, so don't you worry, just enjoy your game, do as much as you can. The side quests will be repetitively boring, but even the conversations with each of the Hashassin guild mate are different!, so you can enjoy a little bit of their stories and their information on your targets. And that's good!
f/ The cities: are well-designed; gotta say I'm pretty impressed with the way Ubisoft has designed them; From the ledges for you to climb, to the positioning and distributions of Hiding places, I've gotta say no wonder the first AC game was a success! You've gotta play the series from the first game through the last to see how the series has changed over the years!
If you have played Prince of Persia before, you will definitely see some common things between the two games, some buildings sure can remind you of some obstacles in POP series
CONCLUSION: 9.5/10 when you take into account this is the game made in 10 years ago. Definitely a worthy game to play if you want to have a nice Assassin's Creed collection.

This game really tries to be the next dungeon keeper 2 with it's laughs and comedy, with managing your squads but it just fails. The whole aggression bar when seen as new and interesting, can become a real irritation when you are trying to manage several groups at once. The idea that you don't only need to use heroes bodies for loot, but also prisoners to earn you treasure or put into a big machine when crunches them into points is also interesting, but again wasted in this game. I got stuck on the level where you were under a time limit because upgrading your units is incredibly costly, especially as you don't make materials, you just steal them from another place which costs time and units. Not ot mention many of the jokes aren't funny. They're kid funny, but nothing really made me laugh out loud in hilarity. No...I'm afraid this game falls waaaaay too short of trying to be a dungeon keeper clone. I suggest a much better one like Evil Genius or A Game of Dwarves. Hell, go buy Dungeon Keeper 2 or War of the Overworld as that one looks far more competant.

The game says that if you die too much you have to start over and although it didn't happen to me it may put some people off. I really enjoyed the added anxiety it added to the gameplay. Everything about this game - visuals, sound, environment, story, is all masterpiece-level. I don't know you or your tastes, but I'm pretty sure you need this game in your life. Premise: You are Desmond, a regular guy who is kidnapped and forced to help the Templar secret society locate a MacGuffin to take over the world. You do this by strapping yourself into

the Animus to launch yourself through time and space and relive the memories of your long-dead ancestor Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad, a Syrian assassin during the Third Crusade who is himself an enemy of the Templars. Altaïr must assassinate nine key templars and stop the evil Robert de Sablé from finding the mind-controlling Apple of Eden; meanwhile Desmond must figure out in the present day what the hell his Templar captors want and how to get himself out of this situation.
The Good: For the time it came out, this is a really, really beautiful game, with obvious care put into the painstaking recreation of the four 12th century cities that most of the game takes place in. This game starting the Assassin's Creed tradition of perching on a high viewpoint and receiving a gorgeous rotating view of the intricate architecture of the surrounding city. There's also a lot of fun, rich history here - not exactly my thing, but even I could appreciate how much research went into this. The story, while slow, was fairly interesting with a few decent twists and turns. This includes the present-day story, which hooked me in and definitely left me wondering where the story of Desmond was going next even as I knew the story of Altaïr was over. The platforming? Good lord, the platforming! Assassin's Creed has used roughly the same platforming for so long that it's a little hard to remember now, but this game did innovative things with freerunning, climbing, and exploration that are still being ripped off by a number of games to this day. There's a lot of fun side missions, and I never got tired of leaping from the rooftops to unexpectedly assassinate a corrupt guard that was giving an innocent civilian a hard time. The side missions don't have as much story as they would in later iterations of the series, but I found them very fun in a mini-game kind of way. This was a game where collecting the collectables and doing the side missions was worth the extra time spent to me, which in all my time gaming I have really only considered to be true for the Assassin's Creed series and the Arkham series - everything else loses me. Finally, the characters of Desmond and Altaïr themselves are a lot of fun. Altaïr walks a fine line between being a "young, hopeful action protagonist" and an out-of-control ego monster, and it's much more fun to have a hero so flawed.
The Bad: Ubisoft had not quite figured out how to do cutscenes right yet, so you get a lot of Altaïr awkwardly pacing around while the head Assassin lobs exposition at him from across the room. The controls were mapped in such a nonintuitive way that probably indicates a lazy porting from console - not gamebreaking, but I did find myself needing to check the controls every few minutes, else I would end up assassinating random peasants when I thought I was pressing the button to blend in with them. Finally, as mentioned, the story is slow as molasses. It's worth it in the end, but patience is a definitely a prerequisite virtue to really enjoy this game.
Conclusion: Parts of this game almost turned me off to the Assassin's Creed series entirely with how clunky they were. But overriding a few glitches and flaws is a unique, lovingly crafted experience wrapped in a deep conspiracy theory storyline with a number of generation-defining stealth and freerunning mechanics.

1. This game isn't good. Sorry you had to hear it from me.
2. W/ that out of the way, the music to this is stellar, absolutely on par w/ the very best game soundtracks of all time. No kidding. Go to Freebird Games's Bandcamp page. Buy the album, skip the game. Win/win.
3. Even the presentation beyond the music is fine. It's done in an old school pixel art style, which is pretty cute even if it doesn't feel all that fresh these days. But even how these simple graphics are done reveals the kind of lack of attention to detail that makes this game a chore to play ultimately. It is  640x480 natively and there is no way to change that. It upscales just fine and I don't mind 4:3 w/ bars on the side of a modern monitor but on top of that, for the majority of gameplay, there is typically a black bar both on the top and the bottom of the window as well. The end result is only about a quarter of the available real estate on a normal screen is being used at any given time and since sprites are already pretty small, things are needlessly hard to see. Lots of games get an old-school feel in 16:9 so I just don't see the reason for this design decision. It is not a dealbreaker on its own but it is just the kind of thing
gets wrong over and over.
4. The controls here are pretty bad too. There is controller support but mouse and keyboard works better, which doesn't really fit w/ the bit-era aesthetic. I can live w/ that but the controls are weird and wonky anyway. I constantly found the mouse pointer getting sort of stuck on a previously clicked object and would report the same bit of dialogue no matter where else I pointed at the screen.
5. One of the small challenges presented (intentionally) by the game designer was essentially a pixel-hunt so number 4 gets really annoying.
6. The other small challenge is these tile flipping puzzles for the first half of the game which are either really simple or can be solved in a matter of minutes by trial-and-error.
7. All of the above technical limitation could be forgiven in such a story driven game, which leads us to the real kicker. The story here is really, laughably bad judged by the standards of any medium but video games. Again, sorry you had to hear it from me.
8. The premise is a pretty solid sci-fi trope along the lines of "We Can Remember It For You Wholesale" or
. There are two technicians who have the ability to somehow actively enter into a person's memories and change them for fun and profit. In this case, this astounding technology is used to improve education and fuel scientific development into even more amazing technologies... Wait, no, it's used to make dying people feel better for the last few moments of their lives by manipulating them into thinking they did things they didn't do. Hooray for science!
9. Predictably, our two technicians run into some pretty unusual things when exploring this dying patient's head-space. Unfortunately, the presumably reliable details of this poor fellow's past are odd enough that it makes it difficult to suspend disbelief--and this is after you've swallowed the idea that people can act as video game characters in another person's brain box. It is hard to explain w/o spoilers but, in my opinion, a hefty majority of the backstory presented would occur only if every actor in it were insane.
10.  There is one joke in this that is actually funny.
11. Even w/ everything wrong w/ it, the story would not be so bad were it not told in such a painfully slow manner. The pixel hunt sections I mentioned in 5 can span multiple screens and really fill up a lot of time. I think this story could easily have been a short story that might take an hour to read and the game is going to take most people 3-6 hours to finish. The game play really adds no challenge and the story is completely on rails so your choices don't add anything to it. I just can't help but feel a game was a really bad choice of medium in this case. It might have made a great comic book.
12. Right at the end,
almost redeems itself w/ an ending that would seem to drive home a valuable life lesson but then takes a hard turn into a swamp of sticky-sweet sentiment and happily gets mired there. I guess if you liked the plot up to that point, this is what you'd want.
13. So here we have it: great music, problematic design choices, poor controls, unbelievable story, unfunny humor.  One could be forgiven if they thought this whole game wasn't just a brilliant soundtrack subjected to death by a thousand cuts but it is somehow not a total disaster. I have spent a lot of time thinking about it since completing it which is something I can't say about a lot of games I actually like. Unfortunately, I am mostly thinking about how no plot points jibe w/ how normal people actually act in real life.

if you like story driven games with a bit of puzzle, this one is for you.

The point-and-click adventure genre isn't one that I hear about much these days. Their heyday was primarily in the late 80s and mid-90s. But in those times the interfaces were clunkier and the games themselves were often 2D or some hybrid of FMV and pseudo-3D. Along comes Syberia in 2002 to deliver us an adventure realized in fully 3D character models, attractive pre rendered backgrounds, and an intriguing premise. It's well appreciated.
Syberia follows Kate Walker, a New York lawyer sent into the French Alps to settle the acquisition of a clockwork toy factory by a massive American corporation. As expected, such routine matters do not go as expected and Kate learns that the owner of the factory has passed away and left information about a long-lost brother who is now heir to the factory. Kate leaves on a journey that takes her across western and eastern Europe, retracing the heir's steps, hounded by phone calls from her increasingly livid boss and faithless fiance.
The interface for Syberia is quite clean. Inventory, notes, and clues are gathered into a single menu that unfolds into a second section depending on what you want to use or examine. I never got lost searching for information or items. Likewise, the conversation system is also simple and easy to manage. Kate has access to a limited number of topics (she can learn more) that can be used on most NPCs. As opposed to some of the adventure games of yesteryear that allowed the player to type in potential keywords and/or questions during conversations, Syberia keeps things mostly linear and self-contained.
The atmosphere of Syberia reminds me of a Victorian era novel. The artwork is often ornate and based in art nouveau with its love for arcs and curves. The clockwork toy factory and its automaton creations evoke steampunk imagery that blends the setting between the real and surreal. Lighting and weather effects deliver a sense that Kate is drifting further and further into an unknown frontier. Civilization grows more sparse and eccentric as she journeys, but not at the cost of tone. Syberia is occasionally satirical and tongue-in-cheek with its dialogue, but rarely becomes so silly that the overall mystery and emerging wonder of the world is lost.
At its heart,  Syberia is a story about self-discovery as much as answering the mystery of the lost heir. Kate's interactions with other characters evolve subtly. Much like her boss and fiance, Kate begins her story focused on business and the superficiality of modern American life. As she delves deeper into the story of the clockwork factory, its late owner, and missing heir, she awakens to feelings and ideas she never expected. Her mission is soon driven as much by curiosity and fascination as obligation to her work. Phone calls with friends, family, and work grow less familiar as Kate's emotional and psychological distance from them gradually matches her geographical distance.
The puzzles are pretty simple and most can be solved with items and clues found nearby. I did have some issues with the conversation system that wasted time, though. Sometimes in the process of solving a puzzle, you must return to an NPC you already spoke to and try exhausting the dialogue options with them again because they have something new to say or give you. The linearity of some solutions harms the game occasionally. I would go through dialogue topics out of order from what the developers seemed to expect more often than not, receiving information and puzzle prompts that weren't properly solvable yet. I would run around confused for several minutes before finally returning and discover that I had to ask about something else that would cause the NPC to give me the item I needed to solve the puzzle they already sent me after. Fortunately, this only happened a few times.
The pacing of the story becomes a bit rushed during its third act. There's a villain character who I would've enjoyed learning more about, but the developers were content to keep their villain mostly one-dimensional. The conflict the villain introduces builds up, climaxes, and then gets resolved so quickly that I wonder now if there had been a longer story arc for this encounter that was abandoned during development. However, the overall narrative of Syberia remains intact and only becomes more interesting, hiccups aside. It whacks you with a big cliffhanger, but I was enthusiastic about it, not annoyed. I'm of the mind that if a game ends leaving you genuinely interested in playing its sequel or even just playing the game again, it's automatically a recommendation.

This adventure game has easy puzzles, and it doesn't get into the steampunk mechanics the way you might be hoping for--like most things, it uses them for atmosphere. But, oh man, does this game have atmosphere.
Playing Syberia is a little bit like reading a book from the 1800s. Slow-paced, a little dated, and a little cliche. But if you, like me, enjoy quieting your mind a little to take in all the beauty of something like that, you're going to find a gem.
The puzzles may be easy, but that isn't for lack of respect for the player. In fact, if you don't pay attention and take notes during conversations with NPCs, you're going to find yourself lost. The game points you in the right direction, but it does so while relying solely on logic. Nothing gimmicky or contrived here.
The mechanics are solid and well designed--nearly every time I ran into a wall with a puzzle, I was soon able to see that I only had myself to blame for not exploring enough or not paying enough attention during conversations. There was one puzzle that used a long-forgotten phone call as a hint that I never would have been able to solve without help, but that's the only frustration I can think of, and it was a minor one.
Unlike many adventure games, Syberia has a more realistic tone. You aren't going to find "punny" puzzles or witty flavortext. It's a calm, grounded little game with some stunning art design and sympathetic characters. If you see the value in slow-paced games and enjoy the adventure genre, give this one a shot.

For how little I bought this game for, I defnitely reccomend this game for someone who is just lookig to pass the time with a fun little game. I completed it in two days, playing for long periods of time, but including the re-do that I had to have because the game crashed on me before I saved (I hadn't saved all day so that's partially on me but.... Some pros and cons:
Pros:
For a game with 2002 graphics, the art and scenery is lovely! Also, the variety and size of locations is very pleasing, so you're not just stuck in one world that gets repetitive.
The "puzzles" are not complicated at all (this could be considered a pro if you are looking for a game that is more for passing the time and relaxation than perplexing your brain). The "puzzle" part of the game is more about finding missing objects and putting them where they go, or figuring out who you need to talk to in order to get where you want to go.
I absolutely LOVE the storyline and steampunk theme! It adds depth and creativity to the game. It is very detailed in my opinion, especially when it came to areas that acted as more of a "buffer zone" between locations of importance-- they were definitely not skipped on.
The main character is very sassy, which made me laugh a lot when she interacts with characters who are... unique.
Cons:
First thing that started bugging me was how she walks reeeeaallyy sloo
and sometimes the area you are in is on the larger side, so you can take like three sips of coffee before she even reaches the other side (I counted lol). However, overtime, I did get used to it, and eventually figured out that double clicking makes her run, which speeds up the process a bit.
Character interaction was very entertaing at times (especially when it came to Oscar), but other times I feel like certain words got a tad too repetitive within conversation, and wayy too lonngg at times.
Most of the puzzles weren't really... puzzles. Personally, they weren't hard enough for me/aren't the ones that I consider puzzles. Again, it's mostly finding things and putting stuff back together again.
Crashes. THis is a pretty old game, so it was prone to a lot of crashes if you 1) left it on too long (like for hours long btw 2) if you switch to and from different windows on your computer. However, if you save often, you should be fine.
*Extras:
Not necessarily a pro or con, but I would have really liked to have been able to control her dialogue-- not to the extent of changing the plot line, but just a tad.

Warning: The game has serious potential problem with crashing with black screen during video playback (like the introduction animation). Solutions / workarounds (e.g. disabling videos, installing codec -- the startup option screen even offers option to disable video) can be found with a quick search online, but it's still a very bad first impression.
Beyond that though, the game is quite OK. The game has a rather humorous overall tone, and is filled with impressive amount of shout-outs and references to Japanese pop culture and actual locations within Akihabara. The development team seems to have put in a lot of effort to incorporate various nice details, ranging from the shops and places in Akihabara to a wide variety of clothing, weapons, and moves. The inclusion of branching storyline, with multiple potential endings, adds replayability. Unfortunately, combat mechanic is clumsy, even when using a controller. For example, it's difficult to consistently target a particular opponent in a group, and direction of player's attack in a crowded situation can get unpredictable. The camera movement can also be annoying, particularly when fighting near transition areas.
In conclusion, the game will probably be a good buy if you're a fan of anime and manga (and thus can appreciate the shout-outs and humor). If you're not, the game will probably lose much of its appeal, and it'll be better to wait for a substantial discount.

Ori and the Blind Forest is an adventure platformer of epic proportions. The art is phenomenal -- with numerous beautiful scenes, vivid colors, and hand-drawn-feeling graphics. The music is moving -- from upbeat and happy tunes to melancholy movements, the music fits the environments. The story is well-crafted and meaningful -- from a narrator using a beautiful-sounding fantasy language to deaths of main characters to friendships and changes of heart to morals of the story to be gleamed to twists and turns. The challenges are real -- such as the escape from the Ginso Tree and several of the puzzles. The game mechanics are well-integrated -- the game uses every ability you have acquired up to that point which makes for a challenging and well-integrated game. The typical infuriation of a platformer is alleviated -- since you can oftentimes save wherever you are, provided you have the energy to do so. In short, the game is a masterpiece. Play it.

TLDR: Just buy Rivals of Aether.
Actual Review:
As a competitor in multiple fighting games, the one that means the most to me is Super Smash Brothers Melee. So naturally, whenever a new platform/smash-esque fighter pops up, my first instinct is to try it. I've dabbled in Brawhalla (though not on this account) and I've played a fair bit of Rivals of Aether. I've played every type of spinoff, Playstation All Stars, Shrek Super Slam, etc. I have a passion for these sorts of games. So it surprised me when Brawlout was unbearably disappointing. Characters didn't have a strong "pop" to them (other than Paco, he's cool asf), stages were designed seemingly with no attention to competitive play or casual play (not enough hazards for casuals, not enough balanced stages for competitive. Really? Half of Smash's battlefield?). Every move has the sound effects of a light slap, yet sends opponents flying off screen. There really isn't much depth here either. Whereas a game like Rivals introduce Parrying, multiple types of cancels, walljump integration, and a quick tutorial to communicate it all, Brawlout has little to nothing. It removes grabs and shielding. "Fair enough," I thought, "Rivals did the same thing and I love that game". But there was nothing to replace it. Nothing was added, things were only taken away. The inclusion of wavedashing seems completely pointless, as if just having such a mechanic in the game will attract players. Melee players don't like wavedashing just because "WE CAN WAVEDASH". We like it because it expands on movement options and how the neutral is played. In Brawlout, it just seems like a weaker version of regular movement, as it is not only laggy, but has similar options as the stock dash (because dashes and dash momentum have little to no endlag). The combo system feels ripped from traditional fighters, but with how far characters are launched, the combos don't last long either. Again, this would be fine if characters died quickly. But every character has an almost ludicrous recovery. When you see the aforementioned Paco, with arguably one of the weaker recoveries, get back from offscreen bottom right/left, you know something is wrong.
Now to be fair, this is the only truly 3D Smashlike I've seen on Steam. It looks pretty standard issue for an early access game. Why then, do my GPU and CPU fans spin up as if my PC is about to take off? I'm running a fairly modern system (4GB GTX970, an i5-4690k, pretty bog standard "VR-Ready") and despite the game looking mediocre at best, it stresses my whole PC. I almost can't hear the generic music and the characters that make little to no noise (Which again, lends to that whole "pop" factor they lack). I know some will defend it, saying, "pretty good for early access". Well with a 20 Dollar price tag, "Pretty Good FOR EARLY ACCESS" doesn't cut it. Premium Price, Premium Product. Similar early access games (Distance, Rivals, hell even Sword With Sauce) have massive jumps in both quality and perfomance efficiency. To my knowledge, they have even SMALLER development teams. It's a shame, because some of the ideas here are really cool. Characters like Paco, Hyper Light Drifter, and (I don't know, I'll just call him Bristleback) have movesets that, set in any other Smashlike, would be incredibly fun to use. But it's Brawlout. So they aren't. Wavedash games is cooking up their new game, "Icons: Combat Arena". The footage from that game's PRE-ALPHA/ALPHA stages looks far more interesting than this game's MID BETA. Sure it may lack the "polish", but that can come with time. A game that is not good from the foundation will not become good. To adapt a rather crude saying,  "You can polish a turd, but you cannot make it gold."
Pros:
+Fun character mechanics (in concept)
+A couple stage backgrounds look nice
Cons:
-Weak movement options
-Poor competition to other games in the genre, better alternatives out there.
-Price is too high
-Characters lack personality

Spoiler free review....
Initial thoughts pre-game: I think I got this game on humble bundle, it was one of the extra games I didn't know about and didn't really care about. A couple of my friends sang praises for it, but I still put it off thinking they were being dramatic and that it wouldn't be that good. So I played anything else. Recently I started achievement hunting a little more hardcore though and figured no matter how it is just finish the game for that achievement.
Gameplay: You can either click around with your mouse or use the arrow keys (even though the game directs you to click, trust me use the arrow keys to move and the mouse to find and click on objects it makes the game flow better and be more enjoyable without the horrible auto tracking of movement that I didn't enjoy before figuring that out.) Other than that you scan your mouse over things to find things you can interact with. Some of these things give you orbs. You need to find 5 orbs to progress, some of these you can get from just exploring the areas which is nice. Every time you get enough orbs you go to the key item in the room and complete a little picture tile flip game to proceed. There's a few other tid bits but it's better if you just take those as they come, it will make the experiance richer.
Soundtrack: It really sets up the mood in a big way, on point if I do say so myself. The use of the piano was an excellent touch.
Story: The story makes this game, the characters are very fleshed out which I love to see in a game. Besides the mechanics of the game work wonderfully to weave it together just so in a way you have to play it to understand. I never cried, but I got goosebumps quite a few times and many suprise moments. There's also many points in this game that made me think about things that not a lot of games do now adays, it was refreshing.
Final Thoughts: If you're sick of the same old routine then pick this game up. The price point seemed high before playing, but afterwards I'd say it's just right. You can even wait for a sale if you want to. It's one game you'll be happy to have in your library. It'll only cost you the price of the game and a chunk of your afternoon to cmplete, it's not a long game, but a good one all the same.

Hammerfight is quite unique.  The feeling of swinging your mouse in an arc to hit enemies with a weapon is surprisingly solid.  There are many different weapons -- blades, hammers, heavy things on chains, even firearms... I think the rock-on-a-chain ended up fitting my flight style the best, but each had their uses and strategies.
Wrapping this interesting combat system together is a very creative setting and story.  I love blimps/zeppelins etc, so a desert warrior society with traditions of dueling propellor-powered hovering craft maneuvering to swing physical weapons at each other?  Count me in!
There's even a branching story with different gameplay twists and challenges.  I must admit, the path I took became far too hard so I modded the game to give me a bit more health... but I'm pretty sure that path was supposed to be harder than the others to begin with.  So try Hammerfight -- there's a demo now (there wasn't when I bought it).  Make sure your mouse is in good condition! :-)

When I started my first campaign, I was spawned at a base as my own unique soldier with his own unique name amongst my other comrades. RIght off the bat the AI began to climb into vehicles, group together, and trek on to our objective which was to take over some district as our general radio'd in with instructions and warnings of where shots were being fired. I followed along on foot with the rest of my team and we found ourselves on a linear street with a brick wall on one side, and a bunch of buildings (tall and short) on the other side. On one end of the road was my team, and on the other was the Brown Pants. Those damn Brown Pants... We were caught in a fire fight for a good 15 minutes until finally my team took over the area and we moved on to a shopping district which featured close quarters combat in alleyways, and often the enemy team would position snipers on the rooftops.
Just as things start to get nasty a local APC on my team drives in and starts launching explosive shells and shreds our enemy allowing us to push forward a bit. A few deaths of me and plenty of dead Brown Pants on the ground, we finally captured the shopping district.
Finally with the last objective we had to make our way up a sandy hill to find a base/camp swarming with Brown Pants. They had the advantage at the top of the hill as we tried to slowly make our way up it, using small rocks as cover. After pounds of blood later we finally won that battle too.
I think it was like <1,300 casualties to take that Island, pretty good I think for my first run. Now we move on the the next island...
This game features amazing gameplay and really good AI at the large majority of times playing this game. Enemies react to fire and find cover, and they use it well too. And more than once did I find myself being blown away by their grenades as my focus was way down the street firing on the enemy, instead of watching my own behind.
As you go through the battle you rank up and the game will continuously respawn you in as a soldier with a relative rank. I've noticed the higher my rank the more squad members I can have, and I can easily tell them where to go by right-clicking.
Only once did I notice my one squad mate have trouble path finding and following me, I simply left him behind and I think later I had another squad member join at some point and replace the last one.
This game is a really great concept. By making you as ordinary and vulnerable as every other soldier on the field, it gives you a wonderful feeling when you do something significant for your team and help them progress.
Will play again and I can't wait for future updates and a chance to play this with some friends.

Competitive Melee player perspective here, so expect some nitpick-iness. So, for being touted as a competitive platform fighter, this game falls well below the mark set by other entries in the genre, ESPECIALLY Super Smash Bros. Let me individually cover every reason this game falls short (in my eyes) of not only being a good competitive game, but an enjoyable experience.
1.) Movement: Movement in this game feels extremely sluggish. Whereas in many Smash clones, you have a dash that allows for quick bursts of movement and dash-dancing, this game has no such thing. The wavedash mechanic also feels extremely finnicky and forced. In Melee, it exists simply as a byproduct of the airdodge mechanic. In this, airdodging into the ground FORCES you to slide. It looks and feels awful, especially since the game lacks the other movement options to supplement it and make it useful.
2.) Combos: They exist...kinda. This game has next to no hitstun, so the only combos you're gonna get are like, jab combos. Everything else is down to reads, due to a combination of no hitstun, and not enough mobility to be able to follow up on things.
3.) Animations: In Smash and many of it's clones, a big part of making the game feel good is having animations that read well. This game doesn't have that. It can be hard to put your finger on at times, but a lot of moves look unnecessarily sluggish, and many action states don't transition well into each other. The game just looks overall clunky.
4.) The Overall Mechanics: I'm glad they listened to the community about ledges (although I don't really agree with how they implemented them), but the game still has too many mechanics that are anti-competitive. Namely rage. I would make rage toggleable (if it isn't already? I couldn't find an option) because in its current form, it isn't exciting to play with OR against. There's essentially no counterplay when your opponent has it other than running away. (which is unlikely to be successful because movement is so janky)
So yeah. I'm not impressed so far. If an update somewhere down the line fixes the janky movement and actually makes this game FEEL good to play, I'll totally be on board. But until then, it feels borderline unplayable to me.

UPDATE 6/15/15
More content has been added and the difficulty levels have been tweaked a bit.  There's still more things I'd like to see adjusted, but as it stands, the game is pretty fun to play and am switching my recommendation from negative to positive.  Kudos to the devs for being very active and releasing content on a quick & regular basis.
---
UPDATE 5/31/15
The game has admittedly improved a bit since the posting of my original review.  More campaign missions and a free play mode are now available, adding a lot of value to the game.  I am enjoying this game a bit more now, though I do think it needs a bit more time to cook before I can recommend it at the $20 price (had it been cheaper, I would have recommended it).
What I'd personally like to see is the difficulty levels balanced...that is, on easy settings (both scenarios and free play) have the maintenance costs of the buildings reduced so that folks can enjoy the game without worrying too much about the budget (yet still provide a "little" challenge).  I also think the maintenance and safety structures aren't that effective and need the amount of maintenance/safety they provide increased or at least, decrease the maintenance costs of having them in the first place as you will need a LOT of them to handle all the pumps, refineries, and etc. you'll have out in the field.
The game is still under development, so we'll see how this all plays out.  For now, I recommend waiting a little longer.  The devs have been pumping out content like crazy, so thankfully the wait should be short.
---
The game has promise, but it's not worth the $15 at this time.  At present, the free play mode does not work and there's only two scenarios available (one of which is a tutorial that doesn't cover everything you need to know).  I believe I figured most of it out through trial and error in that you can sell oil to either the market or via contracts...the former having a variable price while the latter having a fixed price.  Logistics enable you to sell more per day, which is important if you intend to accept a lot of contracts.  Expect to stumble your first few playthrus of the scenarios as it can get a little confusing.  I would have liked a way to distinguish crude from refined oil, for example...they should really have their own separate resource count.  That's not to say that it couldn't be something fantastic some day, but I'd only recommend it to dedicated fans who want to support the developers.  As for the rest of you, I'd say wait a while until the game receives a bit more TLC and content.

What can I say about To The Moon?
Honestly, I thought it'd suck so much. Like A LOT. But I was wrong. Oh, how I was wrong.. I guess the whole 2D sprites thing really put me off at the beginning. But eh, this was a really good game. It's one of those.
But let's get back on track.
Aside from some slight micro-stutters and lackluster game options throughout the entire thing, the first thing I noticed about To The Moon is that it manages to tell an amazing story through a number of perspectives. And it wasted no time on doing just that. It just kept going and going. Giving the player a thorough, yet enjoyable experience trying to understand the story.
Another thing is that I really liked how it got to deal with a lot of genres in a single game. Especially when it tricks the player (this happens multiple times) into thinking it was some sort of psyhological or horror story, when it didn't even need to! I find that as an excellent suspensive plot device to utilize, and this game was released was back in 2011!
One of the perfect things that they managed to pull of in the game was the music. It was top-notch, not gonna lie. Wasn't exactly flawless. But it fitted very well into every scene and atmosphere they were trying to convey to the player. I find that in most scenes, they attempted to give out a certain vibe or sensation that accurately represents the character's emotions and they achieved to do that. I guess there were some cliche parts where they showed bits of a character's life while having some sappy song played in the background, but I digress. Pros outweigh the cons.
I remember a part in the game where they let you attack other sprites using.. Plants. But that's besides the point. Basically, the whole game was semi-linear. With just one story to follow and a myriad of characters to accompany said story. Sure, there were some items and events that they let you interact with. But here's a level in the game where there's enemies, there's traps, and numerous of ways to avoid and/or destroy them. Might not seem like much. But I really appreciate it when game developers have the courage to go outside the box. And show the player the true potential of the story, or more specifically the game engine, but that's neither here nor there.
You get the point.
I think my favourite thing in this game is during one point in the story, it starts to ask a big question to the player. It will question your methods, your goals, and also how you decide to empathize on various characters throughout the game. Essentially there are loads of issues and uncertainties that come into play when I reached this point. And I love that. It really makes you think what you would do, for someone you barely even know. This also happens very subtly. Like it's something you think on and on about behind the scenes, away from the game. Amazing.
All in all, 2011's To The Moon was a complete masterpiece. The story was moderately-paced, but highly engaging. The music was phenomenal and it suited a lot of emotions that comes into play. I really don't know what else to say about this game.. Just play it.
I guarantee you won't regret it.

While Caster can be fun some of the time, there's really no other value there. If all you want to do is spam overpowered weapons while sprinting around at mach speed, this is probably the game for you. But if you like your games with actual value in them, actual story, playability, difficulty, challenge or what have you, then look elsewhere, because Caster lacks all of those and then some.
The graphics are very outdated and the textures/models can be glitchy as they clip a good amount, but even if they don't they're still not pleasant to look at. The character isn't even aesthetically pleasing and that's the one thing you have to stare at the entire game. Not to mention his/her face is just down-right creepy at some angles. The balancing is dreadful, as you get a game-breaking weapon at about level two, and the difficulty spikes up and down more than a heart monitor. Also, once you max out your health and sprint ability (which can be done very early game, mind you), you can just sprint back and forth to avoid every projectile, while spamming you're broken weapon that shoots as fast as you can click (and if you're like me, that means it can be spammed at speeds that will melt bosses in no time).
So there's no balancing and the graphics are bad, what else? Well, the story is worse than both of those cons combined. The easiest way to describe the story is by saying that there just isn't one. You're a new recruit and you're sent on missions to combat what seems to be an evil creature-empire that's expanding and trying to take over the world(?). You go place to place and just clear each level, there's no more objectives than that. Also, there's only like two themes of levels, and they're repeated over and over.
Later game you run into a few levels that are almost impossible given the game's engine, where you have to keep a small ship out of the water even though it goes way faster than you can terraform the ground in front of it, and a boss battle that just drags on so long no matter how much damage you deal per second, and you just have to spam and dodge for like five minutes straight. The game is also very short.
And last but not least, the developer decided to incorporate a destructible environment... everywhere. Weapons that deal a little bit of area damage will also chip away at the ground on every level, so if you max out your weapon and you're spamming like hell (as is the custom) the ground will basically meltdown out from under where you're aiming. It breaks the map and it breaks the game, even though it was already broken from all the other previously mentioned problems.
When it's all said and done, I would not recommend the Caster to- well, anybody. The only reason it's not getting a 1/10 is because sprinting back and forth at mach speed while spamming your blaster like you have some sort of turrets is actually quite enjoyable in a weird way. So because I ran into a little bit of fun there, I give Caster a generous 3/10. That being said, do not buy this no matter what, not only because you'll waste money, but mostly because you'll just waste your time. I got it on sale for pocket change and I feel like I still got ripped off.

Part of me really wants to love this game. As someone who loves both fighting games and party games tremendously. I prefer how this game plays over the more popular Rivals of Aether, with some more polish I think it could really be a solid title.
However as it currently stands, in Early Access it's certainly not worth the full price of admission. The game is still in beta, so expect bugs, some maps are worse than others, but for me I tested it out on the first stage with 4 bots with no issues, then I tried it with the ice stage and was suffering large framerate issues where the game was basically unplayable unless I quit.
The art style is actually fairly nice, simple, but the characters are easily different enough from one to the next, and gameplay wise, this feels a lot more smash-like to me than Rivals of Aether does, and perhaps that's just due to the 2 attack buttons and dodging as opposed to Rival of Aether's 3 attacks + counter system.
I will probably refund this game for the time being, and hold out for more development, but honestly if you're curious there is some fun to be had here. It may vary, depending on the amount of people you bring in with you with the aformentioned frame rate problems, but mechanically this game works decently, it looks decent, and it can be fun. I look forward to seeing the story modes, and polish being added to this someday when it leaves Early Access as I think this game could be a solid pick for playing with friends online or locally.

Teeworlds offers an easy-to-run helping of free crazy competitive 2D shooting action. While it features a small selection of weapons, players really don't need a lot of diverse firepower to get the job done, once they get the hang of using the grappling hook. Player customization is nothing special, yet the game's cartoonishly simple aesthetics and lack of blood/gore allow it to appeal to younger audiences.
However, there are some flaws to Teeworlds. For some reason, grappling hooks can hook into
. While this may sound like it serves as a cooperative purpose in team games, i.e. helping a friend up by acting as an object they can pull themselves onto ledges with/use you for momentum, it often ends up being used as an offensive tool to get in close with enemies and force them to hope that they get in more hits with a shotgun/hammer than their clingy adversary. This somewhat defeats the purpose of using the hook for dodging projectiles or placing yourself in an advantageous position when engaging enemies. On top of that, teammates and enemies alike can actually hinder player movement just because the game hooks into them instead of the intended wall--I've had more than one occurence where I or a teammate accidentally hooked one-another while falling over a pit, killing us both.
Aside from that one game mechanics, Teeworlds also suffers from an overall bad community. People seem prone to kicking one another for no good reason, which is called "funvoting" IIRC. Expect a fair sum of the other Tees you run into to have a bad mood as well.
All in all, Teeworlds is a multiplayer game complimented by it's simplistic easy to play, hard to master formula. Unfortunately, the community and player-grappling mechanics may sour your experience a bit, but it's worth a try.
Also, the map
is this game's Dust2, especially on American servers, so I hope you like that map a lot.

Tl;Dr version: If you play RPGs mostly for the story, and like lots of little details that all fall into place(so many, that you'll continue to connect more with every playthrough), then this game is definitely for you.
[Everything that follows is Spoiler-Free, btw]
I have to admit, when I first heard about this game, I was skeptical of all the hype, but it really is a beautiful story. It's almost like a well-written novel or movie, but turned into a game. Kan Gao knows when to lighten the mood with humor, when to add suspense, and when to slow down and let the emotion of a scene sink in.
Despite what some may say, it has been my experience that you do not HAVE to cry while playing...But you will want to.
As for non-story aspects, the gameplay is not very difficult. As I said, this game is mostly focused on story, and is not like a Final Fantasy-esque RPG with levels or enemies. However, it is rather like an adventure game of old, where you must explore and collect items to progress. There are periodic puzzles, and they can be decently challenging without being stressful. All-in-all, the gameplay is a seamless way to progress through the story.
The game's art style is pixelated, but it's the kind of gorgeous pixelation that looks like a painting, as opposed to the cheap, arcade look. (Sorry, Toby Fox...)
The music, also made by Kan Gao, both fits perfectly with the story and sounds great on its own. I have literally used songs from the OST to relax before bed, and I'd recommend the soundtrack just as much as the game.
In short, this has quickly become one of my favorite RPGs, and I'm looking forward to the sequel, Finding Paradise. Well played, Kan Gao. Well Played.

honestly I'm not sure why so many people are having issues with game performance, I've been playing for about 30 hours and haven't encountered anything of the sort. anyways:
PROS:
+it looks gorgeous
+the gunplay kicks♥♥♥♥♥ the weapons are varied and everything feels satisfying to use
+story is cool, it seems like a lot more thought went into it than in the last game and a few of the story beats will really blow your mind
+surprisingly a lot of replay value, I bet some people won't be fans of the Oberkommando assassination missions but I like them if for no other reason than you get to revisit and really explore the game's levels without having to spend too much time dicking around during the main story
+the weapon wheel was really janky to use in the last game for some reason, this one feels way better
+we've all heard the complaints that the story is just a big liberal circle-jerk and for the most part that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. there's definitely a couple of places where the dialogue gets a little preachy but the vast majority of the story is well thought out, reasonable in its tone, and not cringe-worthy in the slightest
CONS:
-the main story is a bit too short, and the final boss battle was pretty hard yet strangely not very climactic
-the difficulty curve is really weird, the game is almost too hard to play during the period where you wear the power armor, and then gets about 200% easier when that ends. it makes sense in the context of the story but it's still frustrating at times
on the whole I'd recommend this game, perhaps it'd be best to get it at a reduced price considering its relatively short length but the overall experience is probably one of the most fun I've had with a FPS in a while. it's got its flaws, and maybe it's not one of the best games of all time, but at the very least it's probably one of the best games of the year.

The sound design and the visual effects evoke an atmosphere which is quite unlike anything else I've played. It is phenomenally well done, and placed in a plot framework and gameplay which is competent but not the reason that I enjoyed the playthroughs I have done ... which is the atmosphere and character "story".
To get the most from this I would recommend deliberately playing slower than for most games. Wait for the background narrations to complete while you observe around you before moving on, so that they aren't truncated or overlapped (where they are not supposed to be). Running between areas of combat or puzzles is recommended as the walking is fairly slow, but I would definitely say that slowing down while the game is showing things allows you to get much more from the interactions and reduces frustration with missed dialogue or instruction which is mostly given through 'in character' audio.
To solve the puzzles, again take your time, move to the centre of the 'bubble' of hints using both visual and audio cues when present, and while moving look for environment items which form part of the runes, either in their current arrangement or in reverse (look from the far side, or use projected light or shade to create the shape). You need item(s) and position. Doors and other interactives always open if you approach them directly in the middle and activate at a sensible distance from them. Getting too close can cause some minor hiccups in a few places. For the most part you need not use focus while moving around, (though there are a few places where this might help, and you are told to do so), as the cues given to you will let you know once you have moved to the right places and should 'focus'.
Combat is fun and can be difficult if you don't use all the tools you have available - and can be slow if you are dodging too much. Dodging can be useful, but blocking with 'perfect timing' is much faster and gives higher damage in the follow up attack, and an invulnerability frame which is quite generous, so is my preferred approach.
Runs well on an i5 2400 and GTX970 under Win7 x64. Not sure what framerate I got, but I had no 'bad' performance or stutters at highest detail settings.
A must play and a true work of art.

The first name you see on the title credits is the psychological advisor for the team. Decide for yourself what that means.
I have a great fascination with game design as it pertains to the developer-player relationship. That being said, this is probably the coolest experience I've ever had when considering what it means to really connect with a player. Before you do anything, read anything, if you're up in the air about this - GO IN BLIND. No walkthroughs, avoid detailed reviews. I'm serious, this is the first time I've ever recommended that as an ESSENTIAL part of the experience.
The developers knew what they wanted to do, and did it. No gimmicks, no tricks, no pandering to the "standard of success" with AAA titles. Incredible art, total sensory immersion, meaningful story, difficult combat and a committment to consequence. It doesn't tell you how to play while also teaching you. There is no direction, but it builds compulsion to act. This is a revolutionary game in it's execution and design. I have complete respect for any artist that makes no compromises in delivering the story or message that they intended to deliver, and Senua's Sacrifice does this for every moment of the game. 100% worth full price, and while far from my usual type of favorite games, it is easily in my top 5.
A comment of praise and warning: While I do not struggle with sensory overload to a severe degree, I do struggle with auditory overload occasionally. This is how I came to acquire the game, actually - the boyfriend thought it would be funny to push my limits with a game that attempts to capture the essense of psychosis. The moment I realized how in love I was with the game was when I triggered the focus mechanic willfully - a mechanic that quiets the voices and narrows in on Senua's breathing - to escape the sensory bombarding environment to think for myself. I've never been so immersed in a non-vr experience. USE HEADPHONES.

This game is spectacular in many ways through both it's satire of horror games and the very fact it is an effective horror game on it's own.
The satire comes in the form of the jumpscares themselves which if you played the game are rather cutesy looking cardboard cutouts that come out from the walls. It helps show how jumpscares are honestly an incredibly temporary unengaging way of gettng a scare out of a person. The very appearence of the cutouts also show that really anything appearing out of nowhere and making a noise can surprise someone and as a result not truly scary
The effective horror comes from the multiple pursuers the player will face throughout the game as each have an unsettling build up through the form of notes either explaining the disturbing origins of the pursuer or what it does to victims. All of the notes amount to the payoff in which you come face to face with the monster and are forced to use what little knowledge you have from the notes to find a way to escape or simply run for your life and don't look back. What happens if a monster does catch up to you is also in most cases very effective as there will be a screen that  either displays mysterious and almost philosophical sounding block of text or an unsettling animation of how the creature kills it's victim or even a mix of both. To top things off the system of randomized generation also means that once you have escaped one of the numerous terrors within the house you may encounter them again leaving the player feeling uneasy as to when they will have to be chased once more.
Along with a great soundtrack, simple graphics, straightforward controls and surprisingly deep gameplay in specific moments I would have to say that this game is something any horror fan should try at least once and since it is free it is actually quite easy to do so.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I played this game years after it was released because it was part of a package deal.  For that reason it's hard to give a bad review because it was so cheap, but I didn't like this game.  Assassins' Creed 2 is a different story, however.
Anyway, the game is very repetitive and quite short.  There is not even much in the way of achievements unless you want to collect flags but the game pretty much implies that this is a worthless endeavor.
The game had good graphics for its time.  Perhaps that's what made it so popular, and also you can climb on just about everything.  This is the good part.
The problem is that you are always doing the same thing.  It's always about assassinating certain people and it's almost always done in the same way. Yeah, you have to maybe pickpocket, interrogate or eavesdrop on people before you get to the target but in the end you have to keep repeating these activities over and over again.
This game could make you hate poor people since the beggars will swarm around you like flies until you want to murder them even though that's evil and the guards will make your life miserable if you keep doing that.  This is one of the funnier aspects of the game but after awhile it gets annoying.
In the end, I felt that I was just doing the same thing over and over and over again just for slight progression in the main character's (Desmond's) story, and the game doesn't answer all the questions (hence the many, many sequels) so you don't necessarily get a good resolution.

Even after playing just an hour I have to commend this game. I am very interested in proto-Germanic history, religion and mythology and I also happen to be one for psychology, grim stories and slow paces. Needless to say I had to buy this game the second I saw it.
To paint a picture: you play as a female celtic warrior who's going completely insane searching for her dead lover in hell. Even though the protagonist sounds like she should be male, both historically and in terms of narrative, playing a female character helps sell the fragility of your character and gives you more empathy for her, which actually makes it a sensible decision. Don't think this character is yet another 'strong and empowered' feminist stereotype, she is decidedly female and has real depth to her.
The game itself plays as if someone decided to go take a walk. Alone. At night. In the woods. On shrooms.
So far gameplay consists of fighting tree-monsters and looking for the shapes of runes in rock formations or fallen trees which isn't very interesting. It gives a player some goal to chase and a reason to move forward but not much more. The real value is in looking at gorgeous visuals and experiencing a grim story of insanity and fierce defiance. Which is done very well so far.
Whilst going through helheim you will encounter many of the old gods our ancestors used to worship. The myths surrounding those gods are very symbolical and I've yet to see if the developers make full use of this, but so far I love being soaked in this world. It is very dark indeed, largely because we are following the story of one who dares defy the gods, but it seems to do its historical basis justice. There's a lot of narrated slices of mythology to find in this game as well, something I really appreciated.
It is also noteworthy that this game is indie-made. Impressive for such a visually striking title. If you care about more original indie titles hitting the market, even high-budget, you should definitely keep an eye out for games like this one.
I might write an actual review once I finish the game proper, but for now I just want the word out that this game is worth people's attention.

Sat down this morning and started playing Senua from a shared library. Got sucked into the world for 6 hours straight. Even though I won't need it anymore, bought the game just to support a developer that creates such a work of art.
The only thing that could spoil the experience for you is if you in with the expectation of just another hack and slay. This is not run-off-the-mill stuff.

This game is a one of a kind, exploring subjects and topics that would never find themselves in a full fledged "AAA" game, yet is still able to retain the production value and level of detail we expect from big developers.
This is an extremely dark and gritty tale about a young warrior who suffers from severe mental sickness and must fight her way through the Norse afterlife to reclaim the soul of her dead lover. The narrative is central to this experience and I was able to find myself rooting for Senua despite being unable to relate to her in any way. Combat, while limited, is claustrophobic yet satisfying, fitting right in with the tone of the game. Enemies are creepy and disturbing, with the game ending in a truly memorable climax.
In Summary:
While the game is only about seven hours long and the first hour and a half or so are fairly slow, the experience builds and builds, getting better with ever set piece and encounter with a deep narrative that will keep you hooked until the credits role.

It's a spooky house, and it has jump scares. Finally, some honesty in marketing!
While graphically simple, this is a fun, randomized experience with some great tributes to other horror games. Though cute and silly throughout, it's mysterious and unpredictable enough to actually be kinda creepy if you overlook the Wolfenstein 3D visuals. Just digging deeper and finding out what the next encounter is going to be remains intriguing all the way to the end. It's loaded with surprises and feels like a brief, loving history of videogame horror tropes.
I'd strongly recommend going into this one totally blind. The first chunk of the game will seem very innocent, but there is a lot more going on than you might expect. While loaded with cheap (and pretty funny) jump scares as advertised, there's much more than those. You might have to stretch your suspension of disbelief to really get the most out of things, but it's some of the most fun I've had with an indie horror title in a while. It knows what it's setting out to do, and it keeps things simple but has plenty of things to show you.
Being totally free I think excuses some of the technical clunkiness, but even with a few glitches here and there I'd have been pretty happy to have paid a few bucks for this one. Definitely recommended!

Brawlout can be called a spiritual successor to the critically and commercially acclaimed Super Smash Bros. Series. I was a huge fan of the original Super Smash Bros on the N 64 and since I did not buy any Nintendo console after that, Super Smash Bros. On PC was one of my biggest dreams. There were games like Brawlhalla and Megabyte Punch where I have sunk countless hours in. None of them felt as polished or as fun as Super Smash Bros but they were some of the only alternatives. So, what new does Brawlout offer?
For those of you unfamiliar with this kind of gameplay, Brawlout is a competitive brawler where you play against bots or your friends on a platform where the main motto of the fight is to beat down your opponents to a pulp and then push them off the platform.
All the players start from 0 % health and it reduces with every hit taken. Once its low enough, your opponent becomes more fragile and starts to fallback farther. After you’ve reduced enough, one hit will send the opponent flying through the stage to his or her doom. It is a very simple premise and the gameplay is simple enough for beginners to understand.
Don’t expect this to be something like Street fighter or Mortal kombat though. While Brawlout offers combos and variations to counter  your enemies attacks, the fighting is not that deep. The major sell for Brawlout is its roster of characters.
At the time of writing, there are about half a dozen characters present all with their own unique style of fighting. Characters like King Feather can jump upto five times and continue his attacks on the opponent to break his return but is vulnerable to being easily knocked out. King Apu is a scorpion like character who uses his chains to pull his opponents in for setting up combos.
Whenever you hit an opponent or take a hit, a rage meter builds up which allows you to perform special attacks and perform combo breaker. When the rage meter is filled up, you enter into Rage mode where you take less damage from enemies while doing more damage yourself.
Brawlout also doesn’t feature shields or defensive abilities much. It depends on the speed with which you dish out damage to your opponents and get them out of the battle. It is very reliant on offense and that might turn some people off from the game.
Brawlout lacks in the amount of features present in the game along with an obvious lack of stages and characters. It makes sense that since every character is well thought out, the game should release them slowly and surely but for the price tag for Brawlout is very steep for its current state.
You can play ranked matches, casual 1v1 matches, private lobbies, Brawlout TV etc. The online connection is a bit unreliable and I failed to complete more than 50% of my online matches due to the crashes or the unplayable input lag.
While the bots are competent, it does not take much time to figure out their pattern of fighting. Another thing that bugs me is the inability to add bots to private lobbies with friends, a feature which can be found in some other games mentioned above. There is no story mode or tutorial present as of now but is promised to be added in future patches.
All nitpicks aside though, the gameplay of Brawlout is fun, fluid and chaotic. It needs more content, a better netcode and some polish here and there but when it gets going, it is some solid brawling fun.
Brawlout has a cartoonish aesthetic which looks incredibly gorgeous in action. The fast, fluid movements are accentuated by the amount of visual flair present here. In case of Brawlout, more players equals more fun and same goes in terms of visuals. It gets chaotic and colours pop out in every single frame.
While the screen might get busy at such times and it might get difficult to grasp what is going on the stage, it looks drop dead gorgeous. The character models are also colourful, varied and certainly look their part. Visually, Brawlout is simply outstanding.
The sound design of Brawlout is a pretty standard affair. The soundtrack is nice enough with enough adrenaline filled music to keep your heads rolling while the sound effects are all right. There is no voice acting to speak of right now and nothing much to hear in terms of overall sound design.
Brawlout is a fun, fluid and gorgeous looking brawler which suffers from a lack of content and unstable netcode. It needs something more to justify its price tag but it is one of those early access titles which has a lot of potential and is worth a recommendation.
