Assassin's Creed has come very far as a franchise. Is the original game still worth playing? Yes. Absolutely. If you can get it to work.
You can
.
POSITIVES: The roots of everything that made the franchise famous are in the first Assassin's Creed. The parkouring and climbing work well, the cities are large and colorful with unique atmospheres, there are plenty of collectibles to while away the hours collecting. The story is pretty good. It doesn't climb the heights attained by Assassin's Creed II / Brotherhood / Revelations, but Altair's journey as an Assassin who has fallen from grace and needs to redeem himself is great, even if it's been told before in other mediums. Graphics are decent (DirectX 10). The game world actually feels larger than some of the other Assassin's Creed games, since you don't fast-travel from one city to another (not at first); you travel on dusty dirt roads through mountains and villages from one city to another. There is a lot of country to explore, and none of the areas feel re-used (though sometimes they can seem extraneous).
NEGATIVES: The game crashes, sticks, and stutters from a variety of issues. My issues were solved by unplugging my internet while playing. The servers that Ubisoft used to authenticate this game are now offline, causing the game to briefly freeze any time I tried to load a save or the game tried to create an auto-save. Lack of an internet connection tells the game to not even bother checking, so gameplay becomes smooth. Even for a game this old, it's hard getting a constant 60fps. If you're running the DirectX 10 version, I recommend setting the Compatibility Mode to Windows Vista SP2.
INDIFFERENT: Activities and ambient conversations recycle constantly. Stealth doesn't have much variety: hide, walk slowly, or mix with monks. Combat is actually boring – once you get the counter ability, countering everything results in a one-hit kill. If you're out exploring the Kingdom, enemy guards are extraordinarily suspicious unless Altair walks at the slowest speed possible. Takes away from the pace of the game. Oh, and don't fall into the water; Altair can't swim, and dies instantly.
VERDICT: A pretty good Assassin's Creed game whose repetitive side-activities don't undermine a decent first attempt at a stealthy open-world-parkour-hack 'n slash hybrid. Hopefully, you can get it to work properly.

Syberia is one of the most emotional games I've ever played, which is quite a feat considering there aren't that many principal characters and many of them are emotionless robots. There are deeply cutting, overarching themes running through the experience that are timeless: destroyed beauty, flawed ideologies, infidelity, Peter Pan Syndrome, the inevitable march forward of technological progress and the loss of humanity. How Syberia manages to tackle such dark and depressing issues yet remain whimsical and keep you full of wonder is the mark of truly masterful writing and game design.
 
  In a modern context, a video game about economic progress and relationship troubles should rightly illicit some skepticism and groans, as “mature games” have devolved into a sort of subgenre that usually treats it's audience like complete ♥♥♥♥ing morons with no ability to parse subtext and nuance. You could go down a checklist of cliches that would (and should) instantly turn you off: “the environment is a character”, “the protagonist really grows on her journey”, etc. Here they don't feel like buzzwords, however. Syberia is art and storytelling, minus the pretension and virtue signaling.
 
  You play the game as Kate Walker, a lawyer from New York on a seemingly simple mission to get a signature from the last living heir to an obsolete toy factory. Arriving in what initially looks like a quaint European town, things quickly get very strange and her job gets exponentially more complicated. Not only has the heir died, but in her will she confesses that her brother is still alive, her family had faked his death, and his whereabouts are unknown. Kate goes above and beyond the call of duty, launching a one-woman investigation to find the mysterious genius/retard Karl Vorslberg. It's not a simple task, as Karl spent nearly his entire life designing intricate clockwork trinkets and automatons, up to and including a train to take himself to the fabled land of Syberia to look for the last living mammoths.
 
  Kate boards the train, following the clues she's found and traveling from station to station, each stop more surreal and absurd than the next. All of the locations are past their prime, crumbling monuments ravaged by time and forgotten by modern society. The inhabitants she encounters haven't fared much better; lost souls either reveling in their past glory, going through the motions like automatons themselves, or driven mad from isolation and false promises. Kate interviews them, hoping to uncover more information about Karl and the impact he had on each locale. She also grows increasingly distant from the “real” world the further down the track she goes. Faced with majestic sights, essentially becoming the biographer of a genius who would not and could not let go of childlike wonder, her mundane, adult life fades into the background. Incoming calls from her friends, family, lover, and work become either uninteresting or tools to help her on her mission of discovery.
 
  Gameplay consists of fairly standard adventure game interactions; you use the cursor to control Kate's movements, pointing and clicking to guide her. The circular reticle will light up when it's possible to move to another pre-rendered scene, or change icons if other actions are available. Talking to NPCs brings up a dialogue notebook with discussion choices, which will fill out as you obtain more information. All the voice acting is top notch, with a wide variety of accents and personality types. Kate especially is wonderful. You'll pick up items, add them to your inventory, and use them on objects... as is expected from the genre. This really is the sweet spot for adventure games as far as I'm concerned: there is some pixel hunting, but the fidelity is high enough that it's not in the literal sense. Solutions to puzzles are usually common sense, or the game actually wants you to tinker around with complex-looking machinery as part of the experience. There's nothing here that should stump you for days or have you running for a walkthrough; thorough exploration and observation is key, and it's still satisfying to solve the mechanical trials.
 
  While graphically Syberia is starting to show it's age, the sense of awe and beauty still shines through in most cases. The 3-D character models look a little rough, but thankfully the point-and-click navigation saves us from having to deal with godawful tank controls of the era. The 2-D backgrounds are pixelated but gorgeous. Oftentimes you may wonder why certain screens exist, since there are no real gameplay reason for them to be there; just “empty space”. They're there because they're pretty.
 
  Syberia is one of those games that's not technically “perfect”; you could nitpick some pacing problems or a puzzle or two that doesn't pay off, or some dialogue that's awkward or a bit too on the nose, but as a package it's absolutely fantastic. The unique, heartfelt story is something everyone should experience, and it's an adventure game you should play even if you generally don't care for adventure games. It welled me up with emotions, and I'm usually an old, crusty automaton.

Syberia is a really fantastic, classic point-and-click adventure game with an incredible soundtrack. You play as Miss Kate Walker, NY lawyer extraordinaire and slightly prissy investigator compelled to adventure across Europe and the Urals in search of the elusive heir to the Voralberg manufacturing plant. Initially, Kate's interest is as shallow as the sales contract she's been hired to conclude, but your adventure doesn't let that state of affairs last. In a series of beautifully imagined cities, the mystery of the Voralberg automatons, the shadowy Siberian Youkol tribe, mammoths, cold war engineering, and personal drama unfolds in puzzle after puzzle. Each challenge is integral to the world and the story, transforming Kate's character and making it difficult to tear yourself away.
In terms of gameplay, this is classic point and click from the early aughts, and is a fairly clean and easily navigable interface, though it takes a moment to get used to the dialogue setup, which is listed by general topic rather than your opening line. The graphics are great for the time and more than sufficient to show both the details of the puzzles and the creators' love for the environments. The puzzles themselves are straightforward, but may require a little creativity; several objects and areas are only accessible once Kate has spoken with another character to acquire a motive or a key.  The soundtrack is excellent and the English dub voice actors are quite good, so it remains enjoyable throughout and has good replay value. Go ahead and get the sequel, Syberia II, while you're at it, because I guarantee you'll want to keep playing when the credits roll!

Well. After having this in my library for something like 4 years, I FINALLY played it through. I started last fall, then took a hiatus in Jan., then finished it up over the last week. I had bought it as part of the Meridian pack, and there are STILL a lot in there I've never touched--yet. Anyway. I understand this game is somewhat controversial in the favorability department. I hand it a thumbs up, albeit a less than enthusiastic thumb.
First, I found the artwork and character design very good, if not actually outstanding. The steampunk vibe is excellent, and reminds me of Sierra's old masterpiece "Lighthouse: The Dark Being", considered by many to be the most insanely difficult adventure game ever made, and certainly among the best. In fact, at one point, my wife, who doesn't even play this type of game, looked over my shoulder and asked if that's what it was! Said it sounded a lot like it. Another aspect I found pleasing and familiar is that heroine Kate Walker bears a resemblance to Alex Vance, heroine of Half Life 2 and its sequels, probably my favorite game series of all time. And while this is a very different style of game, Kate also has that same tough-as-nails determination and willingness to get her hands dirty. In one sequence, she escapes a ruined underground complex through a ventilation duct -- shades of Dr Freeman himself! In fairness to Microids, let it be noted that Syberia was released more than 2 years BEFORE Alyx was helping Freeman shoot zombies.
I found most of the puzzles to be of satisfying difficulty, right in the Goldilocks zone, not too hard, not too easy, but just right. I believe I only had to go the hints (UHS reader, a valuable classic!) twice, and BOTH involved using the telephone -- I don't think it's a spoiler to say that at least twice you must make phone calls to get necessary clues -- and the first time (if I recall correctly) invokes an absolutely ABSURD coincidence! The other game it reminded me of irresistably was Douglas Adams' "Starship Titanic", with its menagerie of eccentric automatons, and one puzzle involving a mechanical bartending machine with an organ-like keyboard on which buttons are pressed and keys played seemed as if it could have been right from that ill-fated spaceship. One very clever and beautiful gimmick is a sort of music box which when wound up performs a bit of backstory from the childhood of two of the central characters, which sequences segue between the music box display itself and flashbacks to "real life".
Gameplay itself is episodic, and you progress from one city to another on a full-size wind-up train with your mechanical engineer/conductor, Oscar, solving each segment of the game. Oscar generally proves of little help to you, as wherever you stop he is afraid to leave the train because of the windy/dusty/sooty/sandy climate outside. Your quest, as Kate Walker, is tracking down a certain Hans Voralberg, creator of all these wondrous automatons and machines, to obtain his signature on a contract. Spoiler -- you succeed. This climactic moment plays out in paradoxically anti-climactic fashion -- a moment, and it's done. Then -- ah, but then you get the REAL conclusion to the saga. While not especially surprising, there is a dramatic suddenness to it and a tension which grips the player -- although at this point we have stopped really playing and are watching a cutscene play out the game's last moments.
One small issue is sequentiality. A number of times I performed some task only to find, after, characters giving me clues or Kate herself saying something which made it seem that said task still needed to be done -- or conversely, making reference to something I did NOT know yet but in a way which indicated I already had discovered some fact. Another, perhaps larger issue, is that the characters here TALK and TALK and TALK. I understand that this is something of a characteristic of European games of this type. And the accents don't help. I've also seen complaints that it is TOO episodic, and there is little sense of continuity from the beginning to the end, and sequence to sequence. Although I understand the point, I largely disagree, or disagree, at least, that it is a negative: it's just how the game plays, and is no more episodic than Myst or any of the other classic graphic adventure games. However, I must concede that it lacks SOMETHING -- but I'm not sure what. The art and music are good -- the music in fact is outstanding at times, and a musical performance is one of the key events. Some of the cinematic sequences are close to breath-taking -- I'm thinking in particular of the launch of a rocket and the flight of an airship. But the whole thing is lacking a certain spark, that special magic that takes you out of yourself and into the game itself, makes you believe that you really are immersed in a different world. It doesn't ruin the game, not by far, don't misunderstand me -- but it keeps it out of that highest level of entertainment, achieving that true suspension of disbelief. Except -- except perhaps in that final cutscene. That's where it comes closest. And I think too that a lot of players in a way ignored that conclusion, and failed to realize that the heart of the story isn't about Kate finding an old man and getting his signature, the heart of the story is KATE HERSELF. Understand this, understand the final scenes, and I think you'll appreciate this a bit more. In any case, I am now eagerly awaiting Syberia 2 to finish downloading (also part of the Meridian Collection) and look forward to playing it as well. It is coincidence that I've just found that S3 has just been released, and the first reviews and comments I've seen are rather harsh, at least with regard to the English translation and voice-acting. At $40 I'll probably wait a while until it's a Steam Special -- but play it I will!
So bottom line here -- I DO recommend this -- somewhat tentatively, perhaps -- be prepared for a thoughtful, slow-paced ride with Kate, Oscar, and their friends & enemies. It may not be everyone's cup of tea, but will be a rewarding and refreshing cup for some.

(Action-Adventure)
A few of the available options are sliders for brightness, Master Volume, Music, SFX, Voices and Menus; Subtitles (OFF by default), Graphic quality, mappable controls, combat difficulty, and more.
Let me address the whispers of permadeath in the game - I died many times over, and my game was safe, so I can assure you that if you're terrible at combat, you will still be able to play and enjoy this game without worrying about losing all of your progress.
Ninja Theory, the developers of Hellblade, made two games that I enjoyed immensely:
, a true gem with its gorgeous visuals and interesting story; and
with its stylish and beautiful combat. When I heard that they were coming out with a new game, I was excited, anticipating something that would be an epic mixture of the best qualities of these two games.  What I got was not even close to what I had envisioned, bringing me something wholly unexpected.
So what IS the game like?
Reality.  Dark, gritty and full of inner turmoil.  Most games have a very cut-and-dried story line, with a clear antagonist to destroy.  It's not so straightforward in Hellblade... Senua's greatest enemy is her own shattered mind.  The devs did a brilliant job of handing an issue that is so sensitive that most people simply refuse to acknowledge it, much less make it the central focus of a AAA game.  I will come back to this a bit later, for now focusing on...
The gameplay is story-based, with a lesser emphasis on combat.  All fights in the game come at scripted intervals - there are no random encounters or wandering enemies to accidentally bump into.  Senua can see patterns in the abstract around her, and by "Focusing", she can unlock or create new pathways to traverse.
Periodically you will need to seek out rune-shaped patterns in the surrounding area.  When you are close, you'll see glowing red shapes floating around you, indicating which rune you are nearby.  Other times, there are areas that look weird... blurry.  This is yet another kind of puzzle which can be solved by looking at it (focusing) from the right angle.  This is where having a controller gives you an edge, as it will vibrate when you are close to finding a piece of the missing shape or rune (assuming that you have the feature turned on.)
There is only one collectible in the game, which consists of finding "
", and "focusing" upon them to hear a tale.  Basic exploration will reveal the lorestones, and I highly recommend seeking them out, as they not only expand the story, they also add a new layer of interest (I personally found some of the stories fascinating!)
As this is a reality-based game, there is no "fast-travel" between areas, so explore well before moving on to a new location!  There is a button you can hold down to jog, which helps, and the game is semi-linear, so you don't have to worry about getting lost.  I say "semi" linear because you do have choices, at times, of which direction you're going to take, but in the end you'll have to complete everything in the area before you can move on.
Finding all 44 of the lorestones is the only
that you'll have to work for, as the rest unlock through game progression.
Senua is a fearsome opponent and great warrior - despite her slim stature - and the reason is actually explained as the story unfolds, so BRAVO for that, devs! *claps* I do love logic in my games ;D
You have five moves to choose from during combat:
and
.  The "run" button that usually makes Senua jog will allow you to
your enemies. I am not great at fighting in games, and I found that dodging was my best friend, greatly reducing my defeats.
When your mirror glows during battle, you can "
" to slow down your enemies and give you the upper hand.
The battles themselves are beautifully-choreographed, and I found myself frequently stopping the action to take screens.  There is a nice variety of enemies to fight, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, and all intimidating to behold.
I thought that ENSLAVED and DmC had amazingly-realistic nuances and mannerisms for their characters, but Hellblade blows them both out of the water, adding a depth that makes you feel like you're in control of an actual movie.  It's not only here and there that the graphics look cinematic-quality -- it's EVERYWHERE!
The blue paint on Senua's face makes her look odd - even cross-eyed at times - but as you play and the blue wears away, she looks pretty, even stunning at times.
Adding to the feeling that you're in a movie is the built-in
.  You can enter photo mode at any time - even during most cutscenes!  Doing so will pause the action, and you can zoom in, out, move the camera approx. 20 yards in any direction, add photo effects, and much much more!
If you enter photo mode during a cutscene, Senua will almost always be blurry.  Simply adjust the focus to 100% and find your perfect shot!
It's not just the graphics that shine in this game, but the sounds as well.  Every utterance, every sound effect and every tick and hum you hear in the game is brilliantly-placed.  The acting is top-notch, and I especially loved the female narrator.  Senua's friend, Druth, really chewed up the carpet, but it worked with the stories that he was telling.
I won't go into specifics, as I don't want to spoil the game for anyone, but I will touch upon a few things.  Senua's psychosis is central to the narrative, plunging us deep into her perceptions and fears.  Ninja Theory heavily researched the topic, bringing in not only neuroscientists, but people who experience psychosis to shed light on the subject from both sides of the coin.  The result is captivating, giving us a glimpse of what some people live with as a part of their daily lives.
I am not into gore, and though there is definitely some blood involved, it's handled in a way that never made me uncomfortable.  There is a definite psychological aspect aimed at us, the players.  There are moments that are frightening, creepy, downright unsettling... all of it pulling us even further into Senua's world.
Hellblade is a game like no other, exploring mental illness in a setting that is rich in stunning detail and fascinating in its delivery.  Everything about the experience is stunning, from the sounds to the acting to the superb graphics, and everything in between.  I can't recommend this title enough - Absolutely two thumbs up from me!

Well I have pretty mixed emotions about this game so far. I would not recommend my friends buy this game just yet. Its release has some pretty annoying bugs, balance issues and micromanagement/interface problems. But I do see a lot of potential and I think the problems are very easy to address IF the devs see it the way  see it and are going to change it.
The game is not a Dungeon Keeper clone, though it will spark up some fond memories of that game. You are indeed the manager of an evil dungeon and you summon a healthy variety of units which can level up and be upgraded and you can place traps and so on. But the strategy layer is very shallow. You have one room to grow muchrooms, and you can send your units on these simple raids to acquire materials and treasure, which comprise the 3 commodities for building units, upgrading and building rooms.
The rooms are fixed size and shape which is a bit sade, you cant just build a giant storage room for example, but add more of the fixed size storage rooms instead. Digging tunnels is really just for connecting rooms, you dont mine anything.
The dialogue and story in the game is really fun though, which is what you can expect from the guys who made Magicka.
I do find it fun to play and I myself do not regret buying it but I am pretty hard core on these kind of games, I can tolerate a lot to get this sort of gameplay :)
Keep in mind the game only saves your progress on Steam Cloud, so make sure you have that enabled!
If you liked Dungeon Keeper 1 & 2, then chances are this game will grow on you. Same concept, different execution.

I originally saw the E3 trailer for this, and fell in love with it.  I didn't follow the hype train (I had for S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and that seemed to be in dev hell for a loooooong time).  The premise was great - an explore-em-up in a complete universe, with lots of procedural stuff, a storyline, etc.  The main thing that attracted me then was the art aesthetic.
I grew up on 70's & 80's sci fi novels, with the awesome acrylic artwork for the covers - think Chris Foss, Angus Mckie, etc.  This game evoked that golden era to me - not hyper-realistic like Elite:Dangerous, but a more flat-shaded, almost airbrushed appearance.  It was, to me, simply gorgeous.
Imagine my disappointment on reactions to the release.  I watched endless YT vids both in praise and condemning the actions of Hello Games approach to their marketing and release.  The subsequent silence was understandable.  Then, there was an update.  Fixes, improvements, new features.  I kept the game in my wishlist and on my radar to see what happened next.  Another update.
Finally, came 1.3, and also a lower price.  I'd not committed to paying full price given the release hoohaa, and opted to buy at sale if it improved further.  Hello Games have shown commitment to seeing this game grow, improve despite the almost universal backlash from it's troubled release.
With that, onto the game itself.
This is a large game, open-ended in it's approach.  You can follow the quests, missions or just explore.  Often I find myself quite content to slowly fly over a planet, until something pops up.  It is quite relaxing in that sense.  Resources are plentiful, although managing the inventory early on is a massive pain.  Dog-fighting pirates is tense and exciting, and seems to increase in difficulty as you encounter more pirates.  I've not done any combat missions yet, but will get round to them soon.
I've come into this game completely new - although I'd seen what was sorely lacking at release, I was not aware of any story/missions/quests.  As such, it's an enjoyable game if you like an open world to explore.  There's no rush, which makes me happy.  Missions and quests don't seem time-limited, so I take them at my own pace.  I get the impression this is a game that likes to take its time about things - to soak in the atmosphere (and great music) as much as getting on with the story at hand.  It'll take a little time to get a base sorted, then run missions, then do the main quests.
Some of the negatives though:
It's not very well optimised still.  I have a Core i3 6100, Z170-based motherboard, XFX RX480 8gb GTR and play at 2560x1440.  After much tinkering, I've got a reasonable 40-60fps, but there seems to be some artifacting on terrain when it pops in.  Yes, terrain pops in.  The AMD issue is pretty much known, and I hope a subsquent minor update continues to optimise and fix these issues.
Some creatures generated look awful. Hoping that this can be remedied, although some of them do make me smile at the absurdity.
Loading terrain when entering a planet can cause horrendous stutter sometimes.  Not every time though.
Overall, Hello Games have done an excellent job not to abandon a game that promised so much, delivered so little.  Instead they've continued to plug away at it, chipping the rough edges to make a game which I have already spend 24 hours in.  And I've enjoyed every moment of it.  I cannot really recommend it at full price, maybe 29.99, however the sales usually coincide with major updates, and might be worth waiting until then.

Performance is important. It's a big thing in any pc title, and 1080p 60fps is, while not absolutely necessary for enjoying a title, very high on the list of priorities because bad performance exacerbates all other issues with the game. On a modern card, like the 1050ti I have, it can run just fine with a little setting adjustment. On older cards without drivers? Its much more unstable. Do some research to see if it will work properly on your hardware before purchasing.
So lets take it from the top (Minor story spoilers):
Pros:
-Excellent Storyline, well directed and written. Gets the blood pumping.
-Meaty guns with extremely satisfying visual/auditory feedback
-Absolutely solid melee animations for those takedowns
-For the most part solid gameplay and progression (see cons)
-Looks great, and even better, the game looks almost the same with settings turned down. The only thing I noticed when switching my settings from ultra to high-medium was the increase to performance.
Cons (Wall of text but its just explanation, actual list of bare bones cons is short):
-While the story was excellent, some side characters felt like something invisible happened to make you closer to them. Maybe its just me not really exploring the u-boat hub much, but it should be a little clearer how all of a sudden after you just rescued horton he's celebrating your birthday and you are interacting with him like a friend you've been through thick and thin with. Again, might be solved with more focus on hub exploration in a playthrough, but that gets tedious fast.
-The basic soldiers are the bane of my damn existence. The giant robot enemies you can fight effectively because they have damage windup or projectiles or weakpoints, etc that lets you play around them in cool and interesting ways, but the basic soldiers have this absurd damage with no windup, just bam bam bam 200 armor is gone because you missed that one grunt with a damn smg to the side. This is on Do or Die difficulty too, not on Call Me Terror Billy. For some perspective, a grunt in The New Order on Uber (the highest difficulty) would take more than twice the time to gun you down. Also them getting damage and armor piercing upgrades to their weapons is total BS and massively contributes to the issue.
-Cutscenes will very occasionally just black out. It won't be a crash, you can still hear the audio and when the cutscene finishes you can progress but its such a mood-killer when you get it in really crucial moments.
-Ok big stuff is out of the way, minor gripe time: Ramshackles should be a one hit kill for any basic infantry unit. For unarmored ones, it should gib every time. Some areas are lit very badly, making some areas a pain to see in even when in max brightness. Weapon upgrades aren't as cool. Scopes? Cmon, scopes? In the last game your ar got an underbarrel rocket launcher. While you get the kampfpistole for that this time, at least give it something that changes how you use the weapon. This is only an issue on the automatic weapons, because fully upgraded they just feel like "oh cool i have a larger mag and some better damage now, gonna spray same as always tho bc it changes almost nothing." The da'at yichud suit gives you like no upgrades to mobility or combat effectiveness whatsoever, even though caroline (rest well old friend) literally jumps from robot to robot killing them in one punch each in the last game.
Ultimately? Not worth 60 dollars. But that's okay, because I didn't buy it for that much anyway; I bought the digital deluxe edition (season pass and all) for 40 dollars. And I think the full game was worth exactly that (not counting the DLC that will be released later).
TLDR: Its a good but not that good. Buy it for 33% off or more.

I'm a big adventure game fanatic, so I'm picky.  This one is pretty good and I think it's a great one to start out with if you're new to adventure games, because it has a good story and the problems are typically at a beginner level, without being absurdly easy.
One thing I particularly liked about the game is that it shows you very clearly what you can click on.  This is something that a lot of games lack.  I want to pull my hair out when I've been thinking and thinking about how to solve a problem in an adventure game and it turns out there was something I just didn't know I could click on (like a one-pixel wide item or something).  WIth Syberia, that's never an issue and it means that they can't rely on poorly thought-out solutions based on flailing around with the mouse to see what you can click on.
My only complaint is that there were a couple of places in which the solutions to problems were, in my opinion, not terribly intelligent.  I'm perfectly willing to take my hat off to a really clever problem that I didn't get, but it drives me nuts when these games have solutions that aren't at all clever, just non-sensical.  I'll try for hours only to give up, find an online walkthrough and then tear my hair out that the solution doesn't even make sense.  I'd advise that you don't spend too, too long on a problem you're stumped with.  Don't be ashamed to find online walkthroughs, because occasionally it's just that the problem was poorly designed.  Fortunately, those sorts of things are few and far between.
The plot is fairly original, centering around a scientist who made ingenious automata that do all sorts of amazing things and who was obsessed with the idea that wooly mammoths never died out, but still exist in some isolated part of the arctic.  My only complaint with the plot is that Syberia refers to a legendary place, not to Siberia, even though it could easily be somewhere around there.  Nobody once mentions that Syberia and Siberia are different (in fact, I don't think anyone even mentions Siberia at all) and yet, even when they're speaking orally, everyone seems to just get that Syberia means the legendary place, even though it's pronounced exactly the same. That little bit kind of rubbed me the wrong way, but, otherwise, it's quite well done and very creative.
One thing I particularly like is that you have a cell phone and you can make calls any time you want, though only to preexisting contacts, which you can add to as the game progresses.  I thought that was a nice touch.  You also get calls sometimes from people like your boss, who wants updates, and your mother and boyfriend who are both worried about you and want you to come home.
All in all, a good game.  I'd recommend it.

No maps in really convulted areas
Too much boring dialogue
Unskippable animations
More on stairs - Kate has a serious almost crippling phobia of them it seems
Soap opera side plot which ironically provides an excellent example of why the Bechdel test is so important
It's really wierd for me to bring this up as it's not really been an issue since the 80's - I've been gaming since I was 7 which was in 1988, and although some games may have some superficial problems with sexism (GTO being the worst offender, and not superfical about it either), most games by this point are far, FAR more inclusive than they were back then.  My biggest gripe with this as a female gamer is that the femminist revolution seems to be something that happened somewhere else - if the writting here is anything to go by at least.  As most of us are aware this occurred in the 60's, yet the protaganist has this strange twee way of speaking, more akin to the 19th or early 20th century.  Then there's what she's saying;  and we are supposed to believe that this woman is a lawyer?!  She spends the entire game being submissive, impassive and the entire point of her existence seems to be for her boyfriend or boss; both of whom are petulant children who need to be told to ♥♥♥♥ off, like now.  How the hell did this gal get through law school?  The side plot revolving around this is hilariously predictable and the culmination is as dull as its content.  It gets worse, the women in her life can't even get the game passed the Bechdel test (yes they only talk about Kate's boyfriend and boss) - it strikes me as stereotypical female drama (think rom-coms, I ♥♥♥♥ing hate rom-coms) as seen through the eyes of a man, a man most likely born in the 40's - it's somewhere between complete ignorance and straight up contempt.  And I don't know whether this is more confusing for me or the guy that wrote this, it's just frigging wierd.  Even by the time our protagist shrugs off the shackles that is her peer group (spoiler not spoiler - its at the end), you'll stil want to smack her in the face.  Grow a pair of ovaries love, seriously, you're embaressing the rest of us.  Then there's her personality - she's all over the place, and it doesn't really represent the unimaginative arc she's given;  Which I think is, a woman finds herself by being thrown in to a wierd adventure and in doing so realises that she can't keep sacrificing herself for what others expect and demand of her, and finally - but not really - she tells them all to do one.
What about the mechanics?  Aaaaarrrrrghhhhh!  Kate will run if you double click, this is one of the few elements this game has incorportated from more modern adventure games.  However there is no screen wrapping and every time you hit some stairs (and yes they are all over the place), kate stops suddenly as if she's come to a precipice, she then painstakingly prepares herself like an elderly person due for a hip raplcement at the bottom of said stairs, before  ardously climbing them: I'm pretty sure people pass kidney stones quicker than this.  Then there's the inventory system which is clumbsy and no you cannot combine items.  And there's the bugs, I had two crashes for no reason, and if you alt tab to say your media player on your second monitor, the background graphics get knocked out until you change scenary and trust me; you will want to watch something whilst playing this, in order to quench the sheer monotonous boredom.   You will also have to restrict the game to 256 colour in the game.exe properties in order to get it to run on win X (and most likely any OS later than XP).  Finally, beware of the huge amount of content in the form of diaries etc, as it's all as excruciatingly dull and verbose as the verbal conversations and adds very little to the story or as clues for puzzles.
Puzzles?  I can barely remember them as they are completely overshadowed by the extremely slow pacing, there were some good ones in there (I think), but the spread out environments really hurt them and are clearly another exercise in dragging the game time out.  Then there's the multitiude of unskippable animations to conversations or interactions with certain objects, it passes bordering on the ridiculous after about an hour of gameplay.  Of those puzzle's I can remember some are very poorly implemented.  For example, there's one involving a blood sample that I had to read a walkthrough for as the game gives you only one way obtaining the second sample and if you miss it and do what most people would do, you will not be able to fix it and proceed - I ended up going back a save and found that the missed option is only noticiable when you are looking for it and does not in anyway resemble the way the first sample is obtained.  This is not an isolated example and it amounts to some lazy writting and design imo.
Other problems:  The reading, oh my god the reading, there's so much and its written so, so, so badly.  The only time where the dialogue seemed less twee was in a diary, but that's only because it starts in the early 20th century!  The voice acting is nativity play calibre, and that comparison might actually be more insulting to the children.  To make matters worse these uninspired conversations go on for what seems like longer than the aforementioned diary, and they are all frigging terrible.  I wonder whether the acting would be so bad if the actors weren't so clearly directed to speak so ♥♥♥♥ing slowly.  You will roll your eyes to the point of muscle strain.
If you're new to adventure games, I'm again recommending the Broken Sword series, Discworld Noir and more recently Still life.  The modernised telltale fair are pretty good too although I would definitely avoid The walking Dead Michone series and Game of thrones, as they are also boring and eye roll inducing.  The rest of the TWD are great and ignore the horror porn comments about the female protaganist in the second season and frontier, cos guess what?   Kids go though some serious♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes and I dont think it helps anyone by shying away from that reality, especially when talking about a sodding zombie apocolypse!  The wolf among us and Life is strange however, put most of these to shame, so save them for last as they may spoil you in terms of expectations in other games of this ilk.
This however, kill it, kill it with fire.

I'll start out by saying I really wanted to like this game.  The concept is great and original, and some of the core ideas are solid.  Unfortunately, the execution is deeply flawed.  Even though I got this on sale for 1/3 its normal price, I do not feel I got my money's worth.  Much of the hype/marketing is incorrect, so I'll address each point as advertised below:
Speculative, Stunning Vision of the Future - delivers pretty well here, but for some reason, the writing/plot just seems barebones to me.  You get a few lines of exposition, then punch 87 guys in the face, and then repeat.
Play as Nilin - um...  yup, you do.  As to stealing memories to progress, you really only do this 7-8 times in the whole game.  So, true on this point, but not optimal.
Memory Remix - total marketing oversell.  This is used literally 4 times in the entire game.  When it is used, it's actually a pretty cool idea that's executed well.  Using it so sparingly seems like a waste of a brilliant game mechanic.
A balanced mix of combat and exploration - Ummm...  no.  There is no real exploration, first.  There are a series of highly linear levels, each with 1-2 small side rooms with a hidden collectible each.  The platforming is not terrible, but the controls seem very loose.  Then the combat...  BUTTON MASHING REPEATEDLY.  On a PC, it is actually less annoying with a gamepad than mouse/keyboard (shudder).  However, one nice thing is the God of War-esque ability to dodge/abort in the middle of an attack.  That is very cool and works well.  But, my god, the BUTTON MASHING...
Combo Lab - customizing combos is cool, as is the ability to change them up mid-fight.  Literally at any point, you can switch up combos, even in mid-attack!  But, your combos are fixed to punches or kicks per slot, and all you change is whether the hit does extra damage, regen, resets cooldown timers, or chains/multiples the previous effect.  So, this is a high point of the game.
So overall, just a so-so execution of some brilliant ideas.  A darn shame really, as this could have been something special.  Imagine a Deus Ex level of alternative options and exploration.  Oh well, I suppose this was 13 hours that were not *that* badly spent.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is the first game of the series to break away from the tried and true World War 2 setting and into the new era of war, involving constant risks of nuclear annihilation and smaller scale, urban combat. Russia has fallen into civil war as Ultra-nationalists attempt to resurrect the Soviet Union, meanwhile an unnamed Middle Eastern country has been overthrown by a warlord with ties to said Ultra-Nationalists. We play as two main characters, one a US Marine called Paul Jackson and a British SAS Sergeant named John “Soap” MacTavish. Starting off we play as Soap who has just been accepted into a SAS squad led by series’ famous and mustached hero, John Price.
You are tasked with completing some quick practice training before being briefed on your mission to familiarize you with the game. If you have played any Call of Duty game or any FPS in general over the past decade you will have no issues getting the hang of it. Introduced in this tutorial is the new feature of flash grenades designed to disorient enemies caught in its blast. Mastering these will greatly improve your chances of survival since you will now be fighting in small areas instead of the vast battlefields of WW2 and a well-placed throw can decide the outcome. By far my favorite edition is that bullets can now pass through thin objects which makes it a ton of fun as bullets penetrate all your surroundings, causing you to desperately seek cover behind something sensible.
It works the other way around as well so no longer will enemies by able to use a tiny fence as indestructible cover. With that new found knowledge found in your training you are then briefed on your mission to retrieve an object from a well-guarded enemy cargo ship. It is here that you realize that the CoD series has taken a new feel to it. While previous games were more down to earth and grim with the sight of allies being killed being common place, Modern Warfare goes the Michael Bay route with tons of explosions, escaping a flooding cargo ship and jumping into the helicopter at the very last second. It's not a criticism nor a necessarily bad thing but it's a change of tone I felt was worth mentioning.
The journey of playing both US and British forces take you all over Russia and the Middle East, both stories are interconnected and give you a greater view of the story instead of being there for convenient teleportation to another cool location. You play as a few other unnamed soldiers, pilots and even John Price for a bit though those are over very quickly and are just keep the game from getting stale by changing up the gameplay such as you having to provided air support and carefully shooting your missiles. Most of these extra characters feel gimmicky and are not really all that fun except for when you play as Price in Chernobyl, on an important stealth mission. That was easily the high point of the game and a moment I will remember long after I stop playing. And that is saying something as there are many high points when playing as the main protagonists.
Aside from bullet penetration, the gameplay is the same as previous entries only now you have newer weaponry, gadgets and gun attachments such as a grenade launcher added under your assault rifle. Smoke grenades are back and as useful as ever to pass through heavy fire or be concealed from tanks and such. Another new addition that is extremely gimmicky and neigh on useless are the night vision goggles. You could see just fine without them and don't really serve any purpose other than a bullet point on the new features list. You're never in a position where you have to scavenge for items or ammo, they are refilled after every mission or taken away, you will always have what you need which makes sense considering these elite soldiers won't go in unprepared but feels too “hand holdy” gameplay wise.
Especially when it comes to ammo. You are given an obscene amount and I have never once had to switch weapons or take an enemies weapon. That was one change to the series I did not like as you will not use any of the other weapons in the game unless you go out of your way to do so while playing through the campaign. Melee combat has been changed a bit as well, while the previous games had you use your weapons to smack an enemy, Modern Warfare has you automatically pull out a knife and lunge at him which I personally find much more satisfying. The smaller environments both harm and help Modern Warfare, on one hand it is far more obvious how linear the game is but on the other it makes it more in your face and fast paced than ever before.
The campaign is short but sweet, it took me about 5 hours to fully complete though it went at break neck speedy action every step of the way and had a shockingly decent story. There is not much motivation to replay it though. 30 enemy laptops are scattered throughout the campaign and unlock cheat codes after finding enough of them yet the cheat codes are usually very underwhelming such as making your screen black and white or other pointless screen effects. The only cheat code that I've unlocked that was decent was the “Cluster grenade” which causes huge explosions once your grenades detonates. To try to motivate you to reply they also added an Arcade Mode once you finish the game that lets you replay any mission and earn points for everything you do. It offers nothing but racking up high scores and is nowhere near enough to get me to replay the campaign after just having finished it.
Where the game really shined back in the day was in its multiplayer. It's RPG like progression system to unlock titles, weapons and perks was revolutionary and changed the FPS genre as a whole. For better or for worse is in the eye of the beholder. It introduced the problem that those who played longer have a significant advantage over newer players but on the other hand it is satisfying to be constantly rewarded with stuff for playing and helped differentiate each player. One may have a perk that allows them to run further without stopping, another may simply have more health and yet another player may be able to hip fire far more accurately and surprise you. It makes every firefight interesting since you never know just what tricks your foe has up his/her sleeve. Once you hit level 5 you can build up to five custom classes that will be useful for different situations and tons of fun to experiment with.
Be warned though, the multiplayer will crash on start unless right click on your sound icon, go into your recording tab and then enable “Stereo Mix”. No clue as to why but that fixes the issue. Another issue is that if you are playing via Steam make sure to unbind the in-game screenshot key that defaults to F12 as that will also cause your game to crash if you take a screen-shot. Weird steps to make the multiplayer work but it is definitely still worth playing even after all these years and still has a decently sized community so finding a game won't be a problem (as of this review). In a rather cool move by Activision the 1 DLC pack released for Modern Warfare is already included. All in all, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare was a breath of fresh air and finally broke the series free from it's done to death WW2 roots.

Easily one of my favorite games of all time. Absolutely an experience.
When it comes to gameplay, I can understand how this may not be for everyone. Specifically the pacing. That being said, I thought it was perfect. It gives you plenty of time to explore and soak in the environment. If you're used to running from explosion to explosion, fight to fight--this game isn't for you. This is a game for those who want to immersed in a story about an individuals tragic and horrific struggle.
The binaural sound really draws you into the game, especially if you have a good pair of headphones. I'm really happy Epic with UE4 is making this possible and I hope future developers/games follow suit. The soundtrack and scores are utilized wonderfully. The graphics (as you have probably already seen) are amazing and the animation really pulls it all together. All the motion capture for Senua's body and face really help bring her to life and will make you that much more engaged in her character.
The puzzles can be a little tricky at first glance but--as many have already mentioned--not too difficult. Same goes for the combat: it's not terribly complex or hard. You're really just chaining together a series of attacks or defenisive moves. It is however, quite cinematic which is fitting for a story-driven game. Thus, the battles are more rewarding for their excitement or intensity than their challenge. Albeit, more challenging enemies are introduced as you progress through the game. I had a few sighs of relief after a few of the more intense battles keeping me on my toes. Exciting but not frustrating.
Lastly, some people aren't too happy with the end of the game.
9/10, as no game is perfect. There are a few bits and pieces where you could argue the graphics or textures aren't up to par with the rest of the game. The voice acting is great, but falls a little short at a few minor parts. The game also has a few progression bugs that need to be fixed at the time of this review.
It's hard to name a game that really compares. If you love norse mythology, have an interest in mental illness, horror gaming, or just want story-driven experience then I cannot recommend this enough. Zero regrets paying full price.

Ok, so let me start by saying I have never reviewed a game before but at the end of hellblade I felt compelled to share my thoughts.

1. The combat is relatively simple and not very difficult.
2. The puzzles can seem repetitive.
3. Nothing for character customization.
4. It took me an hour or two before actually getting into the game.
Now with that out of the way, this game is an epic experience which depicts the topic of psychosis very well. The story is well written and explores a different avenue of games for players. I trully believe everyone should give this game a try. The end game combined with the ability to move you emotionally once you become emmersed in the adventure is what makes this worth it.
So yes, I recommend this to people looking for an experience and something different from every other genre of game out there despite the gaming aspect being slightly lacking. I for one was incredibly moved at the end of the story... so much so that I felt I just had to review it and give it a thumbs up. If anything the fact that there is no triple A price makes it even more compelling.
In addition, the graphics and atmosphere is well developped. This adventure really is better is you have headphones rather than speakers.
In conclusion, I really did not enjoy this game at the start but it has a way of engaging you. So much so that the credits and the end song made it very difficult not to think about the entire story and what senua had been through... it just really sticks with you.

Cartoony, stylized, simple and easy to pick up its a great "pick up game" for when you don't want to focus all too hard on something. You drop right in a coop server, shoot some bots, earn some XP and they even have a working persistence system for leveling up in multiplayer coop servers.

A lot of fun, worth the $$$!

In my Alien Swarm review I stated that it was easily my favourite top down shooter to date, Well, as good as Alien Swarm is, it's just met it's best contender yet, That being said, Running With Rifles is more of a open sandbox, tactical top down shooter in which you take the role of a simple soldier in a fight of potential hundreds, the old saying "One man can make a difference" is one you should keep in mind when playing.
The main objective of the campaign is to capture all of the areas on the local island the game takes place, but how you go about doing that is completely up to you, there is no set method for you to follow and you're given the creative freedom of how to overcome your current mission, this is what makes the game stand out for me. Would you rather stand with your brothers in arms on the frontlines, directly taking the fight to the enemy? Would you prefer to sit back and support with sniper fire or perhaps manning an Abrahms tank? or maybe you'd like to take a team around and attempt a finnicky yet rewarding amphibious stealth attack? All are viable and all will help bring your team one step closer to victory, best of all, it will be you who had ultimately changed the tide of the battle.
You can easily tailor your equipment to the situation and there are many, many methods of taking care of your enemies, from rifles, grenades, pistols, MGs, mounted MGs, snipers, tanks, jeeps, C4s, impact grenades as well as a number of shotguns, smgs, rocket launchers, more rifles, body armours, silenced weapons and even apc turrets, if you get bored of one weapon, there will be a number of potential candidates to take its place.
The game does have a ranking system which releates to the in-game radio you can use to call in support from your base of operations, the higher your rank, the better support you can request, so long as you have RP to do it - a tradable resource on multiplayer servers that players obtain by capturing bases, spotting important targets such as enemy tanks and destroying opposing communications - you can request down reinforcements to help finish capturing a point, you could bombard a heavily fortified enemy position or maybe you just need that little extra edge of a friendly tank storming the opponents down.
Thats the general gameplay, so how are the controls? In short, very good for what it is.
The controls are very smooth and responsive, there is a slight slide in the game, probably to help emphasise that your soldier is quite heavy and can't just change on a whim, you can go prone and crouch which both increase your general accuracy by a significant amount, you can jump up smaller buildings, climb ladders and hop over fences to your hearts content, but that doens't mean you shouldn't be staying behind cover the second you spot the enemy force.
RWR is a fine top down shooter, I love the art style, sound effects are crisp and war torn and the game itself is just great fun to play, with friends especially, I remember this one game I was playing with two amigos, we had been at this fight agaisnt the Greycollars for 2 and a half hours, It got to the point where we had to use a tactical mindset, one of us stays behind with a squad to defend the base under attack whilst the other two attempted to push the base to relieve some pressure, I love games that put you in a particular mindset, one where you really think about your next moves and RWR does that surprisingly well.

I really fell in love with this game. I first played it many, many years ago and, since then, have replayed it several times since. Each time I replay reminds me of why I fell in love in the first place.
It is the story that took me. It seem strange at first because the graphics isn't that good, the voice acting isn't the best, and the dialogue can be downright awful at times. You'd think all these factors would make the story difficult to get into...and it certainly doesn't help, that's for sure. However, I suppose what I love is the premise, the imagery, the location, and how it is all executed together.
Often, while playing through this game, I get a sense of surrealism. At times, I get drawn into the quaint loveliness of the architecture and people of Valadilene/Barrockstadt then the stark barrenness of Komkolzgrad/Aralbad, and, in the midst of this, the inexplicable impossible spring-operated automatons would be present. It's a weird mixture, but it somehow drew me in. I would feel as if I'm actually in a fantasy world exploring it.
Kind of a strange thing to feel considering that's pretty much what many games essentially is and aims to make players feel. Problem is that it seems to be so rarely achieved. In fact, of the hundreds of games I've played over the course of my life, Syberia is among a handful that actually manages to achieve it.
For that reason alone, I became a huge fan and the game gets my highest recommendation possible.

Syberia is without a doubt my favourite game of all time, the story is beautifuly crafted, the visuals even now are just beautiful and gameplay honestly still holds up.

People seem to love this game and I can partly see why. As a widely recommended title of my favourite genre, it's full of original ideas, beautiful artwork and the opening scene made me feel like I was in for a real treat. The music's nice too. Looking through the Steam reviews you're hard pushed to find a bad one. Unfortunately, as much as I kept trying to love this game, it really didn't work for me.
Sadly, my defining memory of this game won't be the ever-increasing innovation of Hans Voralberg's automatons or the sheer time and effort spent on complimenting the plot via newspaper clippings, diary entries and so on. Instead, I'll remember the tedious and seemingly endless running back and forth involved EVERY STEP OF THE WAY. And I should point out that I mean the word 'step' quite literally.
I'm not sure exactly what happened to Kate Walker in the days or weeks preceding the game that makes climbing stairs such a challenge for her but as she slowly and deliberately positions herself at the bottom of even the smallest flight, before beginning her tortuous ascent, you can't help but try and solve the only truly baffling puzzle of the whole adventure - If a woman walking up some stairs is so disruptive to the game's engine then WHY PUT STAIRS IN EVERY FRAME?!
Solving a puzzle invariably involves walking back and forth through a bunch of frames multiple times in what felt to me like a shameless attempt to make the game feel as though it contains more gameplay than it really does. Don't get me wrong, I've played many point and click games in my time and know that running back and forth between frames to solve puzzles is a characteristic almost all share, but usually this is a case of necessity rather than choice and developers usually try to make it as painless as possible. In Syberia, the designers seem to have brainstormed on the question 'How can we make this game seem longer than it is?' and come up with only one solution; 'Drag every puzzle out as long as is humanly possible until finding the solution is more of a relief than a reward'.
My primary frustrations with this game are as follows:
- In some scenes you can double-click to make Kate run. In others, for some unknown reason, you can't. This gets quite annoying.
- Unneccesary and, more importantly, unskippable animations precede interactions with NPC's, which makes returning to someone you've already spoken to for a quick recap a painfully slow process. The same goes for interacting with objects.
- It's impossible to skip to the next frame with a double-click, a simple feature which would have multiplied my enjoyment of the game ten-fold.
- It takes a long time for NPC's to say anything that might be of value in some of the most wooden dialogue I've ever witnessed in a point and click game.
In short, it takes AGES to do ANYTHING. A simple puzzle that requires little thought and would be solved in seconds in better designed games (ANY Lucasarts title for example) ends up taking minutes to complete which really adds up over the course of the adventure.
This review may seem harsh but I feel that the reviews on Steam are so unfairly one-sided that a counteracting review is necessary to warn people that the slow, tedious gameplay mentioned in some of the other reviews as a potential downfall really IS enough to ruin the entire experience.
Sorry, Syberia. There were so many times when you were so close to being a great, original game but you screwed up at every opportunity by disregarding the one thing that all great games have in common: The continued engagement of the player.
If you consider yourself to be a particularly patient person who doesn't mind spending a five minutes running for every minor hunch that you have then buy this game and enjoy the good things about it. As for me, despite having bought both Syberia 1 & 2 together, I won't be playing the second one until I've finished watching all of my paint dry. At least I can do that without using any stairs.

One of the best, and most unique adventure games. It's a truly memorable classic which helped revive the genre at the time. I remember when I first learned about Syberia, the idea of a plot involving automatons and mammoths didn't excite me, but I was very curious how it all tied together. This is a slow-moving, story-heavy game with strong atmosphere and a beautiful, haunting soundtrack, as lawyer Kate Walker heads east through Europe to find an eccentric inventor. and close a business deal. In many ways this game is about Kate's character development, and you can't help but to go through the experience with her. The game seems to take place around the time it was created (2002) but as you visit the locations, touched with elements of art nouveau, steampunk, and the scars of world war, the game feels enchanting, surreal, and totally out of time in the most endearing way. The intelligent script, mysterious and charming, has it's moments of suspense and humor, too.
Now, the puzzles to be found are somewhat straight forward and will likely give you no trouble. So this isn't a puzzle-centric adventure, which may push some people away. Also, the game has been criticized for having many screens where there's nothing to interact with as you move between points of interest. I can understand that running through 4 screens of landscape at a time with nothing to do, and then running back through them, can be irritating to some people. However, I find this is something that contributes to the immersive and thoughtful tone of the game, like looking at paintings.
I should mention that while this is the must-play gem of the series, the shorter sequel is still very good, and the 3rd game, developed 13 years later and coming out next month, will no doubt be interesting.

An amazing 2D fighting game with great visuals, memorable characters, great humour and solid gameplay.
Skullgirls is probably one of the most underrated games in its entire genre.
Every character has something weird or creepy about them (i.e. they're undead, living weapons, eldritch abominations or something similar), which makes them all quite interesting.
All the characters have their own moves, many of which are references to other fighting games, including references to Scorpion from Mortal Kombat, Dio from JoJo's Bizarre Adventure or several Street Fighter references.
All characters have a different playstyle, as such, you will probably find just the one you like.
Stay away from the online mode though, otherwise you will get absolutely destroyed, even if you've managed to defeat the AI on the highest difficulty.
The Story mode has a lot of effort put into it and as such, I can only recommend playing it!
You should, however, purchase the game with the 2nd Encore upgrade, as this will allow you to play as all the DLC characters and you will also get a few challenges and a fully voiced story mode!
All in all, Skullgirls is an amazing fighting game that truly surprised me with great visuals, a great soundtrack and wonderful characters. Buy this game if you're looking for a solid 2D Fighting game, as long as you don't mind the anime-esque artstyle and the fanservice.

Assassin's Creed is a very strong game that will satisfy individiuals that love history and war, but also the real main story of Assassins Creed.
Setting: The game is set in the Third Crusade times, the battle between Islam and Christianity. It features Desmond Miles, a protagonist in 21st Century America, which is kidnapped by the antagonist company Abstergo Industries. This company uses the Animus, a generic-memory stimulator, on Desmond to recall his memories through his ancestor Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad.
The cities involved are Masyaf, the assassin creed's home city, Acre, ran by the Knights Templars, and Jerusalem and Damascus, both cities ran by the Templars and enemy Saracens. There is one more city however I won't spoil it. The landscape is different for each city, but only noticable in each city. There are three districts, poor, middle, and rich district, and you would assume there are higher quality buildings as the districts become richer, but again, you can only notice them.
Plot: The plot line is certainly intriguing. Having played AC II, Brotherhood, and Revelations, and having not finished AC I, all the storylines from the sequels made actual sense once I completed this. Onto the plot though, there are two separate plots that do intertwine. To clarify that, there is the story of Desmond and the story of Altair and the plotlines intertwine through the story of Altair and Desmond mashing in present 21st century America (hard to explain I know). Just know, the plot makes absolute sense once you play the games. From the perspective of AC's release in 2007, it was very very intriguing to interpret the plot without knowing the sequel storylines, so the plot from that perspective is a massive plus. The finish was very surprising as well might I mention.
Also, I completed the game in 18 hours, which included the core plot and the main side-missions. I did not complete finding the flags and killing the templar guards as I found them to be irrelevent. I had only played 14.9 hours on Steam, however 18 hours came from I playing about 3.5 hours of the game and me realising after three hours that Steam didn't realise I was playing AC, so there was a glitch in the Steam Client.
Only nuisences regarding the plot is the side-missions. As you progress into the game, they become more of a chore than actual for fun, for example, when there is an investigation side mission, the guards keep on coming later in the game and is ridiculous as they are alert, and spot you without even looking at you, meaning you failed the investigation. So yes, there was a few unbalanced AI involved with the missions, but other than that, it relieves you in the end once you know all are completed.
And to note, I realised why I got so bored of the game about three hours into it on my first playthrough last year, and that was because the horse riding from Masyaf to the other cities is so long, it would take at least 15 minutes to travel, ridiculous and boring especially when 'The Kingdom' is just a transition area with no real meaning.
Gameplay: Gameplay is very solid. For a game released in 2007, it is surprising to see how smooth the gameplay is. For a game that emphasises parkour and combat, I see it as a major positive adding to the game. Only negatives regarding gameplay is how basic some actions are. For example, you will notice the same amount of counters to attacks and blocks, something that I felt could have been explored further.
Sound/Dialogue/Graphics: The graphics are very good for a 2007 game. I praise that.
Dialogue is good as there is mostly variety in individual dialogues. Only negative for dialogue is the 'Save Citizens' missions, the dialogue is extremely repeatitive. There was also some minor speech issues that I had noticed.

Sound: Serviceable. There was rare audio issues that I encountered.
Negatives: This review may seem very positive, but gee these negatives are really that annoying. Overall, there are several bugs and glitches I'll name a few, for 'Save Citizens' missions, you would get glitches where you could not trigger the person to speak to after completing the task. Another was camera's getting stuck on the player, especially moderately when walking through doors, completely annoying.
Overall: A very solid game and a good first-entry to the Assassins Creed series. If you didn't bother reading the review, the plot was consistent and intriguing, the graphics were very good, the sound was servicable, the dialogue was good, and gameplay was very solid. There were several bugs and glitches within the game that completely nagged me. The game is currently worth $10 on Steam, I'd say buy it, no harm done, sets up the good foundation for the series. Now, the rating is low compared to what I mentioned in the review as it was not an excellent game by all means. 7.5/10
EDIT: I didn't note, but since the game took me 18 hours to complete, for the individual, I would assume it would take 20+ hours to complete by doing all tasks.

Ok. So I was postponing playing this game for a looong time now (b'cause, you know - ubisoft. Plus I tend not to play highly hyped games right away, unless they are titled Mortal Kombat). And I have to say this game is lovely regardless few glitches here and there.
Pros:
- Action takes place in early middle ages (crusaders in middle east). Personally one of my favourite chapters in history.
- Climate. Impressive, large cities. Architecture is amazing, brings up the spirit of the times. Music adds gracefully to this.
- It's a climbing simulator.
- It has "find the flag" mini-game.
- It has story line! (don't get me wrong. If AC was only climbing simulator with find the flags mini-game it would be joy enough). Story is pretty interesting although not earth shaking. I like the feeling of ambiguity that Altair's last chats with his victims bring in.
- You can try to play stealth if you wish.
- Action oriented. Assassinations are pretty flashy and possible interactions with so many objects in the game can cause interesting twists. (I.e:  scored one templar kill by accident: was being chased, attracted attention of some templar I hadn't even noticed. He fell down the roof leaving me happy, although somewhat puzzled).
- Antagonist and Protagonists: they are interesting in design. They don't feel cliche.
- Open ending.
Cons:
- Weird one time glitches:  Damascus contact's face started to melt down while we were chatting. Altair froze mid jump from horse back, and memory had to be reloaded.
- Sometimes game breaking bug may happen: dead body carefully put on the ground might twitch and fell of the roof, causing havoc on the streets. Dead bodies can even jump high to the sky, before they fall. Pretty creepy.
- Repetitive:  people who might not enjoy flags finding as much as I do can find this game repetitive. In each city there are flags, and sub-quests (view points, rescue civilians, some informer missions) that are either the same or very similar (informer missions may slightly very).
- Out of 3 major cities, Damascus and Jerusalem feel the same (except one has yellow and the other green filter on). Travelling to Acre I could feel that this conquered by crusaders city is different and had it's own western-like touch to it.
- Fighting mechanics is simplified and a bit clumsy, especially when you face a lot of enemies.
- You will not exit this game easy on PC...
In general though: game is fun to play. And I think I do understand now, how this title is so popular. It's just joyful climbing simulator re-skinned packed with action moments. ;)

tl;dr: 9/10. Quality mix of JRPG, visual novel and hack & slash elements. Impeccably faithful and relatable reproduction of Akihabara in many ways, not just the maps. Just take it at face value and you'll have a blast.
I've lived in Japan for a number of years, and I've visited Akiba a plethora of times throughout those years. It's one of my favourite places to go and take people, and I like to believe I'm quite familiar with the area. Upon discovering a game that claimed to faithfully reproduce the town, I naturally bought my copy and proceeded to begin my scrutiny.
Needless to say, I was very impressed. I had no doubts in my mind that I was in Akihabara. The attention to detail on all of the stores and roads is unbelievable. I would honestly believe you if you told me that the maps were constructed from real photos of Akiba, put through a few image filters. I have zero complaints about this, it is 100% faithful. I truly felt like I was thrown back into the Akiba of 2012, especially seeing the
everywhere. I remember these quite vividly, and despite the blatant self-marketing, it was rather nostalgia-inducing.
The quality of the maps isn't the only good point, though. All of the stores and signs present in the game exist in real life too (albeit a little parodied at times) and it was a pleasure to find myself so familiar with the environment despite being dropped into the world of a game I've never played before.
On top of this, Acquire also included a faithful reproduction of more abstract things. One example I particularly enjoyed was a side quest where you had to take revenge on an art gallery for selling someone artwork that he didn't want. I've actually had the misfortune to have visited that very art store in real life and have postcards almost forced upon me. I managed to get away without buying anything, but the depiction of this art gallery in the game left me nothing short of overjoyed. Anyone with a bit of time on their hands can hit up Google Earth and reproduce the town in a game, but it takes true knowledge and love of Akiba to include things like this.
I was also exceptionally pleased with the English translation. It was top notch. I found no mistakes throughout all of my ten or so playthroughs and the game was also localized amazingly. There were no meaningless literal translations, and the dialogue actually makes sense in English. According to the credits, there was a whole team working on localization, as there should be. They provided a glorious reading experience and still preserved the original meaning of the writing. I did in fact play in Japanese for a while, but surprisingly, I found reading the game in English to be much more enjoyable and worthwhile - a first, for me. Great work, XSEED. If there's any mark of a quality translation, this is it.
As an added bonus, the character customization was also nice. All of the armour and weapons are more or less homogenous and will provide the same benefits, so you're free to play dress-ups without compromising your combat prowess.
However, Akiba's Trip falls a little short in a few places, such as the soundtrack. The music wasn't
by any means, but it was mediocre at best. It didn't subtract anything from my enjoyment of the game, but I hesitate to call it
.
Another area I felt could use a little work was the story. I won't spoil anything, but it was largely inconsequential and I didn't really feel like anything was happening. Barring one, the routes were more or less the same thing and the heroines didn't seem very relevant to their own routes. There was also a bit of recycled text that
, and a fair few inconsistencies in the story, which was kind of disappointing. I guess all of their effort was devoted elsewhere; namely, towards recreating Akiba.
That being said, the story isn't really this game's selling point. I felt like it was worth mentioning, but Akiba's Trip wasn't designed to be a rich, story-telling experience in the first place. It doesn't take itself very seriously and if you do the same, you're sure to enjoy the myriad humorous antics that ensue, and appreciate Akiba presented in a faithful light.
A complaint I do see every now and again is with the combat system. I admit, it does have its flaws, but you have to remember that the game is a Playstation port and naturally, running on a non-native engine will inevitably cause problems. I noticed a few issues with the camera when you were near a map transition point, but nothing that affected gameplay really. The combat itself is a bit fiddly, but if you take the time to familiarize yourself with it (or read
), then it's definitely playable.
The game engine also had a few other faults. The visual novel features of the game were quite limited, for one. There's no chat log or text speed adjustment or anything, which only ends up being a mild annoyance, but it really shouldn't be, considering how easy it would've been to implement.  The encyclopedia also could've used a bit of work. It's not fun scrolling through hundreds of items in a list to find the new entry without so much as an indicator to tell you which tab it's even in.
Still, the production quality was rather high in due respect. The dialogue was fully voiced, which was a welcome surprise. The sprites were also animated - blinking and mouth moving when talking - which isn't very common in a lot of VNs. That was another nice touch. There are also a few nice quality of life features, like select all when selling your junk. A few more wouldn't go amiss, though.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game. I mean, I played for more than 50 hours over the course of 5 days. I'm positive a large proportion of my enjoyment was due to my extreme fondness of Akiba, but I still believe you can enjoy the game without any background knowledge. You'll also enjoy your eventual trip to Akiba just that much more. In fact, if you plan to go to Akiba at all, collect and read all of the flyers in this game so you know what to do!
