Let’s start by unmasking the culprit that hides behind the name 'Nordic Legacy' say hi to Carl Olander...
Yes get your double headed snake emoji's ready. It's going to be one of those reviews. Strangely enough though, this thumbs down is more aimed at the developer himself than the actual game he created, I'll explain why later.
Zone 22 is about what life would be like if Hitler had won the war and is kind of broken up into three acts.
Act 1:  The intro scene forces us to watch a single father get separated from his daughter and transported to a concentration camp in Zone 22. You would think that maybe this daughter thing might be somewhat consequential down the track as surely he would miss her wouldn’t he? Wouldn't he be demanding to various soldiers about wanting to see her? Nope he just immediately forgets her and she is never brought into the game again. So why add her in the first place?
From here on it becomes somewhat a concentration camp simulator. A deleted part of the game which required us to drag dead bodies to a refuse pile was deleted by the developer simply because a Jim Sterling youtube video frowned upon it. But none of the bugs were fixed, no proper direction on what a player needed to do was added. In fact there is very little to do in the concentration camp at all. Let’s see...
You go to bed.
You wake up.
You see someone get shot.
You go get some apples to eat or give away.
You take a packet of cigarettes.
You walk over to a man who is talking about the women of the camp and how they are put in a different area also known as district B and asks you to take 15 guesses what B stands for when it comes to women.
Again you might think that a secret area where all the women are kept might become a pivotal issue down the track. Nope... serves to no purpose what so ever. So why bring it up in the first place?
Finally you get to dob someone in for stealing or you become his victim. That's it. That's the end of Act 1. Whole thing should take you 20 minutes maximum. While the concentration camp simulator is an edgy idea. It's rather limp wristed in its delivery. No real hard issues are raised or dealt with? Issues regarding 'Torture', 'Gas Chambers’, ‘Solitary Confinement', 'Segregation’, ‘Tyrannical Control' are never properly explored. So why put us in an area where we do pretty much nothing? The whole concentration camp idea seemed rather pointless and short.
Act2: Because we are a dibber dobber we get promoted to District A, here we are rewarded a small apartment and the ability to do constant manual labour for the Nazi’s in the form of arduous production so that we can get paid a pittance and slowly improve our living conditions. From here on the game becomes a production work simulator. I pity someone who does production work in real life only to log into Steam and do production work in a game. However amazingly it does a pretty good job portraying how cold it feels when you’re just a number, and you have to keep asking yourself why am I doing this.
However here we have our first BIG LIE from our developer. He claims that there are 8 work stations. There isn't, and on top of that only 2 of them work properly to the point where they are advantageous money wise for you. They are 'bullet control' and 'box filler'. To make matters worse levelling up is slow and at first you haven't a clue in the world what to actually level up. So this means that you have to eventually spend about 28 hrs doing production work to get anywhere in the game. I kid you not. The bulk of the game is production work. 2 Boring jobs constantly.
By now you’re thinking this is some type of psychological experiment. But wait it gets worse. The money you do get, you have to spend constantly on high priced things like an apple for 150 bucks. There are basically 'NO' novelty goodies to spend money for yourself other than a broken TV, some uninspiring pictures, a clock and a radio which is probably the best purchase of them all. If you could decorate your house more and even your work stations then maybe it would be more acceptable, but 28 literal fruiting hrs of production work...SERIOUSLY??? And i forgot the best part, the game doesn't allow you to do the same job twice. So if you only want to do the advantageous jobs, you have to keep exiting out of game completely and logging back in after every production day.
Act 3: By now your praying that someone rescues you from this life of hell, now we are introduced to the underground rebels. Again everything they want is extremely costly and requires you to do another several life times of production work. On top of that they are completely stupid and don't know how to do anything for themselves. So after you have spent a whole day on the production line, you have to go around and do everything they can't. This is probably the most fun part of the game. Going around breaking cameras, sabotaging ATM's, hacking search lights. Problem is that most of the quests are bugged or very poorly explained and some don't turn off at all.
Eventually at some point after all your hands are wrinkled because of production work and you’ve seen as many boxes as you can in one lifetime, then finally you can act on all your hard work tearing away at the regime by orchestrating 'The Event'. This is where all your comrades run out onto a field and do a big group hug in front of constant bullet fire and no one gets hurt. Yes the ending is completely bugged and doesn't work. The developer claims that this game has 17 different endings, but not even one of them works. He claims 36 different quests, the game can hardly ever tell you when you've done one of them correct or what you need to do.
So let’s look at what we have...
Act 1 Pointless and Short
Act 2 28 Hrs of long and pointless
Act 3 Group Hug let’s all be shot forever.

Easily one of my favorite games of all time. Absolutely an experience.
When it comes to gameplay, I can understand how this may not be for everyone. Specifically the pacing. That being said, I thought it was perfect. It gives you plenty of time to explore and soak in the environment. If you're used to running from explosion to explosion, fight to fight--this game isn't for you. This is a game for those who want to immersed in a story about an individuals tragic and horrific struggle.
The binaural sound really draws you into the game, especially if you have a good pair of headphones. I'm really happy Epic with UE4 is making this possible and I hope future developers/games follow suit. The soundtrack and scores are utilized wonderfully. The graphics (as you have probably already seen) are amazing and the animation really pulls it all together. All the motion capture for Senua's body and face really help bring her to life and will make you that much more engaged in her character.
The puzzles can be a little tricky at first glance but--as many have already mentioned--not too difficult. Same goes for the combat: it's not terribly complex or hard. You're really just chaining together a series of attacks or defenisive moves. It is however, quite cinematic which is fitting for a story-driven game. Thus, the battles are more rewarding for their excitement or intensity than their challenge. Albeit, more challenging enemies are introduced as you progress through the game. I had a few sighs of relief after a few of the more intense battles keeping me on my toes. Exciting but not frustrating.
Lastly, some people aren't too happy with the end of the game.
9/10, as no game is perfect. There are a few bits and pieces where you could argue the graphics or textures aren't up to par with the rest of the game. The voice acting is great, but falls a little short at a few minor parts. The game also has a few progression bugs that need to be fixed at the time of this review.
It's hard to name a game that really compares. If you love norse mythology, have an interest in mental illness, horror gaming, or just want story-driven experience then I cannot recommend this enough. Zero regrets paying full price.

Ok, so let me start by saying I have never reviewed a game before but at the end of hellblade I felt compelled to share my thoughts.
And wow, I mean WOW!!! This is trully something different. Before discussing the story and game aspects I will get the bad out of the way and tell you that this is not an MMO, this is not a strategy game... this is an experience. And one worth every penny, even if it is short.
So the bad:
1. The combat is relatively simple and not very difficult.
2. The puzzles can seem repetitive.
3. Nothing for character customization.
4. It took me an hour or two before actually getting into the game.
Now with that out of the way, this game is an epic experience which depicts the topic of psychosis very well. The story is well written and explores a different avenue of games for players. I trully believe everyone should give this game a try. The end game combined with the ability to move you emotionally once you become emmersed in the adventure is what makes this worth it.
So yes, I recommend this to people looking for an experience and something different from every other genre of game out there despite the gaming aspect being slightly lacking. I for one was incredibly moved at the end of the story... so much so that I felt I just had to review it and give it a thumbs up. If anything the fact that there is no triple A price makes it even more compelling.
In addition, the graphics and atmosphere is well developped. This adventure really is better is you have headphones rather than speakers.
In conclusion, I really did not enjoy this game at the start but it has a way of engaging you. So much so that the credits and the end song made it very difficult not to think about the entire story and what senua had been through... it just really sticks with you.
P.S. sorry for any bad grammar.

Nothing obvious comes to mind, because this game is not focused on doing one thing. It's a walking simulator mixed with a puzzle game, some psychological aspects and a bit of fighting.
You're a female Celtic warrior who travels into a viking version of hell to try and rescue the soul of your dead lover. Oh, and you have mental health issues, you keep hearing voices in your head telling you to do (or not do) certain things. So you run around, learning about your past, the world you lived in and what happened to you and the man you love.
This game is absolutely beautiful. Everything looks great, the locations, the lighting, the shadows and the main character. For a mid-budget game, this is a masterpiece.
Sometimes, however, mostly during zoom-ins (when I was trying to focus on some elements to solve a puzzle), it looked shattered, like the anti-aliasing suddenly stopped working. That looked bad. But I'm pretty sure it wasn't a bug that was missed in development. It was so obvious, it must've been there on purpose. But I can't understand why, it was just ugly.
The game also doesn't have any kind of UI, but that's actually working very well here. There's no map, no hints, no button prompts, no HP, no inventory or weapon stats. It's just you and the voices.
This is a one-of-a-kind experience, to see how mental illness affects a person's life. The voices you hear in your head, laughing at you, telling you that you're stupid or that you are unable to do something. If you play this at night with your headphones on, I bet you will turn around to make sure there's no one standing behind you. More than once. In one of the levels I got scared... by flies.
There's a not a lot of it, most of the time there's silence in the background with the voices you're hearing taking the lead. But when it's there, it's dark and psychodelic, does a great job of building the atmosphere. You can check out a sample on
.
It's a mix of a walking simulator and a puzzle game. The game is story driven and very linear, not a lot of places where you can make choices or go the wrong way. The puzzles are mostly based on elements in the environment that you have to align in a specific way to form a rune. There are some portals that can alter your perception of reality, allowing you to get to places that were inaccessible before. They aren't very complicated and get repetitive quite quickly.
Luckily, sometimes between the puzzles there's a fighting segment. It's also pretty simple - fast attack, heavy attack, block, roll and a special ability. But it was also a lot of fun for me, I enjoyed those fights and wished there were more of them.
It's a very unique experience, I haven't played anything like it.
The mental illness alone is enough to give this game a shot, and you might actually enjoy the other bits as well.
I know I did.
- the voices
- beautiful graphics
- enjoyable fights
- no UI (hints, map, HP, etc.)
- repetitive puzzles
- some pixelated graphics during zoom-ins
- threat of losing progress after too many deaths

There's nothing I love more in a game than a good story, and oh boy did Syberia deliver.
I don't often play point-and-click games like Syberia since I usually get bored pretty quickly due to the lack of action, but I got it in a Humble Bundle and decided it was worth a try.
This game has everything you want from an adventure game: Interesting, intriguing characters, an exceptional story worthy of a bestselling novel, beautiful landscapes with their own unique style which have stood the test of time considering the game was made in 2005, beautiful music although i would have liked more of it, (maybe have music specific for when you make progress in the story and then different background music in case Benoit Sokal ever sees this) and interesting, fun puzzles which require a certain amount of exploration and attention to detail in order to find and assemble the pieces.
The puzzles can at times seem tedious as there is a lot of running back and forth, but that didn't bother me the slightest and was definitely compensated by everything else in the game.
10/10 in my books, certainly one of the best story games I have ever played.

This is a game with interesting ideas that are boringly implemented, a boring story with boring characters and boring gameplay. It's boring. It's not terrible, but not great. I recommend it if it's on sale. ONLY if it's on sale.

Pros
-The story was nice and I, actually, didn't anticipate all of the twists and turns (like it usually happens with most of modern media)
- I was surprised to find that the remapped controls are universal (once you remap your movement and other controls - they work as intended in the game and all its menus. Unlike some AAA titles (yes, I am looking at you, Witcher!))
- The soundtrack is kinda nice (but the intentional sound glitches in music are annoying)
Cons
- glitchy camera (camera shakes or floats around even when standing still, different sensitivity in different areas, glitches if too close to character, resets to centered position after some time - annoying when trying to look around. The camera feels like you are moving it with a controller stick, rather than mouse. I would consider it bad for a PC game.)
- fixed camera positions (a lot of times the camera will be fixed to a set position, especially annoying if you are trying to look around for secret areas. This brings us to the next point)
- unintuitive controls (when camera is fixed a direction you want to go might not be the button you will press e.g. left can be up for example; other times the game is slow to recognize a button that you have been mashing for a few seconds now)
- poorly thought out combat (combos are nice but it's very hard to execute them in required time with many enemies around: you have to keep track of enemies around you, dodging pretty much every second, look at the combo gauge to monitor the combo progress and make sure that your character is actually doing the combo YOU want while also doing the correct combo sequence and still, the combo sequence will reset for no reason sometimes -_- )
- very linear levels (the game offers no freedom at all, you have to go through the specific narrow corridor that the devs set for you; there is little chance to explore, only preset surfaces are climbable and others are not, just 'cause)
- aiming is terrible (the game has a ranged weapon. It snaps to targets. You will need to use this weapon against enemies that will be right next to you. There will be more than one enemy next to you. The game will always choose the worst target for you ("thanks autoaim, yes, I wanted to shoot that guy on the other side of the room and not any of the ones currently tearing my face off" - every. single. time. seriously!))
- unskippable cutscenes (might not seem important but this game has a lot and if you are replaying a level, or just reloading a checkpoint - you will have to watch all the cutscenes again - and some of them are over a minute. You can't even alt-tab and do something else because the cutscenes will pause too!)
- the QTE-s (they are not hard but having them right at the end of a tough boss battle is highly annoying. I mean I have already fought the boss, I have overcome all his special attacks and waded through crowds of his minions but if you fail one press of a QTE - the game goes 'NOPE!' do some of that♥♥♥♥♥♥again)
Get this game only if it is on sale and you are really bored. Towards the end I actually used a trainer speed things up, get through the final 2 episodes and just be done with the game. The combat in the latter episodes is plain infuriating as the only thing the game does to make it more difficult is literally swarm you with enemies who just spam you with regular attacks.

Incredible art direction and great gameplay make this "Metroidvania" a very fun ride. The game is difficult, but forgiving. Platforming is very trial-and-error with new mechanics getting chained on top of what you already know. Failure usually means you're going to die, but the ability to save virtually anywhere keeps the game forgiving enough. The chase sequences especially put everything you know to the test.
Graphics and music are incredible. It's an artistic vision that all flows together perfectly.
One minor issue is that the controls tend to take some getting used to, especially if you use a keyboard. Especially after you get the Hold-Shift and Hold-W skills, you'll find yourself failing to activate them occasionally or the game just releases it.
Another minor issue is that for completionists, you cannot go back to the game once you've finished. If you're told "no coming back", then note that this is the last section of the game and you should go back and nab 100% of the goodies. Some people may not care, but those that do, it's a nuisance.
Overall, complaints are minor and the final product is great. Got about 10hr of enjoyment trying to grab everything. YMMB.

At game's end, I was left feeling rather conflicted about the entire experience.
Let's start with the story, which is convoluted in a lot of places.
It seems that the writers of
had quite a few ideas that they needed to get off their chest. Using the playground of the obviously insane world that Wolfenstein has built, they felt free to push boundaries in storylines that I don't think a lot of games would have tackled. The wealth of creativity here is a nice touch, but it seems that the story team felt compelled by specific images that they wanted to show case:
SPOILERS
These are all great images, and I'm all for poetic representation over top of gritty reality any day of the week, because a poetic representation often has more truth to it. The problem here is that these images seemingly are only half ideas. They give us a flash of an evocation, without really tying up what in the hell they were actually trying to say in the first place. These are all conflicting images in themselves, which is good when you're writing, but please give us inkling of the statement you're trying to make. This, on top of structural problems:
, no clear climax due to a mission that feels tacked on near the end, and no perception shift at story completion because the central dramatic question slides in and out from mission to mission. . .and there are some problems. I'm not going to get into the political nature of the story, as I'm looking at this from a more critical eye, but be aware that apparently some people are pretty upset over it.
The gameplay is good, with some polishing from TNO, but then there are some drawbacks as well. It seems that the health system feels a little wacky to me. The way it chips away is so random. Sometimes I feel like I can survive twenty waves of guys coming straight at my face, the next time I get shot in the foot and die. Also--the stealth is clunky as hell. Often, I can crouch walk in front of a dude and just get an unenthusiastic, "Huh?" Other times, I'll jump down on a cliff/high up ledge looking out over an impending gameplay area, then BJ must accidentally pass gas too loudly or something, and everyone in the whole damn place is aware of my presence. I could also just really suck at stealth. I don't know, I just know that it was frustrating, but at least I could run and gun whenever I wanted. You know--if my health held out.
Sound is pretty good if you have a headset, but I had to take it off cinema to hifi to hear directionally. Even then it was a bit of a bugger all if I would or not.
Graphics are perfect. ID Tech 6 is a dream, and this is one game I'm grateful to have a higher end PC for, as it is really, really beautiful. Not to mention that the animations are some of the best I've seen in a while.
That's really all I want to hit on. My conclusion? I'm a happy consumer. In certain ways, I had more fun playing this than I did TNO and vice versa. I recommend it, as the story actually takes some risks that reward sometimes, and falter others. Is it better than
? I don't know yet. Not that you'd ever come back to my review to find out, who the hell cares about my opinion,  I'm just entirely conflicted about this game. Do I recommend this for everyone? Not really. You gotta be in a kinda mood to dig it, and I don't even know what the hell that mood is. . .but if you wanna play a weird, pretty game where you get to shoot Nazis, cheers friends. This is for you.

Do not be fooled by the low price of the game. Hellblade is a top tier AAA game from start to finish, pioneering never before seen concepts, albeit with some serious flaws.
Buy it at full price and support them, it's well deserved.
The star highlights are the incredible production quality, animations, voice acting, and the storytelling through the eyes of a mentally ill protagonist.
The game explores some ideas ideas regarding puzzle solving I have never encountered before and though most are novel and interesting, the visual puzzles of lining up symbols against similar shapes found in the outside environment are sometimes overly ambiguous and difficult to solve
The biggest flaw in the game that nearly drove me mad was the combat mechanics. The major issue being that the camera is locked to one target at a time and you have no control over this. All movement is relative to the locked enemy and it is very difficult to quickly switch between multiple enemies surrounding you or get out of the way when you are surrounded. This is infuriating when you need to fight multiple enemies and combining this flawed mechanic with enemies that spawn in from behind you and strike at you immediately caused me to almost want to stop playing the game. Ninja theory, if you are reading this, please, don't continue to use this combat system in future. It is highly flawed.
On a more subjective note, I would also like to add that I am also not a fan of the permadeath mechanic introduced in this game. It adds an unnecessary level of stress when a mistake is made and my character dies. Games should be about learning from our mistakes and eventually overcoming them, without worrying about losing it all just because we had to repeat a section too many times. This especially so  with  some of the 'solve or die' type puzzles in the game as well as many aspects of combat and finiding enemy or boss weaknesses which are not explained to you...you need to listen or watch and find the answers yourself. This may take some experimentation. The last thing you need is the knowledge that you can only get things wrong a finite number of times, before you lose it all, hanging around your neck.
That aside though, you're looking at an amazing game. Contender for game of the year, and a proof of concept that will be discussed even years from now. Great job ninja theory and keep up the good work!

RWR is one of the best indie games i have EVER played. It's also a very mod friendly game, with anyone being able to anything they want with RWR. Well, it's obviously a military game at first glance. You play as three different military factions: The Greenbelts (America), The Graycollars (Germany), and the Brownpants (Russia). But instead of being like most other military shooters such as Call Of Duty of Battlefield, you are not a big action hero soldier sent to the front lines to kill everything that moves, you are a generic low lying foot soldier who is just as expendable and worthless as all your enemies and friends. Every time you die, depending on what faction you are part of, you spawn with a new name that is generated from the bank of first and last names corresponding to said faction. If you are mod savvy, you might know that you can edit this. Because you only take one to two hits to die when not wearing a vest, tactics are a must and can be very rewarding when you plan something out and carry it out correctly. Bases consist of 4 things. #1: The Armory; The armory is a place where you use your currency (RP/Resource Points) you earn throughout the game to purchase new weapons, gadgets, and equipment. You can also sell rare items and weapons scattered throughout the map that you find for some quick cash. You can also deliver enemy weapons to your armory to stock your armory with enemy stuff. This is useful is you want to have some enemy loot that you would otherwise have to go and get from the battle area. Also, some weapons have exp locks. These can't be used until you have a certain amount of exp. You can, however, take the weapons and store them in your backpack for later use.  #2: The Vehicles; the vehicles are an essential part of your advancement to the next objective and can be used as extra firepower against hordes of enemies. #3: The Enemy Objectives; When you capture a base you might notice a large radio tower in the middle of the base. These radio towers are enemy objectives and can be destroyed for quick cash a bit of exp. Specifically, radio towers also block radio calls. This prevents you from calling in reinforcements, armored support, artillery and so on. #4: The Stash; the stash is where you can store extra items to come back to later, but don't let the enemy recapture the base, or the enemy get hold of your powerful stuff! There is ranking system in the game, starting you out as private and ranking you up to higher ranks with more abilities. Higher ranks can use there money to call in artillery, extra troops, deployable cover, and so on. You can earn exp and rank up by killing enemies, as previously mentonied, destroying radio towers, doing side objectives and capturing bases. You might notice the general occasionally saying things like "capture that graycollars supply truck to the southwest!". Those are side objectives. Side objectives are things like capturing vehicles and delivering them to the armory for quick cash and exp. There is far too much to this game to talk about in one review, so here is my final verdict:
10/10!

I love this game! This game is suited for those who love the old style of gaming, with an interesting story line and combat system. You create the combos and evolve your power, how strong you become is up to your own hard work and experience. If you don't do what you can do you wont get far. If you take a relaxed stance on this game it is very easy to die over and over again, this game makes you think about the paths you take. I specially loved the combat style in this game. It has been a long time since I've last played anything with a fist style combat system, these days games rely on weaponry to fight in game monsters, this game relies heavily on martial arts and mind force like abilities. The memory steal features are an interesting addition to a completely unique game that hasn't been seen much since the Sega Mega Drive Era. Please note this review is not based on a play style that looks for the flaws or the techno jargen of a game, but rather for the simple fun of just enjoying a game.
These days people are so busy picking apart a games flaws and techno capabilities that they forget to simply play the game. I'm a gamer who loves a good story line in a game (its what made me fall in love with gaming in the first place), and this game takes me back to those roots.... I miss playing games like this. I miss simply being able to enjoy a game without the added pressure from other players and the way they play the games so competively. For those who don't have time for games that force you to play without really taking in the game, then this is for you. For those who prefer a game where the pressure is on you to get to the next goal and quickly, then this game is not for you. Remember Me, has a mixture of both fast pace and slow take your time pace. For those who care about what other people think, this game is not for you. If you love the old school simple way of gaming, then this IS a game for you. It adds a lot of old school elements and combines them with modern technology and graphics to give you an enriching experience. This game is the type of game we wish certain sequal games had, story line, activity and beautiful graphics.  In short, Remember Me is a very well balanced game.

Syberia
PROS:
+ good atmosphere
+ design and art are superb
+ beautiful music (even though there are like 6 tracks)
CONS:
- for today standards very slow paced, lot of empty walking around
- some areas are hard to notice (like doors or passages)
The game is a must for every adventure enthusiast. Short game that can be completed in 10 - 12 hours. Very atmospheric and will draw you in with its art and music. Story is simple and quite straightforward, but enough to keep you interested through out the game.
Puzzles are all simple and very logical (which could be minus for some players). The main problem for the game in the light of todays standards is A LOT of empty and slow walking. Overall playing this game is like reading a nice art book - it will suck you in and amaze you with its ideas if you give it some time.
On the end of the game you can ask yourself are you leading your life like an automaton or a person who wish to aspire, create and fulfill personal (childish) dreams? Will your time pass by and leave you corroded without will to sing like before? Whatever life you led, will it fulfill you on the end? I guess that philosophical point of the game is that even an automaton can change after all.

A early noughties point and click, Syberia offers almost exactly what you'd expect: a lot of busy pre-rendered backgrounds, puzzles that require the most non-linear of thinking and an incredibly front-loaded plot. But the story takes you to some unique and interesting places and the voice acting is surprisingly solid for almost every character. Definitely worth your time if you are a fan of the genre.

As someone who has played every single Assasin's Creed from start to finish, going back and playing this game was painful in terms of the mechanics, camera angles, repetitiveness.
The main story-line is still good although repeptitive, and I did enjoy the nostalgia seeing how the series got started in terms of the pieces of eden, abstergo, and desmond.
However you are assigned to assassinate a total of 9 people, and before you can kill one of them, you must complete at least 2-3 mini tasks.
There are only 3 different mini tasks in the entire game: Pickpocket a random citizen for info, talk to an informant and complete his task, and beat up a random preacher/well-know citizen to get info from them. You do this NINE times. You literally pickpocket, escort/run through city, and fist fight a citizen a total of 25-27 times, and then assasinate a target. (9 main kills, 2-3 mini tasks before each one).
Once again want to emphasize if you've never played the series, please get this and play it through, as you're starting one of the best and most successful game franchises of all time.
First time played: 9/10
Going back years later after playing the whole series: 7/10

Wolfenstein had a lot going for it after The New Order and indications pointed towards a direction that The New Colossus would add a very strong stylistic sensibility to the formula established in its predecessor.
Lets start with the negative, Wolfenstein II doesn't know if it wants to be a stealth game or a run and gun shooter like DOOM. The game plays with the vulnerability of BJ in interesting ways but even with this I find that it is way too easy to be taken down in some sections of the game. Some parts make you feel like you are untouchable as your dispatching Nazis but other portions you feel like a glass doll. And this would be fine if it made sense for those moments but it seems to be somewhat random. Parts of the game where it is clear your supposed to see BJ as weak are often very easy whereas portions that are obviously supposed to be these shooter sections with heavy weapons everywhere to lay waste to Nazis get you killed in mere seconds of approaching the turrets etc. Aside from that, when the stealth and shooting don't feel frustrating it is pretty competent. If the game was balanced better it would be greatly improved.
My second gripe is something I've never had a problem with in a game. The sound mixing is bad. And not just in the game, but the cut-scenes. Even when trying to adjust the volumes in the settings I could never get it to be okay. The music was often way to loud and would often drown out the dialogue, something that is extremely problematic in the scene with the preacher and BJ.
That said there are some spectacular highs in the wolfenstein, the issue is that most of them are not in the gameplay itself and towards the end I was just running past enemies to get to the objective marker because I was so done with the game portion. But those highs are good enough that I'll say its worth it. If you don't like pulpy stories however I wouldn't go for this game, while it does have a darker tone at times its sort of comic bookish which may turn some off.
The tone is all over the place and in some good ways, camera work in the cut-scenes is very well done. The game felt fairly short and the ending was a bit anticlimactic but the comedic over the top nature of some portions of the game make up for it. One specific section of gameplay was also very impactful.

Cons:
Super super laggy. Game appears to be Peer-To-Peer so I don't expect that to change ever. The whole game stops when someone lags.
Joystick Controls are sloppy for a brawler. There is no tolerance for the inaccuracies innate to support game pads. This means your character may snap to another direction you don't push in. It also makes it incredibly difficult to pull off moves requiring you to hold your joystick any direction but forward.
Matchmaking is very slow especially for a launch day game. Took 5 minutes to get into my first match. On average took well over a minute with many people "dodging" the match.

2017 would seem to be shaping up to be the year of platform fighters (or brawlers or ssb-fighters or PFs here on I'll use PF for platform fighter). Brawhalla, Rivals of Aether and now Brawlout. (Potentially during 2017 we will also get first reveal of the Wavedash teams game) These games have all a lot in common. They are very stylised. Both RoA and Brawlout feature non-humanoids only. Most importantly all of these games are draining inspiration from the one and only king of games like these: the super smash brothers series by Nintendo. Last year was pretty damn crazy for Smash. Melee kept on steady growth pace from the earlier years. Smash 4 had phenomenal growth both in tournament size, participants and technical level.
What does any of this have to do with anything? Well to say whether you should or shouldn't buy Brawlout (and whether it is good or not for that matter) entirely depends on what are you looking for in the game.
I'm going to be writing from my personal perspective. From the perspective of a person who is looking for an alternative, better than alternative, for Smash 4. What I want is a game that doesn't just reach the level of Melee and Smash 4 but bridges the gaps between the two games.
For melee: makes a rooster where actually all the characters will be viable even after 10 years, is modern, isn't stuck up about what people use to play the game and has a developer that supports both the esports, modding/art and casual scene. For Smash 4: make the game a little bit faster, make the movement/tech skill little bit more complex, add offline tournament mode, offline comp mode..
You get the idea.
Is Brawlout that? No. And it probably isn't trying to be. To talk about the game generally it doesn't have any fundamentally "wrong" qualities. The art style is very pleasing, characters are unique aesthetically and play style wise, the game has decent level of polish.
However, the game play just isn't what I'm looking for (albeit it decent fun)
- Brawlout makes quite an interesting choice basic mechanic wise: It has removed both grab/throw and shield functionality from the game. The main interactions of the game consist of attacks, special attacks and dodging (and some kind of rage meter that affects moves and apparently has combo break esque functionality but since I wasn't in the beta I don't know how it works.) This isn't necessarily a bad thing but I certainly dislike it.
- Other option wise things that seem to be different: there seems to be no dash dancing, wavedashing, ledge options, wall jumps, no weak/tilt moves, no crouching and no techs.
These are all in themselves sort of negative things but not deal breakers. What evidently is the biggest issue for me is just the feeling.
In smash when you float in the air, when you perform ground movement (foxtrot, dash dance, PPs, wavedash..), when you  get hit by those Sheik forward tilts, when you hot someone with Bowser forward smash.. there is constantly that tangible feeling of weight. The characters feel like physical objects with mass and the attacks feel like powerful moves with strength to send the characters across the map. It is hard to put in words but Brawlout just lacks this. There is definitely aesthetic element to this but also a feel one.
Aesthetically the attack, hit and knock back effects and the animation don't really sell it.
Feeling wise it is probably combination of many things (attack animations, hitstun, knock back) but the game just doesn't have weight.
This is emphasised by very confusing situations. Sephira's (purple cat) kick that looks very similar to Sheik's forward tilt in Smash 4 can KO from the edge of arena. You'll look at the kick hit you and think "I should probably DI this down to avoid follow up" and the you'll explode on the blast zone. In other hand charged Olaf up smash barely kills from center stage until closer to 200%. Olaf down smash (which looks lighter and like it would spike) in other hand can relatively easily KO from the top by shooting them up vertically (in an almost straight line) (A lot of attacks look deceptive and have really weird launch angles. This is made worse by not having clear visual indicators of how heavy you were hit and how much knockback you received)
A lot of the visual cues just seem weird.
I'm probably going to get shredded by someone from the beta who is going to point out that all the technical mistakes/misunderstandings I have.
This is, however, the impression I got from 2 hours of ranked and quick play. Whether I'm qualified to say this is arguable. I used to play a lot of SF, Blazblue and Melee before fighting games started to get releases in steam. I have probably around 200-300 hours played in Smash 4.
Anyhow my final verdict would be:
- Brawlout has lot of potential to be a fun, polished platform fighter (both online and local play wise)
- The developers got a lot right (pretty stages, interesting characters, most of the basic things like UI, modes etc, the game recognised gamecube pad)
Should you buy Brawlout?
- If you want to support platform fighter genre, smaller developers: yes.
- If you want to buy a platform fighting game that isn't weapon based or pixel art: yes.
- If you want an alternative for Smash 4 and Melee while you wait for Melee HD and emulator that can run Smash 4? Then probably not.
It'll be interesting to see where Brawlout goes from here. There is a lot of improvements they can make in many different aspects. I hope that Mobgames will prove me wrong and make Brawlout the next big Platform Fighter. But for now I'm bit a bit sceptic about the chances of that happening.

After hearing so much good things about Syberia and being in a mood a for a good adventure point and click game I decided to give Syberia a try. What a disappointment it is and a big one at that.
You play as Kate Walker, a lawyer. You travel to a little town in Europe to the mission of completing a deal to buy a Toy Factory which actually makes automatons, which seem like robots but a little different as the game explains it, or tries because it doesn’t really explain it. Here we can begin pointing out one of the first of the many problems of the game, nothing is explained to you.
The developers create a setting that is different from the usual, so if anything they should try to immerse you in it. One good way to do it would be to explain to you how some of these particular things are, how they work or pretty much anything interesting about it but no, better to be left in the dark, I guess.
The story itself is boring and bland. Without spoiling anything while trying to settle the deal for the purchase of this factory you learn about some of the history of some characters. Bare in mind that those characters are either dead or you have not yet met them. To give the game a little credit, this is by far the best part of the game, the backstory of what happened years ago. Of course the game wouldn’t present it to you in a interesting manner, that would be asking too much, instead you are presented with a book to read. About 10 pages or more. It’s not that bad but as it is the best part of the game and the only thing that gives context to many of the stuff that you see and some puzzles one would thing they would do a better job at presenting it.
With a boring scenario and story that leaves us to the characters and I’m sorry to say, they’re also just as bad. First, your main character, Kate Walker. She is alright at best. You don’t get much room to see her being relatable but at least she’s not annoying not anything. There are however some things that could make her seems better as everynow and then you get a cellphone during the game as people in your life want to talk to you, be it your boss, boyfriend, friend or mother. The problem here is that when talking to pretty much any of these people, when you think it would help to create Kate’s character, it does, but in an opposite way one would hope. Everyone gets the last word with her, it almost makes you feel sorry for her being kind of stupid and helpless and aside from her friend, every person that calls her seem boring.
There are also the characters you meet which believe or not are even worse. One of the first characters you have to interact with is a retar... mentally disabled kid which tags along with you for while and you can guess how much depth he has… zero. This only goes on and on with every character which are boring to the extreme with the sole exception being the robot/automatron Oscar. He seems to be the only interesting and creative character of the game and lo and behold, the only interesting character in a point and click adventure game is a robot. Not your character, not anyone you meet but a robot.

What music? It seems the game does have some music but it barely plays. Most of the time you are walking around in a complete silence with only the marvelous sound of your footsteps. Occasionally some music does play and it is beautiful but it’s so rare you barely forget there is any music for about 90% of the time you’re playing.

The environments do have a nice mood to it. They look nice, of course, understanding this game is some years old but despite of that, the game does look nice. What its’t nice, however, is that every item, door, or pretty much anything you have to interact seem to be hidden behind some huge amount  of crap in the front of it or some horrible camera angles that obscures anything worth noting. I do appreciate when developers take the care to not make items stand out so much they are almost shinning in contrast to the background but here they made sure to make it virtually invisible. Most items you can only probably notice when mousing over them, otherwise you would probably miss them entirely.
With all that out of the way, it leaves us to gameplay and partially continuing what I was saying about the graphics, when you can’t see anything in a point and click game, you can imagine how the gameplay is gonna be like. This is the killer for me. Everything is a pixel hunt and that only helps to make the gameplay slow.
Talking about slow, how about mentioning the movement speed our main characters walks? Let me just say, it’s so slow you can probably do something else while she walks from screen to screen and to add to it, there are a ton of screen to walk around with barely anything worthwhile to do, look, or experience. It seems like it’s padding to make the game seem longer than it actually should be.
In fact, it seems like every action Kate does is in slow motion, like climbing a set of stairs, for example. Depending of the stairs they seem to take about 5 to 15 seconds just so she can climb it and another 15 seconds to climb back down. Did I mention there’s a ton of backtracking in this game. Well, then get ready to have fun walking super slow back and forth and waiting for the slowest of the animations to get anywhere.
Only thing left to mention is the puzzles and by god, they are among the worst I’ve seen. Most of them feel like they are completely random, especially when you are giving pretty much zero indication about how to proceed. Recently I’ve heard of the term
and I think it is the perfect way to express my perception of the puzzles in Syberia. They have no logic one could think of unless they lived in the moon or maybe the crazy world from Alice in Wonderland.

I’ve played games that take a while to begin, many adventure games and visual novels suffer from that, the problem with Syberia is that it never gets anywhere. I love puzzle games when they have some thought put into them. Sometimes, you play a game in this genre but one of its aspects leaves something to be desired, a game may have some weird puzzles but a good story, bad story but with good characters, weird characters but nice music, etc. The problem with Syberia is that for me it did everything wrong.

TL;DR: this game uses Comic Sans MS for the subtitles but apart from that it is a great game.
Syberia was one of the highly-praised games I often heard about as I was playing Myst as a teenager. 10 years later, I eventually bought it and can confirm it deserves its reputation.
Thanks to the good writing and remarkable art direction, each of the four locations you visit (a village in the French Alps, an university with a train station in a giant aviary, a former Russian mine town/cosmodrome and a forgotten spa where Soviet elites use to stay) is filled with an unique ambiance, colorful characters and creative inventions (the automate/spring technologies reminded me of the kind of things an imaginative kid would come up with). The soundtrack also deserves praises, it complements well the settings and help create an ambiance. For the time I spent on this game, I forgot everything about my (boring) adult life and joyfully went on an adventure with Kate Walker.
On the downside, Syberia is pretty short (it took me 6 hours to finish it) and has close to no replay value as most enigmas are straightforward and none of them is randomly generated. Because of that, it is worth waiting for this game to be on sales and/or buy it as part of the Syberia bundles. Also it uses Comic Sans MS as main font but I could survive; this misstep was probably done to balance the eye-candy sceneries.
I hope that at some point in the future they will do a true remake of Syberia with true 4K resolution and additional enigmas.

Funny story on how this game came to me. For my brothers birthday a few years ago I was in JB Hi-Fi looking for something to get him. I saw this game, thought he would enjoy it and bought it. On his Birthday I gave it to him and to say the least, he seemed pretty intrigued. I think at the time It wasn't particularly new (or at least not really heard of) so the both of us were a little curious. He played the game, finished it and then said that he liked it but thought combat was a little boring. So I asked if I could give it a go, and he let me. Nek minnut I was up all night playing the game on his computer. Of course, I couldn't keep playing it on his computer because he wanted to use it. And since he activated it on his steam I couldn't play it on my computer (at the time I don't think sharing was enabled) so I left the game mostly unfinished. Until now! Now, the game is one of my favourites of all time, I think it's diverse, unique and refreshing to play for someone casual like me. The Game utilises Parkour in which our heroine uses to get around Paris. She has a very special ability that enables you to do very special things such as

This is not a good game.
Ok gameplay first. It's tedious. The combat bits are fun but absolutely repetitive. You have these x,y combos that you can customize with different elements (when you hit, you will either heal yourself, do extra damage, or reduce the cooldown between your extra powers - you choose which of these forms each hit will take). Then you have your extra powers, like rapid hitting or getting a robot to fight for you for 10 or 20 seconds. All of this is fun but very quickly becomes rinse and repeat. The powers are mostly situation-specific, not really encouraging any kind of creative or improvisatory use. And it's
(I played on normal mode). When you've got combos that will heal you, there's almost never any point in the game where you can't quickly get back what health you may have lost.
There is a boss fight at the end of every level. These all have brief QTEs at the end, which don't bother me. What does bother me is when the fights frequently require you to use one of your special powers to accomplish something which they never accomplished before. The game doesn't make an effort to let you know beforehand that it's even possible to do such things with your powers. An example is your fight against Madame, a prison warden. Late in the fight she creates copies of herself, and you can go around trying to hit them one at a time but after three tries your chance is over and she becomes invulnerable for a bit until she creates more copies and you do the same thing over again. You can use one of your powers to reveal which copy is the real her, but you won't know this until you’ve been going through the cycle for a minute or two and a tooltip finally pops up telling you what to do. This kind of thing happens in at least half of the boss fights.
Again, most of the general combat is fun. It's just nothing to write home about.
When you're not in combat, you're just running through corridor after corridor going wherever the little orange arrows are telling you. There are a few spaces that appear wide open, but are just linear paths in disguise - you can only travel through these areas on one path, limited by whatever scenery is in the way. I'm personally fine with linearity, but there are times when what you can do and what you can't, in regards to level traversal, is inconsistent. Some rail guards you can leap over, when the game needs you to get to whatever is below. But some rails (of equal height) you can't, even if what's below is theoretically walkable space.
There are environmental puzzles (the likes of "rotate a crane!"), but there's almost never any margin for error. Everything you have to do is laid out in front of you, you just have to go through the motions. Rarely will you feel inventive or satisfied. Combine the lacking puzzles with the inconsistent traversal and fidgety platforming and you've got levels that are just joyless to move through.
The brief moments where the game shines are found in the memory altering mechanic. You have a special skill that allows you to hack people's key memories in order to change how they behave in the present day. A scene will play out, and when you reach the end the game tells you what you are trying to accomplish (example: make x kill y). From there, you rewind and fast forward through the memory looking for "memory glitches", little details that you can change to alter the events. Not all of these are necessary, so you have to find the right combination of glitches to change, but even the wrong choices will still alter the scene, so you can see how it may play out in various ways before rewinding and trying again. This is super fun and satisfying and interesting, and it's a real shame these sequences don't come more often throughout the game, though I imagine they took a lot of work to script and animate. And sadly, the narrative potential of this aspect of the game is never fully realized. More on that below.
You are Nilin, a woman waking up in a prison, with no memory of your past. All you've got to guide you is a guy who calls himself "Edge", on the other end of a radio. His voice is your constant companion throughout the game. He tells you that you're an Errorist, a group dedicated to the eradication of Sensen, a technology that converts memories into transferable, deletable data, something every Neo-Paris citizen has taken part in. He helps you out of prison and you get to blindly follow his every order from then on, despite constant doubt over the morality of what you're doing.
It's in this awful relationship that a huge disconnect erupts between the player and the protagonist. First off, he's just downright annoying. Everything he says is incredibly over-zealous, a very "WE WILL BATHE THEM IN OUR RIGHTEOUS FIRE" vibe. He consistently withholds valuable information from Nilin to get her to achieve his (terrible) goals for him.
(Early-game spoiler in this paragraph) Second, early in the game Edge has Nilin commit an act of terrorism. No joke, by flooding a whole district of the city, Nilin engages in
that Edge deems deserving of death because they were living comfortable lives while other people were suffering.
. Yet, despite this, Nilin eventually goes on to be buddy-buddy with Edge, thanking him for his help in… being a terrible person, I guess. But even more concerning is Nilin's direct reaction to what she just did. "I don't know what I'm doing. Was what I did right? Should I trust Edge?" No, you ♥♥♥♥ing moron, what you did was one of the worst things a human being can do, and there was no justification for it, and no, you should not trust the guy who coerced you into doing it. The pathetic wallowing of Nilin's inner mind makes her completely unrelatable to the player at this point.
The other major failing of the story is that it never really explores or even talks about the morality of Nilin’s memory altering. It condemns the memory technology as a whole, but Nilin’s actions in particular are never questioned, even though she is making use of the same technology that brought about this dystopia. The conflict does not go to places nearly as interesting or dramatic as it should when you're going around changing people’s realities in order to get them to fight for you.
(More minor spoilers in the next two paragraphs) Here’s an example of this wasted potential. Very early in the game, a bounty hunter named Olga comes after you and attempts to kill you. Before she can do that, however, you seize the opportunity to hack into her memories and alter her reality. You make her think her husband (who is very much alive in reality) was killed in a way that ignites resentment toward the powers that be. As a result, she immediately joins your cause instead of killing you.
She then helps you out by flying you in her hover craft to a certain location, where you ask her if she will join you on your current mission. She says she can’t, because she has family business to attend to. I assumed this meant she has to take care of arrangements for her husband, and when she finds out he isn’t actually dead, she’ll realize that Nilin altered her memory and Nilin will have to deal with those long-term consequences of memory altering. Logistical is a game that's basically like Euro Truck Sim 2, but without the driving, and instead you can actually finish towns by supplying them everything they want. You buy trucks or tuktuks, load them with goods, and send them around the map. At first it's simple - get apples from an apple grove, bring them to a town that wants apples. Then it's mildly complex - to get magazines, the factory needs paper and paint. And to get paint, its supplier needs oil to make the paint -
You see where this is going. It's essentially a giant puzzle consisting of supply chains. If you're not careful, your entire fleet of trucks will sit around in various towns idling, waiting for you to fill in the missing item that gets production running again.
Now, you're either intrigued or bored by the concept. If you're bored, stop! Turn back! This game is entirely about solving these puzzles and getting everything where it needs to go. If you're intrigued, but put off by the graphics or UI...please try it. All you need to get going is the base game - that has some massive maps in it along with tutorial island, so you'll be busy for a long time before you need the DLC.
In short, it's one of those games where you look at it and wonder why on earth you want it, then you try it, and it's incredibly satisfying. I highly recommend it!
... I also recommend turning off the sound effects, because oh boy they are bad. Bring your own music or podcast, and you'll be set.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This is gonna be a really rambly review, due to me jotting things down for it as I play. I didn't buy into any of the "hype", never cared about "lies", and was just looking for a basic exploration game. I bought after the 1.3 update, so have no experience of the game beforehand.
Overall, I'd say the game is fun, the exploration is neat, but not spectacular, it's a very pretty game, and it's good to relax in, the core gameplay is great, flying around, scanning things, etc, and if it was just that, i'd give this a thumbs up. However, it isn't, and this is the bad stuff.
It's so, god, damn, buggy. Seriously, I play a lot of early access games, and this has more bugs than most Alphas I've played, hell, even more than some pre alphas. The worst part is, most of the bugs I've seen are game breaking, such as getting stuck in infinite warp, all NPCs having the same one line of quest related dialogue (meaning you cant talk to any NPC), quests breaking if you move your base, the "Atlas Path" questline plain not working at all, stuff like that. There are other minor things, like being forced under the landscape every single time I try to teleport to my base, but I'll save the words, or this will be too long.
On top of the bugs, there are just really weird design decisions, like having to HOLD DOWN left click to do anything, even browse the main menu and settings (What???), and loads of seemingly half implemented features, such as a terrain manipulator that only lets you dig and fills holes (with no decent terrain manipulation features at all), or quests giving you the same 3 technologies over and over, meaning you essentially get no reward as you already have damage upgrade sigma, 100 times.
The game is also missing a lot of features, but the biggest ones are mainly customisation, of which there is none. Yes there are loads of randomly generated ships and guns, but what if the best one has an ugly colour (im looking at you, yellow), welp, you're out of luck, you're stuck until RNJesus gives you one in the colour you like, cos you can't even change colours.
Exocraft suck. Plain and simple, they are all completely useless.
Base building could be a saving grace for this game, but like everything else, suffers from weird design choices. First off, you can't build anywhere, find a cool mountain you wanna settle on? Or an island in an ocean? Tough, you have to settle in one of the pre chosen zones. The starting building can't be changed, moved, deleted, editted, or anything, You're stuck with it, smack bang in the middle of the (already small) build zone, which limits a lot of base designs, you could build around it, but base building is ridiculously frustrating and poorly implemented, things are there, but it just doesn't work properly. I snapped a 3x3 grid of cubes together for a room, they snapped, not placed, snapped, ie, they are all in line, however they are all seemingly randomly placed, as each cube is in a different position than the last, making the floors and walls not smooth, and all misplaced, with different sections raised or moved, so much for a nice looking interior. On top of that, base building is so grindy, even more so than the rest of the game, the bases use rare materials, which is fine, but it needs a  LOT of them. You want a glass corridoor? Have fun grinding on an ice planet for at least an hour trying to find enough frost crystals to make ONE of the DOZENS of corridoor pieces you need. Also, you want to put a landing pad as the main feature of the base? Congrats, its super expensive and the last thing you get, meaning you either have to build your base last, or have to redo it at the end, as you cant build around it due to utterly abyssmal snapping.
Overall, if this was a pre-alpha early access game for $15, id say yeah, go for it, but the devs are marketting this as a full release AAA title, which is absolutely laughable. Even if all the bugs, glitches, and weird features were fixed, this wouldn't be anything more than a cheap indie game to ♥♥♥♥ around in, so their marketting is just attrocious. Maybe in a few years this'll be something good, and I know it will, when it works it's fun, but god, at the moment, just stay away.

This is the second time, i am writing a review for this.
The first one was negative as well.
However, despite the annoyances, bugs and bad performance i kept coming back to the game. And after racking a bit of playtime, i felt like leaving a negative review on a game, that i played quite a lot is unfair. So i went ahead and and delted that initial negative review.
Now i have seen most of what the game has to offer.
Built bases, upgraded through different ships. This part was kinda enjoyable - some sense of progression plus a bit of room for creative freeplay.
Learned alien languages. Completed the games storylines. This was a huge downer. It takes a lot of good will, to even call  them story.
And, sadly, i am once again writing a negative review.
The whole thing i pretty much a tech demo. An impressive one, since the demoed tech - the procedural generation - really does work pretty well.
But a tech demo, as good as it might be, doesn't make for a good game.
Pros:
* Procedural generation. There is unaviodable a lot of repetition. Still, there are also many unique, interesting and funny things to see.
* Sense of scale. Huge galaxies, huge planets, huge spaceships. I particulary liked the - once again procedurally generated, kinda - freighter fleets.
Lots of quite impressive stuff.
* Devs are active. There are patches. A couple of the issues were literally fixed while i was playing the game.
Cons:
* Immersion. There is none.
The procedural stuff, while quite interesting and even impressive in places, still feels completely generic overall. The NPC are static, generic, faceless blobs. Despite some of the species being actually kinda neatly designed visually.
They might look different, but they are all just the same zombified providers of meaningless speach-bubbles.
* Story. Literally a badly crafted excuse, for why everything is so generic and there is "not supposed to be any immersion".
Can't deny, there is some dev-ingenuity in this: they are telling us, the games biggest short comming is actually by design.
But it's still no fun.
* Grind. Sure, it's a sandboxy game, it is expected to be grindy, to limit progression hereandthere.
But this one is literally designed to waste time. Prime example - you don't click a button, instead you have to hold a button for a bit (half a second or something), to make it activate.
* I didn't really like the overall visual theme. Oversaturated, outlandish colors. Stuff literally glowing with color and light.
This is mostly a question of taste. However, in some instances it acutally interferes with gameplay. Trying to follow a bright blue trading route line, while the whole space is glowing in bright color - pretty much impossible.
* Bugs. Lots of them. Most are just glitches: a floating tree here a hole in the ground there. Most are harmless, some rare ones might cause you to get stuck and have to reload the last save.
But there are also a couple of really huge ones, mostly connected with the quest lines and potentially bloking progression.
* Performance is terrible. I have a pretty good gaming PC. "Only" an i5, but rather high end as these go. Nvidia 1080. I still had to lower/turn off many of the settings and the FPS still deeps below 20 quite a lot.
* Combat sucks. It's not the focus of the game, i get that, but it's there and it's plain annoying, partly because of the performance thingy - unsteady low frame rates make hitting moving targets a bit of a pain.
* PC controls are badly ported from console, customisation options lacking. Most things aren't too bad, but the overall feel is clunky and slow, requiring lots of clicks, to acomplish simple tasks. Interface management in particular is rather slow and convoluted in places.
* Price. I paid about 25 Euros for this on discount, and looking at my playtime, i'm OK with this.
But the normal price is just ridiculous.

The two main characters were enjoyable enough, but I kept waiting for puzzles or choices or some elements of gameplay and there weren't any. Maybe the story resonated strongly with other people, but I would have rather watched this as a short film than point and click for an hour to get to the story wrap-up. The music was also very generic keyboard-y piano music throughout, never really tied to a particular scene or emotion, and overall didn't live up to the hype.

I really enjoyed my time with Caster.  This is a 3d combat platformer.  Most importantly the game is just fun.
This is a good example of a game that excels without having top end artwork.  The art is decent, and they really like using particle effects.  But, the textures and models are dirt simple.

Play follows through a number of stages.  After each stage, the amount of energy balls you pick up allows you to purchase upgrades for your character, thereby allowing you to specialize your strengths to fit your playstyle.

So as an avid Smash Bros fan in my younger days. It's easy to welcome an inspired version come to the PC with open arms. When I first saw Brawlout I was instantly attracted to it's aesthetic. Its not visually overwhelming and it does a fantastic job of keeping you engaged without many distractions whilst you are fighting. The game runs smooth as silk with more than 200+ FPS for me which you can limit in your options menu and pretty much adjust it accordingly.
The fighting is exactly how you would expect from a game like this. Pretty fast-paced, with a variant of move sets and combinations you can pull off. The game focuses it's attention purely on the fighting, there is no items to grab as of yet that I'm aware of. When it comes to the multiplayer you can private host, Join a quickplay match, or even test your skills in ranked mode. But it's only stable at the moment in a 1v1 scenario which is honestly disappointing. You can also choose from 6 characters and 5 Stages to Brawl with and more expected come launch.
Overall right now I think the game has a ton of potential but the lag issues and the lack of modes such as 2v2 only being in the private lobby concerns me. Being beta I hope these fixes are in the works ASAP. I would keep an eye on Brawlout if you're a fan of these style of games.

The opening cutscene was eerie enough to describe my experience playing.
Syberia is a classic detective story, and one that has our character shrouded in mystery upon our arrival to the hotel. We are introduced by a notable cast that includes the dead all along character (the early reveal of Anna Vozerberg’s funeral), the mouthy kid (Momo) who is referred to as the ‘village idiot’, and the hotel manager. The hero/heroine in which we are playing as is, if not obvious enough, will be the great detective of the case. Apart from this main set of characters, many of the other NPCs you come across will mainly be fillers.
Voice acting was a nice addition to the game, especially for Miss Walker. It gives us a better feel for our characters persona, and enhances the interactive nature to this game.
The art is absolutely stunning. A great amount of detail and texture was added to the rooms, objects and overall settings and it was rich in the steampunk genre. Anyone who enjoyed the design of similar games like Amnesia, or Alice: Madness Returns will agree on that. This includes the smooth effects in the atmosphere, such as smoke, breeze and other animations that occur during the cut scenes or when you interact with an object.
The BGM and sound effects were also well done. It may not be memorable, but they fitted where it was appropriate. Different areas of Syberia would trigger a new audio, from the Hotel of to the graveyard you’ll uncover later. Though this is not a highlight of the game, the story itself added with the alluring atmosphere makes this game a great Interactive adventure game. It is not a short game either.
Syberia is a game that I do recommend trying!
A true classic adventure game, I recommend it highly.

Remember Me is an entertaining game with an interesting concept that was unfortunately not executed to it's fullest potential. Players take control of Nilin, a memory hunter with the ability to "remix" people's memories. She herself has had her memories erased, and is working with a mysterious man named Edge and the "Errorist" cause to take down Memorize, the company that has commercialized memories and is slowly corrupting the population.
Playing as a character who's memories have been wiped puts the player in an interesting place where they know as much as the character knows. This concept is good for story development, however it also tends to be the game's own undoing. The game does a poor job of making the player ask questions about who and what Nilin is, so when the game makes reveals about the story they feel almost unimportant and unneccesary.
The concept of remixing memories is interesting, however if felt almost tacked onto the game in most scenarios. I would have liked to see more applications for this concept, but unfortunately it only comes about four or five times in the game's rather short 8 to 9 hour campaign.
The game's combat and other mechanics are fun, but they seem familiar save for the concept of building your own combos. However, I didn't find myself using that concept as much as I think the player was intended to use them; typically i only needed two or three of the five available combos to get through combat instances. These instances were very fast-paced, however, and were fun to play through, if they were just a tad on the easy side.
Remember Me's soundtrack was probably one of my favorite parts of the game, and really served as one of the best atmospheric elements of this game.
All in all, Remember Me is definitely a fun game that can be played in a weekend. It's not one that you'll be missing out on if you skip it, but it's definitely worth picking up if you see it on sale.

Good story, good setting, bad combat system. I honestly got a trainer just to skip over the combat, to see the end. That said, I also didn't like the Arkham series combat, so it might not be that bad. But if your willing to put up with annoying combat, like the combat style, or are willing to get a trainer, Remember Me is good fun.

Setting/Visuals
The game had me at cyberpunk. I am a huge fan of the genre and an even bigger fan of fully-realized world building (Fallout 3, Deus Ex etc.). So imagine my surprise when I hear of a new setting, a Neo-Paris, to explore. Each character feels unique no matter their screen time and Nilin has some cornball dialogue but overall feels like a solid character and is torn between being a rebellious memory hunter and the conflict in the story ("This red-riding-hood has a basket full of kickass!" per example of bad writing).The textures and visuals are beautiful and the neon is well-balanced with the trashy dim lighting for a cyberpunk vision. Seriously, when you first start each level take a minute to just swing the camera around and view everything. It's all designed with love and the little touches make everything truly come alive. Consider the mass produced Valet androids that are running around holding grocery bags, walking dogs, playing piano. It's amazing and I will definitely "remember" that ;)
Gameplay
It's an old school beat-em-up with some HD visual packaging. Your only incentive to unlock and experiment with new combos in the branching combo system is achievements and dispatching enemies quicker but once you find 2-3 combos that work you won't deviate from them; it's just too taxing to keep opening the menu to try new things. There are a decent amount of enemy types and some engagements are multiple types at a time which keeps things fresh. Platforming is light and engaging but tends to drag on. However, it only seems that way in hindsight perhaps because the environment and atmospheric splendor is so engaging.
