Greatest single player soccer game ever.

PROs:
+ Graphics. The ankle tape and forehead sweat look better than ever.
CONs:
- Gameplay. Look, PES is lightyears ahead of FIFA in terms of gameplay and the control you _do_ get. But what PES gets right is overshadowed by what it gets wrong: trying to be FIFA. Like a pathetic little brother tagging along, PES tries (and fails spectacularly) to emulate its bigger, brighter competition, instead of honing the unique qualities that make it special.
FIFA is the broadcast experience. If you're looking for the gee-whiz factor of a computer simulation that LOOKS REAL, get FIFA. But looks is all you'll be getting, because as a game, it's a joke.
If you're looking for a simulation of actually playing football... well, sonny, you're SOL. There is no such thing. PES could be it, but instead, it feels more like playing a dice-rolling game, but with soccer instead of orcs and elves.
The "player nearest the ball" button doesn't actually mean PLAYER NEAREST BALL.. instead the game has some sophisticated algorithm to determine which player you get. Semi-auto player switch claims it won't switch you on defense, but this is a lie. It WILL switch you, when it decides you need help.
If you are of the sub-80 IQ crowd, all of this is probably immensly helpful. Otherwise, it's one of the most exquisitely frustrating experiences you will ever have gaming. There is no way to configure the game that is fun. Hell, there's no way to configure the game that is COHERENT.
What makes PES so disappointing is how much potential it has. If it were just a crap game (like FIFA), it would be easy to discard as another few dollars wasted and a lesson learned. But it's the tantalizing flashes of brilliance, the minute control over dribbling, say, that wake me up in the middle of the night, drenched in cold sweat, dreaming of what could be...
IF ONLY PASS ASSISTANCE WOULD JUST F***ING DIE ALREADY!
TLDR: If you play with pass assistance, you are worse than Hitler, Stalin, Milosevic, Pol Pot, Suharto, Pinochet and Trump put together.
That's it. If you want to pay $60-70 more dollars for cut scenes, get this game. Otherwise, it is exactly like previous generations. One of the most disappointing purchases ever. There just aren't any good football games.

Overview: 9.8
This game left a huge impression on me in a world full to the brim with video games. That might be in part because this is less of a game in the normal sense and more of an emotional journey through an incredible story with excellent characters, powerful and emotional music, and scenes that both wrench and warm your heart in equal measure. It is a tale that stays with you long after you've finished it.
Breakdown
Bad points
To the Moon is a point & click game, and occasionally you are left simply clicking away at everything in sight just to progress instead of focusing on what's going on in the story. Because you also move by pointing and clicking, moving around the game screens is a little laborious and I feel it would have felt much smoother if you could just press WASD to go from A to B.
My other main complaint is that there are points within the game where you are required to solve mildly irritating puzzles to traverse to the next scene. These puzzles serve no purpose other than (I assume) to mix up the gameplay a bit, but honestly they seem out-of-place and unnecessary.
Aesthetic / Style: 10/10
To the Moon is a retro-style game that strongly reminds me of Chrono Trigger. It's nostalgic, fits in well with the themes of the game and is implemented in a beautiful manner.
Music: 10/10
I listen to video game music all the time: while travelling, while I work, while I relax, when I go to bed. I'm actually listening to the game's soundtrack right now. It is honestly some of the most emotion-provoking music I have ever had the pleasure to listen to. When the powerful melodies are combined with the storytelling of To the Moon you cannot help but be overcome at times with the sheer levels of emotion it manages to squeeze out of you. There aren't many games that truly manage to connect with the player, but this is certainly one of them, and that is in no small part due to this stunning soundtrack.
Game play: 9/10
As I mentioned above, To the Moon is a point & click, and the only negative comments I have about the game are to do with the game play (please see above). That being said, I don't believe these negatives are anywhere near enough to suggest not getting this game. For a start, while the controls are a little clunky etc. the main focus of the gameplay is the story, and the story is told brilliantly, no two-ways about it. I would also like to applaud how the game manages to focus on tough topics, but lighten the mood just enough with truly funny moments exactly when you need an emotional lift. It makes the story even more compelling and I personally didn't find the bad points enough to break my immersion and enjoyment.
Characters: 10/10
I love the characters. They manage to worm their way into your heart with extraordinary speed and once their all you can do is sit back and watch the many twists and turns the story takes. There are no stereotypes or stupidly designed characters. They are all relatable and believable, with well-written dialogue that can be both witty and tear-inducing. I won't say anymore (Spoilers!) but the characters really are very well designed.

This game is easily beaten in 4 hours, but don't let that turn you away this game shows how easy it is to create a beautiful story with just a bit of effort and thought.
You play as Eva and Neil two workers from the Sigmund Corporation that offer a rather interesting promise. When on your deathbed the company can alter your memories to make your greatest wish come true. However an interesting case comes in Johnny, a man who wants to go to the moon, but doesn't know why.
Over the course of the game and in particular the latter third of the game you learn about Johnny and his dream, as well as his relationship with his late wife River. The whole while learning about our protagonists as well and just how hard it is not to get attatched to people the more you know about them.
The gameplay is wonderfully crafted to make you have to learn about Johnny's life. You have to collect energy to travel back further in Johnny's memories by way of examining the surroundings inside his memories. This beautifully allows the programmer to teach the player subtle hints about Johnny such as his enjoyment of pickled olives and his connection with a stuffed platypus as well as his obsession with paper rabbits.
Let me tell you if this well crafted music and story aren't enough to hook you, and if your idea of a game is more than an interactive story I can't help you. However if you found Either One to be an especially touching title then I cannot recomend this enough although the story is more in your face than that game.
People say if you play this game you'll cry towards the end. I for one did though my reason for crying might have been different than most by the end of it you'll be begging for more.

To the Moon is a short role-playing adventure video game developed by Freebird Games. The game focuses nothing more than driving you into story with high speed train. With little gameplay no more than interaction and solving small puzzle.
A story is about two doctor. Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts who have a machine that can grant anyone wish by diving into patient's memories then reconstructing them into what patients want and what needed to fulfill their wish. A machine is capable of uncovering any patient's memory at any life time, even the ones that patients don't remember.
To the Moon, this is one of Johnny's wish, and his wish sounds exactly like that, he wants to go to the moon. The entire story will be involved around fulfill said wish but things seems to not be as easy as it sounds, as the two doctors uncover more and more secrets regarding Johnny himself during his whole life time and the whole things about go to the moon itself.
This is really a game for expressing story and story alone. In order to express story effectively of course, is to use suitable musics. This game have the best set of musics that can narrow every single inches of story they want to present, it's emotion, it's happy and it's sad, they have everything. An astounding of depth in both story and music synced, they enough to touch anyone heart, they simply show how memories could be such things that influence the life of one person and what caused him or her to behave that way.
For a small price like this game, it surprisingly gives me more than I could ask for. I didn't expect this small game to teach me something about life and drive me cry like this. I recommend anyone who want some short story worth of 4 hours that put you in a train and then simply hook your feelings to a heart of this whole story right away.
Another note; Right after you've finished to the moon story, you should also play both DLC mini story. They explain more about two main characters, Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts. Even it's just last 1 hour each it packs with some interesting facts for these two and probably rise more questions. You shouldn't miss it if you have a chance. This is a brilliant game. When I first saw this game I thought it would be a campy fun little game that was just a little distraction for a bit, I soon learnt I was wrong. When I first got this game my friend and I decided to get on a multiplayer server for a bit of fun, and after a four hour session of large scale warfare and small spec-ops raids I can say that if you want an awesome war game that brings you into the action, this is the game. There's just something special about running with twenty or so of your fellow compatriots to the enemy's ground and not knowing whether you're about to face total annihilation, completely destroy your enemy or get caught in a vicious deadlock where ten feet is a gain. Not to forget that none of this would be possible without smart friends and enemies. The A.I. is so good, it reacts to suppersion, it understands whether it is out numbered and should fall back, it knows when just rushing a target will just over power them, and it uses cover in some of the best ways I've seen an A.I. do. My only gripe with the A.I. is it at sometimes does not prioritize the dangerous target and ends up being gunned down, this is a small nit-pick though. This game is so great, it's odd how it manages to be easily picked up and played and at the the same time is actually a pretty hardcore experience that is incredible enganging. This game truly is amazing.

I really want to recommend this game, but right now it's too frustrating and annoying. The game have a lot of good ideas but not well implemented.
-The A.I. is plain stupid sometimes. Your team mates pushes you out of cover so you end dying. And sometimes they just dont show up on batle, they just hangout in the base and leave you alone in the fight. And i don't want to talk about A.I. in vehicles because it makes my blood boil just to think about it.
-No auto-reload when the clip is empty? ... really? at least put an indicator to let you know that your clip is almost empty, like a flashing icon or something easy to spot.
-The objectives aren't clear and there is no correct feedback when you complete an objective. This game needs an easy to access list of objectives mapped to the 'O' key as in other games.
Now, not all is bad, in fact the rest of the game is really good and addictive, just please correct this things because i want to give this game a thumb up when its finished. I'll change my review in the future.
Note: My native language is spanish not english, so i'm very sorry if i didn't write this review correctly.

If you're searching for an assassin game, this is not the game you search for, better check out Dishonored or Hitman or even Shadow of Mordor.
Assassin's Creed is a one-man-army action game with bad voice acting, strange controls, horrible camera movement, repetitive character and world design, boring missions, hundreds of (useless) collectibles and a nice setting where you're facing 20 enemies at once and still win.
Some other "features" like fixed aspect ratio (black borders on top and bottom if you don't have a 16:9 monitor), no subtitles, no regular saves or the need to press 10+ buttons just to quit the game round this terrible package.
I have no idea how this franchise could become so popular.
Don't buy it.

The game could be much better if there would be no combat and less towers. Gameplay becomes repetative after two cities - climb the tower, find the objective, RUN FROM THE GUARDS, kill the target, go to the bureau and move onto the next target. Free-run is pretty cool, climbing animations are smooth. However the climbing process is so simplified that it becomes boring pretty soon. Guards everywhere disrupt the running pretty often and sometimes it is VERY ANNOYING. By some reason regular people (not guards) may throw rocks at you while you are climbing - a person who gave them that ability must be fired. It seems that it was forbidden to drive the horse fast back in these days - the police will chase you if you break the speed limit (stealing horses is still fine). A wast amount of collectibles (420 flags and 60 tampliers) is useless - there is no reward for collecting them.
Combat is horrible - there is no lock-on so you will change your target every time you move the mouse. You can avoid fighting till memory block 6 when you'll be forced to kill a small army (and this is not how the True Assassins™ do). Seriously, it is frustrating to fight more than two persons.
Sound is good, graphics are fine, story exists. The game is playable, but is far from perfect assassin simulator. Get it on sale, play till the sixth block and then uninstall.

My experience playing Assassin's Creed? Well, imagine you're back in school. It's English class and dictation time. You like English and welcome the challenge. So, you master this task and look forward to the next topic. But instead of changing the subject, the teacher forces you to write down the same text he or she has just dictated. Again. And again and again, the very same text, merely replacing a word here and there. Eight times, to be precise. That's Assassin's Creed.
As an assassin fallen from grace, you are given the mission to assassinate nine people in order to bring peace to the Holy Land. Each target sits somewhere in one of three large cities. In order to access missions vital for your task, you have to climb to the top of towers, churches and minarettes and get a view of your surroundings from there. If you are bored, you can rescue citizens from being terrorized by city guards. The actual missions to unlock the target are eavesdropping, interrogation and pickpocketing. Once you completed enough of these critical missions, you move in and kill the target. The actual assassination is the only part with a bit of variety. The rest is. Exactly. The. Same. Nine times. This is where AC transcends ist existence as a game and becomes something a game should never, ever be: A chore.
If you are REALLY bored, you can spend your time finding hidden flags and assassination target, which reward you with more energy bars. BUT: You can get all bars by climbing the view spots and saving the citizens, all things which are marked on your map. So, unless there's some super-secret unlockable I've never heard of, you have zero reasons to do these sidequests. Oh, sure, you get your XBox 360 achievements for them, so if you're after them, feel free to -Wait.
There are good and worthwhile things in Assassin's Creed. The atmosphere is nice, if a bit cold. The cities are well-realized. The animation of your player character is nothing short of spectacular, even now. The freerunning is great fun... and honestly the only thing that made see this one through. Now, I haven't played the second part yet, but from what I've heard, it's supposed to be far superior. And, granted, the game tried something new, and you can't expect it to get it right the first time. But this... this feels less than a fully-developed game than a proof-of-concept. And by its very definition, a proof-of-concept is not supposed to get released.

Remember Be offer a quite interesting future sci-fi story, with some social and political elements. I like that! And the story-driven part is also the most positive part of the game. Unfortunately I can't say any positive things of much other parts of the game. There is another interesting and original part of the game however, the memory remix.
First of all this is clearly a console game, which is very bad ported for PC. The controls feels clumsy, the menus do not support "normal" mouse-mode, and you are forced to navigate in an annoying console-way. And the memory remix is the most bad ported part in the entire game. To rewind in these parts, you literally have to clear your computer desk, to make space for you to look stupid with your mouse, while you make big counter-clockwise movements with your mouse. Very, very bad control!
Another clumsy and glitchy part of the game is the fight parts. And except from that, these are furthermore quite trivial and boring on the long term.
The game is very linear, and have too much of a console-feeling for my taste. The game however, is very pretty, and the scenery is very nice to look at.
But all in all, I can't recommend this game. The story, scenery and memory remix is the best part of the game. But a too linear level designs, boring battles/fights, and not at least a very, very bad PC port, make me incline to the view that this is
a game that I will recommend. Unfortunately, because the concept have potential.

Remember me is the kind of fighting game, that if you're not into fighting games, you just might want to make an exception for this one. Remember me is a fighting game with a lot of RPG elements in it - so much, actually, that a lot of players have critisized it for being too linear, forgetting it's true nature. It's a visual masterpiece IF you're into visual beauty but then again it's just one aspect that makes this game as awsome as it is. Some parts of the level design does feel like a rip-off from other games, for example the beginning totally looks like Dishonored and Bastille looks like Citadel form Half-Life 2 but instead of holding it against them, I felt happy to rediscover those places in another context. I agree with the overall consensus that the main character is one of the key elements, that make this game what it is. We have a female protagonist, racially diverse AND with a compelling history. She fights like a badass and makes tough descisions throughout the game. It's one of my all time favorites. Below are pros and cons:
Pros:
+ Incredibly beautiful cityscape (reminds the movie Fifth Element).
+ Supreme level design.
+ Interesting futuristic story.
+ Interesting character build and choices she has to face.
+ Customizable fighting combos.
+ Really useful powers/ abilities.
+ Visually the fighting sequences are a masterpiece.
+ Tactical approach to battles.
+ Build your own combos.
+ Supreme dodging mechanics that make battles dynamic, rapid and visually marvellous.
+ Apart from many other players, I actually liked the QTE endings of boss battles, that gave a meaning to the cinematic killmoves.
Cons:
- One gamebreaking bug in the worst place imaginable - right after a boss battle, forcing you to replay the lengthy fight.
- Main character's face should have been modelled, textured and animated better since you see it so often in the game.

At times this seems like two different games, one is a smart mindf*ck game (literally!) where you have to remix peoples memories to make them remember events differently to bend their will to your own ends. The other game is a straight up Batman style brawler, made way more complicated than it needed to be by you having to map abilities you unlock to the x, y, a or b buttons and then having to remember and try to pull off button combos in the right order and with the right timing.
The brawling sadly takes up most of the game, while remixing peoples memories you only get to do about 4 times in total throughout your journey through Neo Paris, which by the way made the game for me. This is one gorgeous and very cool looking city. It's sadly also incredibly linear while you are navigated through it while either climbing up buildings or fighting people.
Tonally it seems off as well, with your character and the story being overly serious but then undercut by these larger than life cartoonish villians you have to fight, which seemed totally out of place in this context, that was jarring for me.
The soundtrack was really awesome though, really memorable and hummable, in fact just get the soundtrack instead you'll enjoy it more :)

I would recommend the game to anyone who likes walking around looking at cool architecture, the gameplay didn't really do it for me, but this is one of the few games where i think it's worth playing for the aesthetic over the actual gameplay.

Remember Me - The game that made my feel like never before.
You are a memory hunter. You edit memories for your own ends, usually alturistic ones but sometimes not. You make people believe whatever you want. Seeing this power - and its effects - makes me question my power.
Gameplay is ok, linear but beautiful (I like it anyway), graphics are nice, but why do you play it?
The story.
The story is amazing. Although a single main character seems to be fakey, it makes sense towards the end.
Can't say much because of spoilers, but what you can do, make others believe, see, and hear Nilin say will lead you to accept things that need this game to accept.
The last scene. The last scene made me ~cry, but not really. It made my throat feel like I wanted to cry without the underlying sadness. More like a profound acceptance.
This game may not be able to relieve your pain, but it will bring you at peace. At least it did for me.

Syberia has good graphics (albeit dated), and music but the story and gameplay just aren't on the same level. Maybe it's because it's more of a interactive cinematic experience than a game, but it seems so unnecessarily long. While you'll get ~10+ hrs of playtime, most of it is spent walking/running/climbing stairs and trying useless locked doors around rather than solving puzzles. There seem to be gratuitous long shots and panning shots of scenery that serve no other purpose than to show off the scenery, because there isn't anything that can be interacted with in those scenes, which means lots and lots of walking/running to get to the next screen. There are also lots of stairs and ladders that cause Kate Walker to slow down and climb step by step and normal pace. Throw in some backtracking and the minutes of walking/running/climbing add up to hours.
For a game with a story, sometimes you have no idea what you're doing since it's rather easy to do things before they make any narrative sense, especially in Valadilene where you aren't told much of anything. Mostly, in the first two areas (Valadilene and Barockstast), you're just wandering around trying locked doors because there are no maps or directions to so-and-so place you're supposed to go. You'd think Kate Walker would at least try to ask someone where the notaary was or the rector's office instead of wasting time running around trying to find the place.
The story felt flat to me. It doesn't really go anywhere for most of the game and ends in a cliffhanger. You get Kate Walker's backstory through incessant phone calls that interrupt gameplay, but the subplot or even Kate Walker's story seems pointless in the grand scheme of things. Every phone conversation felt like Kate Walker didn't particularly care, even though her relationships were falling apart. There just aren't any likable characters, except maybe the hotel manager at Aralbad, who seems to be the only person with any good sense.

From the very start Syberia is a cinematic treat. Its unique characters and gorgeous settings are shown in great detail, rich animation and creative design, and this carries on throughout the entire game. In fact, both get even more elaborate. There are a few annoying animations and the occasional empty areas you are forced to walk through that only serve to connect point A to point B, but they don’t take away from the game that much.
The sound effects help bring the world to life and are fitting for each area whether it be beautiful sounds of nature or the mechanical sounds of the city. They help to immerse you in the world that Syberia creates, although there are some volume issues with quiet lines of spoken dialogue or overly loud sound effects but these are few and far between. The music… my word, the music is a treat. Cinematic orchestra swells in and the low woodwind bellows help pull you into this game that only feels like a movie.
Of course, the real treat in Syberia is the story. It caught me off guard. What starts as a story about a toy factory turns into one of the most beautiful dramas about heart and humanity that I have seen in a while topping most movies and TV shows I have seen. Even the subplot between our hero and her boyfriend begins to take center stage and melds with the main plot at the end that could bring tears to your eyes.
If you love adventure games or great stories in general, you are doing yourself a disservice by not playing Syberia.

This game is a pretty nice semi-traditional RPG with a good amount of thought put into it, whose only major flaw seemed to be a a few difficulty spikes / balance problems and a few bugs that actually just got fixed in a recent patch.  If you played the Shin Megami Tensei games, you may find some of the mechanics here very familiar and enjoyable.
The story of the game is strong enough that the premise and personality of the characters feels interesting.   Even if it doesn't get all that deep, it doesn't feel trivial or just there to hold the game together.  The black and white + paper aesthetic ties into this (you are trapped in a magical prison inside a book), but ultimately is just a nice aesthetic choice rather than being relevant to the gameplay at all.  The music is sort of an interesting mix of retro and electronic (but not chiptune) and seems to be disliked by quite a few others, but personally I enjoyed it.  The game performs and controls well at all points, although some menus become annoying to interact with if their contents become too long of a list.
The mechanics of the game are actually pretty interesting in how they both stick to and vary from normal RPG conventions.  MP recharges every turn and skills have independent cooldowns, thus letting you not feel like you have to conserve special attacks but also making it strategic to choose how to use it.  Status effects are applicable to almost all enemies and are actually useful to use in most encounters, as are stat-de/buff spells.  The game lets you build a party as you play the game and choose from a variety of tanks, healers, and both physical and magic dealing types, as well as specialize the main character partway through the game.  These characters can interact very well, with some setting up attacks for the other, drawing aggro, or blocking attacks along with the traditional buffing and healing.  Gear is fairly straightforward stat upgrades for the most part, and any excess money has a sink in useful stat upgrades.  Item drops are random and you can sometimes generate out-of-depth gear that carries you for several floors.  All enemy encounters are set except when specifically noted as random in a few specific areas.
If there are any complaints of the game, it is probably that there are strong difficulty spikes at the early part of the game (second or third boss IIRC) and the end of the game (Lv40 tier Assassin x2 + Sorcerer + Warrior mage encounter), and then later on seem surprisingly non-challenging.  I was able to pass these encounters without too much trouble even still.  There also aren't too many puzzles in the game, mostly a few perception based or riddle based puzzles.  A small complaint here is that a certain game-length chess key puzzle has the unfortunate quality of having your key break when used in the wrong lock.  All that really costs you is a reload and since you can have up to 10 saves it can mean a trivial amount of time lost, so I wonder why they didn't just say that the key doesn't work instead.  Also, said keys are removed from your inventory when successfully used, and all doors close and re-lock if locked upon reload.  Thus it is possible to accidentally shut yourself out of a chain of completed-puzzle-loot if you quit the game at a few awkward points, but you can't get yourself stuck as all such rooms can be opened by a level from the inside.
Overall a really fun game, about 20 hours worth with a modest amount of replayability from trying the other party members you didn't play with or playing on a higher difficulty.  It gets a pretty solid recommendation from me!

I went into this game not sure what to expect. As it began, I wasn't impressed, but after the first couple of fights, things started getting interesting. Eventually, I was having quite a bit of fun. The music is quite good, the "paper" appearance is pretty spiffy, and the fights were fairly strategic. Granted, I suck, so when I discovered that I could grind, I did for about half an hour before taking on the second big area. I felt guilty, like I had cheated a bit when I got to the second boss fight and I was taking hits to my entire party which dealt 50% or more damage to their HP. Despite having two healing characters, one of my healers was dead the next round, and my mage and warrior were dead within two more rounds. My final healer died swiftly after that. I had hoped to play a western RPG so that I wouldn't have to grind, because I want to experience progress moving through a game; not fighting the same crap for hours on end to get to see the next area, effectively making it easy for a developer to make less content but make it take longer to reach to conceal the fact that there is less content than in other titles, as with a Final Fantasy game or a free to play RPG. Perhaps a glorious strategist could do well in this game without grinding, but for me to succeed, I would have to grind for a very, very long time, and that's not entertainment; that's a job. I play games to have fun when I'm not working, and grinding is not fun. If you're quite good at turn-based strategy games or you love having to grind, this game is for you. Otherwise, I would recommend avoiding. I said it before, but great music and visual aesthetic, though...

For starters, only play this game if you insist on playing it.  Other wise, just skip it.  It is not worth your money and it is a terrible game.  Here are some reasons why.
The Bad
Story
The story is very generic and it's ending is laughable.  The characters are almost none existent and the story seems to have trouble developing itself, most notably towards the end of the game where the story just collapes in on itself and doesn't make sense anymore, leaving on an ending that leaves a very bitter taste in your mouth.  The story does have a few twists and turns you won't you see coming and they can be very suspenseful, but none of them last and are only small moments that shine.  As a whole, the story is unsatisfying and leaves much to be desired.
Gameplay
Now, the gameplay as a whole isn't exactly bad.  In fact, it can be quite good.  For example, combat can be fun and satisfying and the free-run system is equally satifying.  However, the game mechanics work 90% of the time, but the other 10% it doesn't work makes the game infuriating.  The 10% is most notable whenever you are running away from guards, and Altair decides to have a panic attack and jump to whatever platform he feels like, coating himself with gorilla glue in the process, in order to stick to every pixel possible at the worst times.  It can be very difficult to control Altair during this instances and leads to possibly broken monitors.  As a whole, gameplay can be fun, but usually results in frustration due to annoying controls and error in game mechanics.
The Good
Story
The only good that comes from the story is the unexpected twists and turns.  I geniunely didn't see them coming and some of them did suprise me, leaving me somewhat interested in the story.
Gameplay
The 90% of the time that the game works, its enjoyable and fun.
Verdict
I only recommend this game to people who just want to beat the game to be able to say that they have played it.  If you are interested in it for other reasons, I say just look up a summary of the story on the internet and go and buy the 2nd game.

Overall an excellent game that appears to have been sorely overlooked. Great aesthetics, great story, fun travel mechanics, excellent fight mechanics, and phenomenal bosses.
My favourite thing about Remember Me is the fighting mechanics. This game makes you feel awesome. Challeging and totally unique, Remember Me forces you to learn and develop a number of highly varied fighting styles to meet some very different challenges. It is impossible in this game to find one easy method of winning fights and just exploit it, all the way through the game you are gaining new skills and adapting your old skills to meet new challenges. There are many fights that will make you go "Man, there's no way I can win this", and the satisfaction of finally beating them is so worthwhile. You feel like River Tam or Buffy playing this game. You are awesome.
The travel aesthetic is quite fun, sort of a mix between Mirror's Edge and Assassin's Creed. It is mostly linear without too much of an exploration aspect, but the cinematic and atmospheric qualities revealed by moving through the world are a good trade off.
The game looks great. Great aesthetics with bright colours and a really strong and cohesive vision. The city looks great, the underworld looks great,the main character looks awesome in particular, and the enemies are interesting and sometimes creepy. Great graphics as well, on par with AAA titles like the recent Tomb Raider reboot.
The story was really good. Coherent without being overly simple. There are a couple of surprise reveals that you get to discover too. Strong themes, and a few good, strong characters. The side characters are really interesting too. Good script, and really good voice acting (English version).
This leads me to the bosses. Along with the fighting mechanic, I think this is where this game really excels and stands above other similar titles (eg. Assassin's Creed, Tomb Raider, Saint's Row). All the bosses are totally unique with complete stories, full characterization, and different aesthetics. You hate some of them, you think some of them are totally awesome, some you pity even as you struggle against them. They all have completely different fight styles and need to be defeated in different ways. They all challenge you by more than just soaking hit points, and you feel great when you finally beat each of them.
If I have one complaint, it would be that the game could have been longer, though not if this came at the cost of this game's sense of urgency and intensity. The game is as long as it needs to be to tell the story, I just wish I had more time to be awesome.
Strongly recommend. Will replay. Would buy a sequel.

I highly recommend Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice. +1
It's a wonderful change of pace for a video game to focus on immersing the gamer into the mindset/mentality/perceived environment of the protagonist—instead of emphasising the "best" graphics or the same-old gameplay mechanics.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice utilized Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response (ASMR) (Google it, it's neat) through 3D audio to make the player feels he/she is Senua. It's truly an amazing experience and amplified the gameplay experience for me fourfold. On top of the emphasis of the story and the immersion, the graphics are amazing and combat feels natural and right—while remaining a secondary feature, a very hard combination to accomplish.
Long story, short: if you're looking for a 8-hour journey in the mind of a psycopath that's like nothing else you've ever played, please buy Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice. If you're looking for a traditional RPG with a different spin, please *don't* buy Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice. You have to understand this game is all about the experience and not about traditional character progression, emphasis on combat, or anything in that manner.

If you liked Elite Dangerous but found it a bit too complicated at times this might be right up your street. It simplifies many of the elements that are in that game (landing/missions/crafting etc) and the planetary exploration is just leaps and bounds above Elite in my opinion.
I’m aiming to get the storyline completed and see where that takes me. Perhaps after that the repetitiveness will set in, but if this game continues to be supported as it has been in the last year then I for one am extremely excited where we go from here.

No Man's Sky has very funny reviews now, overall there are over 70000 reviews and only around 30% are positive, but recently this game have 2000+ reviews and 76% are positive. This game is not for everyone, that's all you need to know. I never expected anything mind blowing from this game, of course i know everything about the Sean Murray's lies and $60 price, and lack of content, so it's understandable where this negative reviews came from.
One day i discovered the game called "Starbound" so me and my friends played it, and enjoy it. I played it for 25 hours and it was exciting, i love space, and i wanted to play sandbox space game and i played it. As time went i forgot that No Man's Sky even exist, so that's why i never played it, until new update came out.  So I bought it for $13, read the reviews and prepared to be disappointed, but i wasn't, I just dived in the space to explore.
Explore, the most important word in open world game, i read that they added 30 hours of story and lore, missions, new biomes, etc. Don't know about other people, but i want to keep exploring, i played tons of open world games, for example in watch dogs 1-2 sometimes i just pressed "walk" button, and explored this beautifull Chikago or San Fransico, slowly, just looking at the city, people, cars, trees, graphics in general. And i was blown away. I did it with every open world game, and now, it's time  for No Man's Sky.
And if you just stop for a while, look around, you can actually see what developers do with their open world games. Open World Game = Exploration, and this is what this game gives you. No Man's Sky is a giant open world game with procedural generation. It's a very relaxing game, you just flying in the space, looking at the amazing view in front of you, gather materials, craft stuff to make your life easier, that's it. You make your own adventure, you make your own story. I had this nostalgic feeling of time when i was playing minecraft, this is my world, the world with no end in it, you are a part of this world, and you have the power to do practically whatever this world offers. You can actually see aliens in this game, you contact with them, learning their language, trade with them, taking missions etc. I especially want to thank 65daysofstatic for this majestic music they put in No Man's Sky, It gives you goose bumps. Developers are still working on this game, not as fast as I'd like, but they do, so i wish them good luck.
This is really "No Man's Sky". People have plased themselves on the highest level on their planet, but not in the space. This game proves that you can own a planet, but you can't own the skies. Everything has its own meaning, and your meaning in this game, is in the skies
Now excuse me, i must fly away, there is an infinite world awaits me.

This is an awesome piece of old-school RPG dungeon crawling game.
You are trapped in a book and must find a way to get out only to be beset by enemies preventing you from getting out, while searching for secrets to help yourself gain the advantage and delve deeper into the stories behind the book itself.
Combat is turn-based and its not just hack'n'slash, it uses energy for skills and each turn that energy will replenish slowly and this makes the combat even more interesting as stated in the description this involves strategy over grinding.
The dungeon itself is real-time and can go anywhere after that dungeon level has been beaten, explore to heart's content and find secrets opening up stories laid behind by previous owner and find out more what really happened.
I find myself engaged throughout the game fighting enemies and finding secrets for almost 15 hours, probably more if I spent more time in reaper's catacombs.
Although in all story and fighting, the UI and mouse interface is a bit clunky and could be improved even further, keyboard is the way to go for moving around and only use the mouse for opening doors and pulling levers and interact items.
I would recommend this game to anyone who likes fighting in a dungeon just to escape from being imprisoned forever. This game is a gem for those who likes to find things on your own as there aren't much clues to be found.
Oh and don't try 1980's difficulty.

Good: Unique game premise, good & amusing interpretation of both Akihabara & Japanese Otaku culture.
Bad: Poor graphics fidelity, simplistic combat, boring main characters
AKIBA's STRIP is essentially a 3D brawler (think Dynasty Warriors, Yakuza etc) set in the real life district of Akihabara in Tokyo, Japan. The core strength of the game being that the game world, while not 100% accurate, is pretty darn close!
The other difference between the previously mentioned brawler games being that instead of flooring your enemy with a K.O. you end a fight by stripping your enemies clothes off..
There is a logical story reason why this happens, think vampires, sunlight etc. In this respect it's an unashamedly quirky Japanese title that you would have seen plenty of around the PS1 import era 1995-2000. If that was your kind of thing back in the day, you'll likely immediately get the appeal of this game.
The combat mechanics aren't fantastic being perhaps even simpler than D.W. Yet there is a sizable amount of weapon collecting & modification (fusing) you can perform. Each weapon has a group type & it's own individual combo string + moveset so it's worth experimenting to see what works with your own play style. It's just a shame this typically ends up being holding the dodge/block button & then mashing one of the three height levels of attack dependendant on which of your enemies clothes you need to damage adequately enough to strip.
XSEED's translation efforts have definitely fallen on the western 'dude-bro' style of the fence & while the game doesn't take itself seriously in anything it does, the story as a whole is very skippable & none of the cast of characters are fleshed out or particularly interesting. The game does encourage multiple playthroughs to complete your catalogue & see all the character endings but in reality, you'll probably be more than done with the title at the end of your first, taking around 10 hours if you also attempt to finish all the side quests.
As I'm currently learning the language, being able to see renders & digitalizations of actual stores with appropriate signs & advertisements in this way is great practice for reading the Kana's & Kanji in its naturally presented form. One of the collectables are real Akiba area flyers some of which are bat♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy & some of the in-game store music is questionably explicit in it's lyrics making me think the original developer didn't quite have a grasp on what it was they were rapping about. It also gives you the option to select either an English or Japanese voice dub & subtitles.
The game itself despite having just had a simulatenous release on the PS4 as well as PC in 2015 does look like a late era PS2 game which could be expected with this type of title & it's hard to remember in this day of AAA or Indie only that mid-tier games did used to exist, once upon a time. It is possible, doing some digging in the steam forum, to increase the fidelity to a certain degree & the game itself has plenty of graphical setting options to tweak to an acceptable level.
AKIBA'S TRIP is definitely not a hentai game & it does give you the ability to play as either a boy or a girl student so unless seeing underwear disturbs you, don't be put off by any notion of this being a questionable, sexist Japanese porn game. It's goofy and silly, other than some poor translation humour there's nothing offensive in the game.
If the fighting mechanics had been fleshed out a bit more, this would have been a gem of a title. As it stands, if you have any interest in the Akiba area or Japanese culture in general, this will probably be enough to keep you going. For me, fighting the entire cast of the idol group AKB-48 with water pistols & dressed in only my underwear & headphones is a gaming experience I'm unlikely to replicate again. In the current gaming scene of sequel after sequel or adventurous (yet low-tier) indie games, I'm thankful this type of game, somehow, still managed to exist.

I feel like this game deserved a review purely from how silly it is and how people may have no idea what it's all about.
TLDR review; If you don't mind tasteless fanservice but a load of hilarity, this game is for you.
Now for the full review...
AKIBA'S TRIP (See the play-on-words?) is certainly a unique JRPG game. It is set in Akihabara; a very popular district of Japan known for it's Otaku culture. For a quick synopsis, man-made vampires called 'Synthisters' are beginning to appear around Akihabara taking life energy from innocent people to use for their own benefits. Your character learns that the best way to defeat these vampires is to utilize a well known weakness; the sun. But how do you get these vampires to bathe in the sun's glow? By stipping their clothes off of course.
Yes, this whole game revolves around fighting people by stripping them of their clothing...
Sounds pretty perverted, right?
You'd be spot on, and I'm certainly not going to deny that it is a bit pervy. After playing the game for a few hours, though, the clothing stripping becomes less weird and more hilarious.
And before you say that this game is extremely sexist and designed for sad guys wanting to see a few panties, there is just as much man-service as there is female fanservice!
The combat is a hack-'n'slash style dealeo where different areas clothing must be targeted and be removed individually after they've sustained enough tearage. It sounds good on paper, but the combat can certainly be a bit jerky and unresponsive at times. The 'weapons' you use are all makeshift ones since you wouldn't be able to carry real weapons around Tokyo. From acoustic guitars to roombos (those little robot vaccum things) and computer monitors. there are loads of funny and amazing weapons to choose from.
The story for the game is average in my opinion, some likable characters here and there but they're very 'generic' and lack real character development. It is also important to note that it also isn't a very long game either. Even doing most of the side quests the game only took me around 15 hours to complete at most.
Positives and Negatives
+ Tons upon TONS of anime and video game references and humor. If you're an anime and gaming nerd like me you'll be laughing your♥♥♥♥♥off from some of these. It even has it's own in-game 4ch.
+ Amazing City Environment: The Akihabara district is depicted well in this game, with anime adverts and vocaloid music playing wherever you go. Makes me want to visit the real Akihabara.
+ Amazing Soundtrack (Especially the opening song)
+ Plenty of 'weaponry' to choose from.
+ Some likable characters.
+ Your character can cross-dress
+- The English voices are hit or miss. For example, Shizuku, my favourite character, has a great voice, but Rin has a pretty poor one in my opinion.
+- Doesn't take itself seriously in the slightest.
+- Combat works for the most part, but lacks depth and can be buggy.
+- Story is nice sometimes but it's pretty shallow as things go.
+- No character customisation, but a lot of clothing to choose from. See someone on the street wearing something you like? Go strip it off them!
+- A lot of fanservice. Some people will like that, some people do not. It does get funny from it's rediculousness after a while. I personally tend to just not think about it too much and as long as it isn't in my face TOO much then I won't complain (I'm looking at you, High School of the Dead).
- Pretty crap port. Sure you get 1080p but it also comes with a 30fps lock.
- The graphics look more like a PS Vita port than a PS3 port.
- Various bugs such as bumping into someone you need to talk to while trying to talk to them makes you unable to do anything, forcing you to restart the game.
- No autosave. Now I know that it isn't something everyone wants but I at least want the option. Especially because of said bug.
- A short story, but the game does have a New Game+ mode so you can try out all the girls' routes.
- Cutscenes are rendered by the game engine with VN-style dialogue. I wouldn't think this was so bad if the graphics were not so meh. If the cutscenes were all animated like the opening movie I would love the game a whole lot more.
- A LOT of loading screens, but they're not too long.
All things considered I'd give this game a 7 out of 10. I'd recommend this game to any anime enthusiast who doesn't mind fanservice or sub-par graphics and are not prone to being weirded out too hard. If you look over the technical issues it's most definitely a fun, quirky game.

Conclusion first: Play it if you like a good story. Playthrough doesn't take too long, even with its sometimes glitchy explore / fighting system (which I don't think is game- breaking.) I got it in a sale, and it's totally worth it. Good job, Dontnod (I'll be looking forward to its next game, since Life is Strange is definitely one of my favourites.)
Pros:
- Story is interesting. Starts from mid-avalanche but doesn't leave you lost in the lingo / story. Fast-paced.
- Nilin. Is. Kickass. Also can I just say, good to see a woman of colour in the lead.
- It's short and linear. Keeps the story going (although you won't get to explore much aside from finding the health / 'special moves' (focus) patches hidden throughout the game.
- Combat system is a throwback to the old Street Fighter / arcade fighting games days where you had to do certain button presses for a successful combo. A plus you get to craft them in an extent for different effects.
- Memory remixes are a treat. Wish we had more.
Cons:
- Glitchy gameplay. Not game-breaking. The combat system requires good timing, considering the amount of enemies that will be swarming you by the end of it.
- Not friendly to backtracking, along with its already limited exploration. (Get them health / focus patches fast. Or they're lost forever.)
- Neo-Paris has a lot of grit and grimeyness. It's subjective to those who view it, but I really prefer my vibrant colours.
ANYWAY, the story is good, so if you're a story junkie like me, I'd totally get it.

I had to get Remember Me, after playing Life is Strange. Remember Me is DONTNOD's first game and it's great solid start :D. It tells the story of Nilin in a beautiful future Neo-Paris, who has lost her memory.  As a fan of sci-fi genre, I enjoyed this story a lot. It reminds me of some awesome movies of the genre. The game is linear and at quite many parts of the story you have to solve some puzzles, climb buildings. Remember Me also features some awesome "rewind" moments, where you alternate memories.
The combat is fast paced, and you can customize your own sweet combos and eventually unlocking more moves. Boss fights include some QTE, which was the only downside for me as using K+M, because the button icons for K+M didn't make it very clear what to press in few moments. Resulting in some retries.
I think the soundtrack is amazing, it fits well in the scenes. The game's story was really good imo and it will keep you interested to the end, as you learn more about Nilin and the city. It made me think how scary it would be, if the technology would someday evolve so far, as it is in Remember Me.
So folks, try to remember and buy this game sometime :).

I was in doubt of giving this game a positive or negative review, but based on what I paid for it (€0.75) and the year it was released (2002), I am willing to give the game positive feedback.

On the one side this is logical, due to the fact that the player will not know where to look for the next clue, on the other side; do not make the doors clickable if the door is no use. Next to that, I did some running around and got to the next clue after 5 'empty' screens. When the clue was found I had to go back the same way.. this really tested my patience.
All-in-all: If it wasn't for the low price I paid, I would be less positive about this game. It is just not worth €10, my advice therefor is to buy this game during sale (at least -80%). I definitely want to know how it ends and start playing Syberia 2.

No Man's Sky has very funny reviews now, overall there are over 70000 reviews and only around 30% are positive, but recently this game have 2000+ reviews and 76% are positive. This game is not for everyone, that's all you need to know. I never expected anything mind blowing from this game, of course i know everything about the Sean Murray's lies and $60 price, and lack of content, so it's understandable where this negative reviews came from.
One day i discovered the game called "Starbound" so me and my friends played it, and enjoy it. I played it for 25 hours and it was exciting, i love space, and i wanted to play sandbox space game and i played it. As time went i forgot that No Man's Sky even exist, so that's why i never played it, until new update came out.  So I bought it for $13, read the reviews and prepared to be disappointed, but i wasn't, I just dived in the space to explore.
Explore, the most important word in open world game, i read that they added 30 hours of story and lore, missions, new biomes, etc. Don't know about other people, but i want to keep exploring, i played tons of open world games, for example in watch dogs 1-2 sometimes i just pressed "walk" button, and explored this beautifull Chikago or San Fransico, slowly, just looking at the city, people, cars, trees, graphics in general. And i was blown away. I did it with every open world game, and now, it's time  for No Man's Sky.
And if you just stop for a while, look around, you can actually see what developers do with their open world games. Open World Game = Exploration, and this is what this game gives you. No Man's Sky is a giant open world game with procedural generation. It's a very relaxing game, you just flying in the space, looking at the amazing view in front of you, gather materials, craft stuff to make your life easier, that's it. You make your own adventure, you make your own story. I had this nostalgic feeling of time when i was playing minecraft, this is my world, the world with no end in it, you are a part of this world, and you have the power to do practically whatever this world offers. You can actually see aliens in this game, you contact with them, learning their language, trade with them, taking missions etc. I especially want to thank 65daysofstatic for this majestic music they put in No Man's Sky, It gives you goose bumps. Developers are still working on this game, not as fast as I'd like, but they do, so i wish them good luck.
This is really "No Man's Sky". People have plased themselves on the highest level on their planet, but not in the space. This game proves that you can own a planet, but you can't own the skies. Everything has its own meaning, and your meaning in this game, is in the skies
Now excuse me, i must fly away, there is an infinite world awaits me.

+ The graphical style (similar to

+ The game does a good job of emulating the old-school dungeon-crawler RPG, with turn-based combat and secrets laid out in the (somewhat small) levels making exploring enjoyable.
- There are many minor negative aspects to the gameplay which add up unfortunately, including:

and its gameplay, those aspects of the game didn't drag the game down excessively; it was still an enjoyable experience (for the most part). Considering how cheap the game is, even if you’re hesitant to pick it up, it won’t leave your wallet much lighter than before.”

Do you like old school Wizardy? Do you like old school RPGs? Do you like cheap RPGs? DO YOU LIKE RPGs?
If you answered "Yes lawd PRAISE THA PAPER!!" then I'd say you're mocking me.. but if you responded "OH HELL YES" to any of the above, then you will enjoy Paper Sorcerer. Playing the role of an anti-hero is a pure delight, and I would suggest this game to any of my friends.

Years ago when Assassin's Creed first came out, I wasn't impressed. I played a few hours of it, only to walk away annoyed and disappointed. Recently however, when the majority of the Assassin's Creed franchise was on sale for less than $5 a game, I decided to give it another try. That was one of the best decisions I've made in gaming and I've been hooked ever since.
The true historical applications of the game, albeit slighty modified, is intriguing, educational, and very well-done. I felt as though I really was fighting an oppressive force during the Third Crusade in the Holy Land in 1191. This game takes advantage of historical events, locations, and terminology in the same way the Metal Gear series does. The ancestoral concept throughout the game was like nothing I've ever seen in a game and brought a uniqueness to it. The protagonist, Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad, is a competent fighter and agile acrobat. The growth of character witnessed during the course of the game was satisfying and gave you a clearer understanding of what the creed means.
On the other hand, the tasks were a little repetitive and stealth wasn't very prevalant. You had very few ways to sneak up on someone and would rather kill someone then have to run away each time. Regardless, the game was immensely satisfying and paved way for numerous sequels that I loved as well.
This is a must buy.

I feel like this game deserved a review purely from how silly it is and how people may have no idea what it's all about.
TLDR review; If you don't mind tasteless fanservice but a load of hilarity, this game is for you.
Now for the full review...
AKIBA'S TRIP (See the play-on-words?) is certainly a unique JRPG game. It is set in Akihabara; a very popular district of Japan known for it's Otaku culture. For a quick synopsis, man-made vampires called 'Synthisters' are beginning to appear around Akihabara taking life energy from innocent people to use for their own benefits. Your character learns that the best way to defeat these vampires is to utilize a well known weakness; the sun. But how do you get these vampires to bathe in the sun's glow? By stipping their clothes off of course.
Yes, this whole game revolves around fighting people by stripping them of their clothing...
Sounds pretty perverted, right?
You'd be spot on, and I'm certainly not going to deny that it is a bit pervy. After playing the game for a few hours, though, the clothing stripping becomes less weird and more hilarious.
And before you say that this game is extremely sexist and designed for sad guys wanting to see a few panties, there is just as much man-service as there is female fanservice!
The combat is a hack-'n'slash style dealeo where different areas clothing must be targeted and be removed individually after they've sustained enough tearage. It sounds good on paper, but the combat can certainly be a bit jerky and unresponsive at times. The 'weapons' you use are all makeshift ones since you wouldn't be able to carry real weapons around Tokyo. From acoustic guitars to roombos (those little robot vaccum things) and computer monitors. there are loads of funny and amazing weapons to choose from.
The story for the game is average in my opinion, some likable characters here and there but they're very 'generic' and lack real character development. It is also important to note that it also isn't a very long game either. Even doing most of the side quests the game only took me around 15 hours to complete at most.
Positives and Negatives
+ Tons upon TONS of anime and video game references and humor. If you're an anime and gaming nerd like me you'll be laughing your♥♥♥♥♥off from some of these. It even has it's own in-game 4ch.
+ Amazing City Environment: The Akihabara district is depicted well in this game, with anime adverts and vocaloid music playing wherever you go. Makes me want to visit the real Akihabara.
+ Amazing Soundtrack (Especially the opening song)
+ Plenty of 'weaponry' to choose from.
+ Some likable characters.
+ Your character can cross-dress
+- The English voices are hit or miss. For example, Shizuku, my favourite character, has a great voice, but Rin has a pretty poor one in my opinion.
+- Doesn't take itself seriously in the slightest.
+- Combat works for the most part, but lacks depth and can be buggy.
+- Story is nice sometimes but it's pretty shallow as things go.
+- No character customisation, but a lot of clothing to choose from. See someone on the street wearing something you like? Go strip it off them!
+- A lot of fanservice. Some people will like that, some people do not. It does get funny from it's rediculousness after a while. I personally tend to just not think about it too much and as long as it isn't in my face TOO much then I won't complain (I'm looking at you, High School of the Dead).
- Pretty crap port. Sure you get 1080p but it also comes with a 30fps lock.
- The graphics look more like a PS Vita port than a PS3 port.
- Various bugs such as bumping into someone you need to talk to while trying to talk to them makes you unable to do anything, forcing you to restart the game.
- No autosave. Now I know that it isn't something everyone wants but I at least want the option. Especially because of said bug.
- A short story, but the game does have a New Game+ mode so you can try out all the girls' routes.
- Cutscenes are rendered by the game engine with VN-style dialogue. I wouldn't think this was so bad if the graphics were not so meh. If the cutscenes were all animated like the opening movie I would love the game a whole lot more.
- A LOT of loading screens, but they're not too long.
All things considered I'd give this game a 7 out of 10. I'd recommend this game to any anime enthusiast who doesn't mind fanservice or sub-par graphics and are not prone to being weirded out too hard. If you look over the technical issues it's most definitely a fun, quirky game.

"General! Italy just entered the war!"
- "No problem, send two divisions to stop them!"
"But  General! They're on our side..."
- "That's even worse! Send them an army!"
After that joke of a german soldier at the very beginning of the game, things start to get ugly. And by ugly I refer to the gameplay which kind of reminds me of a walking simulator with broken legs and a strained neck. For example, I didn't even know that it is possible to mess up the simple functionality of looking around... but somehow the devs found a way to do so!
"Well ok, maybe it's just me beeing silly..." I tried to adapt and continued. Meanwhile I enjoyed the really good german voice over that seems pretty authentic (no irony this time, they did a good job on that).
Arrived at the shooting range for basic training. After listening to some more propaganda about german war material I received a rifle and suddenly I saw why they fu**ed up the camera controls so badly. Simply because using the mouse does not rotate or manipulate the camera itself as you would suggest, but it lets you drag the imaginary aim point of the rifle across the screen, which is then beeing followed by the first person camera. I don't know why they tried to revolutionize a simple mechanic that has worked perfectly fine in thousands of other games before, but they failed.
So already lacking of motivation I tried to convince myself that maybe they where trying to enhance realism, and that's why...
Two minutes later I perfectly hit some targets with an unmounted mg42 from a standing position and over a distance of a few hundred meters.
I quit the "game" and decided to write this review, which was basically more fun than playing Iron Front itself!

So in spite of the very disturbing (or at least foreign) concept of three different young boys showering with their respective dads in a lockeroom shower, this game is actually pretty fun. You get six different minigames, plus plenty of unlockable stuff to power your way through. The reoccuring theme is the concept of running whichever under ten year old boy you are to the correct dad. There are obstacles along the way (puddles, slippery floor signs, pints of beer, adoptions papers, etc.), but the two main modes of gameplay remain the same. Other minigames involve a SCUMM- engine point and click adventure game, a ninja trial game, a game where you fly through the air in a bathtub shooting down other dads in their bathtubs whilst rescuing your own, and finally, a game where you catch falling dads. Overall, the game is like one of those "Game and Watch Gallery" games they used to sell for the original gameboy, but with an overall theme of showering with dads.
Plenty of goofy moments, insane jokes and basic yet totally addictive gameplay.
pedophilia, but plenty of homoerotic moments between the dads. I recommend this game to anyone who isn't a school teacher!

Classic turn based dungeon crawler. That's just the game's description.
What it truly is, is a game stripped down to the very essence of gameplay that defines that description. Everything else from zone traversing to merchant is streamlined into a menu selection.
The gem in this title has definitely got to be the 1980's difficulty mode. It's the time machine that sits older gamers back in time playing RPGs that are unlike the slew of mindless successors that their characters can overpower through.
Buy this, ignore everything but 1980's mode. In it, you'll be pressed to form your party with companions that complement each other and fight strategically rather than having the strongest. You'll clock 10x more play time saving before every fight, but you'll relish every minute of it.

Assassin’s Creed is the first title of the popular Ubisoft Franchise, Assassin’s Creed. Launched in 2007, the game received enormous commercial success on consoles, but only a year later after its initial release, Assassin’s Creed was introduced to PC. Assassin’s Creed is a semi-sandbox, action-adventure-stealth game set in the Holy lands of; Jerusalem, Acre and Damascus during the Crusades.
Assassin’s Creed is a beautiful game, every crack and crevasse is filled with amazing detail, from astounding visuals to overheard cries for help. The graphics are absolutely jaw dropping, despite the age of the game. The Vast cities of Jerusalem and Acre extend into the horizon with hundreds of buildings and thousands of people living out their daily lives. All the while the frame-rate remains constant.
The story, or should I story’s, brings the game to life. On the one hand, you play an assassin during the Third Crusade in 1191 AD, named Altair. We follow his quests as he assassinates nine public figures at the command of his master. And on the other hand, you are put into the shoes of Desmond Miles, whose ancestor was Altair. Desmond was taken in by a mysterious organization for questioning, and put into the Animus. The Animus is a device which allows the user to revisit their ancestors’ past memories. Desmond is forced to relive his ancestor’s life against his will for unknown reasons.
The voice acting is solid throughout the game. Conversations are completely believable and delivered with the perfect amount of solemn dignity. What you hear in the game is more impressive than what you see. In the cities with populated areas, your ears will fill with the pleas of beggars, the din of street vendors, and the occasional humming. At the top of synchronisation points, you hear the wind blowing past you as you climb for the sky, the barking of a far-off dog, and the twittering of birds.
Assassin’s Creed is exceptionally entertaining in that it features a mix of fine stealthy exploration and exciting combat. You start the game off fairly weak, but as you progress through missions, Altair gains new abilities and increased health. Before a primary target can be assassinated, you need to gather intelligence. The methods by which you go about doing so present the most irritating aspects of the game. When you get a mission to assassinate a target, you have to do at least 3 side quests first before you can assassinate the main target. There are an array of side quests that you can choose from, like; Pickpocketing, eavesdropping, interrogation, and target elimination. The problem is that after doing one of the side quests, there’s practically nothing satisfying about it.
After completing three side quests of any variety, you head over to an assassin’s bureau in the city and you get informed that you can now assassinate your main target. The problem is that all the bits of intelligence you pick up while on side quests have little to no impact on how the eventual primary target mission plays out. Beyond that problem, after repeating the process for each target, things got plain, simple and just really boring.
The controls, for me, could have been better. I often found myself getting stuck on a wall, roof top or the side of a building as you can’t just jump anywhere; you have to jump from one specific point to another. This really got on my nerves, especially when trying to run away from guards, the last thing you want to happen is to get stuck. Combat in the game is fun and exciting, but it does have its issues. First off, there are a few combinations that you will need time to get used to. Secondly, the character did not always do what I wanted him to. This did get a tad annoying sometimes but it’s not a major issue.
The player is given five different weapons; long sword, short sword, throwing knives, and a hidden blade. Each weapon is useful in different situations. The long sword is the main tool of self-defence, and is useful for big battles; the short sword is a light and fast blade which is useful when facing small numbers of enemies; throwing knives can be very useful as they kill the enemy instantly, and you can use them for long distance kills; and the hidden blade which is used for assassinations.
Assassin’s Creed does come with a few issues that just can’t be ignored. Firstly, the amount of guards that walk around the roof tops is incredible. It is impossible to go anywhere by running ‘freely’ on the roof tops without alerting a guard. You can assassinate them, but after a while, that satisfaction of watching Altair use his hidden blade to slam down a guard just becomes boring and you just want to get to where ever you going. So then you decide to take the city streets to your destination, only to find out that it’s just as annoying as taking the roof tops. The city streets in Assassin’s Creed are plagued with beggars, drunken people and woman carrying pots on their heads that fall and break if you run into them.
If you are on a stealth mission where keeping your distance or blending in is needed, just wait until you come across the beggars who run in front of you, and you only, and start asking for money, meanwhile your target is getting away as once the beggar is in front of you it’s hard to get them out of the way. Same scenario, but you are confronted with drunken people who walk around and look like zombies from 'Land Of The Dead', if you get close to them they will push you which ultimately gives away your position and you have to restart the mission.
The Verdict:
Assassin’s Creed is definitely not the best game in the series, with its repetitive side quests and annoying NPCs, the game can get a bit frustrating and boring. For somebody totally unfamiliar with the game, it's certainly worth playing. Even though the game does have its faults, it still offers a great mix of exploration and action that is just waiting to be experienced.
+ Good graphics
+ Lots to explore
+ Great story
+ Challenging missions
- No side Quests
- Controls could have been better
- To many guards on the roof tops
- To many beggars and drunk people in the cities
SCORE: 7.5/10

I really got drawn into this game. The art and surroundings are just beautiful and original and the soundtrack is phenomenal. The story is really interesting and has some current themes, but Nilin's character remains a bit superficial because she doesn't get to have that many discussions. The game is also very straightforward -- so much that it's easy to forget to explore and you can easily miss out on valuable health, focus and story collectibles. This game would have needed some side missions and a more open world. The camera angles are also very restrictive, which is a pity considering the amazing views all around. The combat is monotonous, and I recommend using the controller.
The initial feeling and the world kind of gave me the same feeling as the original Mass Effect -- only here you don't have freedom to roam, no side missions, no discussions, and therefore it doesn't really compare. It's frustrating how they invested so much in the art, music and background story only to make it so straightforward and limited.
Still, if you like a good  immersive story with beautiful visuals, I recommend it. I truly hope they make a sequel where the shortcomings are addressed.

Remember Me is a linear SciFi story with batman-style combat and tombraider-style movement. And Lord of the Rings is about a little guy who carries around a ring.
Lets get serious again... it has good art, very nice sound track, nice animations. The world is fancy and entertaining but the real star is the story, it is a rare example of smart scifi which touches heart and mind equally well. There are also some unique minigames like changing the memory of people. Also the balance between exploring, combat, puzzles and mini games is good.
Surelly there is some bad stuff too, the game is totally linear (but trust me you wont mind), has only auto save points (but lots of em), has little replay value, a couple of little bugs (had to restart the game 3-4 times), things sometimes get a little repetitive (but only slightly) and some battles and quick time events are a little bit unbalanced. Also while the "old Paris" scenery was gorgeous there was too much "that sewer again" and "yet another generic scifi service tunnel". Sometimes I stepped through a door which immediatly locks and I lose my chance to explore some more rooms. No serious problems but definitly not perfect.
Would I buy again? Absolutely. I have enjoyed every minute of it. 8 out of 10 points.

Make no mistake, this game is a delight to look at.  The city of Neo-Paris has been rendered in a way that lends considerable creedence to their vision of the near future.  Lots of little details are included that make the environments believable.
That task was probably made easier by the highly-linear nature of the game.  On the one hand, you can lament how incredible this would have been to have the same level of detail in an open-world, but the linear nature allows for a high degree of polish on the path you follow through the world and story.
The story's competent, and told well enough, though I don't think I was invested as the story expected me to be.  Nilin comes across as introspective, yet more than a little cold.
There's a neat memory-remix mechanic introduced early on and it felt like I was nearly halfway through the game before it came up again, though there are several instances before all's said and done.  I'll echo the sentiments of several other reviewers who wished there was "more of that, please."
The combat itself is also competent, in the Arkham vein but with a dodge rather than a counter, with a few nice touches to spice things up.  Depending on your play style, it's easy for some fights to overstay their welcome, but once you become comfortable with the combo system and fight mechanics (or like me learn to stop hoarding your special attacks) you can dispatch with most battles relatively expeditiously.  It's got QTE's, and while the button you press corresponds to the action executed it still feels more like a match game than a act of skill, but they're used to cap off certain battles rather than as a routine mechanic.
I played with a mouse and keyboard and occasionally felt like the game wanted me to be using a controller, but it was never a serious handicap.  (Here's a tip if you're using a mouse and kb like me - the "Rewind" motion is like drawing a counter-clockwise circle with your mouse.  Perhaps I missed a critical instruction, but that really threw me off during the first memory remix.)
I think there was something else I wanted to say, but I just...can't remember.

At first its a fun little game but it quickly gets repetitive. It needs way more maps and needs more inventive ways to win than just literally a dieing fest for position on a map. More respawn gear options would help as well, and it wouldn't hurt to gain RP for going on kill streaks... its annoying to have to drop out of battle, and do a long run, aware you do need to pick up some items to bank for RP so as to make sure you can still afford decent gear.
Also not dieing so quick would make it a bit more fun. Tired of being one shot by an npc holding a basic rifle before they are even on my screen and they shoot 1 bullet. I hate not having a longer view distance, I would much rather have a way more tactical game by being able to see further but accuracy being woeful at the edge of your range or even not being able to target the full distance you can see (although admittedly this would screw up the sniper rifles and such, but perhaps even that could be re-worked(.
