I believe life as a whole is made of many little things, and this applies to games too. If a game repeatedly annoys me or otherwise has a constant flow of unfun mechanics, it probably isn't fun: No Man's Sky is plagued with these annoying little things, and as such I don't feel it is a fun game. As I've played this game for roughly 4 hours now, my chances of getting a refund are over, and I will continue to keep playing in order to see if the game will begin feeling fun soon.
Below are my nitpicks of the game so far. I'll leave a TL;DR section at the bottom.
1. The game starts with the option of four gamemodes; standard, survival, hardcore survival and creative. Rather than a typical menu screen where you would have choices for Play, Options, Quit and so on, I only could choose the gamemode. I went with survival. Next up was about 3-4 minutes of Loading Shaders, during which a VERY loud soundtrack was playing on repeat. I couldn't access the options screen, so I was forced to turn the game volume down with the sound manager on my toolbar; this isn't a good sign. There is a lot more of loud music in the game later on, too.
2. I load into the game now, and am surrounded by two small huts and some broken machinery. This is my first time playing the game and although I know the basics (zap trees and rocks for materials, craft new gear, so on) I don't really know where to start. I mine some iron from a rock on the surface, and a sentinel comes to look at what I'm doing. Turns out sentinels don't like having you mine their ores: Three of them open fire on me and I have to run to the hills. Looks like sentinels will be a large annoyance in this game.
3. Eventually they give up the chase, but the escape meant I was exposed to a lot of radiation. My suit's radiation shield is decaying at a very steady pace, and after a good five-ten minute period I'm low on health but I cannot regain it. There was a machine in one of the huts that allow me to refill my health and shields, but I used it earlier, not knowing it has only a single use. The scanner tells me that there are NO resources nearby from which I could recharge my life support; Either I go out and try to find some, and die in less than a minute, or stay indoors and die in about two minutes. Bad start, I suppose? Or beginner's idiocy for starting on survival for the first time? I don't know, but I choose to make a new save on the standard mode.
3. This time I have an easier start. I'm able to find resources faster than I am dying to the cold, and radiation isn't a factor on this planet. I didn't come up against hostile enemies, either. However, when the idea of the game is to zap trees and rocks and other things like that for resources, it is really annoying when you can't do that to certain things: There were these blue plant things that I could destroy three of (they blow up in a puff of blue smoke and give me exotic materials), but after that any additional ones are invulnerable to my mining laser. Why are they invulnerable now? Doesn't make sense, really. There are also other, larger plants that are seemingly just decoration, as they can't be interacted with in any way. Not a fan of this.
4. I fix my ship, and find out that flying it is extremely annoying. Flying is still helpful though, so I go from marker to marker and eventually find some knowledge stones and aliens, and feel like I'm making progress. Soon I leave the planet and go to a space station. As I enter the "doorway" to the spaceship, VERY loud rock music starts to play. The game is behaving as if this is the coolest moment in my entire life; "You're about to meet alien life! Inside an alien space station! This is amazing!" The music lasts for a while (good thing I can lower the volume of my computer) and I find three aliens playing poker at a table. I think these guys already got over the excitement of meeting aliens.
5. I sell most of my inventory (I didn't mention it before, but inventory management is a ♥♥♥♥♥ to handle..) and while 250,000 credits seems like a lot, two of the purchaseable ships I find on the station are both above 10,000,000 in price. On another planet I find a pillar of gold, and after mining it for several minutes, I get about 400,000 credits worth gold to sell: Getting those new ships won't be easy. Especially so because of the inventory management.
6. I manage to fix my hyperdrive and now I can travel between star systems. The galaxy map screen is a big tell of how the game as designer primarily for console rather than PC: There is no cursor in this menu, and navigating this felt insanely frustrating. I was eventually able to figure out how to warp to a different place, but I'll try to avoid using this as much as I can.
7. Menu screens are painful. When you enter a menu screen, the cursor is in the center of the screen, and "reload last save point" is also in the middle of the screen. If it wasn't for the fact you need to hold down the mouse button to navigate in menus, this'd cause me to reload saves on accident constantly.
Also, holding down the button EVERY time you need to advance to another screen in the menus? This gets old, fast..
TL;DR
Overall after 3.5 hours of gameplay, I've been left with the sour taste of buyer's regret in my mouth. It is absolutely ludicrous to spend 60€ on this game, and in its current state even the 24€ I paid feels like too much. I'll continue playing it to see if it gets better, but I have my doubts. Don't buy this unless it is on a very heavy sale.

I was very eager to play No Man’s Sky when it came out in August 2016 -- not because of the hype, but because of the ability to fly around in space, land on a planet, explore and discover alien creatures, only to return to space and visit another planet intrigued the nerdy kid side of me! I put down the game around Halloween 2016 to kill zombies and play other games relevant to the season. I forgot about NMS until I picked it up in June. I was really enjoying getting back into the game, building a base, and working through the Specialist missions. I had exocraft pads on several planets, was about to start farming, and had plans to save up for a freighter -- and was ready to give the game a glowing, thumbs up review.
That was all before the Atlas Rising Update; this game is no longer simple, chill, or enjoyable!! While the Update has added a few cool new features (like side jobs and improvements to the in-flight radar), much more has been introduced or modified that makes the game a complex mess!. The arbitrary changes to resource names, unnecessary modifications to the Analysis Visor and the interaction interface, the Mr. Fix-It interface to open Cargo Crates & Damaged Machinery [that pulls me out of the game a little], the unwelcome changes to the Discoveries menu, the addition of factions/guilds and system economies, the general wonkiness of flying a ship, and the loss of all the Specialists in my base - and resetting my progress with them - makes me very upset & annoyed! Game updates shouldn’t change things this much… especially for a game not in Early Access!!! (And I thought switching to Iron to recharge the Pulse Drive was going to be the worst change introduced by an update!?)
Actually, with the latest update NMS is giving me EVE Online vibes. EVE was a boring, complex mess that I quit playing after a few months. But, to be fair, EVE updates didn’t change things so drastically.
I’ll move on to other games on my To-Play list. If I do ever come back to NMS, it will be a long way down the road and only after I get the taste of alienation out of my mouth!

Wow, is all I have to say.
There’s something rather interesting when finding out that you've learned something as a result from playing a game specifically from a long time ago.
Sure the aesthetics are okay, nothing bright and attention grabbing at most times, but through this sacrifice, we see a marvelous work spring about. Despite these aesthetics, the artwork and camera angles were brilliant!
The story has meaning and messages of all sorts; from the impact of major wars on small European towns (the guard not seeing the static enemy correctly for decades which reminded me of the cold war as a whole), to how mechanical toys seem to be a thing of the past due to the times ('smart' robots replacing machines, smartphones, etc. in our parallel), to uncovering the mystery of a pre-ice age peoples who have been misrepresented by history. (The parallel of history not always being truthful or correct and the shifting of science based on proper connection).
Even the main character's personal debacles seem to connect in so many ways to the story.
It's been a pleasure playing, and at the same time difficult and rewarding to break out of my ADD shell that seems to be the core mindset that haunts so many top tier games nowadays.
You really get a good sense of the ‘general’ video game timeline that seems to sway with culture and society every year: this one showing the mindset of well over a decade ago. But this is not to say that it will be as black and white as comparing the first video game ever created to the last, but it is a vibe that's most felt through the medium of a solid interactive experience that withstands time...unless all you wish to do in the video gaming world is to level up and play the same player vs. player maps over and over again, then I would recommend it even more so that maybe a sense of understanding can come about!
But that's just me :D

He manages to create a believable steampunk-esq world of automatons and clockwork mechanisms against a backdrop of the real world. When this story is combined with the game's utterly beautiful environments and wonderfully haunting music, it has the ability to take you into another world. The animations are also worth a mention being very fluid and life-like. The animators' attention to detail is very clear to see.
I did have a few minor annoyances such as pixel hunting, the voice acting, while being decent enough, wasn't that great all round and the French to English translation wasn't quite 100%, but they are not enough to detract from what is an otherwise excellent point and click adventure.
If you are a fan of point and click adventures then look no further. Syberia is a very fine and tremendously enoyable adventure game.

*********************************************************************************************************************************
As the introduction to a now well known and defined franchise by Ubisoft {France and other studios}, Assassin's Creed™ is the cornerstone entry into now what has become Ubisoft's flagship brand.
Assassin's Creed™: Director's Cut is the quintessential version of that cornerstone. Ultimately, the game is fun to play to an extent. For those lost in the annals of the Assassin's Creed universe, this game is a great stepping stone to move into the now popular "revenge, passion, and growth" storylines that permeate the modern AC entries. For fans of Ubisoft's work, it can serve as an interesting look back at the mechanics and storytelling that launched a new IP.
However, I would like to stress that this game is not like its future bretheren. The game has little in the way of customization of either character or playstyle. The unlocks are given at defined intervals and there is significant travel time between mission sets. The gameplay is repetitive, taking place through a variety of event types that ultimately lead you up to an extended mission with a difficult situation to overcome tactically. However there is no replay value, as the missions do not change. The graphics are dated 7 years later, and the Director's Cut content does not add anything that changes the way the mission sets play out.
I do want to note that the game places much of stress onto players to approach situations how they want while being given the tools to do so. Two of the 6-8 side missions are required for the player to approach the set-ending assasination attempt, which leaves it to the player to decide how much preparation they want to place behind their precision. The future entries in the AC Universe certainly distill this methodology of player agency and expand on it, incorporating the side missions into the main story, therefore lengthening the story and making the work up to an assassination attempt significant in a different way.
I would also like to stress that the story is different as well. The story for AC was developed following the loose adaptation of Vladimir Bartol's Alamut. The story is not the typified AC norm (emotionally scarring event that leads the protagonist into a catharsis, forging the character and leading to the emergence of an assassin moving to vanquish those who wronged him/her/the brotherhood) The Assassin v. Templar threat is not well fleshed out here in the meta-story either. However, these are tropes left to the rest of the franchise to carry out.
I argue that this story line is the last one that has significant interpretation that can be administered. Although containing franchise staples such as revenge and freedom, the epiphany here takes the length of the game, and the true value is in the growth of the main character, not in the vanquishing of the main antagonist. The assassination's in the mean time serve as the vehicles that propel the character to the objective, without becoming the objectives themselves. It is here that the story shines, even though it is an adaptation of a story written in 1938.
Despite it's flaws, Assassin's Creed™ is a title that enthusiasts and beginners can both pick up and enjoy with the only draws being the repetitive nature of the mechanics. I love the game and certainly suggest it to all interested. With it's interesting and well written story, and fun gameplay with appropriate twists, this title earns and keeps it's place as the birthplace of AC and one of Ubisoft's riskier and profitible entries.
8/10
**It should be noted that Ubisoft took a financial hit in developing AC, losing a significant amount to a lack of sales driven by the release of this as a new IP and the lack of heavy marketing that Ubisoft now relies on. Ironically, the game's mechanics and models have been copied into many of Ubisoft's other IPs and has created an extremely successful franchise that is soon seeing it's next installments in AC: Unity and AC: Rogue, bringing the total number of console/PC AC properties to 8. Vladimir Bartol would be proud.**

I just gone done playing online for several hours and I'm gonna chime in and say that *Running with Rifles is awesome*. Its like Cannon Fodder mixed with Planetside or the Battlefront series. It even has a Sunderer/spawn truck. The gameplay is great, and the AI is a surprisingly challenging opponent, and not really all that much in a "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t!" way. Or at least I didn't get nearly as enraged at RWR as I do when playing Planetside or Battlefront.
It can take a bit to "grind" up the ranks (and the grind is unique to each server), but even the basic assault rifle is a competent weapon, and the first promotion unlocks what has become my favorite weapon in the game (and I've used quite a few in singleplayer), the SAW! You need to be prone or behind cover to fire it, but man that thing has firepower, you will massacre groups caught in the open and it also seems to do a very good job of pinning the AI. I'd blast away at them and they'd stay behind cover, I'd start reloading and they'd vault their cover to try to charge, I finish reload and open fire and they scramble to get back into cover. Its really awesome that suppression seems to work. At one point me and someone with a sniper rifle were holed up in a tower, fighting off waves of AI. I'd pop up and start spraying bullet across the whole group, causing the enemy to stop firing so much and the other guy would pop up and blow a few of their head's off. Then we'd duck back down before they found their courage/brains and started firing at us, hoping to hit while we're exposed.
The AI is really good too, which is good since the only two major servers I saw were co-op against AI factions. They seem pretty clever and will actively try to flank (and cover is really important) or flush people out with grenades. It seems you can also sneak up on them if you crouch/prone and don't shoot until you're close.
Now for the bad part. While playing online on one server I experienced some significant server-side lag/desync issues. Part of this was because there was 25-30 players, and part of it was because we were trying to grind our way into a final enemy base down pretty much a killing field and the place was thick with AI mooks. Worst thing is, every time we'd start to make some progress, the other AI faction (there are 3 teams in the game) would assault the territory we were attacking front, killing our momentum. I'm unsure how much of that lag/desync issue was the server itself or the game code.

Being a French game and all, one can really taste influences of Luc Besson's Fifth Element which is one hell of a compliment. The game is a linear beat'em up & platforming game with some quicktime events and the occasional puzzle.
In total I spent about 70 hours to complete it without worrying about getting all the achievements.
The story of 'Remember me' is based on the concept that memories can be stored, traded, stolen, deleted and altered.
Dontnod Entertainment is really a game developer to keep an eye on. Their other game 'Life is Strange' uses time traveling as a component which all seem excellent ingredients for a good and intrigueing story.
Because of such refreshing game concepts, the end product may feel a bit unfinished as the Sensen Universe really could make an amazing open-world experience. It's good but it could be a lot more.
There are only a few NPC characters in the game and they have very little screentime of back story. All seems to be revolved around the main character who is very likeable.
The graphics are gorgeous and the architecture, interiors, fashion and overall design are very believeable and consistent throughout the entire game. Rendered through Unreal 3 engine and you have a pretty sweet looking game.
The bad thing about Unreal engine is that modding is pretty much ruled out. This is too bad since the textures are a bit outdated as they are between 512 and 1024 square pixels.
The voice acting is done very well though some dialogue seems over the top.
Difficulty of the game is quite low and the only thing that may cause any trouble are multiple enemies attacking at once. The enemies do not have really advanced AI and will attack automatically on proximity.
Despite this criticism, I would really recommend this game. The immersive story is really worth playing and I'm kinda hoping for an open-world sequal with more RPG elements and NPC interaction.
Pros
- Neocyberpunk style rendered gorgeously in Unreal 3 Engine
- Excellent story line
- Very good soundtrack
- Actual swearing - makes dialogue much more believable.
Cons
- Extreme linearity with invisible walls
- Camera will go crazy once hitting an invisible wall
- The fighting system - though pretty fast - doesn't really feel smooth and you end up using the same combo over and over again.

Let's say something honest about this game.
This game makes me sad. Not because it is mediocre (just mediocre though, not utterly shameful), but because it tries and fails.
Caster has a few features which got me entertained for some time despite the poor overall quality of the game. The character movements are well-done and it's pleasant to jump n' run around with actually quite much fluidity. The entire terrain deformation feature also made me have a bunch of fun at it's well-included in the level design (I'd even say this is pretty much the only thing that keeps the lev-des acceptable along with the variety of the environnements).
The first thing which will strike you is the graphics. Jesus. I know it's Elecorn's first game, but the game came out in 2009 and I felt like I was playing an early PS2 game. The textures are low-res (giving by the way to your character the face of an eternal suffering) and the models are quite polygonal.
While I'm at it with the general graphics, the particle and pyrotechnic effects are horrendous. When you cast an attack, you really don't have a feel of empowerment because they just look so weak and unimpressive. Some fire and explosions would be welcome in order to take these pew-pews to the next level. Even the attacks from your ennemies are looking unthreatening, while they in fact at medium defficulty deal a good bunch of punch. This seems like a detail, but that will make the boredom come at you in an even shorter time.
Now 'bout the the gameplay. Like I said, there are a few interesting things which brings some spice to your adventure. But the gameplay is seriously too repetitive. There are tens of levels and the objective is always the same. Either kill all the ennemies, pick up some energy balls or make a dead tree come back to life. And it's a shame, because this game has potential. There could've been much more things to do, especially with the pleasant movement system and the different attacks to gather along the game.
Oh, yes, the attacks. There's a total of six attacks which are, like I said, pretty unimpressive, but fun to use for a little time. You have a basic pulse laser attack, a charged blast attack which deals great damage to both the ennemies and the environnement, an ability to raise the level of the ground, seeking missiles, stunning lasers and a (quite useless) shield.
Not only they look pitiful, but their upgrade system is too classical and bulky, and you just gather these attacks by approaching spheres which are spread in the in-game world. You don't acquire them by defeating bosses or gathering an out-of-the-ordinary object, nah. You just encounter 'dem spheres and yoohoo, magical attack learning. That is and will remain too simplistic and it totally does not give any feeling of accomplishment.
I could bash this game for a longer time, but this is just sad to look at. There's been effort and you can feel it. And I don't want to be too harsh on somthing that's been the output of many hours of work. So I just hope Elecorn will learn from its failures of the past and make us a neat Caster 2 in the future. Because they really seem to have good ideas, and good ideas leads to potential.

Somewhere between a short visual novel, a cute brawler, and an epic RPG, you will find Akiba's Trip.
Although I was worried when I first bought the game that the controls for keyboard/mouse were not liked by other reviews I was quite pleased to find the style manageable, and nowhere near as bad as for example Dark Soul's PC Port. The keybinds are displayed and can be changed before the game begins which is *much* better than getting no instructions at all and having a horrible keybinding set. As for the FPS - yes it is capped at 30 FPS, and it's true the game doesn't always exit entirely (you have to force close it down in Task Manager once you exit for your system to resume modern specs). The Story is comical although not so much that it's completely out of context, the English translations imo are akin to stylized writing being judged for it's errors (ie Intentionally making spelling errors, does not always warrant correction). I won't spoil the story but I will say that there is a New Game+ for those who wish to repeat it with a different character model, although your in-game sister still calls you "bro" and all the pronouns are "He" instead of "She" with a female model. You don't get to change your partner's clothes until somewhere in the middle of the game, and even then you have to wait till ng+ to change their underwear. Game is anime-inspired no question about it. It has several of the typical "dress styles" one will find in most Anime RPGs
didn't bother looking at the male ones lol.) All of which you can collect given enough patience. Undead & Undressed is kinda a niche game, but it's cutesy and not all that intense (except given the foul language on plitter, the game's version of twitter). Would probably be OK for teens (13+) but I'm not sure about what the rating is right off hand (i think it's M, but it's likely only that because of the language). As for undressed, you never see a character truly "nude" - they always retain their underwear.

"The Norsemen will not stop her. She will find what she has come to seek." (or something similar)
Rarely have I been excited enough to buy a game within the opening month, and have found the game living up to my expectations. Nay, outstripping them by a mile. Senua's Sacrifice is one such game, which combines the best elements of Tomb Raider, Far Cry Primal and psychosis (you read that right!) in a nail-biting adventure that neither cuts down on  graphics nor gives into jump scares. Must I point out some flaws ? Yes. So here goes, the very good and the improvable.
Graphics - They said Ninja is a small studio, but the graphics are as good (or better) than the latest Far Cry or Tomb Raider games. You'd think a game about mental illness would have a dreary nightime setting, which would have made the graphics easier to design. But no. Senua's world is vivid. Not always in a pleasant way, but vivid. Seas break on rocks in all their frothy detail, enemies' clothing can be made out to the smallest tear and even the gap in Senua's teeth have been dutifully portrayed. The world is beautiful, haunting and exciting, and does full justice to the psychosis effects shown therein. A masterpiece.
A side note about the aural effects here. In most games I'd jsut pass over them, but here they often take center stage. The devs used a binaural microphone, and advise using earphones. I would give the same advice. The audio effects are nothing short of amazing, giving you a level of immersion that AAA games like Far Cry fail to achieve.
Rating - 11/10! (Graphics - 10/10 + Audio too!)
Plot - Senua is a Celtic warrior with severe psychosis who wants to save her lover. She must journey into Hellheim to find do so. If this sounds like a copy of Dante's Inferno, you had me as a fellow thinker once. And would be proved wrong like I was. Starting out as a kill-the-boss-to-get-to-the-final-boss story, the game produces a masterpiece of showing how a person can make her own  sense of the world, and fight to fix things according to its own logic- her own logic. Storytelling is tight and well-woven, with enough left in the dark (literall) to make you wonder what Senua would have been in a different world, one which treated her more kindly.
The game delves deep into Norse or Viking mythology, which thankfully I had some idea about. Even if you don't, the game will tell you just enough for you to enjoy yourself. One grouse that I have is that given the protagonist is named after a Celtic goddess, a bit of Celtic mythology would not have been amiss. But ah well.
Rating - 9/10
Gameplay - The game is highly cinematic, but not in the Call of Duty "press X to save the world" way. You're driven on relentlessly, but even if you stop, the urge remains. Barring certain parts, the game allows you to move at your own pace, but the urgency remains. Thiings are helped by the devastating simplicity of the HUD, because there isn't one! Your arm tells you how many bites of the apple you have left, but that's it. No health bars, no QTEs, no inventory, nothing. Combat is just parry, dodge and time slowdown. Nothing exciting or too challenging, but again, fits in perfectly. After all, you don't want DOOMesque combat in a game like this.
However, I have one problem with this game. Female protagonists are always shown as "dodgers" ie they can't block heavy attacks, and sometimes, not even light attacks. Whether it is Tomb Raider, Remember Me or Senua's Sacrifice, this remains constant. I understand that women aren't physically as strong as men, but this habit of putting women into a combat stereotype not only seems somewhat dated, it also makes gameplay somewhat repetitive. I don't recall how many times I hit "space" to dodge, when there could have been any number of combinations to stop the attack.
Combat aside, there are puzzles. Some are tough, all are pretty, and all dovetail with the theme perfectly. But then Tomb Raider set the standard for puzzles, and Hellblade doesn't really raise the bar.
All said, the world is a set of interconnected areas, some of which you can backtrack  through, some barred forever once you pass through. So in a way, the game is highly linear. But a game like this couldn't be open world without falling apart. Senua has a purpose and she moves forward relentlessly. So the linearity works.
Rating - 7.5/10
NPCs/Characters - Senua is the prime character,  and I've already given her bio. She is a remarkably relatable person, who has had a rough childhood and a rougher adulthood. Her wishes evolve as the game progresses, and make perfect sense. Her pain, especially in the final section, will tear you up. The voices in her mind, while being useful sometimes, are also confusing. In a way, this is similar to how voices in all our minds work. Again, while the limping girl image is too Tomb Raider to be novel, the expressions and voice acting really make this game come alive without turning it into a movie.
There are others - Dillian, Senua's parents, Druth, etc. They all play their parts well, but this game is happening in Senua's mind (and her world). So they act as useful filler.
Rating - 9/10
Conclusion - Senua's Sacrifice is a masterpiece, even when it was expected to be one. If you're looking for a complex game with leveling up, complex gameplay and branching storylines, don't buy this game. You will find what you seek in a game like Witcher 3 perhaps. This game is highly linear, but the plot, voice acting, aural effects and graphics make it a treat. Moreover, its core message is simple and so well baked in that you don't have to look for it in the game's symbolic haystack. Given the developers' approach (see the Feature section AFTER finishing the game), this isn't surprising.
So am I looking forward to a sequel ? No, because there really can't be one. But do I recommend ? Hela yeah!
Overall rating - 9.5/10

I absolutely recommend giving this game a go, but there are two major caveats.
First:
The level cap is currently 30 (out of a planned 100), some of the higher-level skills are still unimplemented, and many features are still under construction. There are plenty of bugs, though none game-breaking.
Second:
Read the whole description on the Steam page. It is quite openly grindy. There is no Auction House (on purpose; don't bother asking for one). Mana recovery is via consumables only, unless you want to AFK in the inn. Mobs and player characters look and move like little pen-and-paper figurines, and movement and combat are on a square grid. Combat is turn-based. The list goes on; seriously, read the entire Steam page.
THAT SAID:
It's a charming game with a retro, tabletop feel, and a small, tight community. And most interestingly (for me), the devs are very active and very engaged with the community. We chat with them on a daily basis, both in-game and in the game's Discord. We discuss ideas and suggestions, give feedback on what we think is or isn't working, engage in general silliness, and occasionally get into heated exchanges regarding game design that go on for hours.
Give it a shot. Participate in something growing, something a little different. And if you decide to leave, maybe pop back in again after a few weeks, or a few months. See how it's evolved; you might find you like what it's becoming.

Whilest browsing through my library I was looking for something unique to feast my attention on. My eyes fastened upon 'Rememeber Me', third person action adventure game developed by DONTNOD Entertainment (the same guys who developed 'Life is Strange). You play as Nilin, a memeory hunter who has (ironically) has amnesia and is on a journey to not only save Paris from a corrupt corporation, but to discover the truth about her identity.
- Unique setting = Set in Paris in the year 2084, society has advanced to the stage where robots are common throughout everyday life and peoples' memorise can be altered and therefore, commercialised.
- Great visuals
- Good cutscenes
- Good voiceacting
- Good audio
- Decent story - Although there were plot holes here and there, I though the story was good at moving the game forward.
- Collectables - Unlock artworks, intel, 3d models and health and energy upgrades.
- Wide range of enemies
- Fast combat = Reminiscent with Batman Arkham games except without the gadgets or counters.
- Customisable combos
- Unlockable abiilities = Unlocked as you progress in the story, such abilities include : increase combat speed, invisibility and taking control of robots.
- Poor camera = Get annoying during cambat as it isn't positioned high enough to show the entire arena like batman.
- Not much to do outside story
- Poor save system = Saves are done automtically. Health stations are basically save points but are never indicated to player. Checkpoints don't save the game after you close the application down and play again, so you lose progress.
- Poor navigation indicator = A tiny arrow is a bit too small to see and may make you get lost in levels easier.
- Tacked on stealth segments
- Annoying boss fights = Mainly due to the quick time events, but also because some bosses bring their 'friends' along as well.
- Quick time events = Mainly in bossfights where you have to press the correct sequences to win or else you are forced to reduce the boss's health again. Also a few of the button prompts aren't clear either so you are forced to go check your key bindings to see what to press.
- Combat may get stale after a while = The problem is that although you can customise your attack combos, your moves are generally the same through out the game 9witht he exception of your abolities)
- Few bugs = There were rare moments where enemies would become invincible (when they shouldn't be) and when your character gets stuck in the environement.
Overall 'Remember Me' was a good action-adventure game with few issues here and there that prevented it from being perfect.

Just played/finished the game (It's a very short game, took me about 7 hours). It's a very interesting concept and story there's no doubt about that. Although I wouldn't say that it touches on our social media at all. It's more on the verge of talking about advancement in technology in regards to how it might affect us on a physical/mental level, which in this case using human memories to regulate our society. It's a game definitely inspired by many other forms of media like the anime Ghost in the Shell and Deus Ex. Deux Ex imo is a far more polished game that literally trumps this one in terms of sheer story, gameplay, and characters.
I would say that the plot of this game was "average" at best. It was nothing amazing and thought provoking like the 2 forms of media I mentioned earlier. The writing and dialogue is a little tacky, and there's little to no character development. The only character you will really follow is yourself. You don't really interact with many other people at all, and the motives of the people you bring down are quite cliche. I applaud the developers for making an entire world that is ran by people using their memories to get by, but they didn't write a stellar story at all.
Gameplay is repititive, but kind of cool for the first hour. The only unique thing this game has is the "Remix" sequences, which allows you to tap into a memory, and change it resulting in the victim remembering a fake memory instead of the real one. It's kind of cool, but you only get to do it like 4-5 times.
Honestly I would pick this game up if it's on sale, making it like $4. Other than that I would recommend playing Human Revolution, which is a far superior game than this. They're both quite different, but share the same sci-fi like setting, but Deus Ex goes way deeper.

PES 2018 is an excellent football game the best in years for PC. Unfortuantely it is once again ruined by high latency which in my opinion is caused by the automatch system matching players that live too far apart (I'm talking people living in different continents). I don't have issues with any other online PC games.

PES Online 60%    Now 80% (over the past few days the online has improved significantly and I now feel I can recoomend this game).

Visual aspect of this game is probably biggest win this year, unfortunately everything else is still unpolished.
Gameplaywise - through passes are far too strong. Goals scored from crossed are too easy. Finding open space - too easy. Despite great intro, there are hardly any real chants in this game. Something crucial for atmosphere of real football game. For some strange reason home team always starts a game. I pay attention to every detail and such things keep me remember it's just a game (which I could forgot in games like SWOS or PES4 and 6).
Some say that license is not a problem. Well, as football fan I want to play with real teams. Imagine Dragon Ball game without Goku. Sure - gameplay is most important, but lack of basic teams affects gameplay as well. Why Konami can't make around 20-50 empty leagues for modders to make career mode with all leagues, not only few? How can you play European Cups with just 4-5 leagues and some other teams? Unthinkable. License for CL? Well... only for tournament, because teams are not there.
Menu runs so horribly slow. Launching the game takes forever, walking through menus takes forever, everything is so damn slow, I can't understand it. Constantly loading something. Maybe Denuvo slows it so much?
Bugs happen as well - I played against AI, which had very strange formation, no gk during corners, just everything went wrong there. In training mode most teams have just one player - gk, with his clones. Anomalies everywhere. Not to mention that injuries are nonexistent (maybe because there're not many fauls to begin with). And why referee only adds 1 minute every game?
While offline experience with future patches could be great (minus some flaws), online mode is a lackluster. Myclub is nothing like FUT, matchmaking takes few minutes and even if it success expect pro player, who won't give you a chance or at least laggy matchup. Delayed input sucks :( Or is it player responsiveness that's so bad?
Yes, FIFA is almost the same every year, yes - gameplay is for casuals, yes - it's expensive and doesn't worth it, still everything just work better in EA's game. Konami never can't win this war with so many faults and repeating same mistakes every year.
No way this game is better than FIFA...

The story mode for this game is relatively short given that you only fight in a set number of stages for each character, with each providing a piece of the story and various view points on how the main villain of the game (the Skull Heart) had devastated or affected the lives of many. Disclaimer: Actual play time of 8 hours, due to steam offline mode. Single-player only. If your a CoD fanboy, this review is not for you, just vote it down without reading (like you do with everything), and move on.
I normally play more realistic or story focused shooters, but with most CoD fans saying this is the best one in the series, I thought I'd try it (single-player) with modest expectations.
It was still a mild disappointment. Production values were fairly mediocre, not what I was expecting from a highly praised big-budget game.
Graphics are ok, but nothing special, even for 2007 (inferior to Arma1, Stalker1 and Crysis which all came out the same year). Some level environments are quite nice, but most others are fairly bland and a bit too linear. Sound design is also nothing special, and lacks oomph.
The story is ok, but the missions are a very mixed bag. Almost all of them suffer from rinse-and-repeat enemy AI waves. Its all scripted, and seems to be aimed at instant gratification console peasants of below average intelligence. The US infantry missions are just a tedious shooting gallery with a shallow narrative tacked on. No matter what instructions you get from your officer, chances are they are not practical for the situation in front of you. If you deviate from the script even slightly, like attempting to flank where your not supposed to, the mission gets stuck or you get punished. At least there are a few missions with more interesting mechanics (like firing canons from a plane). The only decent conventional mission was “All gullied up” - much more atmospheric and better paced. If only the other missions were as good. You only get to do a (highly scripted) sniper shot once in the game, and only at about 150m. The campaign is quite short at 4-8 hours. The only really good thing was the few jokes your squad make now and then.
Open combat mechanics are not fun - arcade and bland. Almost every time you shoot an enemy a new one spawns right behind him, just around a corner. This creates the ludicrous consideration where you may not want to bother shooting someone to avoid dealing with the near infinite replacement enemy spawns. Weapons look nice and have great reload animations, but lack realistic power. Quite a few times the AI would ignore a bullet to the head or multiple rifle shots in the chest. Certain enemies are immune to damage if they are not “supposed” to die at that time - eg: hit a helicopter with anti-tank RPG and nothing happens. This punishes any player initiative. Enemies move without inertia. This makes aiming at them a pain. The AI will tend to just run at you mindlessly. Enemies throw grenades with machine-like accuracy and occasionally seem to be able to track your movement through walls. during training you are instructed to shoot through weak cover, but I encountered many weak surfaces that seemed to be just as effective as concrete. Friendlies are either invincible bullet sponges or get in your way  (example: grenade falls at your feet and AI is blocking the only door exit).
Overall CoD4 is a fairly mediocre game (but not quite “bad”). How this became the No.1 FPS franchise seems to have little to do with merit.

"The Norsemen will not stop her. She will find what she has come to seek." (or something similar)
Rarely have I been excited enough to buy a game within the opening month, and have found the game living up to my expectations. Nay, outstripping them by a mile. Senua's Sacrifice is one such game, which combines the best elements of Tomb Raider, Far Cry Primal and psychosis (you read that right!) in a nail-biting adventure that neither cuts down on  graphics nor gives into jump scares. Must I point out some flaws ? Yes. So here goes, the very good and the improvable.
Graphics - They said Ninja is a small studio, but the graphics are as good (or better) than the latest Far Cry or Tomb Raider games. You'd think a game about mental illness would have a dreary nightime setting, which would have made the graphics easier to design. But no. Senua's world is vivid. Not always in a pleasant way, but vivid. Seas break on rocks in all their frothy detail, enemies' clothing can be made out to the smallest tear and even the gap in Senua's teeth have been dutifully portrayed. The world is beautiful, haunting and exciting, and does full justice to the psychosis effects shown therein. A masterpiece.
A side note about the aural effects here. In most games I'd jsut pass over them, but here they often take center stage. The devs used a binaural microphone, and advise using earphones. I would give the same advice. The audio effects are nothing short of amazing, giving you a level of immersion that AAA games like Far Cry fail to achieve.
Rating - 11/10! (Graphics - 10/10 + Audio too!)
Plot - Senua is a Celtic warrior with severe psychosis who wants to save her lover. She must journey into Hellheim to find do so. If this sounds like a copy of Dante's Inferno, you had me as a fellow thinker once. And would be proved wrong like I was. Starting out as a kill-the-boss-to-get-to-the-final-boss story, the game produces a masterpiece of showing how a person can make her own  sense of the world, and fight to fix things according to its own logic- her own logic. Storytelling is tight and well-woven, with enough left in the dark (literall) to make you wonder what Senua would have been in a different world, one which treated her more kindly.
The game delves deep into Norse or Viking mythology, which thankfully I had some idea about. Even if you don't, the game will tell you just enough for you to enjoy yourself. One grouse that I have is that given the protagonist is named after a Celtic goddess, a bit of Celtic mythology would not have been amiss. But ah well.
Rating - 9/10
Gameplay - The game is highly cinematic, but not in the Call of Duty "press X to save the world" way. You're driven on relentlessly, but even if you stop, the urge remains. Barring certain parts, the game allows you to move at your own pace, but the urgency remains. Thiings are helped by the devastating simplicity of the HUD, because there isn't one! Your arm tells you how many bites of the apple you have left, but that's it. No health bars, no QTEs, no inventory, nothing. Combat is just parry, dodge and time slowdown. Nothing exciting or too challenging, but again, fits in perfectly. After all, you don't want DOOMesque combat in a game like this.
However, I have one problem with this game. Female protagonists are always shown as "dodgers" ie they can't block heavy attacks, and sometimes, not even light attacks. Whether it is Tomb Raider, Remember Me or Senua's Sacrifice, this remains constant. I understand that women aren't physically as strong as men, but this habit of putting women into a combat stereotype not only seems somewhat dated, it also makes gameplay somewhat repetitive. I don't recall how many times I hit "space" to dodge, when there could have been any number of combinations to stop the attack.
Combat aside, there are puzzles. Some are tough, all are pretty, and all dovetail with the theme perfectly. But then Tomb Raider set the standard for puzzles, and Hellblade doesn't really raise the bar.
All said, the world is a set of interconnected areas, some of which you can backtrack  through, some barred forever once you pass through. So in a way, the game is highly linear. But a game like this couldn't be open world without falling apart. Senua has a purpose and she moves forward relentlessly. So the linearity works.
Rating - 7.5/10
NPCs/Characters - Senua is the prime character,  and I've already given her bio. She is a remarkably relatable person, who has had a rough childhood and a rougher adulthood. Her wishes evolve as the game progresses, and make perfect sense. Her pain, especially in the final section, will tear you up. The voices in her mind, while being useful sometimes, are also confusing. In a way, this is similar to how voices in all our minds work. Again, while the limping girl image is too Tomb Raider to be novel, the expressions and voice acting really make this game come alive without turning it into a movie.
There are others - Dillian, Senua's parents, Druth, etc. They all play their parts well, but this game is happening in Senua's mind (and her world). So they act as useful filler.
Rating - 9/10
Conclusion - Senua's Sacrifice is a masterpiece, even when it was expected to be one. If you're looking for a complex game with leveling up, complex gameplay and branching storylines, don't buy this game. You will find what you seek in a game like Witcher 3 perhaps. This game is highly linear, but the plot, voice acting, aural effects and graphics make it a treat. Moreover, its core message is simple and so well baked in that you don't have to look for it in the game's symbolic haystack. Given the developers' approach (see the Feature section AFTER finishing the game), this isn't surprising.
So am I looking forward to a sequel ? No, because there really can't be one. But do I recommend ? Hela yeah!
Overall rating - 9.5/10

Its weird how Steam ties a negative review to 'Not Recommending' a game in general. I don't want to discourage people from playing this game. You totally should, you woun't know untill you try it.
What I want to do is share my experience wth this game and how I decided to play it in the first place. And this experience is begative.
I decided to try this game after seeing a whole lot of YouTube reviews where pretty much everyone who played this game would♥♥♥♥♥♥themselves while telling how great this game was. Naturally I set huge expectations going into it and this game consistantly failed to deliver on every single one of those. Maybe if not for the level of hype, I would have actually enjoyed this. On the other hand, I most likely might not have enven decided to play it. But I did, and spent the whole game thinking "What the hell is so great about this?"
My thoughts on the game ended up as follows:
- I did not care for the story, it failed to keep me invested into it. Senua herself is blant and uninteresting. She's crazy, ok, there is that, but what else? For me there was nothing else. Her background story failed to compell or make me feel empathy.
- Gameplay is boring as all lving hell. I don't feel like its a game in general. 6 hours long demo is more like it. Fighting generic enemies♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off more than it did anything else. Kept from falling asleep, though. Most of it is just walking, running, ocassional balancing on a narrow board.
- Puzzles are not really puzzles. A brain dead monkey can solve them.
- I do not see where praises towards the graphics are coming from. Senua is drawn very well, the rest looks pretty mediocre in 2k with every setting maxed out. I think people are mixing graphics and art for some reason here. Not sure why.
- Same applies to music. While I can't say anything bad about it, most of the time it is generic absolutely forgetable ambient, nothing special. There is, for example, the piece that plays during the fight with Surt, which is very distinguishable, as well as a couple other, but the rest of it is just there and does the job, there is nothing to praise like most positive reviews do.
Artistically this was very interesting, can't say anything bad about it. The atmosphere and the design of the locations was aso very well done. But while this can be observed and apreciated within the first hour, the rest of the game for me turned into trying to find the masterpiece people overhyped it to be, only to end up with the stuff I listed above.
In conclusion - this was not an enjoyable experience, a total waste of time and a thorough disappointment, which I had to force myself to get through.
So if you want to get this game - you should. But don't go into it overhyped. You might end up, just like me, forcing yourself to like something you do not enjoy.

People often ask me what it means to be an American. I tell 'em it's triumph. Triumph. Triumph when we nuke the disgusting Nazi regime that has taken control of Earth. Triumph when we replace the Nazi flag that flutters in the wind on the moon. Triumph when we peer down from the moon and laugh heartily at Russia. Triumph when we depose one dictator after another. Triumph when we break into the homes of Uberkommando kingpins on the other side of Earth and shoot them in the face. Triumph when we steal Nazi u-boats and use them to nuke others into oblivion. Triumph when we were the main reason the world recovered from Nazi rule in 1961. Triumph. Triumph. Triumph. But it's not just the the big things, see? It's the way I can set up lawn chairs at my friends house on the Texas Rio Grande and share a toast to freedom while watching Nazis charge into gunfire to enter my country. It's the way an Italian cabbie sits up straight and floors the gas when he hears my accent. It's seeing the wide eyes and bead of sweat running down the forehead of a Nazi customs agent when he opens my suitcase and I blast his head off. It's the way a French waiter hangs his head when I refuse the wine and ask for Coke instead, in English knowing full well he understands me (and that they have it). The way an Aussie blushes and leans into the urinal next to me in the bathroom, asking me how I'm such a strong, muscular, dashing Nazi-killer, or the scowl that meets my smirk when I tip a liberated English waiter in the newly printed US dollars covered with Washington's face. The way small mobs of Canadian school children follow me from a distance to see what a free, Nazi-destroying man looks like, or how heads timidly rise and women gather when my accent stops the music in the clubs of Amsterdam. The laughs of my American companions as we burn Nazi flags and paper Reichsmarks intro crisp, black ashes. Triumph. Every bit of it, triumph. That's what it means to be an American.

But To The Moon proved me wrong.
I played through this game non-stop from start to finish. I couldn't bring myself to stop playing. The story just drags you in and you just want to find the next answer, which itself would raise even more questions. The unique way of storytelling combined with an incredible plot, vibrant characters, an atmospheric art style, and a beautiful soundtrack creates one of the greatest experiences you can have with games. If anyone refuses to believe that games can be art, just show them this.
So if you're looking for an experience, a mystery, or even just a burst of emotions, you should definitely pick up To The Moon. Very few games can be called perfect, but I think this one definitely ticks all the boxes.

I WANT to like Stash, I really do. It's a noble attempt, and it's got some interesting design ideas. But when it comes down to it, the game is miles wide and inches thick. It's a worthwhile time killer, but ultimately, I can't see myself devoting serious time into it. There are so many more rewarding games out there, and while you'll have to spend real money for most of them, it's usually worth it.
My motto for F2P games: If it's worth playing, it's worth paying for (supporting the devs in some fashion). If it's not worth paying for, it's not worth playing. And at this time, I cannot see investing money into this game.
Edit, a few days later: I spent some time today chatting with one of the Devs, who disagreed with my characterization of the game being "miles wide and inches thick." He and I discussed the game at length, and we both agreed on a few points, particularly for the newbie experience, that needed some improvements. I gather that he made some changes to the game as a result of the discussion, in terms of reducing cost for early "Upgrades." I also spoke with the people in their Discord channel, about many of the same things, particularly the crafting experience.
But even after all of that, I still stand by my point: The game has many different systems, but they're all fairly simple, not very deep, and not very complex. The biggest problems that you're likely to have are a lack of in-game instruction on how to do things, and running into artificial barriers, called "Upgrades," requiring resources and money (in-game money, not real money - although they're VERY willing to let you use real money to sidestep these barriers) in order to advance, hindering your progress and requiring grind, grind, and more grind.
In its current state, this is going to be an extremely narrow niche game, and the odds of it matching much of the gaming audience is very low. Expect to rely heavily on in-game chat or out-of-game Guides and Wikis to answer questions that will inevitably pop up, questions for information that THE GAME should be giving you. And if you start getting annoyed and complain... expect the loyal followers to turn on you quickly.

TL;DR -> Grinding game with no real fun gameplay early on. Try it only if you are used to grind (and you really like to do it). Be warned tho, other than grinding you are going to be walking back and forth from A > B > C > A.
A: Grinding area > fill inventory.
B: Town (sell loot).
C: Hideout (personal warehouse and crafting place).
A: Grinding area with empty inventory.
Which is not bad, but the inventory fills so quickly that you won't be grinding 10 encounters without needing to go B and C.
----
Now, i'll tell you my story with this game.
I tried to like the game, so far the first few hours are a total and complete grindfest, mixed with a bit of traveling into town to sell loot you don't need.
You start with a very small inventory with an outrageous amount of ingame currency needed to expand it.
So after you kill four or five encounters, you'll need to go back to town, sell stuff, go to your hideout, stash crafting materials, and then go back to grind other four or five encounters until you need to go back to town again.
And i mean you NEED to go and sell things, because naturally you want to buy a bigger inventory to grind for longer.
The game uses turn based combat, yes, but it wasn't fun.
I do love turn based combat, I enjoyed a ton of King's Bounty (sega genesis and then Steam), FFT, Atlantica Online and such, however, this game was pretty basic.
Combat was all about spamming basic attack, one or two skills that only increase the damage you deal (no strategy needed for the early game is guess), and nothing more.
Maybe if the grind wasn't so hard in the early stages of the game then i could have endured a bit more until real strategy was needed.
All i had to my disposal was my basic attack (no pushes, no stuns, no debuffs, no use of the environment).
At least until level 10 or so, you might just be using your basic attack for the most part. Specially if you want to save up on healing items (mana included) because you want to buy that extra inventory.
I mentioned level 10, it doesn't sound that much of a grind tho, but I played it for 4 hours and only made it into level 5. Sadly i cannot endure boring gameplay for too long.
I have faith that endgame can be good, but if the early stages are THAT boring, then i just cannot recommend it unless you are a real fan of grinding.
I even beated the first boss, a rock golem. No strategy at all.
Attack > receive damage > attack > repeat.
The loot was pretty good tho.
By the way, grinding with turn based combat is not for everyone. You'll have so many delays to your grind (wait for each enemy turn, attack animations, encounter animation) you just can't do fast grind on these games. I mention fast grind because early game is way too boring to play it seriously.
It's specially slow if you don't want to go everywhere with a full inventory, and of course you don't want to, since the game is all about grinding and you need to buy that extra inventory slots to grind for longer without going back.
Higher level grinding areas are far away from town, you need a bigger inventory if you don't want to use most of your playtime walking (which again, isn't necessarily bad, but there is nothing to do while walking).

I try not to give negative reviews when I feel a game is actually trying to be good.  I think they are trying.  I just think they are falling a little short.  Below is a slightly long winded account of my first couple days in Stash that led me to my slightly reluctant negative.  If you care not for details and just want a quick summary, scroll your ADHD self down to the last 2 paragraphs.  I'm not moving it up here for you.  Hmph.  Kids these days...
So....I decided to become an enchanter.
I bought an incantation table and tried to place it in my 'BOO'.  BOO being your player home.  Guess what?  You can't.
You can't place the incantaion table in your home until you level up your home because it has to go indoors and your home at this stage is a sleeping bag on the ground.

You need assorted quantities of half a dozen materials to level it up.  Game doesn't tell you where to find those materials.  You go to a vendor to buy some.  Guess what?  You can't.
Vendors don't sell them.  You have to fight mobs for them.  Because everyone knows bats carry bricks.  Riiiight.

You finally manage to find what you need to level up your home to place the enchanting crafting furniture and you click on it to make your first enchantment!  Guess what?  You can't.
You need Twinkling Dust to make your one beginning recipe.  Where do you find that?  Nothing tells you.  Vendors don't sell it, Monsters don't drop it, you can't farm nodes in the world map or dungeons for it.  You check the 'newspaper', which is what passes for a player market.  You search 17 pages to find it because there are no categories or search methods in the newspaper.  You find some.  10,000 Triads for 99 of them.  As a new player, you are making about 20 triads per battle.  So...500 battles.  Don't worry though, mobs drop a LOT of loot.  It sells for an average of about 8 triads per piece.  So lets say 300 battles to buy some Twinkling Dust.  I don't really mind that kind of grind.  Grind is part of the charm of a crafting flavored RPG.  What I mind is players trying to charge that damn much for it.  I won't reward people for that kind of self centered gluttony.  So you have to search a wiki because there is no mechanic to hover over a crafting requirement and get even a clue of where to attain anything.  The Wiki (which is so incomplete it doesn't even have a description of all the classes and covers nothing past level 5) says you get it by putting enchanted equipment in a disenchanter.  So I have to have enchanted equipment before I can make enchanted equipment?  Logic.
You go kill mobs until you finally get a piece of enchanted equipment.  I had had some before this but sold it out of necessity.  I didn't know I would need to keep stuff I can't equip.  Nothing indicated that.  SO I sold it because you are severely limited on storage and each upgrade you buy only gives you 1 additional space.  Have 19 spaces, buy upgrade, have 20 spaces.  Ridiculous.  Characters level up one level at a time.  Do they only gain 1 health?  No.  Storage should not be constrained to that either.  You don't buy a new closet for each shirt you own.  Logic.
Next you have to buy a disenchanting station and place it in your home.  Guess what?  You can't.
Turns out it has to be placed in your yard, not in your home.  Again, nothing at all points this out.
You finally figure this all out on your own (becuase some of us play RPG's for the game aspect and don't like having to use it as a giant chat room to figure out the basics of a system that should have at least some descriptions or hints).
You craft your first enchantment.  Only took 7.6 hours of stumbling through a very unintuitive crafting system.  You joyfully try to apply it to a piece of your mob-loot equipment.  Guess what? You can't.
It can only be applied to player crafted equipment.

So you have to go back and learn how to craft weapons and armor so you can use your sparkly new enchantment.  Guess what?  You can't.
Unless you pay premium currency, you can't learn more than 1 skill.
Now I won't say I don't like the game.  I just don't like where it is at.  It is needlessly vague and cumbersome for no other purpose than seeming to want to force people into seeking help at every turn.  Yes, I do realize it is a multiplayer game.   I  do not, however, see that as a valid reason to force players to 'chat' or get lost.  I don't play RPG's to make new friends, and even the old players get sick of answering the same questions over and over for every new player that wasn't online 10 minutes ago when the last new player asked the same question.  So instead they get pissy, snappish or offer to 'help' the new player by selling them what they need at grossly inflated prices.  Loupe costs 10t from the ONE vendor that isn't selling food.  They'll sell it to you for 1000t. Out of the kindness of their hearts, of course.
I see the course the game is on as being a short road to an obscure ghost town.  That could easily change.  The game has a certain charm.   But when you try to force people in to being friends in order to get what they need, it's going to bite you in the aft-end.  It makes this feel more like a Facebook game than an RPG.  Need a sword?  Invite 12 friends!  No thanks.
Please, allow people to learn multiple crafts without paying for it, put a search function on the newspaper, and add at least a short description of recipe and crafting components on mouse-overs, and it would help the game tremendously.  In the first hour I played this my son said "That looks cool" and he downloaded it.  By hour 7 he said "I'll just uninstall it, it doesn't look like it's worth it to me."  And that is kind of how it feels at this point.  Not worth the time.
So in the end I have to give the game a thumbs down.  Not for the camera angle, graphics, or gender locked races, but for the ununtuitive slog that the crafting is presented as and the immediate need for a premium purchase in order to succeed in that crafting as a solo player.  If that is not the kind of thing that gets under your skin, or if you have a few friends to dungeoneer with that you can pool your crafting talents in with, please, give the game a try.  It is geared towards groups or friends and would probably be immensely more fun with cooperation.  For for a wizened old hermit like myself, it felt punishing rather than fun and I can't recommend that in good faith to other wizened old hermits.
Frogdice, please keep up the updates, take some of the criticisms of myself and other players into consideration, and make a few tweaks to this dusty jewel.  You really could have a gem on your hands.  I would be more willing to make premium purchases from a developer like you who has actively kept up with and loved their game, if I felt there was a future for the game.

There are few games which really stand out. I find that these days story is what drives me most, and most games lack in that. They opt purely for action and fail to show true narrative. This game... This one is on a world of its own. From the very beginning the narrative is rich and filled to the brim with lore. The world is rich with beautiful scenery, and the motion is fluid like water. Yet, there are insanely terrifying moments as well. It's amazing how the world can shift from this calming atmosphere to the most barbaric and hostile environment so smoothly. It's an invigorating experience. I often found myself wanting to stop to catch my breath but, at the same time, craving more. This is one of the most original games I've ever played, and recommend the experience to anyone.
People often say "play this in a dark room with headphones" well, this game is different. Not because you shouldn't play this game in a dark room with headphones, but because YOU MUST do so. The audio is so powerful that it's an experience of itself. And, while definitely not the weak of heart, it's certainly something everyone should experience for the sake of knowing just how truly amazing this games development is.
There is combat, but you can immediately tell that it's second to the story, and not in a bad way. Rather, the combat is simple enough that it "compliments" the story with this concept of a physical struggle alongside the psychological. It's never hard enough that it will seem unfair, but it can be made hard enough to simulate a true struggle for survival. It's very sharp and responding, I never felt out of control or cheated. The devs clearly thought out the combat as a secondary aspect as well, as you clearly have the option to turn combat into Easy, Normal, Hard or Auto to fit your desired playstyle. This way you can completely focus on the story and truly immerse yourself without the fear of frustration.
This is game of the year material and needs to be played by anyone who dares call themselves a true gamer, it's an entirely different experience from the average copy/paste material we've all experienced over the years.

Immersive, original, casual yet challenging dungeon crawler with turn-based combat!
I say casual because it's not too long to complete and it is easy to play (but combat can be hard, especially on high difficulty).
I greatly enjoyed this game. I took my time on normal difficulty, completed it in around 30 hours, died a few times, for a few bosses I had to adjust my party members (you have a pool of extra characeters). There's still replay value because I could try highest difficulty with a different party setup so there is a great amount of content for a casual game.
Story: Loved it. Simple, easy to follow and get into, yet with interesting details along the way.
I really felt like a paper sorcerer trapped in a book / digital world.
Music: Awesome. Electronics inspired by 80s dos sounds mixed with accoustics. Don't expect a medieval fanfare though, it's modern music, to me it fits the game and its inspirations perfectly adding a lot to the immersive factor.
Graphics: Simple, original art style, fits with the whole game atmosphere very well. Beware however it is mostly black and white (some nice color effects here and there make it feel like alive ink art). Environments are extemely simple and repetitive . Not a lot of ennemy variety but interesting drawings...
Gameplay: it's mostly about long turn-based combats, which I love. Don't expect too much in term of exploration and puzzles, there's a few secrets to look for, some involve back tracking if you feel like it but it's all optional.
Controls: Average. With the mouse sometimes it feels like a tablet port. Controller support would have helped especially since this game would be easy to play simply with directions (cross or stick) + buttons for accept cancel and menu. However I was able to customize the controls in the main menu to my liking using mostly just a mouse with 5 buttons so it ended up OK for me.
Overall: Great gem of a game, especially considering it was made mostly by one person. That person was able to express something with this game, I felt it and I greatly enjoyed the experience, very immersive (sometimes repetitive, just take a break when that happens!).

Much like the game itself, this review is going to be very occupied about the non-gamey parts of TNC.
My main problem with TNC is that it lacks the chutzpah of TNO, my second problem is that BJ is far too fragile for the game he is in - though that is perhaps, debatably, the point.
What do I mean by chupatzah though? For me, TNO was, although knowingly silly, a terribly grim game. It was a game that had nazi robots and 60s moonbases right alongside concentration camps, genetic experimentation, monologues on the values of eugenics - all without batting an eye. It embraced the camp imagery of decades of WWII propaganda films and managed to turn it into something horrifying by contrasting it right next to the real deal. That takes conviction, I think, and its a conviction that isn't so clear here. The game suffers from this, not just because I think Wolfenstein somehow has become an important bit of anti-fascist media (which is hilarious), but because, more objectively, the emotional core of Wolfenstein is in the very specific evil of National Socialism. BJ and the Gang as characters are written to reflect the different kinds of suffering that exists within this system, but without that being apparent in the plot or villains, the motivation for the crew becomes a lot less interesting - they took us over and destroyed out cities so they are baaaaaaaaad.
Nowhere in this game do you have anything coming close to the holocaust level (again, hilarious to say out of context), and without it, only the silly campy B-movie stylisation is left. It's kinda vapid, is what I'm trying to say. It's a lost opportunity, really, considering the setting had so much untapped potential. Where's the damn KKK that keeps getting namedropped but never seen? What about the reintroduction of slavery? What about the "best baby" contests that were an actual, real thing in America as part of an early eugenics movement? Where is the complicety that allowed America to accept Nazis in the first place? Where are the Americans who don't want the nazis to go, and would actively fight against a revolution? How could BJ, the lug-head patriot, fight his own "kind"? And can they be called his own kind, then?
Again, I see missed potential.
This is not the end of the game's story problems. Without getting into spoilers, BJ's arc is one that I'm not convinced by. It's not earned. Nor is the "victory" at the end, which comes aprubtly at the end, like an added scene. The game even calls it what it is, An Epilogue - but then where is the ending? It's like the second half of the game belongs to a different body. Haha.
But,
I did enjoy my time. I don't regret buying this game. The enviroments are stunning, filling in so much of the detail the plot leaves out; the cutscenes are all wonderfully directed, one in particular being a stand-out in the midway point; the gameplay is serviceable, the shotguns heavy and hatchets sharp. This is a Good Time for Killing Nazis, and I love doing it as Blascowickz. It's also really funny, far more than I remember TNO being.
But with a plot that doesn't want to take itself seriously, it all feels a little for naught. As the reverend friend in the game might say: "History repeats itself: First as tragedy, then as farce." And that's just a shame.
(Also the game crashed a ♥♥♥♥ton on me like c'mon Bethesda you coulda Q&A'd a bit more and not released it right next to Assasin's Creed and Mario. Hot PR tip, me to you.)

This game has been out there for about 2 years or more, only available at Desura (where it has already got a bit of a fanbase), but now it has finally found its way to Steam. It provides players with a really unique experience by making them seemingly insignificant - in "RUNNING WITH RIFLES" you are not "the chosen one", you are just a soldier, just like the hundreds of others around you. If you think that titles like Call of Duty or Battlefield can give off the similar kind of feelings - you are horribly mistaking; in Battlefield you fight maximum of 32 enemies at a time, while in RWR there can be hundreds of them! Therefore, yes, you will be totally unable to turn the tide of a fight – nobody can defeat 200 hostiles on his own. However, don't think that player's actions don't matter at all: you can take charge of a squad, and then you'll possibly become a real threat, that you enemies won't be able to simply ignore. Your squadron will still not be able to destroy the enemy forces completely, but it will deal significant damage by blowing up their vehicles, radars and other tactical points, capturing their fortifications and slowly depleting their reinforcements.
In the single-player campaign, as well as most of the multi-player battles, the majority of both players' and opponents' teams consists of AI-controlled soldiers. Bots can do everything players can - form squads, drive cars and tanks, take cover, use knives, grenades and sniper rifles. It's worthy of note that AI is really decent, not as good as a real person, obviously, but much better than in most other games, even singleplayer ones, and especially indie-titles. It will try to flank you, use every advantage it can - trenches, artillery, vehicles. It acts pretty much like an RTS AI, which makes it smart and quite challenging to deal with.
But what makes the game for me - it's its community. Online players are very friendly, people often cooperate to achieve certain goals; more experienced players always help the newbies to fit in; low-ranked players are often OK with doing a little bit of roleplaying and executing higher-ranked ones' orders. Even the devs can be found online chatting with the community!
So, if you are looking for something new in Action genre, if you are tired of "standard" shooters and always-angry players constantly yelling at each other, you should totally try "RUNNING WITH RIFLES".
An update? Indeed! More so, a post-release one.
So, what has changed in this game over the course of months? Not much, to be fair. The community has grown a fair bit, but most of the people are still nice to each other; the AI got even smarter than it was previously; the very few issues that there were with the game crashing to desktop seem to have been resolved; the user interface has been partially reworked, and now it's somewhat more intuitive and less confusing for the new players... so, to sum up, the game process hasn't changed much since this review was originally written, which was over a year ago. Instead of adding new features, overcomplicating the game and breaking it with every update, the dev focused on tweaking and fixing, which, in my opinion, worked out perfectly. All the small problems that this game had have been fixed, and nearly all aspects of it have been improved in one way or the other. If you considered "RUNNING WITH RIFLES" interesting, but didn't want to buy an unfinished game, now it might be the time to do it; most likely, it has only become better since the last time you checked.
P.S. My apologies for my bad English, which is not that bad, but still no way near perfect. It became somewhat better since the review was originally written, and yet I'm still kind of dissatisfied with the quality of the review... so, feel free to point at my mistakes if I wrote something stupid. ;)
