Caster is a third person platformer shooter with slight RPG elements. Basically, this is a mission based game. You select levels and get missions upon entering them. Missions are generally things like, collect all the orbs or kill all the enemies. Although there are more complicated missions, especially later. As you go through the first set of levels, you'll learn the basics, get new weapons, and collect in=game currency. You use the in-game currency to buy upgrades between levels, such as boosting your natural abilities and powering up the weapons you have collected. You can walk around, jump, and shoot for basic controls. However, you can also hit jump again and hold the button to do a super jump, which can help for dodging enemies and clearing distances and obstacles. The other special ability is a dash, which allows you to run quickly. This can help run up slopes and across water. Combining these two special abilities can make for some great techniques. There's also an interesting mechanic of being able to destroy and build up the land with your weapons. This can make tough situations easier depending on what you choose to upgrade and when. There are three sets of levels. The first set are there to help you learn the basics. The second set will make you use your abilities in more interesting ways. The third set will challenge your skills. It's a simple design that has lots of potential. The art is very colorful and pretty, even if I had to run it in minimum settings for my old worn out computer. It still looks really nice, and the music is alright too. It also has a low level of story investment.
What I mean by that is... there's only vague story connections from mission to mission, and they don't have much to do with an overall plot. Also, not everyone will be thrilled with the graphical style, as it is dated in terms of modern games. Plus, the level selection method may turn away mordern minded gamers, as well as the simplistic gameplay. The third set of levels are made by the community and aside from the fact that they are very difficult, they're just a bit of a hassle to get. They aren't included with the game download, nor are they available through Steam workshop. To get the third set of levels, you need to go to their site, download the levels, and place them into the correct folder. It's not complicated, but it's a hassle that I'm guessing most won't bother to do, even though it's worth it for more levels. And you'll want more levels because the second set of levels, designed by the developer, is unfinished. There's one mission that, when selected, simply says to be continued. This game, according to the Steam store page, came out in 2009... and it's still not finished. This leads me to believe it's not going to be finished, or if it IS then it's going to have to wait until the developer isn't busy with other projects, which is a shame because this game has lots of potential and I'd sure like to see it through to the actual end to see know what it has been building up to.
Still, Caster is tons of fun if you're into platforming third person shooters. It's kind of like a 3D Mega Man if they had done the Mega Man Legends games differently I guess. It has simple rules that create so much potential for cool and interesting levels and missions. While it's not complete yet, it's still worth the 3 dollar asking price. I got it on sale thinking I'd hate it, but it's actually a lot of fun. You could wait for a sale, but it's worth the money anyway. Just make sure you get those extra levels for some more fun. Caster gets a 7/10 for being a very fun third person platformer shooter similar to those a few generations ago.

The story just drags you in and you just want to find the next answer, which itself would raise even more questions. The unique way of storytelling combined with an incredible plot, vibrant characters, an atmospheric art style, and a beautiful soundtrack creates one of the greatest experiences you can have with games. Strange. You do not know who you are. You know you are alive. But your memories are long forgotten. Thrown into unfamiliar territories and shaken by orders in the face of adversity. How do you adjust to the reality you are confronted with?  A piece missing from the shift of boxes labeled blank and new and old. Constantly triggering new emotions, reactions, and actions, and all that remains? To Remember...
DontNod developers seek to engage gamers in a unique third person action/adventure game featuring a amnesiac female struggling to regain her memories in a world of corrupted corporations and the lingering doubts that plague her consciousness. Remember Me is a fascinating third person, action, adventure, plat-forming game. Featuring Nilin, a memory hunter with the power to remix memories, subjected into a world where memories become products in the daily sci-fiish dystopian world of 2084 largely taking place in Neo-Paris. Where memories are an integral part of human society that can be tweaked, bought, corrupted, and made.
Jumbled, fragmented, hacked, and tweaked. Imagine any precious memory you hold dear, become erased or tweaked to suit the user willingly or unwillingly.
Keeping that train of thought we emerge with Nilin, in an ironic sort of twists starts off with having her memories erased and it is up to you to restore them and take down the corporation called Memorize because a dude compels you to. That’s it. But wait! That’s not all; enter a uniquely crafted world built by DontNod in their own depiction of Neo-Paris which I found to be strangely inviting albeit colorful in the design aspect of the game. No two places I came back to have the same environment used in the graffiti, advertisements, the paintings, slums, the vibe of the combined essence of sci-fi buildings coupled with merging it with past architecture in a sort of high tech, but with a stroke of homage to the works of old. The combination that resides from mélange (meaning mixture) creates a very awe-inspiring setting to behold. Attention to detail not only in levels and cinematic places were carefully fleshed out that for a moment I felt like I was in Neo-Paris a la 2084.So much so that I had “Woah,” “Wow,”during my blind playthrough on Hard difficulty and even moments of “meh.” These moments of “meh,” are primarily in the game-play elements...
First off, I would like to highlight a unique aspect of Remember me in one of their game-play mechanics to go back into a person’s memory; re-live the memory through a 3rd person omniscient observer playing god. You can troll the users in the memories by tweaking it, a nudge of a folder, an open product of which was originally shut-off, or perhaps kill the client outright. It is an interesting mechanic the likes of which I can’t seem to remember a similar game like this. These moments are where the game truly shined. For not only does the memories give some insight into the story itself, it allows a great respite from the tedious combat levels.
However, the game is not just built on a point and click adventure where you can re-mix memories at your disposal.
.
While, I raise an eyebrow at such a design choice, I have mixed feelings for the brawling mechanic, not that it’s bad far from it, but it isn’t certainly exceptional in my eyes. To be frank I spent a lot of times hitting my enemies through the punch and kick style only. Through most if not all the game. My enemies were ridiculously hard. I was limited to only kicking and punching them along with 4 special abilities (60 sec cooldown’s) different from my combos. I mixed and matched my combo’s with a punch here and kick there with a combo spared in there. I felt it was tedious albeit tiresome to complete a level after a cut-scene, plat-forming a bit, walk and gawk at some artwork (Mona Lisa comes to mind) and then come back full circle against spongy enemies just to progress through the main story. I spent a lot of time mixing up my combos one’s that give health, extended combo times, and a lower cool down reduction combo’s helped tide the minor annoyance. In retrospect I think I should’ve gotten the dlc to get more combos... But... I’m a cheapskate so I didn’t think I need it. Nevertheless the game play brawling style didn’t hold a large amount annoyance to merit a negative in the game; I’m just “Meh,” on it.
Since, there were different enemies that progressed in the story that made me think of ways of how to effectively kill or shut them down made such an annoyance to a dull and mixed satisfaction when coupled with intervals of the cut-scenes to move the story along, with an interesting short cast of 10 not including the enemies. A cast of which told enough dialog to get me to become intrigued enough to be focused into the story and enough to move the story that had me guessing of how did Nilin lose her memories and why I have to take down Memorize. The soundtrack also helped keep my interest within the game throughout all of the game which was a plus in my book in adding atmosphere to each level. The boss battles too were versatile enough to not be a generic run of the mill buffed up enemy you see from around the corner. And troublesome in a good way to be different from the previous bosses and later bosses that allowed me to bear a grin on my face after countless failures most of which were my fault for being slow on the Quick time events to finally succeed.
For Remember Me,
Is a bold new i.p.  game that quite frankly is an underrated game. Remember Me stands on a plateau with her head held high that can with time can become a truly great franchise with time and effort. It’s by far not a horrible game, and holds a certain amount of originality to its name to entice newcomers to try Remember Me and satisfy gamers with an appreciation for new Ip’s and action adventure games.

I waited to review the game until I had fully cleared the game,  Akiba's Trip is an oddity in the gaming world and honestly ~ most people are not going to get the anime and otaku tropes, and will just see this game as a weak RPG with some lewdness,  however - that couldn't be further from the truth..more or less, to put it mildly -- you have to be an otaku in real life to fully enjoy and understand Akiba's Trip.
I could mirror everything other people have said about the game, about the story involving Synthisters and Night-Eaters but that would be pointless.  So what I'll offer is the more techical negatives this game suffers from first.
The biggest problems with Akiba's Trip is that the game is quite easy, especially once you max out your equipment although on the hardest difficulty setting (Otaku Mode), even with maxed out items the game can still be a challenge if you don't plan your attacks, and learn how to counter effectively especially when your enemies can do juggle attacks which completely prevent you from dodging/blocking or escaping.
Another problem, fortunately it doesn't really appear until you play the game on higher difficulty settings such as Gamer and Otaku mode is that during major fights, the view can become blocked by scenery or the entire viewpoint can shift completely.
Everything else about the game though is positive,  their are many different endings - a huge amount of character customization, lots of different and wacky weapons to use although, a few weapons are a bit overpowered.   The story and character design is very good, alot of emotional scenes and interesting areas of Akihabara to discover.

So as I buy pro evo and fifa every year, after hearing that pro evo 2018 was going to have the new engine that the consoles have had for the last few years I was looking forward to playing it.. thats where it was a shambles though.
Seeing as I see pro evo as more of a passing game, you would of thought that they would of improved on this but unfortunatley just like the whole game, the AI lets the game down major.
You can have a player right next to you that you press pass too but then the cursor will flick to someone about 20 metres away so the player that you tried passing too just stands there absolutely gormless and you can't control them either. It also has the problem of players recieving the ball just standing on the spot waiting for the ball to land at their feet before moving too.
You can still pass right down the centre of the box and the defending AI will move out the way for you every time or pass it out to the wing and keep crossing it in because the attacking players always seems to win the headers.
I have saw so many howlers on the game regarding the AI already and it's only been out a few days. You know it's bad when you see opposition players online where their goalkeeper and defender are just running senseless into each other to the point of hitting off them into their own goal. Every person I have played has inconsistent records of wins and losses because the game seems to be scripted where your players don't seem to turn up and just stand motionless off the ball.
I will say one good thing is the co op clan games where you can team up with 2 of your friends and play another 3 players which is a pretty cool feature.
Overall it could have been a good game but it is just let down by the AI majorly. It's like the gameplay is too fast for the AI to react and the cursors are too unresponsive to react to the speed of the match. It needs serious tweaking and fast.
You know it's bad when you score 3 goals in 3 minutes gametime because you do the same thing over and over because the AI cannot deal with it (I wish I could upload the picture here).
--- (PRO'S) ---
- Co op clan feature online
- A new team with randomised player feature
- My club where you don't have to spend real money.
- Keepers improved and actually make good saves most of the time.
--- (CON'S) ---
- AI is terrible (way too unresponsive for the speed of game)
- Passing does not always go where you press.
- Cursor problems constantly
- Needs consistency in matches (sometimes your players don't turn up and don't move)

The complex storyline, meaningful choices, and incredible character development present in this masterpiece known as "Shower With Your Dad Simulator 2015" render it worthy of a $60 price tag.  However, the unfathomably generous developers have priced this game at only 99 cents.  The plethora of modes available to players enables casual gamer's to endulge their fun side in "Endurodad", while hardcore gamers can put their skill to the test in race-against-the-clock modes such as the world renowned "Dadathlon".  In addition to the various game modes, Shower With Your Dad provides three characters for you to play as.  These characters are as follows: Thomas and Magnum, Richard and Lefty, and Johnnie and Robin.  Each character includes meaningful choices that directly affect their development, and Lefty's story in particular is rather heartwarming.  Growing up in Chicago in 1952, Lefty defeats his childhood bully and grows up to become a male backup singer for the famed doo-wop band "The Shirelles".  Now now, I don't want to ruin the wonderful tale for those who are yet to play the game!  Thus, I will not discuss the details of each character's story, but I can ensure players that with each and every character is attached a heartwarming story that will take gamers on emotional rollercoasters. All in all, "Shower With Your Dad Simulator 2015 Do You Still Shower With Your Dad" is a complex and beautifully developed RPG adventure with a complete storyline and character development.  This masterpeice is a SERIOUS Game of the Year Contendor; it is my personal pick for the 2015 Game of the Year Award.  I hope readers found this review helpful, and remember, dont hesitate to purchase the game! You won't be dissapointed :)

The beginning scene last maybe a little over 20min which is just a bunch of voices saying random things to you as you wade through this river basin which provides little character overview and gives you little reason to care. The second is "Combat Mode" which forces you into a 1v1 enemy situation where you're locked onto your enemy and smashing the left click button until your imaginary enemy is defeated. Within the first 43 min of gameplay you find yourself doing the same location puzzle 3 times which comes off as boring and uninspired, this game tries to apparently have a psychological affect on you as you hear voices chattering at a constant rate while at first this seems pretty cool it becomes repetitive and annoying.
I wanted to like this game but I can literally recommend any game, every game I have refunded on steam this is by far the worst and I beg you to look at gameplay videos instead of going purely on a friends recommendation.

Short:
Do you like shooting men? Go buy the game and start shooting men!
Longer-ish:
RNR is a Battle-Cannon Fodder-Field kind of gaming experience, combing squad tactics, personal skill and battlefield immersion into one thight and fun package. It doesn't matter if you prefer to be a lone wolf, outflanking and ambushing the enemy or if you like to coordinate with your squadmates to break through that choke point, you'll have plenty of opportunities to do both. When I first saw it on Desura I thought the abstract art style would hinder me get really immersed into the actual game, but the opposite is true. Soon you'll find those green and grey figures beeing more of a loyal comrade or a more hated enemy than any of those high fidelity player models in other games could ever be. It's that little bit of graphic left out, that gets filled by your head automatically as you play, that really helps getting you unto the battlefield, screaming and laughing as you kill and die.
RNR is a multiplayer game at heart, but it also offers a solid singleplayer experience with the AI creating a fluid flowing battlefield for you to conquer, explore and die in. To be entirely clear, Caster is pretty terrible. It’s also a ton of fun, in large part because it’s only just barely holding it together and doesn’t really give a damn if anything makes sense as long as it’s entertaining.
Everything about Caster is more than a little insane and nonsensical. It’s always trying new stuff just because it can, and though this means the whole game feels like a crash course in engine experimentation, somehow it works. It really has no business being as fun as it is, but something about running around as an immensely overpowered MegaMan-reject is so stupid I was barely able to keep it together while playing the game.
I have no doubt Caster would be a huge chore if it insisted on imposing any restrictions on you or ever became an actual challenge (though a few moments in the second half begin to weigh the game down), but for the most part it lets you do whatever you want. It doesn’t matter if it unbalances the game or even breaks it in places, you’ve been put into this sandbox to blow stuff up and run really fast and that’s about all I needed.
Caster might be barely competent but I can’t help but admire how little it cares or tries to pretend it’s anything but a bit of super dumb fun. I can’t stress enough how stupid everything here is and how delightful I found it. So, sure, I could tear it apart as an ugly piece of garbage, but apparently I was in the mood for something so-bad-it’s-good and Caster more than fit the bill.

Akiba's Trip is a somehwhat odd but ultimately lighthearted
game, that intentionally plays into traditional anime tropes because it's a celebration of the culture as a whole. Aside from a few cringe worthy references here and there which I imagine aren't in the original japanese translation, the game ultimately feels like a love letter to otaku culture and isn't afraid to poke fun at it or deconstruct it briefly in the meantime; I swear while reading pitter in this game that I somehow found my way back to a chan website in the middle of the game.
You can tell this game was made on a budget since some side missions are re used by the end of the game with merely an increase in difficulty and a different reward and the story is presented to you via Visual Novel like appearance. On top of this, the combat system is a bit repetitive but when you think of it more like a turn based RPG with brawler elements with a heavy emphasis on crowd control instead of a brawler with RPG elements, it makes a lot more sense within it's context that it'd have repetitive animation as turn based RPGs usually do.
Akiba's Trip is still a genuinely enjoyable experience though if you're into JRPGs as a whole, however. The writing is often flippant, witty and also intentionally campy; Just reading item descriptions is an enjoyable experience in this game. The characters are likeable
, there's a lot of custimization, even down to the color pallete of the game itself and what animations your partner uses.
There's not a lot as utterly hilarious as giving your partner a thug walk/idle animation and having them follow you around starting♥♥♥♥♥♥with random synthisters, which are the antagonists of this game. Basically the reason you have to strip the clothes off of your enemies is because they're vampires of a unique brand who will burn up in the sun only when their clothes are removed.
If you like stuff in this vein, I.E. stuff like Persona or Yakuza, or you like visual novels and or immersive Playstation 2-era JRPGs then you'll like akiba's trip. If you can't stand things like anime archetypes, even though they're presented more subtly here you probably you won't like this game.
All in all, I'd give it a decent 7.50/10, my first playthrough doing every side quest I could see took me about 35 hours. The game's worth your time if you like JRPGs or just colorful light hearted settings. And besides, this game is previously a playstation exclusive; Having it come to PC is kind of a big deal, I just wish it wasn't locked at 30 fps. I forgive it though because it's supposed to be emulating an anime art style, and that♥♥♥♥♥♥s usually at 24.
I plan on doing more than one playthrough because it has NG+ in it and there are different routes to pursue in typical VN fashion.
Sums up Akihabara pretty well.

Next-Gen PES is here! This is a moment long waited for. Konami has indeed put out PES games on an outdated engine for years now, it was about time they upgraded it. Finally, I can say I'm playing a new PES this year. It's absolutely stunning visually, compared to past iterations, and the gameplay itself is much better.
One very positive thing is that AI no longer feels like it's cheating (on Regular difficulty level at least). Yes, sometimes you're frustrated that they get lucky, but at no point do they grab balls from two meters away or score from off-side position without getting stopped by the referee. It's not the best AI, but it's certainly better than past ones.
The only big downside are the licenses for teams in Premier League and La Liga, as well as the missing Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga, Erstedivisie (Netherlands 2nd Division, Jupiler League) and Portugal Segunda Liga. Those are usually fixed via patches done by the community, so in time this will feel like a non-issue, but I'd still like EA not having exclusivity on some of those things.
On the other hand, Konami has exclusivity on UEFA Champions League and UEFA Europa League, so there you have it: Two great competitions, right there, for us to play.
Long live (better) PES!

Let me start by saying this is one of the best football games I've ever played, but that aside not everything as it good as it seems.
Konami released the game with broken servers, an insult to a loyal PC fanbase that had to wait years to even have a game remotely comparable to it's console counterpart. They fixed it within a few days but the fact they hadn't already tested the servers beforehand just shows a total lack of professionalism and I would expect more things to go wrong.
The Computer consistantly attacks and defends in the same way, for every team, on every difficulty. You could be playing Barca, Bayern, Man United or Derby County and they'll all try to do the same things over and over, it all feels the same in Master League and makes the experience boring after 2 or 3 matches. More variation and less lobbed through balls for my full-backs to be waiting to pick off constantly would make such a polished game much better.
There isn't much I can fault on this front, PES 2018 is a beautiful game and it shows on the highest settings, every animation feels smooth and like watching a real game, aside the occassional humurous glitching and clipping which is to be expected in a game.
It's PES, what did you expect?
The players react how they would in real life to recieving the ball, taking realistic touches to control the ball with their entire body and dribble around players, the close control is much improved and benefits from a slower game speed than we're used to, favouring slower build up and creative passing.
The passing feels good, the through balls perhaps aren't as good as previous releases but if you're a good player they present absolutely no issue to utilise.
Unlike previous PES games, you can't just throw everything and the kitchen sink at opposition defenders, you need to play like a real football match and carve out chances. Mix up how you approach attack.
The defending feels clunky, unresponsive and broken at times but again, if you're a good player and don't mind your players not even going for the ball unless you manually do it yourself while contesting with a player switching system that feels unruly at best then it's not too bad.
I'd give it an 8/10 personally, there's a good base to build off for 2019 but as of right now it doesn't feel complete to me, no matter how fun it is.

Remember Me is a Wall crawling and melee combat game set in 2084 Neo Paris.
Very Cyberpunk environment.  Very challenging even on easy mode.  You will need to learn to use combat moves correctly to make it to end.  Bosses and combat gets progressively harder, with larger groups of attackers at times.

Main Character is great at free climbing and jumping and the path has plenty of: ledges, pipes, hand holds, ladders, jumps, leaps, drops, dangerous areas and rides on objects.  MC is a melee fighter, she runs into preprogramed fights a lot along her linear path.  There is health stations and other pickups hidden along the route and the auto save is helpful.  The path is shown by arrows on the Augmented Reality viewer, but hard to see the path sometimes.  The automatic camera system is terrible though, you can use something to move the camera view.
MC has several combo attacks choices LMB is a 3 hit combo, RMB is 6 hit combo, and 8 hit combo and you have other modes that you can activate after gathering focus and has cooldowns.  The combo attack skills are unlocked and can be placed in any order, but there is no clear detailed stats on what each individual skill does.
MC also can steal and manipulate memories, so there are memory remix puzzles and path guides.

I absolutely loved this game. I understood Nilin's sad childhood and it's an overall very depressing game, so the emotional appeal worked for me. There wasn't really any chance to explore Neo-Paris and if they did this like Gravity Rush, I think it would've worked better (missions with a set path but time to explore the city for as long as you want between missions). Spoiler: I didn't actually expect for Nilin to be the daughter of Sylla because I figured that it was just another remix like she did with Olga. I really liked how they did that because it wasn't super obvious until she's calling the little girl in the backseat by the protagonist's name. Another thing that could've been done for Remember me would be to have more chances to remix because it's so interesting, but maybe have slighlty less depressing remixes because I always felt sad after them (especially because you make a husband die, a man kill his wife which led to his suicide, blaming the mother instead of the child for a car accident, and having a father kill his daughter). Overall though, this is honestly one of my favorite games now because it drew me in with an interesting story, awesome character designs (espeically the holographs), and a heck of a lot of emotion. I am definitely going to look for more games made by DONTNOD. (Btw Jax and Nilin were precious together.)

I remember when this game came out in my junior year of high school. Great time. I was an awkward, nerdy little♥♥♥♥♥♥with more time than I'd care to admit and I guess I was looking for something that'd make me *feel* stuff. One night, a couple of buddies were over and we all decided we wanted to play something with a story. Something that'd eat up a couple of hours and keep us all focused.
Enter: To The Moon
As one of my buddies narrated the dialogue, we were absolutely enthralled. We couldn't tear ourselves away. How did we get so wrapped up in what was essentially a move-and-click sprite game with cliche tropes and easy puzzles? By the end of that session, we'd finished the game and, for reasons you'll understand if you decide to play through, all of us sat in the dark and cried for a while while we talked about what we'd just experienced.
I cared about the characters, I loved the soundtrack, and every moment of the game made me feel warm and fuzzy. I've sat down to show it to a few people over the years since then, and even though the magic and surprise is gone, I still can't help but smile like an idiot or get a little teary-eyed while I play this game.
Ladies and gentlemen, regardless of your age, if you buy one story-driven walking simulator this year, don't let it be Dear Esther or one of the seventeen ripoffs of that game; let it be To The Moon.

A bad case of Alzheimers.
Anywho lets get into this review of Remember Me.
In Remember Me you play as a character named Nilin, who has lost her memory and must retain them and bring down the Memorize Corporation with the help of a mysterious asset named Edge.
To be quite frankly honest, Nilin herself isn't really an interesting character, she seems quite bland and boring for my personal taste. Some characters you meet along the way are far more interesting such as Olga Sedova (Interesting Fact: Olga's Character model was tweaked to become Victoria from "Life is Strange") anywho she just like Tommy, Bad Request, are Interesting characters whom you don't get much background from, and sadly they only make very few appearances, although they are your allies, only Edge whom you don't see phsically is in constant contact with you.
The story itself is interesting, I liked the idea of a world where Memories were bought and sold, even stolen or wiped. It was an interesting concept that I enjoyed, and It made me wonder how it became to be and what would happen when we brought down the Memorize Corporation, will everyone be restored to Normal? or will we all have lost memories. The Story is interesting enough to keep you going from Chapter to Chapter, making you discover whats happening next. It was also nice to see throughout the game the restoration of Nillin's memory, slowly getting to know yourself again, before your memory was wiped, there was one major plot twist that I enjoyed but ill let you discover that on your own.
The setting was perfect, the "Neo Paris" fit perfect to the theme at hand. From the  slums to the high class Neo Paris was an interesting place to explore.
Gameplay, well to be quite frankly honest the combat got a bit repetative and at time it was annoying remember combos which you must land perfectly or you won't get your combo buffs. The enemy were pretty simple to kill, only the invisible lurkers were completely obnoxious (I hate invisible enemies). One other annoying factor is when your combo breaks (which will happen alot), when you fight a large group of enemies and your doing your combo, they hit you once and your combo breaks and you must start again, really irritating. The parkour is pretty fun though, jumping around and grabbing onto ledges and items.
In the end I would say this game is "Mediocre" its not Good but its not bad either its average. I enjoyed playing it but did get to a point where I just wanted to finish and get it over and done with, but overall its a decent game.
I would highly recommend buying this on sale, and not at the full retail price.

If I were to compare this game to others, it's Runescape meets Fire Emblem/Final Fantasy Tactics.
The game is great. Levels feel like they mean something further into the game, crafters aren't overshadowed by dungeon/mob drops. They have value. The potions, armor, and weapons they make are better than any random drop you get. But not everyone can afford crafted gear, so the dungeon drops aren't worthless by any means.
The crafting can be a bit tedious, since you're locked to one crafting profession unless you make another character to help craft or use their paid currency to unlock another crafting slot. And that might scare players away thinking the game is p2w since you can unlock more of your character than others by paying money. It's not.
Now I won't say this game's cash shop is irrelevant cosmetics, it has things that make the things a LOT more convenient. Namely inventory space. This game uses a Bag/bag size inventory system, and you can use their paid currency to get better/bigger bags and unlock bag slots. But you can also do that with the ingame currency called triads (just like gold).
There are mounts, just not visibly shown. The game shows your character more like a Figure than a living character. The mounts grant movement speed, like they would in any other game, and can be bought with both paid currency and ingame currency. But the price/effort between those two is incomparable.
And it becomes very apparent when someone has a mount and you don't, and you're both heading to a resource node. And with the bag space, more inventory means less time running back to town to sell and put items in your stash. WIth that said, you can find resource nodes when you engage in a fight.
The fighting system is really what hooks me to this game. It's grid based combat, so you have limited movement area as well as ability range. But that's where the combat mechanics come in to have you plan out your next move carefully. For the battle mechanics, there are elemental attacks and mobs with weaknesses/resistences against those. Without a beastiary or monster journal, you just have to go through trial and error or ask in global chat. Lastly, the battle mechanics I enjoy so much is the monster/player placement. You can be surrounded, pinned, and flanked. You can do these to the mobs as well (surrounded and flanked require a party member) and it makes for a much more engaging fight since these effects place a debuff on whoever is affected by it.
This game also features player housing and I won't sugar coat it. It's very, very tedious to manage it. There are multiple materials needed to upgrade the size of your base, increase how many items you can list on the auction house (which is accessable globally, really nice), how many items your stash can hold, and how many crafting tools you can place. When I say crafting tools, I mean like an alchemists table or a weaponsmiths anvil. There's also farming, but I haven't gotten into that since my current profession doesn't need it.
All in all, this is a great game. It needs work and clarity on some mechanics, but the dev's are VERY active with the community. They have a discord server and always talk to their playerbase. I absolutely can't wait to see what future this game holds.

I applaud the developers of Stash for creating the most original, refreshing game in the MMO genre in many years. Their passion and vision are evident in so many elements of the game. They clearly set out to create something missing from the MMO genre and they succeeded.
The main game elements are turn based combat, crafting, developing your house (called your BOO or Base of Operations), and social structures (clans, parties, and apparently religions too in the future).
They really nailed the combat. It is fun, challenging without being punishing, and as I gain levels I can see more complexity being added.
Crafting is done very well and is more interesting than just clicking a recipe and getting an item. There are multiple steps involved in gathering and refining resources, especially crafts that involve farming (for food or leather). I have not messed around with the market much but it looks like you could be a full time merchant also.
Your house is really incredible. It is almost like a full Sims game here. I have only scratched the surface but it is already very cool.
Social structures like clans and parties are clearly a big part of the game, but again I have only dipped my toe here.
Now I need to specifically call out the community which is incredible. This is something really missing from most online games. Too many games these days have toxic communities and the devs done care. But the Stash developers have very clearly put an emphasis here and it shows.
Speaking of the Stash developers, they are very active in game and on the game's discord. Yet again they show how much they care about this game and its community by being directly involved.
I highly recommend this game and hope you enjoy it as much as I have.

Okay, so I've given this game quite some time before I decided to write a review.  Skip to the end for the TL:DR, because this is gong to be long.  I bought this when it first came out, and found it to be incredibly grindy and the controls and functions of the game were nowhere near intuitive.  Making money to buy any sort of ship (or buy a whole lot of anything really) is insanely difficult if you don't grind your rear off for hours, some mission-vital resources are incredibly scarce, and storage is so miniscule for some items that you can barely carry much of anything aside from the essentials.
The Foundation Update was quite nice, but the sheer amount of stupidly long fetch quests you have to go on is rediculous just to get a few pathetic blueprints.  Also, Rigogen, now called Kelp Sacks or something, was a major setback in my ENTIRE progression through this update, and there was no crop you could make for it either. (Not sure if they added it in the Atlas Rises update because I could not bring myself to get that far through the fetch quests again, but that's for a later section)  I did like the addition of bases, but it felt like something that should have been there from the start.
Next we have the Pathfinder Update.  Again, ground based vehicles were a welcome addition, but there were still more detriments to be added.  More fetch quests, and expensive summoning platforms if you can't find the blueprint for one of the key resources (this falling back on my previous point about money making being difficult).  I loved the vehicles themselves though.  They are fast, can harvest resources fairly quickly (after the fetch quest to get the mining laser blueprint), and allow you to safely traverse on land and in water (the only thing that makes collecting Rigogen slightly easier).  This is probably my favorite update so far, but does not make up for the grievances I have against the rest of the game.
And now we have the Atlas Rises Update.  Where to start...  Portals take a lot of resources to activate (okay, not that big of a deal), but to use them you have to scour every cave you can find so that you can get fragments that you have to use to dial in a portal.  I tried to find some, but there is nothing that comes up on the HUD to help find these dead explorers, not even clues as to which direction to go.  That aside, the economies introduced are confusing and the resources that you can trade between systems take up a whole slot EACH in your inventory, which makes having a large amount with you when you go back to sell them nearly impossible.  I tried to go back and forth selling valuable goods, but after making only 10K in profit, I decided to say screw it and move on to the new missions.  The mission "board" in each system is a nice addition, and a nice way to get credits and items, but there is no real direction as to what you need to do.  "Mine a Resource", "Kill Wildlife".... Okay, but what resource, and how much wildlife???  The same now goes for the fetch quests; they don't tell you how much of resources they want you to collect to bring back to the quest giver anymore.
TL;DR -
Look, I gave this game an entire year of playing off and on, and I just can't say that this game is good.  I love the idea, I love that they're trying to make things better, but at this point in time, it's not playable in my eyes.
Pros:
- Lots of exploration
- Diverse creatures and planets
- Base building
Cons:
- So much grind
- Unrewarding fetch quests
- Incredibly difficult to gather any real amount of money
- Certain rare and hard to get resources not farmable (literally)

I went into this game with very low expectations. Frankly, I only got it because there was a ridiculous sale that dropped the price down to 14 cents. Upon playing it, I was pleasantly surprised. The gameplay is simple but very fun. It's a third person run and gun action game that puts you in arenas of varying sizes, each with a simple task to complete. There isn't a lot of variety in these tasks, it's either collect orbs, destroy monsters or a boss, or shoot a tree... it makes sense in context. The game isn't very challenging or long, I beat all the currently available missions within three hours and a good chunk of that time was just faffing about running and jumping for fun. The mobility in this game is what makes it so fun. Running and high jumping all over the map kept me amused and entertained throughout the whole game. There's also an arsenal of weapons that range from rapid fire homing bolts to terrain morphing blasts that make the gameplay more unique. The art and design style leaves a lot to be desired. Everything is blocky and unpolished. It looks like an early PS1 game in alpha. Still, it doesn't really affect gameplay so it's not a big deal. There hasn't been many updates to this game even though it's pretty old so don't expect new content. There are community mods, however, so you're not limited to the main game. Even then, this game is reasonably priced so you're not getting ripped off if there aren't any more updates. I'd say, give it a try. It's far from perfect but for what it is, it's fun. Plus, it'll kill a couple hours if you're bored.

I bought the alpha of RWR back when it had just come out. (Before release on Desura) A few weapon varients and some grenades were about all you had back then and it was thoroughly enjoyable. Since then it has become quite a beast, improved graphical fidelity, multiplayer, ranking and a basic inventory system all creates a game which has a lot of potential.
There are some gripes, no abilities for lower ranked classes, the AI being a little perculiar when it comes to vehicle movement and the aiming (Which has actually become much more user friendly since the last time I looked at it.) but these are simple gripes which will, I am sure be figured out as they go along.
Apart from those small things, Running with Rifles is a geniunely unique shooter that has some fantastic arcade graphics and game mechanics that hide its' hardcore inner beast.

I've played the Desura release of RWR for probably at least 100 hours (and most of that's just in single player) and can confidently recommend it to anyone looking for a fun shooter with some very unique qualities.  More to the point, I've described this to friends as a combination between Cannon Fodder, General Chaos, and War Hawk.  On top of that, the game really gives a sense that you're a tiny soldier in a big war.  You won't be able to Rambo your way to victory, but instead will need to work with your team (even if they're just AI) to achieve objectives.  Speaking of the AI, it's really good and constantly being improved.  I believe the developer even had an interview somewhere about developing the AI.  It reacts to situations dynamically and can do almost everything the player can.
All of this comes together in a really fun way.  If you like pick up and play shooters but long for something a little more dynamic/deep then this is the game for you.  I find myself just enjoying watching the AI soldiers fight and it's satisfying knowing I'm a part of a larger battle.  There's really nothing else like this out there.
Edit (as of June10/2014): A player experessed some concern that RWR isn't very similar to Cannon Fodder, so I want to make a note here about my comparisons to other games.  Read on.
Cannon Fodder: Cannon Fodder's movement feels "floaty" to me (in an arcady good way), and the mouse aiming, while less precise than RWR's, is similar.
War Hawk: Mostly because RWR is a fairly large-scale multiplayer game, but also because even in singleplayer, as I've mentioned in my review, RWR makes you feel like part of a team. That's something I felt quite strongly in War Hawk as well.
General Chaos: Probably the least warranted comparison, but hey, obviously I like General Chaos and wanted to make some connections.  General Chaos has been described by some as an RTS, and certainly it has tactical elements.  You control where your soldiers move and then just hold down one button to shoot (which you absolutely do NOT do in RWR) but in commando mode you control one character directly.  Again, the movement is similar and there is cover.  The battlefield is isometric, so not quite the same perspective, but close.
Net War: I sincerely doubt many people played Net War, but basically it was one of the first online only shooters.  It was overhead, had team based modes and there were vehicles.  Pretty similar actually, but RWR is better.

This game is the best game I've ever played. The controls are tight and responsive, yet Ori's movement remains fluid and swift. The art is incredible; every area hints at a hidden history that you can only wonder about. The music fits perfectly with the mystical forest Ori journeys through, and makes the story all the more memorable. One thing about this story (I won't spoil anything): As simple as it is, the story of this game is one of the most evocative stories I've ever experienced. I almost cried at the end, and I'm not the type who cries at the end of movies (let alone games).
The puzzles were fairly intuitive, but still were challenging. Simply figuring out how the puzzles work is half the challenge. You also have to figure out how to get through them without dying or dropping something.
The combat is brilliantly designed; it gives the player several ways of defeating their foes and lets them discover ways to use them. I frequently found myself using dash and bash in combination with Sein to defeat enemies quickly, and often felt like my skills were superhuman, even when I barely got by.
The game is practically open-world. The only things keeping you away from the more difficult areas are deadly enemies and locked abilities. Every area is revisitable, except for the escape sequence from the wind temple (which is partially revisitable). The save system is very unique. It allows you to venture wherever you want, and set up checkpoints almost anywhere, at a cost. If you checkpoint too often, you'll find yourself low on energy when you really need those checkpoints (which can be very devastating). If you don't checkpoint enough, eventually you're going to die to something minor and have to go through all the stuff you did since you last saved, including story clips.
The only issue I had was some minor difficulty spikes at a couple places, mostly due to bad checkpoint decisions on my part. I highly recommend it to...anyone. The gameplay is flawless. The level design is clever and always interesting. The story is evocative and memorable. The art and soundtrack are fantastic. It's an incredible platformer for all gamers, new and veteran. Ori and the Blind Forest is a masterpiece.

Its been a while since I've written a legit positive review, so heres a legit non-satire one.
Remember Me is CQC Combo-centric game that has arena combat and combos at the center of everything. The two-button combo system is simple, yet complex at the same time. Its not about doing rediculous inputs, but rather keeping time and a steady rhythm while dodging other enemies. The game throws 5-6 enemies at you at once and expects you to keep track of every one. In between fights there are some parkour segements, and if you have played Uncharted 2 or 3, its basically that, just more linear.
The story, was absolutely amazing. Although confusng, if you can peice it together, its a very good story. It stars Nilin, a memory hunter who has had her memory wiped, Throught the game, on her mission to end the corrupt force of M3morize, she finds out about herself and wonders if what she is doing and what she has done is right or wrong. There are several plot twists I wont spoil, but they have little build-up and no foreshadowing, makng them some of the best plot twists in any form of media I have ever experienced.
The visuals are an ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for your eyes. For a 2013 game, its extreamly sweet to look at. From the run-down slums of Neo-Paris to the busy commercial area, the game looks amazing. The lighting effects are some of my favorite things to look at in this game.
The soundtrack. Why cant I buy it. The soundtrack is just absolute genious. Its dynamic with combat, as in the music will get more exciting when you preform combos or use special moves. It is a prefect mix of classical instruments and artifical music, something I did not think was possible, but the composer nailed it and needs an award.

Like all games that take place in the future, Remember Me is set in a dystopian-esq world where the rich are richer, the poor are poorer, zombies exist, and memories are a form of currency. You can remove bad memories and relive good ones over and over again, perhaps even other peoples.
Nilin is a freedom fighter in Neo-Paris in 2084. She's fought against the destructive nature of memory monopoly company Memorize and the way they've allowed their technology to be used as punishment, to remove the memories of a negative event even though it had a major impact on that person's life, and to turn normal human beings into zombies who've lost their mind and can only destroy for as long as she can remember...or so she's told. All of her memories have been erased and she's in the most secure prison in Neo-Paris, the Bastille. Then, a man named Edge, who is able to communicate via the memory plug located on nearly every human's neck, instructs Nilin how to get free and return to her old self. For the rest of the game, you uncover Nilin's lost past and attempt to free everyone from their fake self’s.
Combat is similar to a 3D fighting game. You press buttons to do combos, called pressons, that either allow you to steal health from enemies, reduce cooldowns on special skills, or straight-up do more damage. You also, eventually, get what is essentially a gun, Spammer, to shoot switches that open doors, turn on/off lights, or just to do a little damage from afar and break shields of certain enemies. She also has access to skills, S-Pressons, which can affect battle by giving you more power, blowing-up enemies, and several other effects.
It's somewhat of a clunky system as you can only continue combos on one enemy at a time but, since you're constantly getting hit and having to dodge around without a target lock, it's easy to lose said combo. It can turn simple battles into a bit of a grind if you're only allowed to hit someone once or twice doing barely any damage. This is easier to overcome late game when you realize you gain more presson options to make a short, powerful three attack but mid-game it can be frustrating. If you're against one to three guys, though, it can be pretty fun, assuming you're getting most of the frames per second and not lagging like I was.
Character depth is, for the main characters, amazing. Nilin is a strong female lead who, after the prologue, isn't a damsel in distress and is a legitmate ♥♥♥♥♥kicker. She shows her emotions but when the world around you is, literally, falling apart, most people would show some concern for the brain annihilated zombies or innocent people being pillaged. You also feel for all the bosses in the game. They all have some pretty heavy baggage which you get to see via the Memory Remix sections of the game where you manipulate the memories of certain characters for the reasons Nilin needs. The only issue with the Memory Remix sections is they're not very open ended. There were plenty of options for several endings to them but there's only one and it can take a while to reach. There's so much stuff to do in the mixes, and most are interesting, but sitting and twirling the joysticks for 30 minutes trying not to miss the two frames you need to catch to continue gets boring.
Remember me tries to keep things fresh by changing levels up a bit. Sometimes you're fighting but often you're Assassin Creed style parkouring, albeit in a linear fashion, from ledge to ledge. One level has you running from a maniac in an attack helicopter. Other times, you're reliving memories to avoid bombs or open doors. There’s also a fair bit of walking around that allows you take in the amazing backgrounds and appreciate how much time and effort was spent into developing the artwork.
The music fits the futuristic tone but isn't drum and bass techno. The dystopian nature of the game doesn't allow for much "dropping of the bass" but it works and works well. Most of the tracks were recorded by an orchestra and written by the same guy who wrote the music for Assassins Creed IV - Freedom Cry DLC, Olivier Deriviere, so if you liked Assassins Creed music, give this a listen. The soundtrack is mostly ambient but enhances tense and depressing moments.
During the game, you're able to collect 40 Mnemist Memories to find out more about the back story and see concept art that reminds you how amazing graphics of the game are.
Some people are mixed on this game but if you're patient then you can enjoy digging into a revolution and political upheaval and you turn Paris upside down while exploring an idea that I haven't seen much of - memories. I'm so glad DontNod Entertainment didn't go with the climate change idea.
Word of warning though, the game has unskippable cutscenes. I totally understand if that is a deal breaker.

So... the best parts about this game are often understated:
1.) The storyline is imaginative, compelling and well told through cinematics and voice over - actually decent voice over!
2.) The graphics are gorgeous, the music and sound effects are well done and the controls (for the most part) are smooth.
3.) The UI is pretty informative. As a bonus, it's even tied into the storyline, which is something a lot of games don't do.
4.) Combat can feel pretty satisfying when you've statted up your customizable fighting combos appropriately.
5.) Speaking of combat, the game does a fair job of trying to spice things up by adding a lot of new abilities, mini games and puzzles to try to keep things interesting. Notice I said "fair," more on this later...
6.) The 'leveling' system feels appropriate. You often face monsters you've encountered before and when you meet them again in later levels, wrecking the monsters that wrecked you earlier feels, oh, so cathartic.
Are we done gushing? Ok, onto the terribad:
1.) Game is repetative, Repetative, REPETITIVE. Did I mention, redundant? Oh, it's that too. Every episode, EVERY EPISODE follows the same sort of segmented sections: fight, "explore"/puzzle, story time. Sometimes they come in different combinations, but you can always tell which segment you're about to encounter next.
2.) Despite the variety of activites the game presents, it tend to want to overwhelm you with combat, which normally isn't a bad thing. The combat in this game is primarily a brawler style combat system, so be prepared to mash X and Y. A LOT. This by itself isn't bad.
However, the key to fighting is pulling off combos, which would be awesome if you weren't always fighting ABOUT 10 people who ALWAYS interrupt your combos. This greatly limits one's ability to pull off, say, a 6 or 9 string combo, making approximatley half of the features in the Combo Lab practically pointless. This also means a lot of time is devoted to flipping around the battle aimlessly whilst trying to avoid getting slaughtered by a huge mob of minions.
And while I think the designers and artists deserve kudos for making the protagonist a lithe and fiesty brunette, I just don't think watching her flip around with her legs in the air is enough to excuse such tedious battles. Call me a feminist, I guess. Or a "hardcore gamer." But I digress...
"What about bosses?" you ask. "Aren't you fighting them one on one?"
Yes, but typically there's a lot of dodging and special activities that are required to make them vulnerable first- then when that happens, they typically call for reinforcements. Wash. Rinse. Repeat.
3.) CAMERA. ANGLES. FROM. HELL! Luckily the game never freezes in one of these angles, but it can be frustrating when you're trying to keep an eye on 6 monsters, navigate obstacles in the environment AND fight a boss that's shooting bombs at you from across the screen.
4.) So the "About this game" section kinda of lies. A LOT.
--- It mentions "A balanced mix of combat and exploration." Firstly, I think if I had to log all the time I spent doing either activity it would be something more like 70/30 respectively. Plus, I'm not sure following a discrete path through the environment really counts as "exploration."
--- It also mentions the "Memory ReMix" feature, which I will openly admit is one of the best parts of the game. However, I think you use it a total of 3 times in the whole game. So, returning to that previous note about "balanced mix" I think the break down becomes something like 70/27/3.
So here I am, about 10 hours into the game, only about 75% of the way through and I'm asking myself, "is it worth it to keep going?" As it is, I have to drag myself to play this game over the 50 other games I've stockpiled during flash sale events.
And a game that makes you ask yourself, "Is it worth finishing?" has problems with its fun factor.
--EDIT 12/13/2015--
So, less than a week later it seems my decision has been made for me. During a particular boss fight in Episode 7 th e game started to glitch out. "Combat time" continued to play even when I'd defeated all the enemies in the area and accomplished my mission goals. I had to burn a focus power to trigger the end of combat (luckily).
Not ten seconds later I was unable to interact with a focus powerup. I thought it might be because I had to clear another conditional trigger because the Aug-Eye icon was flashing, indicating that there was something I needed to look at by pushing the down button on the D-Pad. Unfortunately, that wasn't working either. I managed to clear it by completing the next section of the area and unlocking a ladder.
I ran back to the focus upgrade and still couldn't interact with it. Defeated I returned to the ladder, only to find that I COULDN'T INTERACT WITH IT EITHER! Effectively trapping me in the level.
After having spent at least 5-7 minutes wading through a half dozen minions at a time to defeat the previous boss (not to mention the prior 3 bosses) I did not relish the idea of starting the episode over.
So this game experience ends now.

Один из лучших 2D-шутеров, которые я когда-либо видел. Игра вышла в свет еще в далеком 2007 году и появилась в стиме лишь в 2016. С момента выхода игра почти не изменилась, и все имеющийся плюсы сохранились по сей день.
1. Геймплей. Он прост, но в тоже время весел и динамичен. Игрок управляет существом, внешне напоминающим колобка, который умеет прыгать, бегать и использовать крюк для того, чтобы зацепиться за поверхность или другого игрока. В игре присутствует всего 6 оружий, что немного огорчает, но не так сильно, как это могло быть. Играть в Teeworlds очень весело, особенно в компании друзей.
2. Системные требования. Они просто смешные. Игра весит каких-то 9Мб, требует пол-гига ОЗУ и проц в 1.4GHz. Игра замечательно подойдет тем, у кого слабые ПК.
3. Пользовательские текстуры. Если вам наскучили дефолтные текстуры вашего колобка или оружия, то вы всегда можете заменить файлы игры на понравившийся вам скин, который вы нашли в Интернете или же нарисовали его сами.
4. Пользовательские режимы и карты. Если бы не они, то играть с набором в 6 оружий было бы совсем нудно. В игре присутствует куча различных режимов и разнообразных карт, на которых можно пофаниться с другими игроками.
5. Маппинг. Если вам захочется создать свою карту к этой игре, то разработчики создали для вас внутриигровой создатель карт. Придумывайте, создавайте, делитесь вашими творениями с другими.
Думаю, все основные плюсы перечислены. Но, если вы в Teeworlds, то найдете в нем что-то другое, что я не перечислил. Настоятельно рекомендую опробовать эту игру.

FULL REVIEW:

I spotted this game through the E3 trailer and I was quite interested in it right away.
This game sets the mood right at the start with an atmospherical/philosofical ride through an amazing story that uses audio like not many games do these days and especially since the main character has a mental illness this allows for a really awesome surround sound effect (headphones recommended).
Fair warning includes some SPOILERS.
The best parts about the game are:
- The story, you get to go through the same experience as the character and you too wonder what is and isn't real. Although it isn't a very long story (took me 7.9 hours) but it is filled with many great puzzle mechanics (will come to that later).
- No UI elements/healthbars floating around, which could make it slightly more difficult for you to know if you are nearly dead or how close to dead the enemies are. But this is done VERY well, visual effects are in place to indicate whether you are almost dead and the character movement will also change the closer you are to dead which I think is really immersive.
- Puzzle mechanics, since the character is experiencing a psychosis the world around her and the puzzles that she creates in her head make perfect sense to her to try and save her beloved. The cool thing about these puzzle mechanics is that they are all visual related, sometimes it has to do with finding symbols 'hidden' in the surrounding, where other times you are faced with illusions. These kind of puzzles portray the elements of a psychosis very well atleast what I would think it would be.
- Some boss fights, I really liked battling the Beast and the seperate stages it has even though the combat it self is pretty straight forward the bosses (especially The Beast & Valravn).
The "worst" part of the game really is the combat, even though I didn't mind it that much.
I would most certainly recommend this gem of a game, its absolutely one of my favourite games of this year (and probably of the last few years) and because it is a much smaller game the price is also much smaller!

AC is the game that started it all, mixing some excellent open world action / parkour with an overarching story (and meta-story) that could easily be the screenplay for the next big sci-fi film.  It also nailed the basic open world action gameplay mechanic of combining primary objectives with optional side quests (batman), climbing towers to make nearby objectives appear on the map (farcry 3), and fluid hand to hand skirmishes that become more complex as the game progresses (batman).  AC nails these mechanics right out of the gate.
The meat of the game is exploration of the game world, set in the middle east some time during the crusades. There are 3 cities to explore, each with similar architecture but a distinctive feel.  The player can only access a few sections of the city initially, and more become available as the story progresses.  Being an assassin, the primary missions involve dealing death to some high profile victim in a specific city and section.  Secondary objectives are a mix of "protect the citizen", "assasinate these minor dudes", pickpocketing, evesdropping, and parkouring challenges.  There are also flags scattered around that you can pick up but there was little incentive to do so.
Story sections and major missions feature a brief cinematic that is rendered in the game world.  Often you can switch to another camera position by clicking a button on the joystick.  The cinematic then seamlessly returns control to the player.
There is also an overarching "meta story" that is told from the perspective of a young man who is apparently a descendant of the assassin you are playing.  There is a device called the "Animus" that you lie opon... it then allows you to access and play out the memories from the past, and also influence (apparently) the original outcome.  I won't reveal anything else about that... you will need to discover that for yourself.
All is not perfect though there are some annoyances:
> The gameplay is repetitive, with only minor variance as your level increases.  The "boss battles" tend to become more complex but the meat and potatoes are samey.
> The cities have some differences but honestly if you plopped me in one city and asked me to correctly identify it, it would be difficult.  They don't feel different enough, adding to the samey-ness.
> The textures and character models are a bit crude.  I would definitely recommend the hi res texture mod, which you can find on the steam forums.
> This game was designed with an XBOX controller in mind... you will NOT want to use a mouse.  Not necessarily a huge annoyance but I for one prefer mouse and keyboard over joystick.
All in all I enjoyed the game immensely and would definitely recommend it.

The original Assassin's Creed game is what started a franchise that can be recognized almost anywhere. I honsetly believe it was this game that served as the catalyst to boost Ubisoft Montreal into creating the multiple other AC games.
I wanted to include my own story overview, because in my opinion you'll want to play this game because of the gameplay (Parkour, Freerunning, Combat) first and the storyline second. This isn't because I thought the story was bad-- it is just the least interesting in the series. However this story was what started the Assassin's Creed lore and, well, Creed.
You start off by waking up inside a machine known as "The Animus", a device developed by a company called "Abstergo". To be more clear 'you' are Desmond Miles, a young man who claims to be a bartender. Abstergo kidnapped Desmond as a means to probe him with the Animus to recover memories of his ancestors, which would lead them to something (something of value) that was lost to time (as Assassin's Creed I is set during the Crusades, in 1191 AD). Once inside the Animus, you play as Altair, a master Assassin who loses everything he built up in the Brotherhood by breaking key Tenents set by the Order's leader, Al Maulim, and Assassins from a previous age. Abstergo follows the memories of Altair, searching for a device created by unknown people (speculated to be supernatural beings) that has the ability to control the minds of others. Towards the middle of the story Desmond realizes what is happening, that the company called Abstergo is actully run by Templar Knights, who are still bent on ending the war waged by Assassins and Templars, even after a thousand years, by using the Apple (as the mind-control device is called).
So does Desmond or Altair do something about it? You'll have to buy this game and play it to find out.
Beyond Story, this game has very nice gameplay and graphics for a game made in 2007-2008. I can still consider it a Next Gen game, as the details and cinematics are very well done. This game isn't seamless, as you have to load every time you change locations-- thats another thing: While this game is tagged as "Open World", the game is devised to give you the first few levels complete control over where you go. After this, you can quickly travel between the main cities in the game; Masyaf, Acre, Jerusalem, and Damascus. The area in between these places is called Kingdom on the map. You can always travel through Kingdom, but you always have the option to teleport to the cities' outskirts after you return to Al Maulim at Masyaf. This game, in this case, becomes both Open World, and Linear. But because this is a small detail, it doesn't really add up as a problem in-game.
Parkour is always fun in AC, as you can freerun up any place so long as there are handholds of ledges to hold onto. The game's "Leap of Faith" idea wasn't bad, but it makes the game seem unrealistic in my opinion, not that this game should sound "real" at all. Basically a Leap of Faith is when you climb up onto a veiwpoint, spy your surroundngs, then leap down into a nearby haystack. Its a very fun feature, but looks very impossible. Ignoring the aesthetics of the Leap of Faith, it's a great way to get players to explore without feeling rushed. You don't just walk around and unlock map bits. You have to climb up and look around to know where to go. This is also great because you don't complete missions if you don't explore-- you have to complete three side-quests before the target is avaliable to kill. So viewpoints and Leaps of Faith are very much-- gameplay wise-- critical.
I've played Assassin's Creed through once now. It can go quick if you want it to, or rush through it to do the most important thing you can possibly do once you complete AC1-- play the next game.
I give this game a 8/10, because its fun to play, but just ends too quickly!

**Assassin's Creed** should be considered a classic in *stealth* games in my
opinion. There aren't many games out there, executing and implementing the
meaning of a stealh game in such a good and interesting way as the
**Assassin's Creed** series, but even so the first *AC* has its flaws.
Considering that the game is from *2008*, the graphics are actually pretty
good and the level design is really awesome and feels authentic (I don't
actually know in how far they're authentic to the original cities, but they
sure look good and feel realistic).
The story is really awesome and interesting, leading you, the player, to think
for yourself which side you prefer or rather whose cause is right and whose is
wrong.
As I said previously *AC* isn't without its flaws either. Some of the
*challenge* missions you get throughout the city aren't really that different
from your average mission, just that there is a timer running now and they seem
to be added just before release because it is simply weird that Altair doesn't
seem to respond or say anything to them. Totally one-sided discussion.
The investigation part quickly becomes boring as it always follows the same
pattern and it doesn't really add that much to the story of the game. So I
actually have to say that trying to get 100% in every memory is actually a
waste of time as it doesn't really add much value to your overall gameplay or
your understanding of the game world.
What I absolutely don't like also is that you as a player can't really decide
for yourself how you want to accomplish a mission. I personally would much
prefer to eliminate my targets without any suspects or at least without the
whole city knowing about it immediately but the game doesn't give you any real
option. That makes the missions still pretty linear, the only thing is that you
can somewhat decide from where you will strike, the end-result will stay the
same.
Even though *AC* has its flaws, it also has many positives and I can only
recommend this game.

Long, long ago, I made a promise to myself to never review games on Steam; there's too many unnecessary reviews and I didn't want mine to get lost in the shuffle. I felt this game deserved my review regardless, because after 395 hours playing I am still as addicted as the first few days. It reminds me of how I felt playing Final Fantasy Tactics for the first time, grinding for hours and hours with a grin.
As a fan of tabletop RPGs and video game RPGs, this is a fantastic blend of both. It has a lot of the features that you find in your AAA title MMORPGs; crafting, clans, etc. all wrapped up in a turn based combat environment. It doesn't hold your hand or babysit you, you have to think for yourself, read things, and learn some of the more complex game mechanics as you play.
You get to make up your own story as you go, or not if you just want a mindless grindfest with clan mates. It doesn't give you a tutorial, just a text manual that takes minutes to read, and player written guides are available for more detailed information. It's fun and highly addictive, and to top it off an amazing community (ironic, considering most MMORPGs, I avoid the community like the plague).
I know what you're thinking, "I've heard it all before." This is the first game I've seen in a long time where the community isn't trolls, bots, and gold spammers, but actual people bantering and having fun. The developers willingness to talk to the community, get feedback, implement feedback, and actually fix things is awesome. They are prioritizing improved game mechanics and fixing glitches as well as starting to host RP events to start bringing lore in.
This is a diamond in the rough, but it's being polished as we play, and every update it shines a little brighter.

Okay, so I've given this game quite some time before I decided to write a review.  Skip to the end for the TL:DR, because this is gong to be long.  I bought this when it first came out, and found it to be incredibly grindy and the controls and functions of the game were nowhere near intuitive.  Making money to buy any sort of ship (or buy a whole lot of anything really) is insanely difficult if you don't grind your rear off for hours, some mission-vital resources are incredibly scarce, and storage is so miniscule for some items that you can barely carry much of anything aside from the essentials.
The Foundation Update was quite nice, but the sheer amount of stupidly long fetch quests you have to go on is rediculous just to get a few pathetic blueprints.  Also, Rigogen, now called Kelp Sacks or something, was a major setback in my ENTIRE progression through this update, and there was no crop you could make for it either. (Not sure if they added it in the Atlas Rises update because I could not bring myself to get that far through the fetch quests again, but that's for a later section)  I did like the addition of bases, but it felt like something that should have been there from the start.
Next we have the Pathfinder Update.  Again, ground based vehicles were a welcome addition, but there were still more detriments to be added.  More fetch quests, and expensive summoning platforms if you can't find the blueprint for one of the key resources (this falling back on my previous point about money making being difficult).  I loved the vehicles themselves though.  They are fast, can harvest resources fairly quickly (after the fetch quest to get the mining laser blueprint), and allow you to safely traverse on land and in water (the only thing that makes collecting Rigogen slightly easier).  This is probably my favorite update so far, but does not make up for the grievances I have against the rest of the game.
And now we have the Atlas Rises Update.  Where to start...  Portals take a lot of resources to activate (okay, not that big of a deal), but to use them you have to scour every cave you can find so that you can get fragments that you have to use to dial in a portal.  I tried to find some, but there is nothing that comes up on the HUD to help find these dead explorers, not even clues as to which direction to go.  That aside, the economies introduced are confusing and the resources that you can trade between systems take up a whole slot EACH in your inventory, which makes having a large amount with you when you go back to sell them nearly impossible.  I tried to go back and forth selling valuable goods, but after making only 10K in profit, I decided to say screw it and move on to the new missions.  The mission "board" in each system is a nice addition, and a nice way to get credits and items, but there is no real direction as to what you need to do.  "Mine a Resource", "Kill Wildlife".... Okay, but what resource, and how much wildlife???  The same now goes for the fetch quests; they don't tell you how much of resources they want you to collect to bring back to the quest giver anymore.
TL;DR -
Look, I gave this game an entire year of playing off and on, and I just can't say that this game is good.  I love the idea, I love that they're trying to make things better, but at this point in time, it's not playable in my eyes.
Pros:
- Lots of exploration
- Diverse creatures and planets
- Base building
Cons:
- So much grind
- Unrewarding fetch quests
- Incredibly difficult to gather any real amount of money
- Certain rare and hard to get resources not farmable (literally)

You begin your adventure after a number of introductory cutscenes intermixed with putting you on control every now and then. Given the current trend in the industry of over explaining everything as though you have never touched a game before I was a tiny bit bewildered when I was suddenly left in control after the first cutscene, since the game is so beautiful and nothing had left me to know I was in control except nothing was happening until I pushed a few buttons. I do not hold this against the game as this is just not something I am used to anymore, so it was good to see a game that do not treat as if I have no clue what I am doing. Furthermore it helps to not break immersion with different unneeded UI explanations.
You start the game being able to only run and jump. Slowly more mechanics are added to your arsenal and the game is a perfect "school book" example of how to introduce and teach new mechanics to the player without ever making you feel like you are in any type of tutorial. It just flows naturally along with the game and storyline.
I'd recommend playing it with a controller. I changed from keyboard+mouse to Xbox 360 controller after the first 'escape or die' event. Be aware though that after learning the charge skill in order to charge off walls you need to grab them (RT) and the use (LS) to point in the direct off the wall and then press (A) to charge off the wall.
Lastly, it is really amazing how the game manages to change character from making you feel more or less powerful with challenges where you can easily save every now and then to these "escape events" that are very brutal and punishing and leave you feeling so powerless. It does something on a higher level that I am still digesting. A direct relationship of this is also manifested in the difference between your (Ori's) size and Kuro's.
