So.. AKIBA's TRIP, is probably easiest described as a close but not quite a clone of what we know as "Persona".
With the twist of actually having to fight enemies in the actual town of Akihabara instead of going into "dungeons", as we know it from other JRPG's. Now firstly this was announced for consoles, but I am very glad to see it appear on steam as it was unfortunately NOT available for Europeans on the console market as it didn't support the European "PAL" system.
With that said, this is probably one of the most fun times I've had, once you get through the awkward and weak introduction to the game and it's protagonist. Also the controls are quite awkward at first and I strongly recommend the use of a controller for this one, otherwise, you might have troubles ever getting through the persistent introduction tutorial that will nag at you in the beginning of the game, not to mention the annoying camera angles the game sometimes throw you into when you reach the map edges of the game during fight sequences and scenarios.
This is also one of the harder games when it comes to the fighting, so if you get easily frustrated over such things, pick this game up at your own risk.
Over all I recommend this game to everyone interested in JRPG's especially if you're into Persona.
As for replayability, there do exist several endings depending on your reputation and "actions".
This game gets a 8,8/10.

This is a very lovely tribute based on the Arma 2 engine. You will enjoy all the richness of features - open world scenario with an editor for unlimited possibilities. All troops and vehicles are high quality and high in detail. Weapon and vehicle sounds are also pretty decent. Playing the mission "Normandy crossing" gave me that immersion, only the Arma series can provide. Laying there with my team at dawn, covering in the grass and behind bushes. Looking at the wonderful colors of the sky, listening to the beautiful soft wind breeze around our helmets and for a short time I remember how it was playing in the wilderness as a young kid. But then reality forces me to focus ont the gravel road to the west. My team hears it - I hear it. There it is. The terrifying whistling and twittering of German tank tracks coming closer and closer. They are less than 200 meters away, but we still have no visual contact. Oh god, save our souls. I order my team to hold fire. Then we have visual contact to a German halftrack fully manned with troops. I know, that the only possibilitiy to survive, is to take out the gunner first, because he can erase our whole team with one single blast. They come to a halt, just 50 meters away from us. This is our chance! Quickly I focus on the gunner and order my members 2 to 5 to attack him, the rest of my team will handle the two guards on foot to the left and right, Open fire! Lucky us, the gunner and guards drop immediately, but the whole squad now disembarks the halftrack, running for cover. A fierce battle ends as we empty our last mags into the one Kraut calling for reinforcements. We check the dead Germans for ammo, gear and weapons and say goodbye to our fallen comrades. Suddenly we are shocked to death. There it is again. The whistling of death....

Hellblade is a gorgeous, psychological experience. I am going to mention a few things I found interesting, and maybe a bit off-putting. First, I felt myself wanting to experience it more as a film than a game. Like I wanted an autoplay switch that would allow the game to play itself and I could just watch. The game mechanics felt like something thrown into a film unnecessarily, the puzzles and the combat. Also, I think the strength of Senua's character was so intense that I felt strange "becoming" her, controlling her. I wanted to see how she reacts without me. I don't know if this is positive or negative though, but it's not something I've ever experienced in a game. I thought the "voices" were an interesting touch, but were maybe a bit too hand-holding sometimes, like it was functioning as the game's way of telling me what to do, and once I became aware of it as a device, it started to get annoying, and not the way I think the devs intended. Overall, I think the game is definitely worth $30.

Remember Me is a game full of interesting ideas, some of which work and some of which unfortunately do not.
The story is both interesting, and does that thing all good science fiction does by feeling like a relevant reflection upon the difficulties in our lives. I feel like it would have benefitted more from really focusing on that aspect rather than proceeding as it did, however.
The combat gameplay is akin to that seen in the Arkham Batman games, except without the countering or dynamism. It includes a system of designing your own combos that manages to feel very limiting as opposed to the freedom an idea like that should give. The combat camera is also less than helpful, often causing enemies to begin their attacks from off screen which obscures the visual warning. One aspect I did like however was the special "Pressen" attacks you could use. After charging a gauge in combat you can opt to unleash one of several special attacks for a variety of devastating effects.
The environmental traversal gameplay is a case of follow the clearly marked climbing path with literal flashing arrows telling you where to go and being unable to deviate in any way. Cinematically this is okay - watching someone climb is more interesting than running down a long corridor I suppose - but it would be nice to be able to actually explore the world a bit more or for there to be some kind of a challenge involved. The gorgeous landscape absolutely begs for it.
Overall, Remember Me is worth playing for it's excellent sci-fi memory dystopia world and for it's memorable "memory remix" segments. It has some good cinematic set pieces and graphically looks great but don't expect to be impressed by the combat or climbing.

Probably the best first person shooter I've played this year, although with some caveats.
The core gunplay and sneaking, the bread and butter of slaughtering Nazis, has been polished to a mirror sheen.  The level design and high damage (at least on the higher difficulties I played on) made for some intense fights where speed and aggression, both while in stealth and openly fighting, are encouraged and enjoyable.  All of your weapons feel weighty, and some great gore effects, fire, explosions, and so on make the whole thing very visceral when you're playing.
If you're into story and aren't a Nazi yourself to get offended at the implication that fascism is evil, the plot and cutscenes are great too, successfully mixing a dose of the absurd with heavy character development and good old-fashioned dystopia.  It's a step back from the long, fully-fleshed out masterpiece that was The New Order, but it's still leagues better than what you'll find in most video games.
That problem with story relates to another issue, however, which is length.  The main campaign of The New Colossus is noticeably shorter than The New Order, but I unfortunately don't have any personal metric on how much.  Whether or not you'll get what feels worthwhile for a $60 single-player only game depends on your opinions on two things: completionism and story.  The game has tons of side quests and collectibles in the same levels you complete in the main story, which massively extends the longevity of the game.  I reached 32 hours finding everything and doing every "remix" level in just one of the game's two "timelines" (different supporting characters and minor changes to events).  However, a lot of people don't like that kind of extension, which I'll respect.
The game also has persistent stability issues for me that last I checked weren't fixed.  Certain graphics settings can trigger frequent crashes, so be sure to test and tweak the settings thoroughly in your two hours before a potential refund.
Overall, Wolfenstein 2 is a good game with some persistent problems that keep it from the kind of overwhelming recommendation I usually give the first game.  It's viscerally satisfying in gameplay and often fascinatingly sincere in the story, but it feels like the parts were assembled in a hasty head-transplant near the end.  Buy it if you like replaying good shooter levels and can look past the technical issues, wait for a sale if you only care about the main campaign, and return it if crashes break your patience.

Mechanically, Vector is a fine runner game. With fluid animation and simplicistic visual presentation, it really doesn't do too much wrong. But it also doesn't do enough right or even interesting to keep me playing. Levels get monotonous and repetitive way too fast. The "tricks" part of the game just really didn't do it for me. Unlocking new moves which don't do anything to break up levels other than play an animation, doesn't make up for the glaring lack of variety in level design. On top of that are the uninteresting and even annoying sound effects. Considering how engaging Canabalt was in spite of its simplicity, I think it says a lot about how much better this game could have been. Canabalt felt intense, driven and had a kind of physicality that Vector sorely lacks. Only get this if you LOVE runner games. It's probably not bad for a game to chill out and listen to music to, but overall it's not a game I can heartily recommend.

Vector; one of the original breakout indies that made a name on mobile and eventually PC. I remember playing this and it's many copy cats back in the early half of the decade and found myself amazed by the smooth, kinetic animations and intensive scenarios. Five years later, Vector still holds up. The 1984-esque opening still looks great, and while the early mobile trappings like the three-star system remain, the game is still a solid, thrilling experience.
[Please note that I played this and many others offline while I was in the process of moving, as my hours do not reflect play time. In all, I probably spent about 2-3 hours and got about half way through the game. As of now I haven't had a chance to touch the free DLC, but in all this should already sound like a recommend, and hey, free bonus stuff is always a plus]
As mentioned before, Vector has a stunning array of fluid motion animation coupled with a slick minimalist art style. This was most effective on a smaller screen, as now playing on a monitor accentuates the various moving parts and rough edges. While for me, this highlights the simple mastery of the game's design and explanation of flow, I will not that if you may put off by the fact you can see the various shapes making up a character in motion. The UI further emphasizes how this game wasn't intended for PC; everything is in big blocky letters, and the overall layout seems far more utilized for pudgy fingers than mouse cursors. This is an extremely minor complaint, and other games I've covered that have been ported from mobile are barely seem to be able to change the tutorials from "tap" to click. Vector is over all, an extremely solid port.
As far as the game? It's still innovative to the "runner" genre, even today, but it has its faults. Jumping is possibly one of the most difficult aspects of this game simply because gauging a precise jump while in motion can be a bit of a pain. This can be overcome with skill of course, but the game also suffers from something a bit more irredeemable; input lag. For whatever reason, hitting the up arrow key does not garuntee an immediate jump.
While there are certain factors that are rule bound, there were a few particular spots that I had to learn to hit the key earlier than the jump would technically trigger. Fighting the game's own mechanics is not my idea of fun, and it could simply be my own lack of skill or something, but I did notice a disparate result on a few occassions that muddled the experience. This goes for much of the games other on-cue demands; there are tricks you can perform at given points on a level, but on some occassions they simply wouldn't trigger when they should've. It's not an end of the world thing, but later levels can be brutal about precision, and as you usually have to start over from the very beginning, even the barest of input lag can detract. As I said, it could be just me, but it did detract a little. Once I learned to start hitting my buttons just a little earlier than I "should've," levels went by much better, but the inconsistancy of this lag was always off-putting.
In general however, Vector is an important footnote in gaming for a variety of reasons, but the wonderfully realized parkour system always had a new surprise somewhere down the line. The fact that skill and not microtransactions gets you through the game faster is so nice, after all. The sequel is definitely worth your time as well and further improves upon this one in every way, but since this is the only one on PC and it goes on sale often, it's absolutely worth your time. Minor criticisms aside, it's one of the premiere 2D runners for a reason. Check it out.

Back when this game came out last year, I had my pre-orders ready, a couple merch items ordered, even got a tattoo of the atlas on my back a couple months before release. Everyone was hyped beyond hyped... and at release, the negativity and backlash was incredible, and in my opinion out of proportion. Did they neglect features intended on release? Yes. Did the game look exactly as it did in the videos? Not very much. I will say though, I absolutely loved it. And now, with the free updates and flow of bug fixes, and the new 1.3 update that creates a whole new experience for a game already a year old... There is hardly a thing not to love. I had it on PS4 until recently when I built a pc and bought it on steam. Even though I feel that a fraction of the hate towards the game in the beginning is somewhat understandable, it was blown out of proportion. What Sean Murray and his team at Hello Games have created is a simple, but brilliant experience. Explore a galaxy in your very own starship, trudge through dangerous weather or tranquil pleasure searching for alien citizens to trade with, discoveries of all kinds to be made. Buy and sell in the newly upgraded market and trade system. Upgrade your ship, suit, and weapon. Enjoy a new and (believe me) amazing story that had me honestly captivated. So, so much more is waiting, and from beginning to end of what was intended to be a game of massive scope, simple and enjoyable all the way until your experience ends, if it ever does... It turns out to be just that. Hopefully, more and more people will find out why!

Ok, I've had a bit of a blast with this now and thought I'd throw in my tuppence worth.
So straight in with my major gripe... Why is this costing £55 pound on Steam? I mean, seriously? You can see I used a key, which cost me less than half this price. That is absolutely scandalous! It is as if actually giving us the Fox Engine version for once means that Konami feel we should now be paying a heck of a lot more for what we should have been getting for a few years now anyway! Cheeky sods.
Anywho, I'm an oldschool gamer. I have played football games since forever and am definately a bit bias towards Pro Evo. I did switch to Fifa for a while when I had thought they had made enough changes of their own, and stole the good bits from Pro Evo that I liked. It was when I became a PC gamer I felt a bit let down, of course we all know that the PC version, until now, has not been the shiny new Pro Evo that was seen on PS4. We were getting some slightly inferior game which was ok but you felt cheated and that rubbed, it was clearly a business decision. This means it was about money. Konami are not quite the kings as a company anymore, and probably just don't have the resources they would like. Priorities weren't with us.
So aside from the politics, what's the game like? And this version isn't a lot different from the last if truth be told, which I own on PS4. All I will say is that almost immediately after picking up the pad and running around I noticed how much better it felt. Player movement seems much tighter and fluid, passing seems more accurate. Some will argue that this game is a bit easier. Keepers spill the ball a bit more than I remember, and it is true that the refs seem more lenient. These things are something I wish there was a slider for or a setting, so that could adjust the overall balance.
I am not a online gamer really. I dabble in these modes but don't like the grind. I understand why they are there and why people like it, and that playing online is a useful way to play "friends". I play with my actual friends in the lounge, pads in hand, co-op or against I don't mind, it's the way many my age group grew up playing these games and Pro Evo still annoys me a bit in this regard nowadays. It's not catering for us Local Multi-player/Couch players if you will. Why only a few strategy setups can be saved per team is anyones guess, this doesn't help the couch players like us. There's no loading of multiple player accounts at once, which is a shame, like I had seem in the past on Xbox 360. Steam doesn't allow that so it needs to allow for local accounts whereby couch stats can be recorded. You need a separate mode for local play to be honest. And why can't I create a league for local play, with as many players and as many matches against each other as I want? Like I always used to in Sensible Soccer! (Told you, I am oldskool) I just wish it catered better for us that play the game the same way we have always done!
Anyway, waffle over. Gameplay here is great, it just feels and looks like football more than Fifa ever does, and the behaviour of the AI teams is varied and changes in a way that makes it interesting to play against. Also tactically there are more options and ways to tweak how your teams behave, and that is great, they actually work! Online modes are probably not on par with EA's effort, and it still has those annoying quirks it always has done, like the slightly crappy looking menu's and the Master League that never seems to understand how real football works. I would also kill for an ISS 64 style return of the tactical change request, which pauses the game only when the ball goes out of play. Make that an option, in fact gives us more options and flexibiliy and we'd all be happy.
In my mind this is the closest thing to football in video game form, even if it lacks the licenses (mods "cough") and some of the flash and bang. It now looks and, most importantly - feels, better than before and for all the niggles and quirks, I'd rather play this over anything else.

This is one game i picked up on a whim as i had enough in my wallet to buy it and thought "OH THIS LOOKS DIFFERENT I WILL GIVE IT A GO",and boy i am glad i did.
The graphics really do,do the game justice and the way they suit the name of the game "PAPER SORCERER" is uncanny.When you are walking round the different floors of the prison you have been incarcerated in the game looks really good and flows really smoothly.It does look at times (when in fights and stationary in the sanctuary) that the art work has been drawn on paper and then transferred into the game,with the artwork reminding me of the artwork found in the old D&D books i used to read and play through with my friends when we played D&D when i was a kid.This works really well and the music in game adds to the feeling that you are actually playing a D&D board game but in actual game form,the graphics effects for spells are all ok and each one looks different.
The characters you amass on your journey all look different and all have different play styles from the heavy classes which include the "MINOTAUR" who is good at heavy attacks and powerfull special attacks to the defense classes which include the "SHADOW" who has great defense magic and also spells that prevent status effects.
The music in game (what is there) does a good job like i have said of putting you in that world of sword and sorcerey and never does outstay its welcome (could have done with some more sound effects in game though).
The story is both entertaining and a joy to watch as it unfolds the further you progress through the tower and it is both a mysterious and wonderous journey to take as you progress from level to level.The further you get the more the enemies change and the more you have to look at your play style and change up the tactics you have been using as what worked on the floor below might not (and usually doesnt) work on the floor your on,this forces you to look at your team and make changes accordingly as you get further into the game.
This brings me to the difficulty level which at first can seem quite punishing,but believe me it isnt,the more you play the game the better you get (YEAH OF COURSE DUH) and the more you learn the little intricacies the game can throw at you.Many a time i have got to the gaurdian who stops your progress to the next level just to be beaten (sometimes by my own lack of in game time to be honest) and therefore have to load up again,but then when you do you learn what he/she does and when he/she does it and what they are vulnerable to and also when they summon companions to fight you and also when they are going to use spells (some of them use certain other spells to prepare for the spell that they usually crush you with "WHY YOU PAIN IN THE A...") and with this you learn and evetually you will "CRUSH THEM AND TAKE THEIR SOULS".
There are a few in game quests to do that you dont have to do to finish the game and my favorite is finding the "LOST SOULS",when you do find these you hand them in to the creepy old man who lives in the abandoned house (all by himself so run away kids if you know whats good for you) and he then opens up a level of the "REAPERS DUNGEON",these are worth doing and handing in as you get the oppertunity to explore a level of the reapers dungeon and this means you can find some really cool gear and other items that just cant be found in the main game.
Will you like this game,well yes if you like a good sword and sorcery romp and have the patience to play through what can be at some times quite a tough and challenging game then by all means "STEP FORWARD ADVENTURER" if that doesnt sound like your cup of tea then look elswhere as this wont be the game for you.

Syberia neatly packages creativity and wonderful storytelling into a compelling point-and-click adventure. Offering stunning artwork, engaging voice acting, and supported by beautiful music, it is very well crafted. In addition, the puzzles require a decent amount of thought.
Syberia does have a few minor faults, although nothing game breaking. The low resolution graphics quickly show off its age and in certain spots makes it difficult to see objects. There are a couple spots where the screen scrolls as you walk toward the edge, however there is no indicator that identifies that aspect. Lastly, some of the puzzles just end up being frustrating because they get overly involved--almost anal retentive in a way.
Overall, the story is what makes this game great and it leads perfectly into the sequel. It was definitely worth the time spent.

- Full review.
If you're in the market for something that's a little Wizardry and a little Shin Megami Tensei, may have a thing or two for you. The first-person dungeon crawling is pretty much everything you've come to expect from these kinds of games, but the combat demands strategic use of all your party members' abilities and strengths. In fact, combat is really the best part of Paper Sorcerer. It may take the same amount of time to clear some normal packs of trash mobs in this game as it would to take on a boss from any other RPG, but the battles themselves are worth it and are infrequent and varied enough to keep from becoming too repetitive.
Unfortunately, my recommendation of this game comes with some SEVERE hesitation. The entire user interface is an uncategorized, unformatted, and at times non-functioning mess. Thankfully the menu bugginess is mostly limited to non-combat situations, but it's still a major pain to work with such an aggressively bad UI. There are also a number of bugs that can occur while exploring the dungeon that may require a restart of the game, which will also re-close any doors you've opened making it harder to re-orient yourself afterward. There's either some slight inexperience going on here or the game needed to get booted out the door to satisfy Kickstarter backers.
If you want some engaging as hell combat and party customization and don't mind wading through some annoying bugs and terrible menus, by all means have a go at Paper Sorcerer.

Summed up in 1 sentence, this game is a riveting journey of a character through many trials that the character imposes on herself through her illness. Grief, anger, sadness, despair, determination and love. All in one package. Visually stunning, audio-wise setting a new standard (the binaural audio on a 7.1. headphone set is truly a treat), with an atmosphere that just screams loneliness, and wrapped up in a story exploring new, delicate grounds in a very gritty and honest way.
Yes, the game might be too slow at times, but it serves a purpose. And yes, the combat (or camera focus, in particular) can be more chaotic and annoying than it really should. But the overall experience is truly something you have not experienced before. When I said a while back in my Spec Ops: The Line review that there should be more games focused on the mental states of the characters, as well as a thought-provoking storyline, Ninja Theory have upped the ante. One of the best games of 2017 for me, no doubt about it!

I'm more of a casual gamer, and don't frequently play games at all (and haven't ever written a Steam review before). I wasn't sure what I was expecting when I purchased Ori and the Blind Forest; maybe something pretty casual, based on the trailers, right? I mean the game looks really artistic, the music sounds nice, no difficult looking gameplay in the trailers, so that means a perfect game for me, the casual gamer!
Well there's lots of enemies to fight, and spikey thorny barriers, as well as some laser beams that cause instant death.... So I died a lot! (Maybe 100-150 times?) In order to save the game you need to use an energy orb to create a "soul link". If you forget to do this frequently, you may need to re-play a fair bit of the game again (I forgot to do this twice, and had to repeat about 30 minutes of gameplay). This shouldn't detract you from the game though, I loved the art work, the music, the story, all of it. It's a solid 2D platform adventure, full of puzzles, RPG-like ability trees to unlock, some minor boss battles, and some close call dungeon-like escape sequences (where if you press the wrong key once or twice you may die, and have to repeat the entire escape sequence over and over again).  Many elements remind me of the gameplay style of old school NES/SNES/Sega games, but with nice graphics, and a nice soundtrack. All up, it took me 10.5 hours to finish the game, and I'd give it a solid 9/10. A fantastic game, that left me wanting more!

So, let me preface this review by saying that yes, you can get this game for free on your cell phone. However the free version has less content, requires a purchase to get everything you have in the Steam version, and has microtransactions. I say this because most of the negative reviews focus on this besides the game itself. With that being said, is it worth it to spend your money on this version? Absolutely.
When I first played the demo of Vector years ago, I didn't like the flow of the game. But it ultimately came down to me not understanding it. I would eventually get around to playing it again and it impressed me enough to get the full version. It's not your normal game for sure, but for what's here you should get a lot of enjoyment and hours out of it.
The story is pretty simple (and unfortunately, it's ultimately pointless to the game). In the future humanity is under totalitarian control, as we are conditioned to think, work, and act alike. Your character decides to break free and runs away, with guards from the government in pursuit of him. Your objective is to escape by reaching the end of multiple stages, laid out over three areas. The appearance of the game is minimal. Backgrounds are static, and the models of your character, your pursuer, and all objectives are cast in a black sillouette. The music is one track that repeats in every stage, with a different track for the menus. It *can* get a bit repetitive but just slap on some techno or metal in that case and it works just as well.
What you're after here is the meat of the game. It functions similar to an endless runner, as your character will move on their own. However you press buttons at certain points to make him vault, run, and jump around the various obstacles in the stage, in order to keep up your speed and eventually escape the guard who is after you. It may sound simplistic but a lot of stages are set up so you need to hit your buttons at the exact right time or spot, otherwise you'll collide into a wall, fall into a pit, or be captured. There is a restart button which you'll be finding yourself pressing quite often.
But that's not all there is to it! When you complete a stage, you get one star. Throughout every level there are grey cubes to collect, and collecting all of them gets you one additonal star. These may require you to take a different path, and jump and vault at different times. *On top* of that you collect coins as you progress, either in the stage or by completing a new stage, and these coins allow you to purchase parkour moves. These moves can be triggered at certain spots during each level, and if you trigger all the moves you get another star. So in order to three star every level you need to get every bonus cube, have all the moves unlocked, and successfully hit every move. Sound easy? It's not.
You need to gain a certain number of stars in each area in order to unlock the next one, even if you clear every stage. *Plus* there are bonus levels in each area and to unlock the bonus levels you need to get so many stars, *and* each bonus level also has stars to gain by collecting bonuses and hitting the parkour moves. PHEW. Yeah so there's TONS of content here.
Oh yeah, and once you do all that, you also have "Hunter Mode" which allows you replay every single level again but as the guard instead of the guy running away. This presents an EXTRA challenge as not only will you need to get all the bonuses, hit all the moves, but you have to be better then perfect in your timing because you need to catch the guy before he reaches the exit, otherwise you need to start over the stage. I only got three stages into Hunter Mode before I had to stop due to the difficulty. So yeah, for what you spend on this game? You have hours of enjoyment (or frustration even).
So if you want to succeed in this level go hit the buy button and add this to your library. You won't regret it.

The King is back!!!
Having been heavily involved in the early days of PES by providing PC modding tutorials and playing the life out of PES4, 5 and 6, I took a long break after PES2010 which was my last purchase before this one.  I am glad I am back, it seems the game is back on track too.
The rhythm of the game is slow and methodical, teams tend to build the action rather than relying on an individual except in the case where the player is called Messi or Cristiano Ronaldo, The artificial artificial intelligence seems refined, with players behaving more logically in the management of the ball and show greater predisposition to respect the tactics and strategies chosen by the coach. In this way you have more intelligent movements that follow the natural evolution of the action. This also translates into a greater ball control, a sign that Real Touch+ works. Defending in general seems tougher but more satisfying.
One of the most noticeable changes is the new system for dead balls. Gone is the ghostly indicator that showed the general trajectory of the ball, meaning its final destination is much more about guesswork. To help, at goal kicks the camera defaults to a higher vantage point, although finding a man wearing the same shirt seems to be almost pure luck unless you pass out from the back. Corners have a similarly low success rate, although that’s in line with the real-life stats, and while the free-kicks have lost the angle indicator too, it doesn’t seem so hard to get them on target anymore.
Pro Evolution Soccer 2018 has excellent graphics, far superior to the previous PC edition that was similar to PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 editions. On my laptop it works at 1080p and 60 frames per second on high settings.  The faces of the most famous players in some cases touch on photorealism.  The stadium graphics are hit and miss, which in the case of generic ones are mostly on average, while the ones covered by an official license are absolutely spectacular. Being a die hard Liverpool fan, playing at Anfield the game gives me all the atmosphere of the stadium and the feeling of really being there.
Team licensing hasn’t improved from last year, so only Arsenal and Liverpool have their correct kits in the Premier League, I'm not too bothered about licensing as its easy to mod on the PC version with the option files and using the Editor.  My major gripe is commentary is still awful and very repetitive, this is the games biggest letdown.
Aside from this, this is a superb game and a must for a football fan to buy!

Pro Evolution Soccer 2018 is without doubt the best football game since the PES 4,5 and 6 glory days. Not only is the PC version finally on par with its PS4 counterpart; it is actually far superior with an excellent technical performance and astonishing visuals thanks to the latest Fox Engine build.
Graphically; the game looks almost photorealistic at times and the attention to detail is phenominal in places. The animations of players is an remarkable achievement and the immersive feel of the stadiums just offers an incredible experience. It is a groundbreaking step up from the 'hybrid' builds we've had in recent years which is just polite terminology for 'PS3 port'.
In terms of gameplay; the pacing is a bit slower in this outing and it feels spot-on. Matches are less erratic and everything flows much better. Players are more composed in their play and the ball isn't bouncing around the pitch like a hot potato. You have to be more tactical and patient in your approach instead and it works really well.
Unfortunately, despite a string of key improvements to the game; the user interface is still incredibly dated as is the recycled commentary which drags the presentation down. It's not a major issue but Konami really need to improve this aspect next year. Online server and connection issues still persist as is the poorly supported online entity which is a shame.
Overall; PES 2018 is a stunning game and Konami's best effort for over a decade. From a gameplay and graphical standpoint, it's simply outstanding at times and if you're just looking for a football game to enjoy; it's an absolute must buy despite some dated elements and a disappointing online portion.

This game is OK as long as you're playing arcade or quick matches as single player. But I, like the next guy, don't really like getting stuck in a combo which doesn't stop till you drop. In campaign, once you reach the end of a certain character's level, the opponent gets majorly buffed, blocks constantly, and once they get an opening, they quite literally smash you till you're gone, this being on easy difficulty. I think the game expects you to be an expert by this point, but i'm not which is why I chose easy mode. I hope that at some point it's nerfed, but for now the story is far too difficult despite it being "easy". Oof. My bones. They hurt.
By the way some pros and cons before I end this off~
Pros- Really nice graphics, amazing single player features (excluding final boss story mode characters) Really nice artwork in the gallery, and smooth gameplay design.
Cons~ Story expects way too much out of a player. Difficulty should be escalated by setting (e.g. Sleepwalk should litearally be accomplishable by someone blindfolded, Easy being more difficult, Normal more-so, and so on), not 100% by story level. Multiplayer is a bit of a pain to understand. Spamming is easily rewarded. Spamming infinites more-so than that.
Overall, I like this game, but only for the graphics and arcade mode fun. And sometimes playing with friends. But this game hurts when it comes to story. I recommend this to people who basically like graphics over gameplay or people who like a switch-in 3v3 style combat game. Otherwise, if you're looking for a good story, this isn't quite the place to look. Plus, the story itself is a bit confusing for some players to understand.

The ending itself isn't as strong as the earlier parts but the journey was enjoyable overall. A lot of people complained that combat was pretty simplistic/repeatitive which is kind of true but in all honesty it isn't that bad. On top of that, while you have only a few preset combos to use, you do get a lot of diversity in how those combos help your character (basically you four "power ups" you can attach to your combos so that your combos heal you, do more damage, or lower your cooldown for special abilities, and the fourth is just a multiplier effect that amplifies one of the three powers). I also LOVED a special ability that your character has which is that they can alter the memories of individuals. I think that was something really unique to the game and it is great to recreate things and see all the different ways you can make the memory play out.
I also thought it was great for the game to have good diversity in terms of gender and race. You don't see that much in games, and we gamers get a lot of flak for that sort of thing. Honestly, I will definitely refer to this game as a good counter example showing that games can have that sort of thing and still be a ton of fun.
tl;dr if you are into a good story definitely pick up this game. If you hate linear games and/or despise gameplay that is a bit repeatitive then you may not like this game but honestly the gameplay wasn't that bad at all to me.

TL;DR - This title certainly doesnt get enough credit. It is actually quite a fantastic game, it just has a few pimples. Great atmosphere and story with gameplay that is only kind of weak.
The visuals and setting are truly second to none. It is set in a crazy future version of Paris. The style ranges from a dripping rotten underground to a sterire futuristic magnificence. Every location could me a painting for all the subtile details and raw artistic effor put in. 10/10
The story is extremely good and well told. The world removes and adds memories to themselves at a whim. Think a combo of Eternal Sunshine and Total Recall. Some people have not fared well with this and have turned into brain damaged Gollum like creatures. You are an Errorist, sworn to take down the people resposible. Great characters and acting throughout. 9/10
The gameplay really breaks down into two elements.
First, is combat. It is a 3rd person beat-em up that functions a lot like Arkham. Except your combos are set into 4 specific ones, plus you have a dodge. Now, where it gets interesting is the effects you can attach to the combos. You can assign each button on each combo with a different perk. You can have it be strong, heal you, or reduce the countdown on your specials. Plus there's 5 different special attacks and your little gun-like thing. On the whole, it is a lot of great ideas, but it is fairly clunky until you get used to it and still clunky even then. 6/10
The other part is a lot of platforming which is pretty par for the course if you have ever played a game like Uncharted. Jumping, hanging, maneuvering around a space. Works well. But then there are these Memory Remix segments where you go into a person's head and alter one of their memories to suit your causes. This is possibly the best part of the game. You make small changes, like moving a table or releasing a lock, and they end up changing the scene entirely. These parts were so much fun. My only complaint is that there were not enough of them. 10/10
On the whole, this is a great game that you can get for pretty cheap that should chew up a solid 7-8 hours of your time.
8/10 Overall.

As a resume: well designed world and charakters, animation are good and voice actiong excellent*. The combat system is okay, but the default camera makes it more awful, than it is. The game could have a bit more enemies. Performance is good and i had only one bug in 10hrs gameplay.

Summed up in 1 sentence, this game is a riveting journey of a character through many trials that the character imposes on herself through her illness. Grief, anger, sadness, despair, determination and love. All in one package. Visually stunning, audio-wise setting a new standard (the binaural audio on a 7.1. headphone set is truly a treat), with an atmosphere that just screams loneliness, and wrapped up in a story exploring new, delicate grounds in a very gritty and honest way.
Yes, the game might be too slow at times, but it serves a purpose. And yes, the combat (or camera focus, in particular) can be more chaotic and annoying than it really should. But the overall experience is truly something you have not experienced before. When I said a while back in my Spec Ops: The Line review that there should be more games focused on the mental states of the characters, as well as a thought-provoking storyline, Ninja Theory have upped the ante. One of the best games of 2017 for me, no doubt about it!

Amazing. Sometimes you spend so much time weeding through the big box ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t games out there looking for that experience you had from one game 10 years ago and never thinking you'll find it again. Well I found it. If I play a single player game it is to immerse myself intoa story that grips me. This game does such a great job of slowly dipping your feet into an emotional pool of hoplessnes and then out of no where pulling you under and leaving you begging for air. There are these sparse moment of extreme beauty amidst a sea of dispare. When you've spent 3 hours in a dark corner of Senua's miond and all of a sudden the sun shines and a voice in your head says "What is this place? I like it here" it just makes you want to sit down and never move another step in the game.
The first hour of the game does not do it justice. It's a light introductory to the world to come. Make sure you put on headphones, turn of the light and completely imerse yourself in the story. Just let go and let it take you on the journey and you won't be disappointed.
Now for the details:
Graphics - 9/10 Excellent quality, runs at a smooth 60fps with eveything cranked to the max at 1440p with my 980TI
Sound - 10/10 The audio production in this game is fantastic! You must play this with headphones or you are going to miss 1/3 of the games magice
Gameplay - 9/10 They through you in with no tutorial, hints, or any guidance besides the voices in your head. I will admit I played all the way to the first boss and halfway through the boss fight looked at the control scheme to see if I was missing something. Low and behold I weas only using 1/4 of the combat mechanics. This actually added a bit of charm to the game in my opinion and I'm glad I stumbled through the first hour without looking. Other than that everything is very fluid, entertaining and fun. Some of the puzzles are so simple that it makes them hard and frustrating(so you of that "duh" moment once you figure it out) but I'm not a real puzzle fan anyways so I'm just being critical. You will find the experience very linear and I find that a plus because the game really focuses on the story it is telling.
Overall I am very pleased with what Ninja Theory has done here. I can only wish that there was another game to fill the emotional void that this game will leave me with now that I have finished it. If you don't like this game you are not a human. Two thumbs up!

No Man’s Sky.  Probably the biggest flop of 2016 but not as bad as the Atari ET game that was released way back in the day.
Let me start with this: is NMS perfect?  Absolutely not.  It was a dumpster fire when it was released last Summer and barely improved with the Pathfinder update.  Sure, it performed a whole hell of a lot better, but it felt and looked nothing like the trailers released in 2014.  I’ll also preface with my view on all this.  I never fell for the hype train for NMS.  I took the game for what it was and enjoyed it (thus my low hours on Steam; I tried it with another friend who owned the game well before I bought it).
After the 1.3 update however, NMS is slowly turning into the game that was promised (I.E. NO MULTIPLAYER WAS EVER ACTUALLY PROMISED.  GET THAT INTO YOUR HEADS, FELLOW GAMERS.  YOU COULD “BE IN THE SAME PLACE” BUT NOT SEE EACH OTHER).  Textures are slowly becoming less blocky and awkward, gameplay elements are improving.  The developers ♥♥♥♥ed up last year – and horribly so.  Yet they’re still trying to get NMS on track.  Do it *right*.  I’ll give them a hell of an ovation for that; not many other developers would bother.
So here’s my list of Pros/Cons for NMS in its state.
Pros:
+ gameplay IS improving, albeit slowly
+ planets are less of a bore to explore
+ the world does feel slightly more alive than it did (planets not so much, besides wildlife)
+ dogfights are more exciting
+ some features are starting to become implemented
+ naming your ship!
+ there’s a better “customizability” to your ship; instead of chucking all your upgrades into your inventory, there are actual menus in place to organize all this
+ menus feel cleaner
+ the UI, though mostly unchanged, has gone through a mini puberty
+ the game runs REALLY well.  Everything feels smooth and how it should have been from the beginning
+ the new filter options makes the game surprisingly pretty
+ the game offers a slightly better beginning with a mini tutorial on what to do
+ Multiplayer I guess?
Cons:
- there’s still a LOT to be done to make up for last year’s blunder
- wildlife looks like God got drunk and ♥♥♥♥ed up an entire universe
- many textures still look like playdough (mostly ground textures but they’re getting better)
- game will have a few lag spikes/slight freezes but nothing major
- resource hunting can be a major pain in the♥♥♥♥♥br>- “survival” mode was never needed
- base building defeated the purpose of a long journey through the universe; you were never supposed to stop and settle down (or so I figured)
- planets offer little variation and aren’t often pretty to be around
I bought and stuck through with NMS because the developers are trying.  The game has a LOT of potential to improve and grow into something fantastic.  Someone who tries to fix their mistakes earns plenty of respect from me.  Hello Games may have ♥♥♥♥ed up pretty bad, but they didn’t quit.
1983/2016: Would play an incredibly broken game and stick with the developers who are seeing their game through again (maybe)

Fun 'runner' game where the controls are simple but the execution is challenging.
The premise is simple. Your character runs from an enemy that is chasing you. If he catches up, you're tased and you have to restart. Along each level or 'route' are cubes scattered throughout the level. If you collect these cubes you are rewarded with 100% completion for that level. Also there are coins that you can collect; these are used to purchase additional parkour-style moves for your character, many of which are also required to '100%' a level.
It's fun but at the same time incredibly frustrating, especially if you plan to master all achievements this game has to offer (57 in total). You will fail, and end up restarting levels constantly. It's a lot of trial and error, but the payoff is sweet once you pull off moves with precision.
Overall a fun time-waster that's worth it, and is pleasant on the eyes as well (the fluid animations are great). I believe this is also available for smartphones, but I find it to be more enjoyable with a controller on PC.

I'm very behind the times. This is the first Call of Duty game I've played since the very first CoD way back when. When it comes to shooters, I've always leaned more towards the realistic Insurgency/SWAT4 type shooters where tactics are key. So, this game is a bit different since its very linear and methodical with how it plays. I've seen enough of the CoD community to know I don't have any interest in playing multiplayer CoD.
The single player campaign, however, is very interesting. The overall plot is decent. But, where this game really stands out is how it varies the game play. The player assumes the roles of multiple people doing different things from doing basic ground missions, to firing at insurgents in a AC-130, to stealth missions in radiation-soaked Pripyat. The campaign never felt boring.
There were things that ticked me off, though. At several points in the game, you get the sense that the game is waiting for you to get somewhere before things happen. So, at certain points, I could just stand perfectly still out in the open and the game would eventually become quiet. But, as soon as I jumped off a balcony or entered some room, all hell would break loose with soldiers popping up out of nowhere. Kind of immersion breaking. Your AI team is mostly useless and will just sit around waiting for you to move the story along or advance in the mission and are completely incapable of doing things themselves and prefer to sit in cover than help (plus, their aim is terrible). A few times this annoyed me so much I cheered as one of my team mates got mauled by an attack dog or blown up by something. Sometimes I would throw grenades at my teammates or push them out of cover intentionally, just to try and get them to do something. Of course, they're invulnerable to all damage. So, unlike in SWAT4, the threat of losing your team and the possible repercussions from that never even appears on the radar.
All that aside, the single player is still great and worth a purchase on its own.

Cons~ Story expects way too much out of a player. Multiplayer is a bit of a pain to understand. Spamming is easily rewarded. Spamming infinites more-so than that.
Overall, I like this game, but only for the graphics and arcade mode fun. And sometimes playing with friends. But this game hurts when it comes to story. I recommend this to people who basically like graphics over gameplay or people who like a switch-in 3v3 style combat game. This is not a game that stands the test of time at all. It has nostalgia factor but playing through it today only serves to make me realize how far the series has come in terms of pure playability. AC has never been known for great combat, but this game has combat you'll avoid at all times because it will make you impatient. Waiting ten seconds for enemies to hit you is not tense, it's an annoying filler task that serves to make the game boring.
The climbing is also very problematic, Altair will get stuck on things for absolutely no reason forcing you to drop and then try climbing all over again. The game also places a very large emphasis on stealth without having any practical stealth mechanics. The mission structure was cool in theory but it's poorly executed. It gives you no freedom and every assassination is extremely scripted.
I'd LOVE LOVE LOVE to see this game updated for the modern audience on say, the Unity engine with better climbing mechanics, combat that doesn't suck and actual open ended assassination and info gathering. As it stands, this game feels like nothing more than the beta for the second game which improved things exponentially (except I was disappointed that the second game went for a less ambitious structure, but considering everything else it fixed I can forgive it).
Read up the story of this game on Wikipedia then play the second if you want to get into the series. The reviews may hold this game in high regard, but this was the difficult dark age of 2007.

Amazing. Sometimes you spend so much time weeding through the big box ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t games out there looking for that experience you had from one game 10 years ago and never thinking you'll find it again. Well I found it. If I play a single player game it is to immerse myself intoa story that grips me. This game does such a great job of slowly dipping your feet into an emotional pool of hoplessnes and then out of no where pulling you under and leaving you begging for air. There are these sparse moment of extreme beauty amidst a sea of dispare. When you've spent 3 hours in a dark corner of Senua's miond and all of a sudden the sun shines and a voice in your head says "What is this place? I like it here" it just makes you want to sit down and never move another step in the game.
The first hour of the game does not do it justice. It's a light introductory to the world to come. Make sure you put on headphones, turn of the light and completely imerse yourself in the story. Just let go and let it take you on the journey and you won't be disappointed.
Now for the details:
Graphics - 9/10 Excellent quality, runs at a smooth 60fps with eveything cranked to the max at 1440p with my 980TI
Sound - 10/10 The audio production in this game is fantastic! You must play this with headphones or you are going to miss 1/3 of the games magice
Gameplay - 9/10 They through you in with no tutorial, hints, or any guidance besides the voices in your head. I will admit I played all the way to the first boss and halfway through the boss fight looked at the control scheme to see if I was missing something. Low and behold I weas only using 1/4 of the combat mechanics. This actually added a bit of charm to the game in my opinion and I'm glad I stumbled through the first hour without looking. Other than that everything is very fluid, entertaining and fun. Some of the puzzles are so simple that it makes them hard and frustrating(so you of that "duh" moment once you figure it out) but I'm not a real puzzle fan anyways so I'm just being critical. You will find the experience very linear and I find that a plus because the game really focuses on the story it is telling.
Overall I am very pleased with what Ninja Theory has done here. I can only wish that there was another game to fill the emotional void that this game will leave me with now that I have finished it. If you don't like this game you are not a human. Two thumbs up!

Vector is a runner. It's more puzzle and timing based than reaction speed. After the initial run that is; The opening cut-scene informs you of a world not dissimilar to a cyberpunk “1984”. It's essentially a 2D Mirrors Edge.
Simple and easy to grasp. There are only three basic main controls. Up to jump, down to slide and right/left to dash faster. You are always perpetually running. The main objective of Classic mode is to get to the end of the level and this will grant you one star along with any money you collected along the way. (I'll come back to the money)
There is a 3 star rating system for each level and this is where the hidden depth comes into play. Completing the level will get you 1 star. Collecting all the gems will get you another and performing all tricks will net you the last. Tricks need to be unlocked through purchasing them with the aforementioned money and activated during the level by pressing up when they prompt you. So they aren't real tricks per se but they are indeed about learning how to traverse the level to collect all the things.
The thing is you have to do all 3 things in one run and the path you need to take is almost never obvious to accomplish this. For instance vaulting over the desk rather than jumping over it to grab the gem and be in the right position to do the trick afterwards is quite a feat for the mind. You must also be aware that you are being chased and you must keep your speed up. Climbing over a water tower instead of sliding under to get into a new path to grab that gem just out of reach feels ever so satisfying once accomplished.
The game has this very “Trials” feel, where you are constantly restarting to get something right or to do it better. I have to mention failing is also quite brutal at times. Smashing into a building at full speed is quite the sight given the physics.
There is also an additional mode in which you play as the chaser and not the chased called “Hunter” which is fine but I had far less enjoyment playing this. I always felt as though I was one step behind.

If you play it casually, i.e. just getting to the end of the level without getting caught, it's an easy, enjoyable time-waster. But if you try to attain the highest score in each level (and you may want to eventually to get the most out of this game), it can be a very challenging game.
Getting all 3 stars requires memorization of the level and good reflexes. Basically, it's trial and error. What I find frustrating is the lack of checkpoints, which means you'll be restarting the level a lot to get those stars. One technique I learned is to use the static objects in the level's background and/or the small dents on the ground or walls as "indicators" to know where to execute the appropriate move.
While I do like the game, I don't understand why it costs 6.99 USD. It's barely any different from the Android/iOS version, which only costs 0.99 USD. Nekki once mentioned a WIP level editor that would have Steam Workshop support. It would justify the price tag, but it was never implemented and info about it can no longer be seen anywhere. Nekki has most likely scratched it.

Hello Games fell victim to what happens a lot in the games industry. Murray and the PR effort promised more than they could deliver, and showed footage at E3 that was far beyond what came out at release, they were rightfully scorned for that. However, that doesn't mean to say that there isn't a team of dedicated passionate devs working behind the scenes that did the best they could, and over the past year or so, they have really worked their backsides off to bring the game closer to what was promised.
The game has features in it now that make the experience feel much more open and varied. The story content takes one path, base building takes another. Progression is stronger and you don't feel quite so lost yet not so guided that it becomes linear.
I look forward to  sinking far more hours into this game since space combat has been given more purpose along with sentinel combat and there are features, like purchasing freighters, that make me want to continue to explore and develop. Tech is not so easily acquired which has increased the longevity of the game and additional features enabling you to teleport and return to your favourite systems is a welcome addition.
The UI also seems massively improved, and there seems to be an increase in life on planets (albeit far from the initial E3 trailers). There are some features I haven't even been able to access yet like land vehicles and terrain modification which I am excited to see.
Overall the huge effort from the devs is welcomed, and people who haven't played the game since its release will more than likely be pleasantly surprised, and new users now have a reason to actually buy the game. Well done Hello Games and to Sean Murray, if for whatever reason you see this.. please learn from your mistakes, and do not become a new Peter Molyneux who pulls this stunt time and time again.

Replay value: I'm not going to, anyway
Verdict: pick it up on sale if you want a simple, story-driven game
A nice little game that integrates its cental story conceits into gameplay. Fighting is incredibly simple, with a linear, highly directed story.
Where this game shines is in the world-building, a nice distopian future, with a french theme. The characters are relatively dynamic, despite most villains being introduced in the same episode they're defeated, and some characters with potential for interesting interaction are very lightly represented overall.
Where this game fails is in its story. The presentation of the story is ambitious, with focus on characters and a few key reveals. The problem is, in a game where a central conceit is the ability to rewrite, delete, and alter memories, the main character is never deceived, and reality is never in question. Story-wise this idea is used in a way any form of powerful science or magic could be used; creates monsters, has an exploit one bad guy can use to rule the world. It also gives an explanation for the tired trope of an amnesiac main character (which is doubly unnecessary in a video game, as the same sense can be accomplished with a silent protagonist ala zelda or half-life) but the revealed past, as these things come, is incredibly low-impact.
Overall the game leads you to an overwhelming question: where did all the guns go, and why has nobody shot me yet?

During the Steam Summer Sale, I happened to stumble across this game that I had never heard of before for somewhat cheap. I wanted to try something new, so I decided give it a chance; and I'm glad I did.
First off, the soundtrack is perfect for the game. Olivier Derivière really deserves more props for this. Second, the world design is absolutely fantastic and one of the highlights of playing the game. Third, the story is decent and helps to carry the game to the end. All of these combined provide a great atmosphere to the game, and the biggest reason I would recommend it.
Now, here's where it falls short: gameplay. It's very linear and repetative. It's not terrible, but it's definitely not the reason why I enjoyed this game. There are occasional puzzles to solve, and the Memory Remix sequences really provide something unique to the game, but most of the gameplay is arena-style combat and repetative bosses. But it looks great!
All in all, this is a really good first effort for Dontnod Entertainment, who went on to develop the very well-recieved Life is Strange and is currently at work on their next game. I would love to see more of the Remember Me universe, particularly if it were open world (and maybe a few changes made to combat).

I guess I can recommend this game. It's got a decent little story line, but its the combat system that actually kept me playing. With a nice world to play in as well.
While the game is about as linear as a game can get, the Devs did a really good job building the world. Every scene felt alive beyond the path you walked. People walked the streets, and drones flew around doing their daily tasks. It was really nice walking around in the game cause it felt so alive.
However it was also the visuals that made the game's largest issue. Because the game uses a, lets say Mirror's Edge style, blinding brightness it made combat difficult. You couldn't see the icons above the enemies heads because everything blended together and made it very difficult to see in some areas. Especially in the Kid Xmas fight.
When the lighting and the scene didn't make combat hard to play, then the game shined. The fighting is fast paced, forcing you to change in and out of combo styles to fit your needs at any moment. This kept me on my feet, and interested in playing. I'd be using short power combos to fight off the little guys, and then a long healing combo on the bigger enemy. Only to then switch the short combo to a (whever they called the cooldown one) combo to make my skills come back faster for crowd control. On top of that adding in the 3rd person cannon was fun to throw into combat. I found myself wishing for a Megaman game in the same style.
Is the game perfect? No, but it is still fun to play. I wouldn't buy it full price though. Only cause it took me 10 hours to beat, and if it hadn't been for the lighting making combat harder than it was, I'd have beat it in less.
I'd like to see a 2nd game, only because the ideas in this game were really cool, just not fully developed.

It was tough for me to decide whether I should recommend this game or not. I can legitimately say that there were as many good things as there were bad things. And with so many great games coming out these days, I would tell you to not bother with this one, unless you're really looking for a tearjerker.
First of all, the gameplay is irrevocably bad. Whenever the action was left to me, I wasn't having a good time - for multiple reasons: repetitive uninteresting tasks, limited exploration, clunky controls, pathetic key mapping, etc. If you want to tell a story, fine. But you have to respect the medium. And in that aspect To the Moon did a terrible job.
Now let's talk about the story itself. Although the premise is original and appealing (two "doctors" travel through a dying old man's memories to artificially alter the course of his life and ultimately realize his dream of going to the moon), I didn't find the story to be worthy of the praise it has received. The dialogues were very inorganic and most of the jokes were either too obvious or simply fell flat. The ending was cheesy and just plain uninspired. The thing I liked the most was the honest depiction of Asperger's syndrome. The music was rather good although sometimes overpowering but the art direction was poor and boring.

Paper Sorcerer reminds me of so many games (and memories) from my childhood.  The music takes me back. The turn based combat takes me all the way back to Bards Tale III - Thief of Fate and Wasteland (1) back on my Commodore 64 in the late 80's.  The graphics are striking and actually quite beautiful in their simplicity (I really like the shadow effects and the feeling of looking down over the edge into the blackness with just a few lines of white going down is amazing).
The combat is both interesting and involved ... and whenever you seem to feel that you are overpowered and don't have to worry this game seems to throw something at you that reminds you to pay attention.  The wide variety of summons/minions that you get to pick from (limit of 3 at a time) gives you a huge range of different party types.  Don't worry about out levelling old minions though as they actually level up with you regardless which means you can swap minions in and out at will (outside combat) and try out new combinations for particular situations (for example the Abomination is perfect for dealing with spellcasters but only does light healing compared to the Witch) ...
Don't be fooled into thinking this game isn't trying to trick you!  The secrets go from being simple and obvious to being down right fiendish (and you can stuff up and permanently be unable to find some of them!!!)
This game is fantastic ... it is potentially the most fun game I have played in a very long time and the developer has done an amazing job bringing the Kickstarter to its full potential!
The game is $5.00 ... if you don't try it you are missing out on one of the best games for a long time ...

What a fun game and a hidden gem. I picked Paper Sorcerer up on a whim and enjoyed my entire 20+ hour playthrough on normal. Probably will pick up again when the developer makes a few updates. You play as an inprisoned (inside a magical book) sorcerer able to summon 3 party memebers (thralls) to help you on your quest to escape.
The combat speed can be a little slow but I didn't mind. The variability of the thralls you choose to aid you is what I feel makes this game great. 3 healers, 2 (main) tanks, and several dps and buff/debuff characters to round it out keeps replayability high.
I had a good romp with my team: Vampire (dps/heals), Skeleton (tank), Ghost (buff/debuff), on my playthough. I feel this game is about taking out or incapacitating your enemies before they take out you VS. a give and take of damage with a balanced party with a tank and healer. My opinion could change on a higher difficulty playthrough or if the developer changes the balance of the game.
Combat remained fresh, really satisfied that RPG itch I didn't know I was craving. You constantly feel your team growing stronger through levels and new loot which is great.
I also appreciated the visual style and music - different and maybe repetitive but I was sold on what the developer was conveying the moment I started the game.
Like I said, a little game updating is necessary (some translations, which would make the ending more understandable / maaaybe a combat speed modifier / savable video and control layouts) but the developer seems to be on top of the community requests. Recommendation: Definitely Play - best 5 bucks I've spent in a long time.

So I just purchased this the other day. I thought I'd write up a review of it.
Pros:
* Old-school dungeon-crawl feel.
* Nice art.
* Neat little storyline.
* Turn-based combat, which makes strategy easier.
* Quite a bit of potential with skill training. Casters don't have to stay quite so "squishy," which has helped me in boss fights.
Cons:
* Combat can be a little repetitive.
* Minotaur minion seems a bit overpowered at the beginning, but he seems to balance out and be on par with other characters by around level 11.
* Slight issue with the save function--it doesn't automatically update and show me my new save. I have to hit "back," and it shows me the new save for exactly one second, so it's hard to confirm if I've saved the game unless I watch it like a hawk.
Additional: This is not a complex game. Some people might see that as a negative thing, but in this case, simple is better. The precept of getting out of the dungeon is straightforward. I have a few slight complaints, namely that I would dearly like to see some sort of enemy status bar so I know what debuffs I have put on them, but ultimately, if you're looking for an old rpg dungeon crawl game, for $5, this one isn't too shabby, not too shabby at all. I'd recommend it. It's actually a pretty good deal for only $5.

If the game were released in this state, I think the legacy would be a very different one. For the time being, I look forward to seeing where the developers at Hello Games take this game. Don't get to caught up into seeing this as "the game where you get to HACK people's brains! To death". As fun as memory remixing is it doesn't make a majority or even a decent chunk of gameplay. Typical game combat ranges from a beat-em-up where you customize the best combos to cheeze your way through to brick wall boss fights where you'll die a dozen times until you figure out the one routine that the game will let you use to pass them. Though as rare as the memory remixing sections, the puzzles the game gives (of both visual and linguistiv nature) are admittedly fun asides - if too easy (unless you're completely culturally ignorant).
If I'll be honest the game really shines in the audio and art design. Cyberpunk avec une touche française, I've never seen a cyberpunk themed game look so beautiful (sorry Deux Ex HR). And this is demonstrated everywhere, from the architecture and environments, to the fashion and character design. As cheesy and cliched as the countless baddies are, their visuals are well assembled. Setting this all against a magically ambient score only heightens the beauty of the game.
The plot can get a little too meandering. I'll admit I loved the dynamic between Nilin and her parent(s) as well as the ending twist, but you better bet I'd have liked it a lot more if I hadn't wanted the game to end four 'episodes' beforehand. As an aside the game is beautifully cinematic if played with French as the preferred language (given the Parisian development team) as the French voice actors give some emotion lacking in the default version.
Overall an underrated classic that's beautifully rendered but definitely may not be everyone's cup of tea given the gameplay.

If you are like me and prefer story-oriented games over complex gameplay, this game is for you. The story is interesting and the graphics are pretty good. If you combine those elements with a cyberpunk theme and a linear progression, you will enjoy your time while you explore Neo-Paris and steal memories from people.

First thing, this game is barely released.  Frog Dice is actively adding content every patch, which are frequent, and someone from Frog Dice is often logged directly in the game.
Overall:  This is a game with lots of potential that I am already enjoying.
Pros:
This is a game where you will build your character up.  Leveling doesn't give you much.  You need to find better equipment, and most of what you will want will be crafted, either by yourself or from someone else, or will be obtained from loot drops.
Very much a player-based economy.  Players have easy access to a global market place, so there are few barriers to players selling what they craft.
Turn-based combat.  I like this a lot.  I prefer strategizing to twitch-based shooting.
No hand-holding.  Pro or Con depending on your likes.
Devs are online a lot, and there is even a Discord VOIP channel.
Con:
Very little instructions or guides.  You will find yourself asking in global chat how to do things.  Fortunately, the community and the devs are very responsive.  There is a wiki, that is being grown.
Small community.  It's definitely growing, but still small.  This is to be expected considering this is a small company without a big name like EA or Bethesda.

Let me start by saying I LOVE this game, it has an amazing Tabletop Turn based fighting system simalar to FF tactics, it has an EXTENSIVE crafting and housing system, a HUGE open world with plently of room for additional zones/content as time goes on, a very possitive community, PvE Dungeons and Boss's, and the typical gear/experiance ladder you would expect in am MMO-RPG, and some great Developers who listen to feedback and interact with the population regularly.
The negative reviews of this game with 1 Liners from kids with less then 1 hour played are hilarious, but please see them for what they are, COMEDY, not actual relevant opinion.
THINGS YOU SHOULD KNOW:
This game is Grindy, on purpose, it is not a game where they expect you to be max lvl in a matter of days, crafting and experiance take time.
This game does not have a tutorial and hand holding, you are meant to go explore out of the gates and learn about how things work, that being said there is a "help" section in the menu which will explain a few key details to help you figure those things out, as well as a player made guide on how to get going in STASH, and a great Community to help in game (but please do a bit of looking/reading ingame yourself before logging in and blindly spamming "HOW TO PLAY?").
This game doesnt currently have a "Hardcore" mode, but at higher levels DEATH is punishable with xp debt, which is not a huge deal =D but if your expecting a glass cannon yolo game with no consiquences this might not be for you.
Stash wont be for everybody, but if youre a fan of a Long term friendly community, D&D, FF tactics, and tons of Favorite games from the 90s this game will hit home with you. Either way give it a shot for yourself.      ~~~~IGN: TimeKop

First impressions after completing the 1st chapter in story mode briefly. (not all 3 stars yet).
I played and completed the 3D 'First Person View' game 'Mirrors Edge' on both X360 and PC back when GFWL was at it's peak. What some may remember was that there was a 2D 'side scrolling' game of 'Mirrors Edge' as well. I haven't spent as much time with that and although I don't remember clearly but think you may have had control over the players movement, not sure. Anyway, I quite enjoyed the 'Mirrors Edge' games and the uniqueness of them.
So, if you also have fond memories of those games then you may also like 'Vector'.
This game is a 2D 'side scrolling' 'runner' game. I say 'runner' because you don't get to control your characters direction of movement. You only control when you jump, slide, and do tricks over obstacles based on 'timing' of your key presses, etc. This might sound 'simple' but a few things keep it challenging;
If you want to '3 star' all levels and collect everything then I can see a lot of replayability here.
Sometimes you probably have to play a level 10 or more times to get past it so there is some repetitiveness. If you are ok with that aspect then you may enjoy the challenge. It can be funny sometimes seeing the trouble your character or the 'hunter/chaser' gets into. Assassins creed has many awesome mechanics and a very interesting story.
However, the mechanics mostly fail and the story is extremely predictable.
The combat goes from extremely difficult to super easy after the first mission. The freerunning often causes you to jump off random ledges killing yourself, the set up missions are extremely boring and repetative, and the world - being set up in the middle east - looks like a poorly textured sand dune.
Here is why I recommend this game: The story, while predictable, is great. Its extremely interesting and it sets up the world fantastically, the side characters are well developed and have strong motivations, and while the set up missions are boring and repetative, the main missions are interesting and pretty solid.
Im really hoping that as the series develops the mechanics tighten up and the story continues in a similar fashion, but with less predictablity. The only thing that I would change is I would add a stealth mechanic. The missions could be far more interesting with one.
If you are interested in playing I would recommend just doing the minimum amount of set up missions per area and rushing through the game and enjoying the story. Im only a few hours in Assassins Creed 2, but most of my complaints are answered by it so far.
I give it a 4/10. Blamo.

It's not without issue, some sections will be frustratingly hard, and you might survive based on absolutely no skill and pure luck; but aside from the limited segments in game of this, it is a very fair, if a bit difficult game.
Story is a bit on the vague side, some stuff not even being explained, which is fine, because who really remembers the plot of any Metroidvania game outside of the fact it controls great and is pretty fun.
Gameplay is real smooth when you're in control, hectic when you're not trying to die. Endgame you may feel a bit OP, but by then you've basically earned that right, as you will constantly be hanging by a thread and carefully choosing when to save, as this game has one of the most frustrating, but understandable save systems I've seen in a while.
Technical performance is really not my lane, but the game appeared to run at 60fps at 2560x1440p nonstop, no screen tearing(v-sync enabled), and very limited in the settings menu, but the game seems to run fine in my case (i7 4790K,32GB DDR3,GTX980). So YMMV, but it seems to run okay.
Overall, 8/10; well worth your time with some weird design decisions, and some run from death twitch puzzles with cheap deaths galore, but definitely worth your time otherwise.
