It was tough for me to decide whether I should recommend this game or not. I can legitimately say that there were as many good things as there were bad things. And with so many great games coming out these days, I would tell you to not bother with this one, unless you're really looking for a tearjerker.
First of all, the gameplay is irrevocably bad. Whenever the action was left to me, I wasn't having a good time - for multiple reasons: repetitive uninteresting tasks, limited exploration, clunky controls, pathetic key mapping, etc. If you want to tell a story, fine. But you have to respect the medium. And in that aspect To the Moon did a terrible job.
Now let's talk about the story itself. Although the premise is original and appealing (two "doctors" travel through a dying old man's memories to artificially alter the course of his life and ultimately realize his dream of going to the moon), I didn't find the story to be worthy of the praise it has received. The dialogues were very inorganic and most of the jokes were either too obvious or simply fell flat. The ending was cheesy and just plain uninspired. The thing I liked the most was the honest depiction of Asperger's syndrome. The music was rather good although sometimes overpowering but the art direction was poor and boring.

First impressions:
Paper Sorcerer is one of those games that people generally miss out on. The game has a fantastic, unique art style and fun, classic turn-based battles
What really sold the game for me though, was the interesting style used. Never played a game with a style such as this, and Paper Sorcerer pulled it off well. The game has you going about a black and white world that you, the sorcerer, has been trapped in. You'll end up building up a party of mythological creatures and monsters to fight alongside you in turn-based combat against various foes. There are plenty of puzzles scattered throughout the game, usually leading to some pretty cool loot.
I'm not usually one to enjoy turn-based RPG's in this style, but this was a fantastic experience. It was just so much fun. Also, the game is only $5? What's not to lose here?

What a treat this game is. Highly focused, it does not burden the player with collection quests, crafting, leveling or any other tedious diversions that bog down other games that superficially look similar. The combat is basic, but well executed (play on Hard difficulty, it's not difficult at all!).
The production values, from visuals to sound far, far exceed what you would expect from a relatively tiny independent production. In fact, through it's relentless focus on Senua and clever solutions like video layovers and faceless enemies this is turned into one of the best looking games I ever played. Gameplay and thematics mesh well.
If I had to criticize anything, I'd say that some of the game beats still come across videogamey, e.g. some battles seem to be inserted more for giving the player something to play than story reasons. It's maybe 10% too stretched-out through repition, but I guess people would complain even more about the length if the game were any shorter. Personally, I much prefer these short, trimmed down experiences.
All in all, I highly recommend this game. It does not waste your time, it has a story to tell and it dazzles with its presentation.

I hate that I didn't like this game, honestly.
It's absolutely beautiful, and the storyline and characters you see are very well-developed, but the gameplay is just not for me. The combat is very restrictive and at times, a bit dull. There is cinematic value, but there isn't much gameplay value.
There are tons of puzzles throughout the game. Every new area you reach will have a puzzle, but they are all similar in their own way. You look at runes, and you match them with the environment, and you unlock more of the story. And then you move on and repeat it over and over. Again, this is GREAT for some people, but it becomes too repetitive and boring for my style of gameplay. If you like puzzles and a rich story, you'll probably like this game a lot. If you don't care much for puzzles and prefer games to move at a quick pace with a lot of action that feels like you're actually playing the character, you may not like it very much.
It seems like a lot of time was put into making this game, and the majority of reviews are from people who loved it, but I just couldn't fully immerse myself with how slow the pace was due to constant puzzles and fights that didn't feel inclusive. I would definitely recommend buying it and playing through at least an hour to see if it's right for you. If it isn't, you can always ask for a refund from Steam (just make sure that it's within their timeframe for returning and that it's under the max. amount of hours that they allow). If you decide you do like it in the time you spend playing it, then it's a win for you and you'll probably enjoy a full playthrough.
This isn't a bad game, it's just not the right game for me. It seems there are a handful of others who feel the same way.

To put simply, this is a game that is engaging in an unusual way. It puts you in the head of a woman in psychosis, to see what she sees, and hear what she hears. To anyone who has a very rigid view towards mental illness, you may be surprised how quickly you can acclimate, as it rapidly becomes 'normal'. I think that it is a fascinating way to introduce such a (sadly) controversal subject and was accomplished spectacularly.
To break down the stictly game aspects though, the combat is satisfying and rewards you for quick thinking. Reminded me a bit of Assassin's Creeds' type of melee combat. The puzzles are not extremely difficult or anything, and there are not a lot of hints given (besides all the symbols in the air to show you are in the right area), which is a good thing. The story I would say is a rather sad one. The protagonist has gone through hell (pun intended) and back in her journey through life, forced to have a unique view of the world, warped in psychosis.
I took for granted some of the things that are in the game as just part of the puzzles and such to be entertaining, but once you finish the game, watch the little feature. It discusses why they used certain things and how some people with mental illness live with those aspects every day.
I would say it is definitely worth the money and they easily could have made the price point $40. If you want to support the developers, pay full price. I am sure that it will go on sale at some point though and then you should definitely buy it.

No Man's Sky is such a valid game. In this brief review I want to talk about the game itself and avoid all the drama that revolves around the "unfair" release of the game when it clearly wasn't ready.
No Man's Sky offers to the user the chance of exploring the universe. Not a fictional one, but a real, living universe. It's not the most realistic game about this topic, nor the one with the best variety of things to do, but as far as I'm concerned, it's by far the one that offers the better experience of feeling like an explorer, a wanderer, a pirate, a wreckage-survivor. The whole thing is elevated by a terrific soundtrack, that always keeps the right tempo.
No Man's Sky makes you feel so human, tiny and vunerable, inside a universe packed with beautiful spots and environments, but also with dangerous creatures and people.
I recommend this game if you are fully aware of what you are about to spend money for. You're not gonna get amazing graphics or a tremendously fun gameplay. You're spending money to buy an experience and a feeling.

Let me give you a little insight into how I organize my steam games. I've got a folder for multiplayer games; that should be self explanatory. I've got a folder for currently installed games; that also is self explanatory. There's a folder for games I wish to play, a folder for games that I may play at some point, a folder for games I won't ever play that mostly consist of the extra, unwanted humble bundle games, and then there's the last folder. This folder is called "Absolute Garbage Full of♥♥♥♥♥" There are only two games in this folder, two games that are the worst of humanity and deserve nothing more than to be displayed in Museums where they display rotten games. One game is Deus Ex: Invisible War, the game that marked Ion Storm's downfall as they pandered to consoles, much like Crytek. The other is Assassin's Creed.
Don't get me wrong, the Assassin's Creed series is not a terrible one, or so I've been told. I have only played this one and Assassin's Creed 3. I did not like Assassin's Creed 3, but dear god does it fail in comparison to this piece of flaky bull. You start out with a rather interesting concept of a story; you're in a laboratory undergoing a simulation to relate to your knife-oriented ancestors in some plot involving Templars. You go through an intro with some heavy fighting and you're thinking "Oh, okay, this definitely is not a stealth game. This is a hack n slash." But whatever right? You suppose it can still be fun, right? Wrong, ♥♥♥♥ you. You get these awful controls and repitive combat that make you yearn to go play with a toaster; at the very least the toaster would be responsive to controls. But that's really the only thing it has going for it. When you enter a city, the side quests are by far the most boring, repititve, garbage nonsense that half the time doesn't even make sense. Why am I capturing flags? Why is there a time limit? I'm a trained assassin, not a crazed blue coin collector. There's tons of people being harassed and you can intervene, but why? I'm willing to change my review in the future since it seems like updates are pretty common, but LOTS of games wind up in that limbo of "well the updates keep coming, it might be good eventually" and never seem to get out of it.
But enough of that. Here's what I think of the game.
Pros?:
1. Reminds me of oldschool runescape, basically what you do is grind and talk. The downside is all you do is grind and talk, and that's if you can find people to talk to.
2. Has the charm of a simple, older RPG, but this hurts as much as it helps. It can come off as very generic or charming in its honesty depending on your perspective.
3. Grid turnbased combat is something I like to see, it's always satisfying to maneuver your tuns in such a way as to maximize your damage output and minimize damage intake. Unfortunately most combat circumstances like pinned/surrounded/etc have so little impact it's almost not worth the extra time spent thinking about it if you're worried about your exp/hour.
Cons:
1. Everything in this game is a headache. Grinding takes forever, for every skill and all the time and it only gets exponentially worse. Finding resources to gather is a pain because they spawn randomly all over the place and by the time you've seen it, someone with a 20$ mount rides over and takes it.
2. Economy is basically all the badsides of an auction house with none of the positives. I've never liked auction houses because they remove player interaction, it's a soulless way to handle an economy. This takes it a step further though by making it an absolute headache to navigate. Tabs loosely organized by item type, but only based on items advertised not based on the general inventory of a player's shop, no search function, prices are anybody's guess because there's no general trading going on, it's a nightmare. You'd think this might not be a big deal, "oh fine I'll avoid trading" but we get into our next point....
3. Loot is trash. Always. Monsters only drop items at 60% quality, and bosses can only drop 80% quality goods. So, player made items go up to 100% and have more enchanting slots. On the one hand I like that this validates the player crafting professions, on the other hand there needs to be some kind of middle ground where you do have a CHANCE at some decent gear while grinding. It wouldn't even be such a problem except that because the game is so young and there are so few good makers/weapon smiths/armor crafters it's almost impossible to find the gear and enchants you need, so you wind up getting smoked for several levels at a time while waiting. To wrap up that point, I can't emphasize enough how awful it is that all the gear you get from enemies is garbage. Grinding is already a chore, but in the carrot on a stick genre grinding becomes bearable by the few "Oh holy crap, THAT item dropped! What are the odds!" moments.
4. Community. I'm not saying anyone is mean, in fact most people are really nice, but I more mean that the community is already sabotaging itself. Clans have already formed and the bigger ones are literally bribing people with high crafting levels to join their clans and not sell their gear, so as if it wasn't hard enough to get anywhere in game, the already tiny community has fragmented into clans that largely don't interact with eachother, removing incredibly needed skills and products from the player economy. Because these clans have their own chats as well, the tiny community feels even tinier in the general chat since everyone's off in their own groups. Ask anyone who is looking for a group how long it takes to find people to even just talk to, it can be a real chore. Putting together a PUG in most games is a headache it just feels worse here for some reason. Honestly gaming communities in general have really gone down the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but that is a different discussion entirely.
5. The game doesn't seem too diverse. Most areas have the same enemies, just with higher levels and maybe some color swaps. For a game that has skimped on so much already you'd think maybe we could get some variety, but even the bosses are just larger versions of either smaller mobs (skeletons) or golems, which I've seen all over the place.
6. Free to play. I hate - HATE - the free to play model. Basically, it's free to play, but pay to have fun. The grinding is made intentionally terrible so you feel pressured to buy exp potions. You're going to want to buy mounts so you can finally get a small chance at resources before other people swoop in and steal them all. You're going to want to buy more inventory space so you don't have to go to town after 5 seconds. Crafting (which I'll cover next) is so painfully slow - but you get the option to complete it instantly with a small financial donation, separate for each crafting instance of course. I wish we could go back to the days where you could just buy a game and play it but hey, ♥♥♥♥ me right?
7. Crafting. I've talked about this indirectly already. Grinding resources is a pain. You can't find anyone who sells the right tools, can't find people to sell resources, and your production is limited by the level of your hideout making the grind artificially terrible, but it gets worse - whether you're cooking, enchanting or whatever, it takes time. Beginner recipes taking 30 seconds, level 10 recipes (which is NOT a high level) start to take several minutes. It'll take what feels like an hour to make a stack of food you'll eat in 10 seconds. Devs said they're going to change this, but it has to be for EVERY profession. Sitting in my hideout and spending a half hour grinding a portion of a level of exp to an arbitrary level point with no progression while not being able to do anything else except occasionally type is miserable.
8. Progression. Crafted gear and potions go from 1 - 5 - 10 -15, etc, by 5's, so you've got 4 levels of limbo where every level gives you basically nothing if you're using crafted gear or trying to grind a skill. Takes forever, it's not great. Crafted 100% gear is so good too that a 100% level 10 gearpiece is usually better than a 60% level 15 and that gear wont come with enchants. It's awful.
9. Partying directly harms your grinding. People are slow enough as it is, but exp bonuses for being in a party don't exist. They recently changed it so that parties get a higher chance at encountering leutenants and elites, which give more exp, but the exp difference feels so small it's hardly worth it. Every time I'm in a grou[p I think to myself &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥ I could farm this exact dungeon by myself but faster and I'd even get more of the loot". Needs to be a bit more encouragement for partying because right now if you can even find someone it doesn't feel like it pays off.
10. Character customization is lacking. I don't give a damn about the cosmetics (though it would be nice if my healer didn't have to look like a weird leathersuit gimp), but the racial differences are entirely negligable and heritage choice doesn't seem to do anything. Basically any character of a given class is interchangeable. On one hand some might like that they don't feel forced to pick a certain race to play a certain class, but without ANY real differences it feels cheap.
I could go on, but the tl;dr version is that it plays like a mobile phone game and right now there isn't enough strategic/game depth. If you're like me and you sometimes enjoy a bit of a brainless grind like maplestory and oldschool runescape, you might get some fun from this, but where maplestory/runescape had enough charm or polish to make the grind enjoyable, I'm not really sure I can say the same for stash. There's definitely the potential for a good game here but everyone on steam knows what a game that "could be good" usually winds up being - not very good. I'll keep an open mind though.

Thankfully a far cry from the usual overwrought attempt at a titillating experience, unless you really get off to the digital equivalent of swimsuit Barbies. Rather, Akiba Strip (let's not kid ourselves, that's the real name) is about... the plot, surprisingly enough, with a clumsy as hell combat system tacked on as the selling point. You've been kidnapped and turned into a vampire - sorry, synthister - that normally must feed on other people's positive energy, but thanks to a fateful blood pact you are able to retain your free will, and thusly go about your business of vaporizing other synthisters by stripping them of their clothing, exposing them to sunlight. It's equal opportunity pantsing of both genders whether you like it or not so it doesn't come across as horribly sexist, but for the majority of this game you go about brutally murdering your less fortunate kin via clothes removal with little hint of remorse. Rather morbid, really.
But that's okay because you get to buy keyboards and giant novelty items to use as weapons and it's slapstick ha ha and there's the mandatory forced romance subplot and... well at least the characters are amusing and the translation's good. Combat, sadly, is the worst attempt at a ripoff of the Arkham games I've yet seen, so again, the best you can hope for from this is an amusing story and lampooning of otaku culture. Does crash on load screens occasionally though.
If nothing else it's a comfort to know that I'm not quite so far gone as to identify with any of the wackjobs in this game in the slightest.

I have nothing but love for this game.
To The Moon handles some heavy issues in a very good and respectful way, but it doesn't end up feeling too serious or boring at all - it captivates, makes you want to push on, both because it's well-written and fun and because you won't feel satisfied until you know how it ends.
The puzzles balance nicely on the edge between being challenging and probably not being so challenging you'll have to close the game to find a guide, and the story itself is beautiful, motivational, and reads like a book you wouldn't be able to put down until you finish the last page. The gameplay consists primarily of walking around and exploring, interacting with the environment, unlocking and unpuzzling the various mementos in the different memories, and while it's not generally very action-heavy, chances are you'll be surprised every now and then at what the game has done this time to change it up.
In all honesty, I could go on forever, but suffice to say - I would heartily recommend this game to anyone who likes time-travel, well-written stories, and giving other people happy endings. And, well, everyone else, too.

Pros:
The atmosphere is really unique.  I like the mix of horror and Viking lore, which is definitely something you don't see every day.  The graphics and character design are great.  I think the overall artistic style makes a big difference, and this game does that really well.
Cons:
There's some random whispering at the beginning of the game, which I thought was a little off-putting at first.  It does become less distracting and annoying after the intro, and of course the volume can be adjusted for the voices separately.
I'm not a huge fan of the combat system.  To summarize the combat, you have to identify an enemy's next attack, and react within a very small window by blocking, dodging, attacking, or stunning.  That's it.  It's pretty much a serious of quick time events, and it relies heavily on having very quick reflexes.  There's not a lot of room for developing strategies, or just having fun with it.  It all has to be done a certain way, unless you want to lose all your progress.  It doesn't help that a lot of enemies attack while spawning.
There's also the perma-death.  If you die too many times, you lose all your progress.  I get the impression that not all areas count deaths the same way.  I didn't seem to get penalized as much in boss fights.  In other areas, if I were about to die, I would just exit to the menu, and reload the game.  Ultimately, this game mechanic is supposed to increase the tension, but it's just an added hassle.
The game is also a little short.  It's supposed to be an 8 hour game, for $30.  That makes it $2.75 per hour.  I'd like to see it a little closer to $1 per hour.
Summary:
It's a great game, which I would recommend, but it might be best to wait for a sale, due to the price per hour.

Remember Me was not very well received and the reviews were mediocre. To each their own, but I thought the game was very enjoyable. It looks great – it’s really cool to see the familiar Paris landmarks in a futuristic setting. It reminded me a little bit of how Earth is portrayed in The Fifth Element. I appreciated the story because it was something different from the norm. The specifics were kept a mystery for much of the game and you didn’t always know if you were working for the right side, so it kept me intrigued.
The combat is fun, and quite similar to the Arkham series with basic melee attacks, combos, dodging (instead of countering) and a couple ranged abilities to take advantage of. However, unlike the Arkham games, I never felt like the fights were excessively long and hand cramping. Every so often you get access to a new special ability which kept a sense of progression throughout the game. You can also create your own combos which gave combat a surprising amount of depth. You can add attacks that regenerated health or reduced the cooldowns on special abilities, allowing you to tailor combat to your enemies or your personal preferences. Aside from combat there is also a lot of fun, though not particularly challenging, platforming. All of the action is very fluid and slick-looking.
The one part of the game I have the most issues with is the memory remixes. Though this was a very innovative idea, I don’t think they are executed all that well. It is interesting to watch them, and see how a small alteration could result in a vastly different outcome, but they aren’t that fun to play. The controls are irritating and the solutions were pretty much a guessing game. However, there were only four of these sequences in the game so they didn’t detract too much.
Overall I’d definitely recommend the game. Nilin is a great main character with lovely voice acting, and the story will keep you entertained. Some of the dialogue occasionally veers into melodrama, but I found those instances rather fun and campy. I really recommend playing with a controller rather than mouse & keyboard, the controls are 100x better.

Since Vector is one of my first steam games, I felt that I had to make this game my first review. After 33 hours clocked in game time I've finally collected every achievement, got all the stars and also finished Hunter mode completely. So I feel like I can give my full opinion on the game. (without spoilers ofcourse)
Quick Game Summary:
Vector is an action packed 2D sidescrolling parkour game, with a basic but kinda gripping (atleast to me) storyline. You wanna break free from control by ''The Man'', in this case ''Big Brother'' and the hunters are after you. Basically all you need to know is in the description in the store page.
Gameplay:
Vector as I said before is a 2D Sidescroller, but not one with free controll like, let's say Mario. No, Vector is an on-rails autoscroller where, depending on the situation, you either press down to slide, up to jump or hold to the right to sprint. You also have these parkour tricks you can purchase to do cool tricks in the level by pressing up when you land on a trick. Unlike the Facebook port and free version on the mobile phone, you get enough money at the end of the level, to purchase all the tricks that are needed for the next level. The game gets pretty hard and challenging which is a good thing, but the hardest part of the game is the Hunter Mode, where you play as the hunter and try to hunt down Vector. I like to call this part the hard mode since thats the reason why it took me so long, but it's extremely satisfying when you get Vector at the end and it adds for lots of replayability.
Vector is in the end a fun timewaster and I recommend you atleast try it out, it's worth the price and you may end up liking it.
I'm still waiting on that level creator though... Oh and also super psyched for Vector 2.

I'm a big fan of old-school dungeon crawlers, but Paper Sorcerer ultimately attempts to crib a lot from 2009's The Dark Spire, and instead delivers a buggy and underdeveloped slog. The trailer, screenshots, and overall aesthetic are impressive to be sure, but they belie a cumbersome user interface (for a genre that is 90% menus, why are the menus so annoying to use?), a sluggish battle system, and overall very dull mechanics that offer little in the way of exciting character molding or customization. A dungeon crawler must dangle the excitement of pushing forward and advancing your characters bit by bit, but Paper Sorcerer's skill system has no appeal and the battles are a chore of poorly-telegraphed information and so, so much waiting.
I want to like this game, and I truly do appreciate the efforts to bring more dungeon crawlers to the market, but Paper Sorcerer is a meandering and unfocused product in serious need of more thought-out game design and revised UI design.
As a $5 game, it is admittedly worth a try, even with the simplistic gameplay & numerous bugs (none of them game-breaking so far, at least) -- but if you value your time even moreso, my suggestion is to try out Legend of Grimrock on Steam or The Dark Spire on DS, two games in the same style that deliver a much more captivating experience.
In short: be wary. The paper aesthetic is so fresh and appealing that it's easy to assume the rest of the game is just as polished, but unfortunately the core gameplay is miles behind what I would expect from a 2014 Wizardry-like. Will you find it fun? It's hard to predict -- but if you keep up with the scant few post-2000 dungeon crawlers like I have, the answer will probably be No, because Paper Sorcerer decidedly does not want to do anything unique with the core genre.

The one that started it all. I've played through AC1 - Revelations on consoles and have decided to revisit AC1 - AC3 and eventually the rest on PC with 100% completion.
There are two mind sets I would review this game in; 1. Completing purely for the story and background. 2. Completely the game 100% (All collectibles and missions etc..).
If you're more of a number 1. then by all means purchase this game and enjoy the backstory to the others and if you're like me then play the rest. The only real downside the completing the game like this is sometimes the parkour movement will seem clunky especially late game. I won't spoil when I started getting frustrated with it.
However if you're the wanting to full clear this game with all collectibles found and all missions completed then you may or may not want to skip this one depending on your patience.
Problem 1. As I said the parkour in this game can be clunky if you're not going straight forward. As can be expected it's only the first in the series.
Problem 2. The side missions are very repetitive. You will essentially have a cookie cutter copy of missions through each district in the game (a total of 9). The only thing changing will be the final assassination.
Problem 3. Since I had decided to do a full completion run I found myself constantly Shift+Tabbing to a steam guide for all the locations. Now for some reason this game does not take that too kindly and if you remain in the Shift+Tab state for too long the game will simply crash. I have tried to numerous fixes I could find but not of them stopped the problem entirely. Thank fully AC1 auto saves after every collectible pick up so I never lost data. Just patience.
Problem 4. Speaking of the final assassinations (don't worry no spoilers here). I found that most of them cannot be "stealth" killed. Now I don't entirely remember if the following games have improved on this to allow the player to stealth or styalise their final kills but in the first game it is essentially find the target, kill all the guards and then kill the target.
This is a great game for the first in its series and I highly recommend it for pure story playthroughs. If you are willing to go through 25+ hours and occassional crashes + clunky parkour at times then it will also be great for a full completion (all collectibles / missions).
Enjoy and Happy Assassinating!

7 Wonders: Treasures of Seven is a standard casual match-3 game themed after the 7 Wonders of the World, where it's unique mechanic involves moving a heavy box  to and endpoint around the field that can not be directly moved, but will fall once pieces under it are matched. This box doesn't appear until you made enough matches/points. This box is then stuck in a "track" in the level that it can't escape- so you have an idea of where you need to move the box. The playfield can be rotated which is needed to move the box at certain angles. Each level has differently shaped playfields and tracks, that adds a bit of challenge to figure out how you need to match gems. You have a limited time to move the box to the end point, though I've rarely lost more than 1/5th of the available time, so I'm not even sure what happens if you do loose time - you'll have a lot of assistance thanks to special gems, an NPC that points out matches to you, and a shuffle button that activates after a few matches are made.
Look, the game is solid and does what you expect, but it is extremely average. Not bad, and certainly a passable time waster while watching something else, but playing it actively can be boring for somebody who expects more depth like out of the Puzzle Quest games. The only reason I even bothered is I saw a friend who played this series alot. You certainly can do worse, but unless you get this from a bundle or are a huge fan of casual puzzle games, you shouldn't waste your time or money.

I remember playing the original 7 Wonders game and several of the follow ups in the past. I can't remember where I played them, but I do remember the art style, and building the "Wonders".  So, let's get into it here...
-Game is exactly what it is advertised as: A
Match 3 Puzzle game. (And by Casual, I mean VERY Casual...)
-Nice music
-Nice graphics
-Runs smoothly on a toaster, or a potato, or a turnip... would run well on a mobile device (which is what it seems best suited for...)
-Workers are still as cute and annoying as always, annoying enough to be cute or vice versa
-Board rotation (allowed constantly w/o needing to earn it), and needing to move a special piece through a set path, to lock it into a specified location to finish each level is different from many Match 3 games, so a few twists on the standard.
-EASY, with a very generous timer and power ups (This is both good and bad... good if you want very casual and easy...)
-EASY, possibly TOO easy for anyone looking for a challenge. Timer allows far too much time to really ever feel any imperative to make matches quickly, power ups are almost too easy to get and too plentiful. Totally subjective.
-
- I got a key for free, so I can't complain. But I would NOT recommend this game at full price ($10 USD is way too much), would not recommend unless you get it for 75% off or more.
Game has replayability to a degree, since it does rely on random placement of the tiles you have to match.  I have played for a few hours, 15 minutes at a time. I could keep playing this as a pure, casual, relaxed time waster. But it is at the bottom of my list if I want a challenge tbh.
Fun little game, but don't get this thinking it is as "difficult" as earlier versions of the game, The frustration and challenge were removed in this version. That said, it would be a great game for kids, because the satisfaction of completing levels and successfully building a Wonder are almost guaranteed. But a possible disappointment to fans of earlier versions of the game.
6/10 Overall   Would buy at 75% off or better, would never buy at full price of $9.99 USD

I have been playing Skullgirls since release. Though my Steam playtime may say otherwise, I have been enjoying this game on console mostly, since I originally purchased it on my PS3. This game is a delight. A throwback and respectful nod to the 2D fighters of old, while managing to contain the ferocity of newer 2D fighter titles.
I found out about the game when it was still in development, through a college friend who was doing clean-up animation on it at that time. One thing I will always remember, is the claims Mike Z and the animation team made about how the animation of the sprites would be top notch. They did not lie. This game holds some of the most beatiful HAND DRAWN animations you may see in a fighting game, or any other genre for that matter. I think it is obvious to understand that I believe this game to be artistically flawless.
The cast of the game is, for lack of better word, amazing. The concepts for each fighter are well addressed and easily understood. Their designs are amazing and the lore that accompanies each individual is satisfying. Although many people were not happy with the inclusion of the male fighters, I welcomed the addition as a fresh breath to the game. I only wish there were more on the roster.
Mechanically, this game hit the mark. Many patches plagued the release of it, but what shortly was given to us was a fighting game that in my opinion would be the most balanced fighter in the market. As I said before, the game is a nod to 2D fighters of old. This means many of the commands will be easy to figure out and complete. Thus, many critiziced the mechanics as "already done". I was quite happy with seeing mechanics as good as MvC2 tossed into a salad with the likes of mechanics like the ones in Guilty Gear X. Because the mechanics were so familiar, the game became one of the most user friendly fighters I have played. The tutorial is also very good. Only thing I kinda wish for was a bigger roster and a moveset list. But nothing that really hurts so far. Trust me. Playing the game before all the DLC characters were introduced was a deal of love for it.
The lore in the game is amazing. Each character has an amazing story and frankly I want more. The writing was pretty darn good. The voice acting was on point and no character sounded like the last, for which I was very happy.
Overall, the game is a must for any fighting game afficionado. No other fighting game currently has been as polished as this one. I bought it on the PSN and bought it on Steam. And if it meant ensuring this team of amazing developers got the recognition they need, I'd purchase it again.

Paper Sorcerer is a turn-based RPG and dungeon crawler with a stylistic flair. First off, there's a somewhat monochromatic theme throughout the game, alongside heavy contrast thanks to fairly common shadows. Thus when colors do appear, they're much more striking. While the sprites and animation themselves aren't the best, the total effect of the game was a minimalistic experience which I found rather refreshing. The developers are still sorting out a few kinks with the game, such as being able to adjust game volume and the like. That wasn't a problem for me, as I found the soundtrack helped set the mood of the game and all told was a fan of it.
As for the gameplay, you are a sorcerer bound in a magic tome, with the objective of fighting your way out. Your party consists of minions whom you summon with your arcane powers. Some of this game's stylistic charm comes from the fact that instead of the cut-and-dry mage/fighter/thief, your minions are themselves monsters: minotaurs, vampires, ghosts, imps, and the like. This comes off across a lot less as anti-heroes as you'd think it would, but it was another thing I found quite refreshing about this game.
The combat itself is quite fun and has depth, while managing to keep things simple enough. One of my qualms with the normal difficulty setting was that after a point, the combat was a bit too easy, though there are harder difficulties to fix that problem. A good deal of the gameplay comes from exploring dungeons and finding secrets. These can range from easy to very puzzling, with the harder ones being more rewarding to complete. This aspect of the gameplay fits in very well with the rest, the result being an excellent dungeon delving experience.
So I can't tell you this game is perfect, but I don't really think it tries to be. When I first saw this game, I got "art game" vibes from it, but actually playing it, Paper Sorcerer comes off much less pretenious than that. The final product here is a laid-back (if somewhat minimalistic) dungeon crawl. It has breadth without being overly complicated, and most importantly it was refreshing. For five dollars, this is definitely worth picking up: if you're a fan of turn-based RPGs, Paper Sorcerer is a solid game that you can sink both your teeth and your time into.

Iron Front : Liberation 1944 is a pretty nice looking total conversion for the ARMA 2 engine. The majority of the unit graphics are debatably nicer than that of some vanilla ARMA 2 units. Likewise, most of the units available in Iron Front : Liberation 1944 look authentic and there is a fair amount of equipment from late in the war. Sadly, these are the only real compliments that come to mind when I think of this "game."
So what's the real problem here? Well, first off: The AI is pretty anemic. A hallmark n00b gripe with ARMA is that of the omnipotent and almighty - "Uber Cheaty" - AI (with eyes in the back of their collective head.) Sadly, this isn't the case for the AI in Iron Front : Liberation 1944... In fact a major complaint about this "game" is that the AI is dumber than a box of rocks and as a long time (since 2001) ARMA player, I'd have to disagree...
Despite the fact that Iron Front : Liberation 1944 is built on the ARMA II engine and despite the largely identical command menus, I feel as though something was lost during the total conversion... So much so that the AI in Iron Front : Liberation 1944 appears to be dumber than a dump truck load of boulders.
As an example: I watched two opposing tank platoons pass right by one another without firing a shot. Being the commander of a lead tank, it was my experience that the command menu in Iron Front : Liberation 1944 is almost completely useless. Due largely to the inept, incompetent and insubordinate nature of the AI in this "game."
After watching the enemy tank column pass by my platoon at point blank range, I tried giving each of my tank gunners their own specific targets. No results... Ok, well how about each of you try opening fire? No? Not interested? Ok... Maybe we can all just stand around, hold hands and discuss how we feel? Would you like to do that? Guess not...
Don't worry though, the AI's lack of sighting, reporting and automatic engagement skills isn't likely to result in any casualties... Realistically, I don't think that any of the AI driven units in the "game" actually pose a threat to the player. However, I do think that boredom is a serious threat to anyone who plays Iron Front : Liberation 1944.
Which brings me to my final point, is this a "game" or a "paid total conversion mod?"
As a standalone game, the AI is pretty lacking, there is no default CTI mode and the majority of the maps are pretty small... Even if you consider this as a paid total conversion mod of ARMA II - it lacks the depth of content you're likely to find in some unpaid addons, mods / total conversion for the various versions of ARMA...
Which ever way you approach this - I think that if you really want an ARMAesque, WWII experience, you would be better off finding your own collection of WWII addon units and maps for ARMA I, II or III...
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Is Iron Front : Liberation 1944 a decent, large scale land / air WWII sim?
Absolutely! If you could consistently get enough players together for huge multiplayer battles it would probably be a pretty fun game.
Is Iron Front : Liberation 1944 a complete ARMA II experience set in WWII?
Nope... Too much functionality and challenge was left behind... The reason the ARMA series has been so successful has been its community, both in terms of players and content makers... Which is something that Iron Front : Liberation 1944 currently lacks.
Unless you've got money to burn - this game is a pass.

I haven't played many match-3 games so far, so I don't really know what's standard and what's considered exceptional among them, so let's get the basics out of the way first.
A gridded board is filled with stones of various shapes and colours. Switch adjacent stones around to match three or more in a vertical or horizontal line to remove them and make all the stones above drop down. In each square of the grid (underneath every stone) is a tile. For every match that's made over a tile, that tile is then removed. Remove all tiles on the board to complete the stage. As far as I know, that's the bare minimum for every match-3 game? But this has some extra features.
As you clear the tiles, you reveal a maze-like track hiding beneath the board. When all tiles are removed, a "7 block" appears at one end of the track, and a goal at the other where the block has to be moved to. Conveniently, you can rotate the board 90 degrees at any time to orientate the block to drop in the desired direction. At a certain point in the game locks are also introduced - coloured rings that cover the goal preventing the block from resting in it and a match of the same colour must be made within the same space in order to remove it. None of these hurdles are too troublesome at first, but when the size and shape of both the board and tracks start to become more elaborate, then things can get a little messy. Thankfully, though, there are special items to aid you in your task.
There are rewarded for matching more than three stones at a time. If you match four, an item appears on the board that will clear an entire horizontal line of all stones and tiles in one go. Matching five will give you an item that clears everything in both a horizontal and vertical line. And at random points a die appears, which when moved, will clear a handful of random squares scattered across the board. On occasion you'll also be given the optional objective of completing a match of a certain colour within an allotted time. If you succeed the clock will be frozen momentarily. But given how much time they give you for every stage, this is something of a none-issue and I don't think I ever even came close to the halfway mark on the timer, so you shouldn't need to worry about that.
The unique spin the game tries to put on its presentation is that all of these tiles you're collecting goes towards the assembly of a Wonder, with every stage you complete getting you closer to building it. There are nine Wonders to build, with seven stages each, the first six taking place on the outer surfaces of a cube, and the final stage being inside it, which is a nice little touch. But aside from the visuals and theme, there's nothing special or particular about it that actually adds to the gameplay in any way.
This isn't the most challenging game in the world, and truth be known, I did find myself getting a little bored and going through the motions towards the end. But I still never actually had a bad time at any point and found it was just the right length to not entirely wear out its welcome. So if you're looking for a casual little time killer and can pick it up at a decent enough price, then you could really do a hell of a lot worse than this.

I've played through two other 7 Wonders games. 7 Wonders II was too rough and simplistic, and Alien Makeover was too complex (although I enjoyed it a lot).
Treasures of Seven is possibly my favorite of them (until I get to play the other ones, of course). By no means is it any hard (you can't turn off the timer, but it runs out after, like... 45 minutes? You'll finish most levels in 5 to 10), but it's relaxing and offers a fun challenge when it comes to rotating the view. Which reminds me of the mechanics in Ron Gilbert's most excellent pirate match-3 game, Scurvy Scallywags. And then you get to the moment where you have to navigate a tile around the board to try and make it reach a specific spot. That's the best part in most puzzles: some of the layouts can be tricky, especially in the last few 'wonders'. It's not very hard either, though, because (as I realized in the end-game), the teleporter tiles can be used in both directions (you'll know what I mean when you see it). Overall, each level has 2 to 3 different 'stages' that you have to go through, and it helps break monotony, which is often a problem in match-3 games when, well, you'll just want to play "one more level" and end up spending your evening on it...
I want to say a word about level 6-6. I went through a bizarre 'series of unfortunate events' with that one, and was unable to quickly unlock the target spot, even after dozens of shuffles. In the end I spent about 40 minutes on it, 4 times more than the hardest next puzzle. It's not that it was hard -- it was just pure bad luck. I really don't think there's a point in having a timer here. If it runs out after 45 minutes, I'm positive you're not going to replay that level any time soon. Ah well, a LOL moment.
TLDR: very easy game, very relaxing, fun puzzles here and there, I enjoyed it a lot, just as much as I suck at describing game rules.

The problem with that is that while you might think it's an interesting variant on match-3 gameplay (the board rotates to assist in this), the time limit is INSANELY generous. I don't know if I ever went down further than a third of the meter, and that was while I was passing out and zonking out for a few seconds at a time every so many moves. I can see reasons to play earlier 7W games, and the later ones redefine things in their own way, but god, this one's a relic.

I played the free version of Vector on my Android tablet and found the controls frustrating; too often I'd miss the jumps due to the game not responding to touch. I'm very glad I bought it for PC!
Vector is a great side-scrolling parkour game. The controls are very simple, run, speed up, slow down, jump, slide, and fall. In some situations you can do a wall climb, and that's about it.
Each level has three special parkour moves that you can do once each in a set location in the level, assuming you have enough coins to unlock the move before attempting the level. These moves are activated by pushing up in the same way as a regular jump, but some of them are pretty impressive, and they add extra flair to the game.
The intro is cool and sets the mood for the game well, and the story gradually progresses as you play through. I'm not finished yet, but each time I've encountered a little plot hook so far it's made me smile. I'm looking forward to seeing what happens next.
The graphics in Vector are very simple, but the animation is fantastic and works amazingly well. It reminds me of the original Prince of Persia animation: very fluid and flowing; perfect for this game.
Replayability of levels you've already beaten comes in the form of retrying the levels to get more coins, which are then used to unlock moves in later levels. Getting a perfect score in some levels will take many, many replays.
I definitely recommend Vector. I don't know if I'll ever finish it 100%, with all levels perfect, but for now I'm enjoying the attempt.

I've enjoyed other FrogDice games, they always seem to land squarely in the "flawed but fun" category so I was excited for this one. Unfortunately, in it's current state all I can describe it as is painful. Let's list the issues:
-Painful to figure out
It gives an ok combat tutorial and points out a few things. That's it. Hope you like randomly clicking on stuff in the hopes you can figure out what it does. I couldn't even figure out how to heal, or exit a dungeon at first.
-Painful to read
Holy tiny font, batman. Seriously, the miniscule font size on this game gives me a migraine. The game even supports resolutions too small to actually read the game text at all.
-Painful to move
Like watching your character slowly inch square by square like a lazy chess piece? I hope you do because it's all you'll be watching.
-Painful to craft
I made a Hunter/Farmer, so the sensible crafting profession was Chef. Bad choice. I placed a baited trap and stared at it for a while, nothing. I dungeon crawled and got 2 sacks of flour, came back to no bait and an empty trap. I looked at the newspaper and found ingredients going for 1,000s of triads apiece. I have a grand total of 650. Crafting is currently for the rich and overleveled so what about combat?
-Painful to level
The combat is flawed, like when you click slightly off the monster occupied square so the game completely deselects your skill, but it's not horrible. What is painful is the amount of grind needed to get anything worthwhile is only made more painful by the fact that you will be fighting the same things in the same dungeons over and over and over. Also the loot that you pick up? Most will be vendor fodder but the bit that is sellable?
-Painful to buy or sell on auction -err- newspaper
There's no auction house, which I appreciate, but in its place is a bulky "newspaper" that lists highlighted items being hawked by players. Not a bad idea until you realize there's no easy way to find what you need and once you do find it, it will be so far out of your price range it won't matter. Perhaps you want to sell? Well the game will give you a small "cart" to start as well as give you the starting price for your items. Unfortunately, this price will be far below the current going price amd there's no good way of figuring out the going price.
Painfully dull
- There's no reason given for your existence. You are plopped into the world and ignored. No mythos,  no story, no destiny, no one cares. It all feels like a board game without the fun of a free night spent with your friends. If I want to do hard, boring work for little gain and no recognition I'll go to my job. I play games for an escape, not more punishment.
So, yeah. I plan on trying it out a bit more for old time's sake. Maybe it will grow on me or maybe an update will make it better, but I can't say this game is fun, because it's not, it's painful.
While definately still a work in progress, this game is enjoyable to play.  The developers really seem to care about what people think and are always willing to listen to the players.

It'll also probably tickle the itch of the really old school MMO players who constantly bemoan the fall of old games like Everquest.  But, I'm not that crowd, so I can't review through those rose tinted lenses for you.
Anyway, for the game itself, its suuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuper grindy.  Duoed 90% of it with a friend, who suggested we try it.  And, after my almost nine hours, I'm the proud owner of two alts at levels... *drum rolls*  5 and 3.  Out of a level cap of 100.  (And technically uncapped as there's some sort of infinite post-cap leveling system.)  Woo?  I've heard from chatter in chat that it takes ~100 hours to hit level 15.  Yes, 15.  I've also managed to level my base once, once of my gathering skills once, and my crafting?  Nada.  On top of this, there's backwards progression in the form of XP debt, which I saw someone commented can set you back by DAYS of grinding.  And also on crafting:  I logged in before this review to double check some things and my plants and animals for getting crafting mats had died since I last logged on and took all their drops with them.
Woo.
...not that I could do anything with them yet since I needed multiple machines for processing the stuff, each which cost 1k in in-game currency.  I was looking at probably a 3-4k investment just to make some eggs and potatoes.  And then try to sell in the auction hou-  ahem, sorry, the Newspaper for like... 30 a pop?  ...assuming if things were that simple since this game is really friggin' poorly explained.  Some of their patches are helping it, like a recent one which explains what low level Elementalist skills actually do besides damage, but this game is way too convoluted to have so little explanations.  Wouldn't have bothered with cooking had I known ahead of time I'd be sinking tons of cash for little gain
Speaking of, the economy sucks, plain and simple.  If its not evident yet, this game is a super hardcore grinder.  And the newsaper (which is merely a really inconveniently designed auction house, all in the name of economy, despite how hard the devs will argue its not and will launch tirades about how auction houses are the worst possible thing to ever exist in a MMO) is dominated by super hardcore players mostly charging super hardcore prices for items.  Not that they're making items for my level anyway, and the few bits of junk around my level are simply racing to the bottom of the price and are merely dropped loot (crafted stuff is always better in this game.)  Why?  People are hoarding all the crafting goods and vendor trashing most everything they don't need.  And the developers are making it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for both buyers and sellers to get their goods to each other all in the name of it being better for the economy.
There's... also some other weird decisions done by the devs.  Healing, for example, is super freaking frustrating.  Your only free option is to go back to town and AFK for about ten minutes in the inn, because there's no other source of out of combat healing and its extremely slow to encourage you to spend money.  You can buy camp materials to make a camp anywhere and then AFK and do something more fun in the mean time on the go.  Or you can buy food and potions and fill up your extremely limited inventory space with food items.  I saw a dev comment they did this so cooks would actually have a place in the economy.  But, food raises stats and supposedly does other things too later, so... shouldn't that be the draw?  Except dedicated players are claiming to have already maxed their stats, oops.  And lowbies like me can't even raise their stats yet, so double oops.  And cooking takes an investment of thousands of triads (I'm not mixing up my in-game and premium currency terms, am I?) to even get going for a modest gain, leaving me, a cook, to decide between spending money on stuff to heal and slowing down my crafting progression or spending money so I can craft to heal, maybe make a profit in the future, and be forced to AFK for hours in the mean time.  >.<   So cooks are getting shafted economically from the get go as far as I can tell.  Of course, you can alleviate this by bringing a pocket healer, but they still need food for mana and, since they can't heal out of combat, except to be doing silly things like leaving one monster alive just to heal.
Okay, so, tangent on healing aside, grouping is weird.  Group members don't participate in the same things unless they "stack" on the group leader and then auto-follow them into combat.  As such, in between stuff, it is their job to take their hands off the controls and wait for the next fight or gathering node or whatever since, if someone starts a fight without them, they cannot participate in that fight.  Ever.  There also appears to be no Round Robin looting, meaning you're going to have to trust someone to actually share stuff, whether it be your leader or other party members.
Also also, movement itself.  Its slooooooooooow.  And the maps are not designed well.  Like, in town, I started at the entrance and took a stop watch and timed my trek to the farthest merchant NPCs.  it took a full minute, moving optimally, to get there.  Why is this designed like that?  And why are their no walking animations?  It looks really weird and bugs me.  Why is there a separate move command in combat when you have to move before attacking if you want to, why can't I just click like out of combat?  Why do my movement commands randomly cancel, even after the patch that was supposed to fix it?  And why do cat folk use stock wild cat sounds from the 80s that are so out of place?
*deep breath*
...okay, this review went a lot longer than I planned.  And a bit ranty.  But, this game has a lot of problems and really only caters to an extreme niche crowd.  And the developers, while super friendly and seem to be in the actual game interacting with the community often, I feel that they seem to have their heads firmly stuck in the clouds as well about their vision for the game and are missing the reality.  (Yes, the article you love to link to says the auction house was bad for Star Wars Galaxies, which is why you opted against a functional one, but did you read the full article and see where it says auction houses aren't bad for all games?  Not saying you should go the auction house route here, if you're actually reading this, but still.)  So, I can't recommend it and I don't really see myself coming back to it unless there's some really massive changes that make it friendly for more casual play, since I really don't need a MMO to hardcore sink my life into right now.
So bottomline:  I don't recommend it unless you're the very tiny minority this game caters to.  But its free, so try it yourself if you want as it'll only cost you time and bandwidth.

I have been playing Skullgirls since release. Though my Steam playtime may say otherwise, I have been enjoying this game on console mostly, since I originally purchased it on my PS3. This game is a delight. A throwback and respectful nod to the 2D fighters of old, while managing to contain the ferocity of newer 2D fighter titles.
I found out about the game when it was still in development, through a college friend who was doing clean-up animation on it at that time. One thing I will always remember, is the claims Mike Z and the animation team made about how the animation of the sprites would be top notch. They did not lie. This game holds some of the most beatiful HAND DRAWN animations you may see in a fighting game, or any other genre for that matter. I think it is obvious to understand that I believe this game to be artistically flawless.
The cast of the game is, for lack of better word, amazing. The concepts for each fighter are well addressed and easily understood. Their designs are amazing and the lore that accompanies each individual is satisfying. Although many people were not happy with the inclusion of the male fighters, I welcomed the addition as a fresh breath to the game. I only wish there were more on the roster.
Mechanically, this game hit the mark. Many patches plagued the release of it, but what shortly was given to us was a fighting game that in my opinion would be the most balanced fighter in the market. As I said before, the game is a nod to 2D fighters of old. This means many of the commands will be easy to figure out and complete. Thus, many critiziced the mechanics as "already done". I was quite happy with seeing mechanics as good as MvC2 tossed into a salad with the likes of mechanics like the ones in Guilty Gear X. Because the mechanics were so familiar, the game became one of the most user friendly fighters I have played. The tutorial is also very good. Only thing I kinda wish for was a bigger roster and a moveset list. But nothing that really hurts so far. Trust me. Playing the game before all the DLC characters were introduced was a deal of love for it.
The lore in the game is amazing. Each character has an amazing story and frankly I want more. The writing was pretty darn good. The voice acting was on point and no character sounded like the last, for which I was very happy.
Overall, the game is a must for any fighting game afficionado. No other fighting game currently has been as polished as this one. I bought it on the PSN and bought it on Steam. And if it meant ensuring this team of amazing developers got the recognition they need, I'd purchase it again.

Remember Me is the First Project by the French Developers DONTNOD Entertainment, and are certainly shaping up to be a very successful Team with 2 outstanding Games [Life Is Strange]. It has certainly got me excited for the 3rd Game rumoured to be released in 2017 "Vampyr".
The Game takes place in Futuristic Paris, and comes with a very unique and interesting Story, with some solid Visuals to take in. For the first half of the Game, I found myself to be walking through the streets purely to take in the sights of Neo Paris. As Beautiful as it looks, I just wish it had more interaction to it.
It is heavily Story driven with a unique and interesting setting, topped with some very nice Voice Acting. The handful of Characters it has won't be seen much, but they were still well made, and fit in perfectly.
I read many comments about how "Linear" the Combat is, and personally, Action Games are my least Favourite so I decided to play it on Easy so it was less painful for me. However, I found the Combat very interesting, and more importantly, fluent.
Most Games have their general "Rotation" for best DPS, and I find this Combat System to be no different from that except you don't have freedom to "Button Mash". Infact, you have the ability to Edit the Combo's to add certain effects to each blow. Besides the Normal Combat, you also have a collection of Special Abilities to counter certain Enemies.
The Combat reminds me a bit of Assassins Creed. Being surrounded by Enemies, and having to dodge an incoming attack while fighting through, with some allowing a finishing blow "Overload". Difference being that unlike Assassins Creed, you don't have the whole Group standing around waiting while 2 Attack you at a time. In Remember Me, ALL of them are going for you, and you need to always be thinking about your position, which Combo to use on who, and which Ability to use on who.
My only dislike I have for the System is that you only get a total of 4 Combo's to Edit, unless you buy the DLC. However, it's not a big problem at all because 4 is definitely enough to get by.
Besides the Action side of it, it's main focus involves jumping from ledge to ledge with a Waypoint every 10 Meters [which at first I didn't like, but dealt with it]. It has a couple of simple Puzzles, and a few interesting Riddles which I enjoyed, as well as the a few unique scenes to alter Memories.
All in all, Remember Me was a very solid experience in all aspects.

I will start by saying that I can't understand how anyone can tell this game is realistic.
I've played PES since the PS2/PS3 era, switched to FIFA around FIFA 11 but always kept an eye on PES. Current-gen came and PES has got my attention again on PES 2015 on PS4 and by that time I couldn't play FIFA anymore. Everything felt fresh on PES while FIFA was sluggish as hell. I really enjoyed PES 2016 and PES 2017, but can't say the same about this new iteration.
***The Pros***
- The game still feels good, if not better, than previous ones.
- Tactics are still a thing although they aren't effective as before as I'll explain in the Cons.
- Graphics are improved for the PC version this time, but since I played the recent ones on PS4 it wasn't THAT much of a surprise. Still, PC looks better than console, especially on 4K.
- Gameplay is alright.
- New animations.
- The most famous players' faces are good.
- Online is improved.
***The Cons***
- Menus. Well, it is the weakest point as it's always been. They basically only changed menu colors.
- Licenses, as everybody knows, are lacking. Fixable by using OFs. Not a big con.
- Menu design is still really bad. Except for some new additions, menus are the same as last year and could be heavily optimized. The devs don't seem to bother considering it's been like this for a long time.
- Establishing connection. Do I need to say more?
- Rocky launch. No info about release date on Steam. No preload. Servers were down.
- This game has no midfield play. Sure you can pass the ball around if you want to, but you don't need to. The gaps in defense in every single match are so big you can run through the opponent's lines with ease. Just run to the side line to your heart's content and then cut inside. If you have a little bit of timing you're always gonna get one on one situations with the keeper.
- Often the AI will prioritize marking a player without the ball than try to close down on a player WITH the ball just about to enter the box to face the keeper one on one. They back off almost every time.
- Players often don't intercept easy balls and have a hard time understanding when and to where they should be moving after a through ball has been sent. They can't tackle/Intercept unless you press the assigned button, even when the ball is right on their feet.
- You can bypass the midfield with lofted through balls. End to end game.
- Different AI teams are playing the same tactic. Lofted through balls and crosses every game.
- AI never misses a pass.
- AI Freekicks at shooting distance = 99% chance of being goal.
- Keepers are not consistent. Impossible saves and silly mistakes can be committed by the same keeper in a single match.
- Stats don't matter anymore. It feels like the AI just ignore that said stats. Weak foot is just as good as the strong foot here among other things.
- Master League is untouched. Same stuff different year. The Regen problem is still a thing, prepare to see young Totti, Messi and whoever retires on your save come back as a 17-year-old player on your youth squad.
- MyClub got all the attention this year, but I couldn't spot many differences.
- Player collisions are still off. When a player loses the ball, he enters on "Stun Mode". It's better than last year but it's still there.
- Switching needs fixing. Too slow and unuseful cause it doesn't switch to the best positioned player. Ignore this con if you use the R stick for switching.
*** CONCLUSION ***
A lot of missed oportunities here for KONAMI cause they don't seem to listen to the fans.

The game was released 7 years ago, and my interest has always been big, although other games always end up being purchased first. This year I finally bought tne entire AC Series, and of course, started by the first (even with all AC II fame).
I regret to have taken so long to buy the game.
Even on 2014, Assassin's Creed has a huge counter weight when compared to newer games, with more advanced technologies and more detailed graphics. With a unique artistic production and game system, you initially see yourself stuck to climb buildings all the time. Then you begin to sink into the story, and your bind with Altaïr only grows.
You watch an assassin make his path to redemption and, along with him, begins to wonder about the course of history, and if what you are asked to do is really the right thing.
The combat system is initially somewhat confusing. The complexity of it, however, is quickly outmaneuvered as you progress in the game, it even becomes a little boring and instinctive. Still, when confronted by multiple enemies, a wrong move can cost a lot. And if you need to flee, the adrenaline is guaranteed (specially with the amazing soundtrack).
Definitely I'm not disappointed with any aspect of the game (a little with the combat system that gets a bit boring along the way). But the story makes it completely worth it. Ubisoft made a game worth every minute of playing.

The first part of the famous stealth action-adventure series. It laid out strong foundations for the following games but sadly can't stand on its own.
Pros
* The scenario show the Templars as ambiguous enemies rather than just as evil monsters
* Many historical characters are involved and you can visit culturally-important places like the Great Mosque of Damascus
* Videogame elements such as checkpoints and regenerating life are interestingly part of the story
* The graphics are still strong for a game that was released in 2008
Cons
* The PC port is awful - you can't exit the game quickly, game-breaking crashes will happen several time and an option to display subtitles is lacking
* The handling is poor and too often you will die or be spotted due to the game not registering correctly your intentions
* Extremely repetitive gameplay and the bizarre need to fill the ending with combat
It's sad but the game is really just a tech demo for the rest of the series. Assassin's Creed is extremely frustrating, which is a shame considering the story is good and taking place in such an underrepresented setting.

Paper Sorcerer is a tale of two vastly different experiences. One part being the popular genre of dungeon crawling turn based role playing games. The other part in the exploration of a sleek monochrome three-dimensional environment where areas are set apart more by their flourishing shadows than light sources. Each different stage you fight your way through and clear leads to widely varying stages both in combat to look of the three-dimensional environments.
Your player character, a sorcerer stuck in a magical book, summons a party of your choosing and sets off to escape. The game features difficult turn-based combat which serves as blarney for the grognards and a hit off the nostalgia bong for the rest of us. These two experiences juxtaposed to each other are quite disjointed, but in the end it’s a game criminally under-priced. You should really give this game a try.

and some new tracks.
There is no real need to describe what the game is about being as how the description on the Store Page is about all you need to know. To be brief,

I recommend this to anybody looking for a new casual game to play, also for the achievement hunters, this is a very fun and doable game to try and acheive 100%.

This game is boring. The whole parkour concept is pretty cool, but there's just not much content here. It's very repetitive.
Basically, the game, which I believe originated as an iOS game, is broken up into worlds and levels. I think it's three worlds (at least that I could se before I gave up), each with 12-13 levels. I got about halfway through the second world before I gave up.
Each level, you have an enemy chasing you. Your character auto-runs, and it's up to you to hit up (jump), down (slide), right (speed up) or left (slow down) to navigate obstacles. You die and restart the level if the enemy catches up to you or you fall to your death or run into obstacles at high speeds.
Along the way, you must collect bonus boxes and complete special tricks (typically just hitting up at the right time) to collect additional stars. You get one star just for completing the level.
Sometimes there are different routes, but there is clearly a "correct" path, as the bonus boxes are typically only along one path or the other. Sometimes, the other route is a dead end and leads to auto death.
Maybe I would have a slightly higher appreciation if the developers took time to beautify the graphics. On a mobile phone, it's fine. On a big monitor, it's just overly simple.
In any case, at core, the game is just dull. The mechanics are fine. The physics are fine. But every level is the exact same thing, and it wasn't exciting to begin with. If you're a fan of auto-run games or endless runner, then maybe you'll enjoy this. But just hitting four keys every couple of seconds is not my idea of fun, especially when it requires a fair amount of precision.
2/10

I'm level 10 almost level 11 now, more than 65 percent of my way to level by now, and will so be level 11 within a day or two, and as I type this, there is one dungeon as a solo player which is a level 10 area and scales up, 10-15, but after you clear it, there are really no dungeons, and the ones you find literally anywhere on the world map which are random appear in four locations, one to the north, east, south, and west, which are all on long timers. The game is full of little annoyances.
I played a healer and even though there's an out of combat action bar, you can't actually heal outside of combat. That bar is only available if you're in the inn (where you regenerate health/mana), your house area, or a resource node. None of those really help when in a dungeon, so most effecient healing is actually to kill all but 1 mob, then just spend turns healing up the party while everyone else passes.
Player economy is very cumbersome. There are player stalls to sell things, but there is no way to search all the stalls for a specific item or even pull up a specific players stall. There is a newspaper that advertises items, and you have to click through every item to visit that particular store to see if they have what you want.
Description of crafts/abilties/debuffs are lacking. The elementalist can "shock" something, but there is no description what that actually does. Some enemies "mezzed" me, but mousing over that icon doesn't actually tell you what that does. Biggest complaint would be for crafting, I picked up enchanting. Only to find out I have to place the enchanting table indoors, so I had to upgrade my house area to level 2 to get an indoors slot. I finally make an enchantment and you can only use it on other crafted goods. None of this was explained in the description for learning enchanting.
All of these things plus the grind, just made it to bothersome to continue playing.

This game drew me to it the first moment I saw it.  Stash is the first game I have EVER kickstarted and I do not regret that decision for a second.  Is this game gonna be for everyone? No.  It is a much slower paced, laid back game with more of a focus on grouping and community than the majority of MMO's you see these days.  Is it a grind? yes. But I feel that makes gaining that next level in a craft or class that much more rewarding.  While I realize that kinda of view isn't shared by all I personally enjoy it.
As for the community in the game.  It is one of the most helpful and welcoming ones I have been a part of in a long time.  It reminds me back when a lot of MMO's were new and fresh and players worked together and helped each other instead of mocking and belittling for asking questions.  Most asks in help are replied to in about 30 seconds and usually by multiple players.  Also the Devs are among the most active I have ever seen in a game. They are on EVERY day and constantly talking to players about balance issues, suggestions to game changes and actively seeking to find and fix bugs as quickly as possible for their small team.   It is a refreshing change of pace to see a team actually CARE about the game once it is released and are so passionate about their creation.
The graphics may not be the prettiest and it may not be fast paced but I feel Stash is a unique gem to those that actually care to examine it for awhile.  If you prefer Tactics style combat with a bit of depth and a community that is enjoyable instead of toxic, I would invite you to give Stash a try.  I'm glad I did :)

Don't take my low hours for granted, it doesn't take longer than an hour or hopping into this game to realize what a gem it is. With an intuitive, unique "tutorial" system that lets you learn at your own pace, I found myself playing a turn-based game in ways I never thought I would!
Combat mechanics that other turn-based games strive for, Stash sets the bar for future turn-based games in many ways. A unique positioning system, aggro, buffs, debuffs, multiple phases to a turn... This game has it all!
The game boasts a modest amount of character customization, even equip with a slider to fine-tune your hero, you have full control over how your character looks. Make them beautiful or... not so much.
The game does have microtransactions, but don't let that dissuade you, everything you can buy with real money you can earn in-game as well, the only except being a few cosmetic "transmogs".
On top of that, the Developers of the game are some of the most active I've seen in a game. You'll often see them talking in chat with other players and helping them. They even have an active Discord!
If you enjoy Indie MMORPGs and are looking for a new, fresh take on turn-based combat, definitely give Stash a try! You won't be disapointed! :)

Not much to say here. I enjoyed this game. I would probably play it again. I will definitely play the two sequels. It's a simple block matching game with a few unique features. You can rotate the board 90 degrees at a time as often as you want in either direction to control how the blocks fall. There are some decent boosters that can clear out an entire row or column. Once you clear the the board, a special block appears and an exit slot appears. You need to clear blocks around the special block to move it toward the exit. It can be a little more challenging than it sounds. As the levels progress, the configuration of the boards make you work around obstacles. It's a fun game. Total play time to completion was around 9 hours.

Set in the Canopy Kingdom, Skullgirls tells the tale of eight female warriors as they fight to reclaim a wish-granting artifact known as the "Skull Heart" from the monstrous Skullgirl. As legend has it, every seven years this enigmatic Skull Heart grants a wish to a young woman... but this power can come at a terrible price. If her heart is impure, her wish will be twisted and she herself will be transformed into a Skullgirl.
Developed by newcomer Reverge Labs, Skullgirls is a fast-paced 2D fighting game. Starring a cast of feisty female warriors, Skullgirls is a multi-layered fighter featuring all-new game systems for veteran fighting game fans while also making the intimidating genre enjoyable and accessible to the casual gamer.
Building on its established game systems tried and tested by veteran and casual fighting game fans alike, Skullgirls 2nd Encore includes new systems, new stages and music, balance adjustments, gameplay tweaks and more. For the first time, the game's story mode is fully voiced in Skullgirls 2nd Encore, with performances by some of anime’s best and brightest stars. Skullgirls 2nd Encore’s new Survival Mode pits players against an endless procession of foes – how long can you last? And for all the trophy hunters out there, Skullgirls 2nd Encore will have a full Platinum trophy set.
