This game draws you in with its unique simplistic art style that allows just about anyone to play it. There's a player run economy where users can sell items they've crafted according to their profession. When I first downloaded the game, I thought it was going to be interesting, not trash. This is because I've been fooled once before.
There's another rpg game that I first thought wasn't going to be fun but was proved wrong later on and this one is definitely second on that list. (the game's called RPG Mo)
So I start the download and I stream some porn while I wait for it to finish. After completion I boot it up. I start, register and then create my character. He's a warrior with brown hair and unmatched good looks. Green eyes too, I dont know why. I didnt notice then that there were different races available. It was only after that when I realised there were around 3-4 to choose from. Only one of which other than Humans which I can remember the name of- catfolk. (khajit memes should clearly be a thing in this game)
I name my character GreatGatzB, from the movie I never watched because why not, people will think I know pop culture, and then start the game itself.
This is when I've decided to say "Hello" in the chat, which was already filled with activity.
I met a player named Stoneheart and he was pretty friendly- all of the chat was, to be honest. They even linked me to a player made guide for new players! how thoughtful was that? granted, that was probably to make me stop asking questions but still, I got a guide as a nice gesture, I'll sure as hell take it.
Which brings us the first thing that caught my eye once I started the game and accidentally closed all the tutorial popups (I read them later on) and went inside the capital city of Askagard. (ask a guard..? hah! Greatgatzb is amused!)
There are professions for your character. Other than classes of which more will be added in the future, your character can have one profession that he/she may learn the craft of in order to start making items to sell/use. The overall quality of these items get stronger the more they practice the art, but to do this they would need to buy the necessary tools and the specific crafting station for their Base of Operations first.
(you can have upto four characters for free and your stashed items can be shared with those characters I believe but if you want one character to have two professions or more you'd need to spend 12 dollars on their store to purchase 100 medallions, which would let you learn up to 2 additional professions for a specific character. But don't think of this as a cash grab, as this can easily be circumvented by having character alts with different professions, which many users openly make use of. As long as nothing is being abused, using alts are for anything is okay, according to an admin/developer of the game who frequently gets involved in the chat himself)
They also need materials which can be gathered from nodes and fallen enemies with tools that need to be equipped before entering the instances. (this is somewhat of an annoyance and perhaps will get changed in the future). But if you're lazy like me and have a lot of triads, the ingame currency you get from selling off your unwanted loot, you can just buy the materials from the newspaper, a nifty tool that lets players advertise their most valued items for sale.
Anyway, I get into my first combat situation and almost die where I retreat. I am immediately greeted by the message saying "You ran away bravely" I sit in my chair, sinking ever so slightly as I rest my head on the back support.
"I'm brave even when I run away...?" I spend minutes brooding, contemplating my decisions in life and
I soon realise that I need help. I hit the chat up and ask for a party and soon get invited to one. led by a very, very, very fair maiden whose the healer of the group. Her name, Lordpsyy. Between you and me, she says she only in it for da money but she heals me anyway, she digs the gatz.
Other than her, theres this other valiant warrior by the name of valoraunt who speaks in the third person and in an old english accent that always cracked me up. "Perchance you could spare a heal, madame". this isnt what he said, I dont quite remember the conversations we had, but he was hilarious. There was also another player but I dont remember his name, but I'm just a forgetful person.
The game has some neat combat mechanics that remind me of the times I used to play Final fantasy v, mainly when you and your party get ambushed and your entire group is suddenly surrounded, rather than having to start from the same side every time a battle starts. its' fun. when a game does that, it mixes things up. there are battle quests that pop up every once in a while whenever combat is initiated, and are entirely optional. they mainly yield loot bonuses
The only downside I have at the moment with this game right now is the limitation on the stuff you can do in instances, mainly combat ones. Hell, I cant even try to open my inventory without getting a pokemon reference! perhaps this should be changed so that we can only view our inventory, but not alter anything within, so that we can sometimes check if we have equipped the right tool for sure or not, and still get the pokemon reference! win win!
But this isnt really a game breaker at all. It's a minor annoyance.
Backtracking a little bit, the enchanter profession lets you enhance weapons/armor with stats that make them a lot better to use as opposed to non enchanted ones. there's alchemy too, where health, mana, and other potions are made. Every profession has a lot to craft and if I start listing down each and everything we'll be here all day, so let's move along.
Your Base of Operations is where all the magic happens. you build your house, decorate it with furniture that drop from monsters/that you buy from the newspaper, and place down the workbenches that are needed to start crafting.
There's a lot more to this game and it surely has a lot of potential. This was a brief summary of my first time playing this neat game, and I really enjoyed it.  Also tried giving details of the features that I found in the game. 10/10. But if it was a movie, 5/7 "great".

Hospital Manager is an even more satirical Hospital management simulator than the highly sought after nostalgic Theme Hospital from Peter Molyneux and Bullfrog Studios.
This game sets you up in a pre built hospital in which you decide which pre built rooms will be what. From diagnosis, treatment and restroom facilities.
The reason the game is satirical is you are not treating any sort of typical 'real life' ailments. You sort out Zombies, possessions and some sort of affliction in which people moonwalk whilst wearing an unconvincing Michael Jackson get up. Among many other sorts of silly ailments.
The treatments of these ailments is equally silly. If someone walks in holding their amputated leg, send them to “surgery” which is actually just a huge sewing machine. Are you a zombie? Well hypnosis is the answer (that one actually kind of makes sense if you use the colloquialism definition of Zombie in where someone is predisposed with something relatively unimportant. However the sprite is most certainly a traditional zombie.)
All of that on its face its actually an interesting premise. I don't NEED a serious hospital simulator. I just want a good one. You'll need to manage patient moods, doctors training and maintenance workers as well as clowns. However the clown is more of a middle man between doctor and patient rather than a new age Patch Adams.
- You cannot build the hospital. They are all pre built and because some issues arise in which multiple types of diseases show up you need multiple types of treatment rooms however there are not enough rooms to satisfy the demand. So you must now manage changing over rooms do deal with new things. Instead of making an actual functioning hospital.
- There is no sandbox. The only mode is mission challenges.
- It gets needlessly hectic. Constant pop ups telling you things you are already working on or things you can do nothing about until you have more money.
- Staff management, research, and doctor training happens too often. You have to research diseases in order to increase the percentage your doctors will be able to diagnosis the disease properly. I had to research the zombie disease upwards of seven times in one mission just to get it at a reasonable diagnosis level to the other diseases in the hospital at the time.
- The art repeats, there are only two doctor skins. This is a minor complaint. But as the game gets so hectic so quickly it makes it much more difficult to remember who is who and what everyones level is, so that in some vain hope of trying to keep the order I attempted keep all my doctors on the same skill level. So that I don't know.. I could make a successful hospital.

Update to address comments:
I couldn't agree more Do_Be...
As for for the developer, I understand this is personal for you. I can only imagine. As such please know I understand and respect your passion for your creation. I must respectively state that while I understand and appreciate your free to play model, I believe you have been a little too aggressive with the purchased "conveniences".
As for "examples of purposely designed annoyances":
1.) Shared stash is one slot and can only be expanded by spending real life money.
a.) In my opinion this is a purposely designed annoyance meant to force the players into purchasing gems to counter this.
b.) Again, this would be manageable if it were a little more reasonable. 1 slot is too few. Show the players you have good intentions and they will reciprocate in making purchases.
2.) There are 6 crafting types but a character can only learn one. All knowledge is lost when switching.
a.) Only way to expand crafting slots is by using real life money.
b.) This would be manageable if the shared bank/stash was reasonable. (See #1 above)
3.) Players can't change harvesting tools in combat.
a.) I can't comprehend why this would be designed this way. This isn't enjoyable at all. Nor is requiring us to equip the specific tool in order to perform the harvest action. Again "in my opinion" this should be redesigned to make the experience enjoyable for players. As it stands now, it's just another annoyance without any perceivable reason (that I can see anyway).
I still stand by my opening statement. This game has so much potential to be a great game. I'm perfectly fine with the typical free to play model and I have a history of supporting developers by making real life currency purchases. (I've spent thousands within individual games)
I believe it would be far more enticing if the limitations put in place to promote purchases were rebalanced.

In this game, you play as a Syrian man named Altair Ibn-La-Ahad, and he is part of an order of Assassins (hence the name Assassin's Creed). You start the game in real time, as a man named Desmond who has been taken by a company known as Abstergo Industries, a company where they are secretly part of the order of the Knight's Templars. The Templars are enemies to Assassins, and since Desmond is an ancestor of the previously meantioned assassin Altair, the head executive and his assistant Lucy put Desmond into a machine called the Animus. The Animus lets a person delve into his ancestor's memories, and since Altair is an ancestor to Desmond, the executive (i forgot his name, but lets just call him Bill) puts you into the Animus so he can monitor Altair's memories and find a secret that the Templars need that only Altair know. Once you are in the Animus, you finally play as Altair. You start in a mine looking for a Templar named Roberto, and once you find him, you see he is planning to steal the holy artifact known as the Ark of Covenant. You fail to kill him, and your other Assassins are left to kill him (one of them fails by the way). You go back to your master, Al Mualim, and he finds out about the attack. Suddenly Roberto and his fellow Templars are attacking, and you send a diversion to help. After you send the diversion, they flee, and Al Mualim punishes you because you did not remember the three strict rules to being an Assassin in the earlier mission. He stabs you, and you pass out. You are still alive and you must kill 9 other Templars to redeem yourself and be one of the master Assassins again.
The game is overall very good, but there are a few things I did not like. First of all, I know it is set in the First Crusades Period (somewhere around 1000 A.D it started) but Altair cannot hold any type of currency. Your gearand weapons are gained from each of the 9 Templars you kill. Also, in the trailer, Altair is seen to have a crossbow as one of his weapons, but that crossbow is nowhere in the actual game, so that got me dissapointed. Another thing is that youdont carry any types of medicine or potions or things like that, which would be useful in fighting because Altair isnt the best fighter without ALL of his weapons. Speaking of health, you dont have an actual health meter. Your health is displayed in something called a Synchronization Bar, a bar that fills as you do good in the game. If you commit crimes, your Synchronization Bar goes down. If you lose fights, it also goes down. Basically, anything bad makes it go down. Those are basically all the problems i have with this game.
To wrap it up, Assassin's Creed is a fun game with a really cool and exciting storyline, not alot of  situations i was mad or angry about, but it is old. The graphics are from somewhere around 2000 (i dont know when the games came out by years). So if you dont mind about graphics and want to have a fun action-adventure game with enticing storyline, Assassin's Creed is the game for you.

(That's it, go and get a copy. But if you want more details read on....)
___________________________________________________________
EXCELLENT EXECUTION.
It's a culmination of excellent art, story telling, sound design, acting (specially in the part of the main character), and software engineering. The execution is EXCELLENT to say the very least.
As I play the game I can see and feel the dedication that the developers put into the game. Actual patients and doctors were consulted to make the experience more immersive, therefore powerful.
During the game, I actually felt empathy for people suffering mental illness. :(
___________________________________________________________
MUST PLAY WITH HEADPHONES
OK, you can play it with normal stereo speakers, but I highly recommend playing it with a decent sound system. Preferably headphones, THE SOUNDS EMANATING FROM THE GAME IS CRITICAL TO THE EXPERIENCE. So you don't want to miss that.
___________________________________________________________
STORY TELLING:
If you love a good story (albeit one with a darker tone) this is a MUST PLAY.
This game further justify my belief that video games might surpass other media (movies, even books) in delivering a story. With games like Witcher 3, Mass Effect, and console games like The Last of Us, this could happen sooner than later.
___________________________________________________________
CONS???
For me the game is close to perfect, but yes there's a couple of things that I believe could've been done better.
- FIGHTING MECHANICS: The fighting mechanic is not bad, but I thought of it as simple and easy.
There are no huds, no life bars, nothing to distract you from the beauty of the carnage happening in your screen. I loved that.
But I wanted to do more than just dodge, parry, and/or attack. I wanted to jump behind one of the creatures and stab him repeatedly in the neck!.I want to execute my enemies Shadow of Mordor style! How about God of War style finishing moves?
- GAME LENGTH????: I finished the game in about 8 hours on my first run. Puzzles became easy since you don't have that much of a variety (of puzzles). Enemies, even bosses are horrifyingly grotesque but  once you get the dodge / parry and attack timings. They are easy to defeat even on the first try.
To be fair, with that length you'll be left satisfied yet wanting for more. Why prolong a good experience if it will become repetitive and boring in the end I say.

I'll keep it short and sweet: I thoroughly enjoyed this game. Without doing any of the extras and on normal difficulty I got about eight hours of play. Given the quality of the single-player campaign I would say that this game is absolutely worth the $60. If you can get it on sale, it's a no-brainer. This game has no multiplayer.
Presentation: the game looks, feels and sounds phenomenal. The graphics are top notch. The game runs on the id tech 6 engine and it shows. Impressive motion blur, impressive particle effects and lighting, top notch shadows, etc. The sound is also suprisingly fantastic. Most guns have a great punch to them and the reverberation inside of rooms sounds incredibly realistic. The HUD is minimalistic and doesn't get in your way of enjoying the game and the rest of the UI is decent. Everything is styled appropriately to match the game's grim setting of a 1960s alternative future where Nazis have won World War II and it is a marvel to experience.
Story: while a little outlandish and ridiculous, the weight of the performances given by the characters single-handedly carries the plot of the game. you will grow to hate the antagonists and care for the protagonists and their plight. some characters have an arc and progressively change as the game moves forward but for the most part it's a straightforward story with fantastic acting.
Gameplay: wolfenstein's game loop isn't groundbreaking. that being said, machinegames did a great job designing a shooter that feels like a faithful successor to shooters of the past. it's a clever hybrid of old school arena and modern day shooters. your character holds about six different guns all at once with the exception of three or four heavy weapons that you can pick up from challenging enemies. there's a variety of enemies to kill, but mostly you'll be fighting standard foot soldiers with decent AI. they'll flank you, attempt to flush you out from your position, take cover and spray you with bullets at any chance they get. it never feels unfair and the gunfights are extremely satisfying. the ricochets of the bullets are clear and most of the environment will react accordingly to your gunfire. enemies will react to getting shot. bodies will be dismembered if overwhelmed with gunfire. tougher enemies have weak spots and the art style reflects those weak spots accordingly. the game plays extremely smooth on my rig and it was a really enjoyable and challenging experience on the higher difficulties.
Things I disliked:
I didn't like the headbobbing. It would have been nice to get an option to disable it altogether. Headbobbing in video games does nothing for me and really just detracts from the amazing visuals so it would have been nice to be able to remove it.
I also didn't like the default keybindings. Pressing J and G were awkward and the game was finally playable after tweaking the settings. The lean also felt shoehorned and the game could have completely done away with leaning. Unless your game uses Q and E (right alt trigger and left alt trigger on a joystick) for leaning, then just don't include leaning in the game.
The main hub was fairly boring. I would have liked to see additional content in the hub. Like RUINER, Wolfenstein doesn't utilize the main hub very well at all. There are no clever side games or interesting story lines and the missions you do eventually get tend to feel grindy and unnecessary to the end goal. While you can do these and have a great time if you really enjoy the game, I didn't feel compelled to do any of the extra missions towards the end. In the future I'd really like to see the main hub fleshed out with things to do aside from the main game, and to be rewarded accordingly for being in the main hub. The characters who sent me on small tasks inside of the hub just thanked me at the end and gave me no reward. Work on this Machinegames.
(THIS WILL GET INTO SPOILERS FROM THIS POINT, STOP READING NOW YOU'VE BEEN WARNED)

I haven't played very many Wolfenstein games, so I'm unsure if this is following a trend, but there were certain moments that the level design opened up and became an arena, at which point I expected a boss to appear only to find that some of the tougher enemies would spawn alongside a legion of other enemies.

The Good:
- An imaginative and well realised setting
- Fluid combat, ala Batman
- Nice visuals, enhanced by clever stylisation
- Excellent soundtrack
The Mediocre:
- A limited number of cards to play regarding content, you fight, you climb, and you get to mess with people's memory a handful of times
- Lack of emphasis on storytelling and characterisation makes the game's "big moments" lack emotional impact
- Upgrade system is too limited to sustain interest
- Having to continually re-configure combos is frustrating
The Bad:
- Completely linear. Once you've played the 8 - 10 hour campaign, there's nothing to draw you back.
The Verdict:
A good game that could have been great. With a longer, non linear structure, a more robust upgrade system, and a little more time on the story, Remember Me could have been great. Still, hats off to the development team. As it stands, it's a worthwhile game, that's worth picking up if on sale.

Vector is basically a combination of BIT.TRIP RUNNER's gameplay with the artstyle of Canabalt. It's also a bit less difficult, because I was able to beat it! ;)
In short, it's a game of fairly limited controls (generally just up to jump/vault/trick over things as they come, occasionally down to slide or left/right for speed running, wall-jumping, or turning around in certain stages) but the game is in using these controls at the appropriate times, needing both precision and correctly deciding what approach to take. It manages to have some very interesting level layouts and well-executed (if very stylized) art, thus keeping the game quite interesting over the 33 levels that make up its story mode.
The only frustrating thing about the game is the unlocks, as most of them are tied to stars, which are mostly obtainable by playing levels near-perfectly - you get one star if you complete a level at all, two if you get either all the pickups or do all the tricks, and all three if you both get all the pickups and do all the tricks. Some of the unlockable things require most of the possible stars you can obtain in a given area, meaning you need to do almost everything in that part of the game perfectly. The coin-based ones are less frustrating, but can be somewhat grindy because the main source of coins is getting stars for the first time. Unfortunately, the primary coin-based unlocks are new tricks, which you'll need to unlock in order to even try to get three stars on levels, thus ending up in somewhat of a vicious cycle. That said, this is mostly going to be an issue if you feel you must complete every single bonus level as opposed to "just" beating the game, so it doesn't lower my recommendation.
The only thing I can't really weigh in on here except to note it is that the game is available for free on mobile devices and on Facebook; I haven't compared how those work with the Steam version to be able to say whether or not the Steam version is particularly better.

Pro Evolution Soccer 2018 is without doubt the best football game since the PES 4,5 and 6 glory days. Not only is the PC version finally on par with its PS4 counterpart; it is actually far superior with an excellent technical performance and astonishing visuals thanks to the latest Fox Engine build.
Graphically; the game looks almost photorealistic at times and the attention to detail is phenominal in places. The animations of players is an remarkable achievement and the immersive feel of the stadiums just offers an incredible experience. It is a groundbreaking step up from the 'hyrbid' builds we've had in recent years which is just polite terminology for 'PS3 port'.
In terms of gameplay; the pacing is a bit slower in this outing and it feels spot-on. Matches are less erratic and everything flows much better. Players are more composed in their play and the ball isn't bouncing around the pitch like a hot potato. You have to be more tactical and patient in your approach instead and it works really well.
Unfortunately, despite a string of key improvements to the game; the user interface is still incredibly dated as is the recycled commentary which drags the presentation down. It's not a major issue but Konami really need to improve this aspect next year. Online server and connection issues still persist as is the poorly supported online entity which is a shame.
Overall; PES 2018 is a stunning game and Konami's best effort for over a decade. From a gameplay and graphical standpoint, it's simply outstanding at times and if you're just looking for a football game to enjoy; it's an absolute must buy despite some dated elements and a disappointing online portion.

*Note: I only played the tutorial levels and the first three missions and my experience of this game is therefore limited.
Hospital Manager is about running your own hospital. The game is divided in a number of levels where you build rooms and hire staff to treat the patients that come to you with their ailments. You cure the patients by first diagnosing and subsequently treating them. Both actions reward you with money to improve the hospital and reputation.
You can improve the hospital by upgrading the staff, (re)decorating the hallways to keep the waiting patients happy or by spending money on research.
A certain amount of reputation is needed to complete the level. You gain reputation by diagnosing and curing patients and lose reputation when patients walk out on you.
Let me start of by writing about what I like first. I do like the way the game does not take itself seriously, opting for a comical take on the hospital simulator. This ranges from the over the top injuries the patients have to the proposed treatments and the vibrant colours used, as wel as the notion that no matter how bad the injury may be, enough benches, flower pots and clowns on site will keep the patients happy. I personally like this kind of humour.
This, however, leaves a lot to dislike for me. For starters, The layout of the hospital is predetermined and you cannot choose the size and content of the rooms you build and can only build in predetermined spots, severely limiting player creativity. After the room has been built you need to pick a staff member. They have three attributes (speed of treatment, profit per patient and number of patients helped before the doctor needs a break), but some staff are twice or even three times as good as others, whilst costing less in wages.
During gameplay you get frequent (and I mean frequent) popups with tips or pointers, but they take up a rather large portion of the screen and hinder gameplay when you are zoomed in. There is no way of disabling the popups.
Also worth mentioning is that this is a mobile port and it clearly shows. Aside from the removal of the microtransactions the game is identical to the mobile version. This means that all the busywork in the form of tapping is still in place, therefore each level forces the player to constantly click on vending machines, staff and patients.
I would also like to draw your attention to the inaccuracies written down in the "Key Features" on the Store Page. For instance, this game has no
in any way, shape or form. Just build rooms, hire staff, decorate the halls and keep the research going, whilst doing your busywork and closing the popups. And their claim that this is a
just boils down to cause and effect: If you choose to, let's say, hire a clown in January he starts working in January. If you however hire the clown a month later he starts working in February. Seriously? This is worth mentioning as a Key Feature?
All in all, this game is not good. It is a mobile port with shallow gameplay, almost no management whatsoever and severely limiting player creativity, with a nonsensical Store Page to boot. Not recommended.

I originally wrote a positive review on this game, but realised how urking the game itself is.
I wanted to fill my "theme hospital" craving, and was brought here (and Hospital Tycoon, urgh).
The game was pretty nice to start off with, but as the game got "harder", the limited spacing and patients just became a nuisance.
PROS:
- Game has some nice graphics. Clear and colourful.
- Pretty unique symptoms that I found funny sometimes.
- Some animations for various rooms are pretty cool. (Such as a sewing machine for surgery)
- Every character has a bust, including patient types. I like the art style.
CONS:
- Main 2 characters are pretty... stupid. The female looks like a Hippy with a syringe, and the male looks like he belongs in a nerd show or his mothers basement. In short; neither look qualified to guide you in running a hospital. Also, humour gets stale pretty fast.
- Pre-built sections. If you want to build a room, you can only choose from selections given. This makes later levels extremely tedious since you have to start sacrificing rooms for other rooms. Want to help that annoying group of patients? better remove my research facility because why not.
- Having to keep rebuying the same furniture every level. In order to unlock better benches, vending machines and stuff, you spend your in-game money to unlock them. This resets every level, so it becomes pointless later. And tedious.
- Can't assign extra staff. If you surgeon takes a break, your surgery is left unattended. This if awful when your staff like to take breaks just as an event of a bajillion patients want to come in.
- AI is pretty dumb. My Janitors seemed to want to avoid the rubbish and puke throughout my hospital instead of picking it up.
In short: The game itself is enjoyable to start out, but it becomes tedious (not hard, tedious) later on once you realise certain mechanics don't work or all freedom of build is removed.

I'll keep it short and sweet: I thoroughly enjoyed this game. Without doing any of the extras and on normal difficulty I got about eight hours of play. Given the quality of the single-player campaign I would say that this game is absolutely worth the $60. If you can get it on sale, it's a no-brainer. This game has no multiplayer.
Presentation: the game looks, feels and sounds phenomenal. The graphics are top notch. The game runs on the id tech 6 engine and it shows. Impressive motion blur, impressive particle effects and lighting, top notch shadows, etc. The sound is also suprisingly fantastic. Most guns have a great punch to them and the reverberation inside of rooms sounds incredibly realistic. The HUD is minimalistic and doesn't get in your way of enjoying the game and the rest of the UI is decent. Everything is styled appropriately to match the game's grim setting of a 1960s alternative future where Nazis have won World War II and it is a marvel to experience.
Story: while a little outlandish and ridiculous, the weight of the performances given by the characters single-handedly carries the plot of the game. you will grow to hate the antagonists and care for the protagonists and their plight. some characters have an arc and progressively change as the game moves forward but for the most part it's a straightforward story with fantastic acting.
Gameplay: wolfenstein's game loop isn't groundbreaking. that being said, machinegames did a great job designing a shooter that feels like a faithful successor to shooters of the past. it's a clever hybrid of old school arena and modern day shooters. your character holds about six different guns all at once with the exception of three or four heavy weapons that you can pick up from challenging enemies. there's a variety of enemies to kill, but mostly you'll be fighting standard foot soldiers with decent AI. they'll flank you, attempt to flush you out from your position, take cover and spray you with bullets at any chance they get. it never feels unfair and the gunfights are extremely satisfying. the ricochets of the bullets are clear and most of the environment will react accordingly to your gunfire. enemies will react to getting shot. bodies will be dismembered if overwhelmed with gunfire. tougher enemies have weak spots and the art style reflects those weak spots accordingly. the game plays extremely smooth on my rig and it was a really enjoyable and challenging experience on the higher difficulties.
Things I disliked:
I didn't like the headbobbing. It would have been nice to get an option to disable it altogether. Headbobbing in video games does nothing for me and really just detracts from the amazing visuals so it would have been nice to be able to remove it.
I also didn't like the default keybindings. Pressing J and G were awkward and the game was finally playable after tweaking the settings. The lean also felt shoehorned and the game could have completely done away with leaning. Unless your game uses Q and E (right alt trigger and left alt trigger on a joystick) for leaning, then just don't include leaning in the game.
The main hub was fairly boring. I would have liked to see additional content in the hub. Like RUINER, Wolfenstein doesn't utilize the main hub very well at all. There are no clever side games or interesting story lines and the missions you do eventually get tend to feel grindy and unnecessary to the end goal. While you can do these and have a great time if you really enjoy the game, I didn't feel compelled to do any of the extra missions towards the end. In the future I'd really like to see the main hub fleshed out with things to do aside from the main game, and to be rewarded accordingly for being in the main hub. The characters who sent me on small tasks inside of the hub just thanked me at the end and gave me no reward. Work on this Machinegames.
(THIS WILL GET INTO SPOILERS FROM THIS POINT, STOP READING NOW YOU'VE BEEN WARNED)
---
I also didn't like that there were no bosses in the game in the traditional sense. I haven't played very many Wolfenstein games, so I'm unsure if this is following a trend, but there were certain moments that the level design opened up and became an arena, at which point I expected a boss to appear only to find that some of the tougher enemies would spawn alongside a legion of other enemies.
I really enjoyed this game and I think it deserves your money. I had only one minor crash when I first opened the game and never experienced a problem again. It runs great, looks great, and plays great. I would definitely recommend this game.

Stash is a Free-To-Play MMORPG with turn-based combat, crafting, dungeons, and base building.  The developers have built the world around their previous works, with lots of history and lore to come with.  They are dedicated to bringing constant updates, bugfixes, and content to their players; even hosting events and interacting to get feedback and provide special bonuses.
Being a Free-To-Play game, they do have an RMT currency in the form of 'Medallions'; however this isn't a paywall and you can obtain anything important to gameplay through the in-game loot and currency.  It's mostly there for ease of progression and cosmetic features.
On a more personal note, I have followed this game since the kickstarter campaign, and when they first had working builds I wasn't that excited with what was there; but the developers have been hard at work to provide better and better gameplay, and now I have a blast.  I expect that this trend will continue, as the team seems devoted to making this game the best they can envision it.
So if it sounds like something you might enjoy, give it a try, it's free. =)

A great platformer, similar in terms of game mechanics, to BIT.TRIP.RUNNER.  You control a runner as you traverse the top of buildings, construction sites, and parks to escape the hunter who is chasing you. There are no checkpoints, so if you get close to the end and die, then you'll have to start all over again.  Although, I don't particularly mind seeing as the animations for all of the moves are so smooth and fluid.  I enjoy playing through the same levels again and again.  You also collect money which lets you buy fancier moves so you can get higher ratings on levels.  Overall it has a lot of replay value especially since they added the new hunter mode where you get to play as the chaser instead of the chasee (It's a word).   However after playing a few of those levels, I'm still not entirely convinced that it's possible to complete them...Or at least to get a 3 star rating on them.

It looks like all the other positive reviews pretty much said what I was going to say.  I will just add that I also really like the design of this game over all.  I love the graphic style with the future art deco buildings and clear colors.  Using silohuettes for the characters and foreground elements is brilliant.  One of the other things I especially like is that, since some levels are kind of long for me, so I end up failing a lot.  When that happens, the game takes you right back to the beginning to try again.  No menu, or lodaing thingy or even a pause.  I really like that because i can stay in the headspce of doing the level and not be interrupted.  I also like how you buy gear and moves with game money (not real money) so you feel a little more accomplished when you get something.  Plus, you can then go back and complete an already completed level with more fancy moves.
The controls seem just fine to me.  One tip, and the only real learning curve that I had, was to learn to just tap the control to activate the move instead of hodling it down or repeated tapping like you might do in other games.

I think this is basically a platformer where the focus is on free-running to try to escape the police of an oppressive society while performing Parkour-type moves to get past obstacles.  I've played it longer on mobile than Steam, but assuming it's designed the same, there are three worlds with around 12 levels each (I forget exactly).  As you run through them, you'll pick up cubes for points and coins that you can use to buy more Parkour moves.  To get a 3-star score on each level, you have to collect all the cubes, which isn't always easy, and perform all of the Parkour tricks, whose locations are marked for you so they're easy to spot (but you still have to time them right).  Since the tricks are purchased, you may have to grind for money in order to buy them.  Grinding isn't really necessary in the beginning, but as the games goes on and the cost goes up, you'll probably need to do more grinding.  Each of the three worlds has specific game moves, with the second and third building up a little from the first -- IIRC, the second one introduces stopping and lets you jump back and forth between walls to reach higher areas, and the third introduces reversing direction and using elevators to go up and down.  For the most part, the game is linear in that most levels seem to have only one way to clear them, and it's mainly a matter of practice and timing to learn how to do that.  They're usually not too long or frustrating though, which is a good thing.  I'm not sure exactly how the game ends though, because I didn't finish it on mobile (I got tired of grinding after a while).  But even after finishing it, I think there will be some replay value, because you can keep trying to get that perfect 3-star score, beat your previous fastest time, and/or go for Steam achievements.  Also, I see a Hunter Mode in the game's menu, which is unlocked by earning 50 stars, and that new mode should add some variety and replay value as well.  While I would have preferred a bit less grinding for money to buy moves, the game is good overall and I'd recommend it.

Well, I've been warned that this is the most dull entry in the saga.
There's repetition in the "quests" you'll have to undertake - but most of them are optional and may be avoided. (You may not want to avoid them in the beginning, because you'll benefit from them.)
But the world! It's a fantastic place and the cities are a sight to behold.
Also, even I, clumsy as I am, had a blast jumping, climbing and stalking through these scenes - this games makes you feel much more competent than you are, which adds a lot to the fun.
The story has an interesting spin (you'll see right at the beginning).
All in all very recommended. I'm looking forward to the other entries in this series.
Here are some play tips (very mild spoilers):
Don't try to collect all flags. This is seriously madness and not needed, unless you are unhealthily obsessed :-)
You can skip "save the citizens" sidequests BUT every 15 finished sidequests (informer quests, view points scaled, citizens saved) your hit point increase by one and you may even gain extra abilities, which helps a lot. You max out at 20 (two bars), so plan accordingly.
I'd always scale all view points. These discover side quests and reveal the map, which is helpful when fleeing or planing to strike.
You don't need to do all informer quests (3 out of 6). The info gained is not that helpful either. But - see above.

It is a light bit of fun and some of the medical conditions are interesting. The first actual mission that you will get a 1-3 star rating out of is Mission 5 'Cursed Hospital'. All missions can be passed on first attempt if you are careful though you may not get a good star rating until your refine some techniques. The only mission that gave me significant issue attaining a 3 star rating was mission 11 'Fairy Tale'. This mission disallows you to have a negative bank balance which makes investment in treatment rooms more strategic especially with reguard to end of month payments maintaining a positive balance. I had to play it several times to make the end goal of 30,000 credit prior to April 1st. Other missions of note (ones that I will drop you a hint of two about how to pass). Mission 12 has zombies which vomit everywhere but it doesnt matter if the hospital is unclean. Mission 15 'Quarenteen' has an odd wing off to the left, that is the one you want to contain the parasites as you treat and research the condition. Mission 16 'Sacred Elephant' I recommend you pause at the very beginning and rearrange the existing hospital assets to configurations more suited to expediant care delivery. Mission 17 'Rural Threat' in the last month the Exo condition pops up which takes time and money to treat and a 3500 investment in a treatment room. Mission 18 'Energy 9000' (AKA Brawndo) very easy just deal with speed delivery. Mission 19 'Seasonal Virus' The parasites are back so section off part of the hospital to prevent the infected from mingling. Best of luck!

Wildlife Park 3 is the third installment in bAlive's Wildlife Park series. The game tasks the player with building their own zoo. Many animals are available to adopt. You construct your own exhibits and visitor facilities in order to create your zoo.
It is my opinion that this game is much better than both of its predecessors. The original Wildlife Park feels like a copy of the original Zoo Tycoon, and Wildlife Park 2 feels like a copy of Zoo Tycoon 2. However, this game feels completely unique.
The graphics are stunning. Many mammals have legitimate fur in layers, giving them a fluffy look. You can see individual blades of grass on the ground. This can create lag, so if you don't have a dedicated gaming PC or laptop I would turn down the graphics settings.
The game is much more in-depth than Zoo Tycoon games. You need to keep things like ground hardness, temperature, and weather into account. This creates a more detailed experience.
Some things- such as what certain enrichment items do- aren't explained in-game, so you'll have to figure them out on your own. They aren't difficult to figure out though, so it won't cause any issues. Overall, Wildlife Park 3 is the best in the series and I would recommend it to any animal fan.
List of animals: bison, gazelle, gnu, meerkat, zebra, elephant, giraffe, leopard, puma, grizzly bear, hippo, jaguar, lion, polar bear, sea lion, chimpanzee, king penguin, rhino, snow leopard, tiger, panda, gorilla, mammoth, Elasmotherium, and Smilodon.

So I figured this game would be one of the best zoo/park games I could probably find, and at the start it really lived up to my expectations! As I clocked in about 20 hours of playtime (I don't have a life) I started to really notice all the flaws with the game. I'll only touch on the main ones, though, because I am known for nit-picking.
1. Herds
All different types of animals have different amounts of their buddies they want in a group with them. Thats pretty understandable no matter what but it just gets tedious near the end of the game when you are constantly having to go back to your rabbit enclosure because your only female rabbit had 8 kids and now, counting the breeding male and female you probably have, you have ten rabbits. The limit to them is 8 per group, despite the fact they breed like flies. Thats something I noticed while I was building my first zoo. The animals that produced the fastest or largest amount always seem to have the lowest herd/group members allowed, which just so happened to normally be your starter animals, like the gazelle or zebra. While I was still new to the game I figured the size of the enclosure would probably partially help determine the size of the herd and they would complain if the size was too small for the current herd or something along those lines, because I figured some thought had to be put into space. They do complain if the size of their enclosure is too small, but it doesn't affect the herd size at all. The animal will get mad at you but not at the space its four other buddies are hogging.
2. Human AI
I started a small playthrough of the game with only 1 star and 10k, the lowest amount possible, with the goal of just getting filthy rich. I hadn't payed much notice on an earlier game I had where I had set my money to somewhere close to 1 million, so the idea of pleasing the people so they would throw cash at me was nonexistent. So I figured the people would use the path as a sort of boundary, showing where they should and shouldn't be while I was building other enclosures. Boy was I wrong! While I was completing a cage for an animal and was just going to start building the path and decorations, I see a crowd of people forming already on the grass. The path they had come from was about a fourth of the way across the map. Now I had to deal with an angry mob complaining about hotdogs, ice-cream, and the lack of decoration because they couldn't walk back to where they had come from where there was a four-star restaurant because AI. Now I have to place an object for every one of their needs every two to three enclosures, which I tend to make small. It is a very annoying process to have to constantly place more shops because the AI refuses to go back to a place a few feet away.
3. (Last one) Lack of content/Map size/Updates
This is where most people complain. There is a lack of animal variety and object variety for the different environments. You normally have to wind up buying heaters or climate control units to have enough animals for the space you are given to please the people. You also normally have to put the same decorations over and over because there aren't any others that are similar that you like more. The map isn't big enough for the size of enclosures a lot of people want to make, and at a certain point it feels like you are abusing the animal with the lack of space you are giving it. For certain animals I wouldn't think the size of the map would even be enough. Finally, the lack of updates fixing the problems. Since I have gotten the game there hasn't been a single update AT ALL! The only thing you could count as an update is the dlc, which cost about as much as the game itself.
I wouldn't really recommend this game. Sorry for the extremely long review. Just passionate about this stuff. Think I'm going to get Zoo Tycoon 2 or Wildlife Park 2 instead, because there was much more effort made with those games than it seems there ever will be with this.

When Wolfenstein: The New Order came out, it was one of the biggest surprises of 2014. Yet another attempt to renew the doom precursor turned to be a meaty shooter with an amazing story, a game that had a clear and striking identity, instantly overshadowing a horde of throwback FPSs like Hard Reset and Serious Sam sequels.
Since then, two things happened. Firstly, neonazi ideas had a minor resurgence in the worst parts of the internet, dripping into the real world in the form of absolute ghouls riding the wave of right-wing populism around the world. With that background, any game providing enough opportunities to smash virtual nazis would be cathartic - and New Collossus seizes the moment in the best way, being very uncompromising and very pulpy about eradicating white suprematists in alternative America.
But, on the other hand, just last year, from nowhere came DOOM and took the throne. Compared to the lean, minimalistic and, at the same time, daring design of DOOM, the dual wielding action of The New Order does not look that striking anymore, and New Colossus fails to improve the gameplay much. Hitscan enemies and no benefits to takedowns, bad stealth options, manual pickup of items - many moving parts of the core FPS action feel very clunky when you've seen the perfection from the same publisher and, I assume, some of the same devs (Machine Games did level design in DOOM).
Still, it is not a bad shooter, just an ordinary one now, elevated by the story (that goes into some INSANE places) and a great cast of characters, deserving a way better vehicle.

I eagerly awaited to play Dragon's Lair 2 for many years, eventually catching it on sale on Steam, snapping it up instantaniously.
For starters the graphics are just as amazing as the first, and the inclusion of collectible objects throughout add a speck of replay value and depth.
But I can't say I enjoy this game unfortunatly. Dragon's Lair 2 is more difficult than the first, you really can't afford to blink or twitch. But the problem isn't the onslaught of commands needed, but the problem stem from the lack of structure unlike the first game. Dragon's Lair 1 had you travelling through room after room, they're relatively short save for a few that last a little bit longer.
But in Dragon's Lair 2 you're not following this structure, you're just moving foward in rather large sections that feel like they last forever and with checkpoints not being as abundant as the ones found in the first game mean that, especially if you're going for the special items, you're gonna have to see the game over screen a lot. I mean, Dragon's Lair 1 will only have you repeat a 10-20 second sequence, whereas this is much more stingy; being forced to repeat a few minutes worth of gameplay.
But honestly, this wouldn't bother me too much but what makes it all a grueling experience is the inclusion of voice acting. The majority of the first game has very little voice acting. But this game has a lot. Due to the amount of deaths you will have to listen and listen to speech that is repeated every time you retry. Its irritating. I can't play the game longer than just a few minutes at a time because of this. It may sound trivial, but when you play it, you WILL know the pain of repeated voice clips. I honestly do believe this pulls the game down, the first game is hard on newcomers but was never annoying. This annoyed me, and as a result upsets me.
Is the game that bad? Not really. Not recommended doesn't necessarily mean the game is bad, but between this and the first, I would 100% ALWAYS recommend the first Dragon's Lair to this. Its much more balanced, its funnier, has a thicker atmosphere and is simply more enjoyable as a whole.

After downloading the new Atlas Update, I am super impressed...Like, I'm actually kinda dumbfounded.
Firstly, I didn't expect an update AT ALL, second I didn't expect it to make my experience so much better. I haven't even touched most of the new content, not even the rovers from the last update, but just the way the game plays and feels is so good right now. Its not quite "there" yet, but that's just because this game has such potential to be better than many other games. Let's get into this.
PROS:
-Performance is 100% better for me (I used to get 12-34FPS, now its like a solid 60FPS except when landing sometimes)
-The aestethic is more pleasing (it looks better, in my opinion, maybe a shader changed?)
-Zero crashes in about 2 hours of play-time (this session)
-The new UI is gorgeous and functional (Its simplified, its organized, it makes more sense)
-Story mode feels like a story now (Before it was all very vauge in a way that didn't work. Now you feel more attached to the character)
-The character's inner monologue with him/herself really helps you feel that you're in a strange place and you must know more
CONS:
-The creatures/plants/worlds still vary too little for my liking, but that's random generation for ya
-This game still feels like its Early, not in a broken way, but in a way that screams for it to finally hit its potential
-The Galazy Map is still kinda clunky in my opinion, it doesn't feel intutive like the rest of the menus
-I would like to see more races in the game. Right now I think I've seen 4 unique ones, but I feel like a universe should be full of varying races
What NMS Needs (In my opinion):
-More ship customization, if just aesthetic. I LOVE customizing vehicles and this game would really benefit from that, it adds another layer of resource management
-More races
-More ships
-More variance in creatures per planet
-Continuing performance updates
I can't wait to see what's next. If you made it this far, thank you very much for reading.

Bought this during the 60% sale with the recent Atlas Update (v1.3). Played it for the 2 hour period and initiated a return for the following reasons:
1. Runs like crap- playing on an OC G1 980Ti and 4790K and could only muster 60 fps on 1080p medium settings on my 1440p screen.

well uhh,,, i spent more time with this game than i expected to, leveling up the different crafting  job to level 3 and experiencing each player class up to level 7.
Stash is an mmorpg that transfers the aesthetics of a tabletop rpg into a mmorpg setting, through looks and some mechanics. i found it enjoyable and recommend it, however it needs work to live up to its' potential and get where it wants to be.
Starting out youll be creating a character with the overly familiar 4 classes (mage, cleric, warrior and hunter), a choice of 4 races (which affect your early game more than they affect the higher levels, by the looks of things) some cosmetic stuff in form of your character's look, heritage and  your figurine's pose.
the game world acts similar to old tabletop rpg's, having player characters and interactions(dungeons, monsters, resources etc') marked with figurines, and movement being tile based. many mechanics involve rng, allowing for "fails" in movement where you encounter ambushes or your crafts end up a disaster (and the obvious rng loot).
combat is turn-based, and features an interesting flank-surround-pin mechanic where positioning can mean a lot for your success in a fight, bringing disadvantages or benefits depending on coordination between teammates. outside of this it is very basic and most of your solo fights will be trading blows with npcs and montsers until something dies.
the pros:
-flanking mechanics in combat bring an interesting value to positioning most games forget about.
-each class is viable even if you did not choose a specific class and race combination for the stat bonuses.
-the dev team interacts with the players and are open about their plans for the game's future.
the neutral:
-enconomy is very much player based, with everything besides the most basic of tools being drops or player crafted(and player crafted items being the stronger option)
the bad:
-combat is very bland at this point.
-gathering materials often involves guesswork, where despite carrying the proper material in your bag you cannot use it if you did not equip it prior to the encounter (personal taste ofcourse, as it is a gamble mechanic and in the situations you bring the correct tools you have potential to earn more than you would when gathering normally)
-the intro to the game is very confusing, and goals are entirely up to the wants of the player. while this is good in a sandbox game, this also scares off a great deal of new players who are not in the mood for reading the guides when starting the game. a simple tie-in tutorial, with use of the player's heritage, would allow an easier and more welcoming learning curve.

Vector is an example of the auto-runner sub-genre of platformers that have really exploded on mobile devices. As such, it is one of the best of its type, with very fluid controls and animation, and a decent (although overly repetitive) soundtrack.
I personally found the entire genre of auto-runners to be slightly less fun on the PC than on my tablet or phone, but I must admit, even with PC controls this was a blast to play in short spurts. My only real complaint is that you have to be doing nothing else to pick up the tricks you "need" to collect throughout the level. If you have another button pressed even for a second of the window for the trick pick-up, it won't register.
Also, it would be nice if you had more control over your character, being able to use the tricks you get when you want, maybe even combo them for points or something. Instead, picking up and unlocking the tricks seems to be largely a waste of time, as the tricks you know don't carry over level to level. This last complaint is really a complaint with the whole auto-runner genre in general, though, so its hard to fault Vector for it.
Ultimately, if you like auto-runners, Vector is a sure win for you, if you don't normally care for them, its still worth checking out, as its professional layout, excellent graphics, and high replayability may make you reconsider the genre.

I enjoy the concept of free running games.  I'm not sure how alone I am on this, but I really liked Mirror's Edge.  So when I saw Vector I figured it would be right up my alley.  Unfortunately, it's proven to be pretty disappointing.
They went with a very similar approach as Mirror's Edge in that you play a man living in a world that has been cleaned to the point of oppression.  So you're constantly running from the cops, and they're always right on your heels.  So ok, I don't really mind that.  It seems interesting to me that free runners are so frequently depicted as anti-oppression rebels because they want to run free, but really who cares.  This isn't about the story, it's about the game and the gameplay stinks.
For all the freedom from oppression rhetoric, Vector has very severe limits on what you can do.  You don't control anything.  Your runner just runs and you push buttons to make him jump, slide, vault or accelerate based on what sort of obstacle you're up against.  It's purely a timing game.  Push a button at the right time and get a biscuit, I mean jump over an instant death pit.
There are some decent production values put into this game, and I wish I could recommend it, but at the end of the day they have managed to make a concept like free running across building tops boring to play.

I've seen too many bodily injuries from all of the Parkour Youtube videos for me even to consider putting myself though that sort of punishment.

So here's what is odd.  If this review was written after my first play through when I played the game back on a PS3 some many years ago, I would only half-halfheartedly recommend this game.  However, after a full play through and many years to consider what had been bothering me before about the game, I finally had the proper mindset for this game.
You see, in this game, a game about stealthy killing (or in my case, not so stealthy killing) all the mechanics feed into that activity.  For example, it annoyed me in the original play through that I couldn't just pickpocket money to give to beggars to make them go away, or to buy knives from merchants.  Now I realize in my second play through that these things are mechanics meant to make being sneaky that much harder; the drunks, mentally impaired, beggars, etc are all there to make it harder for you to kill and silently blend into the crowd.  It bothered me that the game seemed more interested in making me run than stand and fight; with this newest play through, I see that they are trying to teach that discretion is the better part of valor, sometimes.  In other words, running from a fight is not a bad thing.  Not that that kept me from killing over 20 guards in a row, but it takes a bit of finesse, and full command of all your abilities.  This isn't God of War or Darksiders or some spectacle fighter, you aren't meant to hurtle towards foes (though near the endgame you certainly can).
The game feeds that need for moving fast, for speed and alacrity that is fed in other games by battle, but here it's fed by efficiency.  Be it moving over rooftops, through streets, killing guards, hiding, climbing, assassinating, escorting, whatever you do, the game expects you to be as efficient as possible, to make choices and change those choices as the situation demands.
In other words, even 6 years after its release, this game still is very good at forcing you to know all your tools.  You can't just know one attack, one move, and expect the game to work fine.  You could still get through, but the game would be much less fun.  No, this game demands that you know it well to play it well.  In that, it demands knowledge, and the intelligence of when to use your knowledge.  Much in the same way Altair must learn, you to must learn.
And to me, that is a possible mark of a good game.  Highly recommended, especially with those for the patience to learn.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is, as many people have pointed out, not a game but an experience. It's an experience because you're not actually just playing a game, you're also living a life in the shoes of someone suffering with psychosis. And as awful as that may sound, this game is a fantastic tool to help understand those who suffer from that mental ilness. By the end of the game, the voices that you hear really do get on your nerves and for a fraction of a time you have a deeper and different perception of how this disease can affect your day-to-day life. I got annoyed by them in a 10 hour game, now imagine someone that has to live an entire life with it.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifce also hooks itself onto the clichés of hack 'n' slash games and uses it to its advantages. All those corridor symbolize an obstacle that Senua has to overcome, in order to maintain her sanity and not give up to her darkness.
Talking about the game itself - it's not a very long game. It's about 8 to 10 hours (depending on how much of a explorer you are) and after beating the main story, there's nothing left but a "behind-the-scenes" video where you can watch the developers talk about the game. However, it's fairly priced - clocking at 30€ for a new release.
The gameplay and combat are not very deep and you will get the hang of it pretty quick (some might even get bored). But it's clearly intentional, because the developers wanted to focus the game on the story and sound design.
The sound in this game is simply phenomenal and one of the best in the market right now. Not only has a gorgeous soundtrack that follows the gorgeous scenery, but the quality of the sound is unbelievable. The binaural sound that is used on the voices that Senua hear are frightning. Not only because you feel like there's 2/3 people beside you, but because it feels like they are whispering in your ear. It's mindblowing. Next on, are the environment sounds which are just spot on. Rain, waves, wind... Everything is crystal clear. If you have a good quality headphones - use them on this game. You will not regret it.
Finally, in terms of graphical fidelity - it has a AAA game quality. Not only are the textures and models pretty great, but also the animations are fantastic. Shout out to the actress who gave life to Senua. Fantastic performance.
It's also very well optimized game, with a variety of graphical options on the main menu that you can tweak to maintain the desired frame rate.
Overall, it's an amazing game and for now my game of the year.
9/10.

If you like trans-humanism. The story revolves around implants that let people share their memories, and the inevitable moral complexities that arise in this. The technologies involved allow overlays on the screen, a la "augmented reality", which is how most of the UI is played, but it brings up an interesting point: The technologies involved are what lets characters fight each other. Overall, just a very good action game.

When Wolfenstein: The New Order came out, it was one of the biggest surprises of 2014. Yet another attempt to renew the doom precursor turned to be a meaty shooter with an amazing story, a game that had a clear and striking identity, instantly overshadowing a horde of throwback FPSs like Hard Reset and Serious Sam sequels.
Since then, two things happened. Firstly, neonazi ideas had a minor resurgence in the worst parts of the internet, dripping into the real world in the form of absolute ghouls riding the wave of right-wing populism around the world. With that background, any game providing enough opportunities to smash virtual nazis would be cathartic - and New Collossus seizes the moment in the best way, being very uncompromising and very pulpy about eradicating white suprematists in alternative America.
But, on the other hand, just last year, from nowhere came DOOM and took the throne. Compared to the lean, minimalistic and, at the same time, daring design of DOOM, the dual wielding action of The New Order does not look that striking anymore, and New Colossus fails to improve the gameplay much. Hitscan enemies and no benefits to takedowns, bad stealth options, manual pickup of items - many moving parts of the core FPS action feel very clunky when you've seen the perfection from the same publisher and, I assume, some of the same devs (Machine Games did level design in DOOM).
Still, it is not a bad shooter, just an ordinary one now, elevated by the story (that goes into some INSANE places) and a great cast of characters, deserving a way better vehicle.

Full Review:
While the game is still in very early stages, it already has a lot of fun to offer. It has a "table top miniatures" art style and feel to it, which is very appealing for those of us with backgrounds in pen and paper RPGs or tabletop mini wargaming.
The combat is sequential turn based on a grid. Players have a basic attack and accumulate new abilities as they level up. The game takes into account details like having enemies pinned against a wall or surrounding them (or being on the receiving end of that kind of thing!).
There are several different crafting trees to try out, one at a time, along with many gathering skills. The crafting system has more depth than you'd expect at this stage, which is great.
The dev is like a machine. He's almost always logged in, in chat, talking with (and LISTENING TO!) players right at the door to the main city. Dev involvement like that is worth its weight in gold. He freely gives out an e-mail address you can send suggestions to, and is always quick to engage with the player base.
You also get a home base called a Base Of Operations, lovingly referred to as your BOO. You can level it up to expand it, store things there, and decorate it for cosmetic appeal. You can also add functional things like crafting stations, gardens and animal pens for fun or harvesting, etc.
Overall the game is pretty great conceptually, and is already in a great state even this early in development. Over time there's a lot of promise here for a casual to intermediate-intensity gaming experience. I recommend it highly. It's free to play it, with a cash shop, but without the pay to win feel.

Man, where do I even start...?
The idea is okay. Not great, but just okay. It suffers from a lot of things, namely a lack of player direction. You're dropped into the world with no clue as to what you're meant to do, who to talk to, nothing. You're given a "help guide" when you go into something new (combat, base of operations, etc.), but it lacks so much detail that it essentially is just there to tell you "Hey, this is *insert name of thing here*, here's a couple of things that can be done, good luck."
Combat is kind of okay. Sadly, it gets incredibly boring very quickly, and becomes a repetive snorefest after a few minutes. 1, click, 2, 1, get attacked a few times, repeat. The first few dungeons offer some crafting materials, but nothing in the way of usable equipment. You can also get housing stuff, but you can't even place them without a house, which requires materials and "triads" (the game's currency, earned through quest completion and selling loot). Like, a LOT of triads. Your inventory and stash also start out so small that you're essentially forced to take maybe one or two things to avoid filling them both up. While you could upgrade your stash, that, too, requires materials and triads. Again, more grinding.
The game world is devoid of any sort of interesting PoI's. You'll find nodes for gathering crafting materials (which require a bunch of different tools), some battle nodes (with color-coded difficulty "peg" bases), dugeons (private, world, and random varieties), and towns. Other than that, it's mostly flat land, some plateaus, and that's it. Nothing particularly interesting.
Dungeons are...well, painful. They're a pain to navigate, a pain to fully explore, and a real pain to work in with other players, especially since so many will continuously farm enemy nodes for XP and drops. The camera's wonky view and controls certainly don't help either. You can't zoom out to see the whole dungeon. Instead, the camera switches to a top-down view, and only shows a small portion of the area. Like I said: Painful.
Give the devs time to get this game more fleshed out before you consider playing it. At the moment, it's just simply not worth the time.

At launch this game was a huge disappoint to me, as it was to many others also. Massive amounts of promised things for the game didn't release at launch, and the result of that was seen across the entire internet.
But now, with the Atlas Rises Update and Patch 1.31, much of that has changed. No, we don't have true multiplayer yet, as much as I'd like to see that become a thing eventually, but they've fixed a huge hell of a lot issues this game had. You'll still be "grinding" out resources and searching for better ships, weapons, and etc., but it will be much more lenient than it was before. In addition to that, they've added a ton of content that, at least I can hope, gets the game back on its feet and on its way to what the game designers truly intended the game to be. There are tons of missions and thought out storylines to follow now, an entire new dynamic alien race to learn about and grow standing with, and the best part of this update, base building that you can allow other players to find and check out. These changes don't make up for the game we didn't get shipped at launch, but they definitely go to show that the game designers over at Hello Games care about keeping their game as alive as possible and earning back the trust and respect of their customers. I applaud Hello Games for their efforts and attempts to revive their game, and this update will hopefully go miles for them.
With that I recommend this game to anyone who's looking for an eye-candy space exploration game, but would like to make one last important statement. You should not go into this game expecting an immersive mulitplayer experience. Hello Games did not fix this issue that they previously promised, and it is still very much a single player game. If you're looking to explore extremely dynamic and eye-catching planets while gathering materials to survive and get farther through the galaxy to research and learn about the alien life throughout the universe. then this game is for you. But if you expect to team up with other players and shoot down enemy ships and raid space freighters as a team (and etc.) then this is a game you'll want to pass on.

Dear Developers of Vector,
Your game captures perfectly the parkour-freerunning feeling. So it could have been a 10/10 game. But right now it's a 0/10 game. The reason: YOU CAN'T SEE WHERE THE CHARACTER IS GOING!!!  The camera always zooms in, to give a more "cinematic" view, so the only way to play the game is to memorize the levels. Every time you jump, you don't see what follows, so you jump randomly hoping that you land correctly.
This is the most silly mistake I've ever seen in a platform game. The fun and the challenge in a game like this, is to perfectly time your jumps, not to memorize every step of every level.
The good thing is that the solution is easy: KEEP THE CAMERA ZOOMED OUT!!!! Or at least give the player the option to choose between the "standard" camera and the "cinematic".
Vector is a beautiful game made with a lot of love for parkour. Developers, please keep the camera zoomed out and your game will be a perfect 10/10.

Assassin's Creed is an action-adventure stealth game with open world environment from Ubisoft.
The first of the series, this game tells the story of Desmond Miles, an assassin descendant who tried to escape his life as an assassin and try to live like normal people. Instead he got kidnapped by the Abstergo Industries. There, his real adventure begins. Desmond is forced to interface with the Animus, a device that is capable to replay genetic memories of the user's ancestors. The Abstergo seeks to uncover information about Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad, a legendary assassin from the Third Crusade.
The gameplay of Assassin's Creed is quite interesting but also very repetitive and linear. It's repetitive because before you assassination missions begin, you need to conduct some side mission to get information for your main mission. The side mission include pickpocketing, eavesdropping, interogation and completing various task of your fellow assassin's which include, killing guards, race or flag capturing. You will do those side missions everytime you're going to assassinate someone. The good part is, you are free to choose which side mission you want to complete, only 3 from 6 side missions needed for the main missions to unlock. The freedom of the game is also quite big. You can explore the whole city of Damascus, Acre and Jerusalem. Kill guards from behind, help civilian from rogue soldiers, find and kill templar soldiers or climb a tower and perform a leap of faith. You can travel from a city to another city with horses. Despite all these freedom, the game is till linear.
The graphics are beautiful and amazingly detailed. The textures are just, amazing. The animation are also very great. The physics effect are also good, you can watch dead guard roll over the rooftops and eventually fall to the ground. The lightning is perfect too. The environment combined with the AI make the game feels more alive with the civilians walking around, the guards patrolling about and some beggars will try to annoy you.
Assassin's Creed is a good start if you want to dive into the world of Assassin's Creed series as this game contains the foundation of the whole story. Even with linear story, you still have the freedom to do many things in this game. I recommend this.
Rating 8/10

I loved Wildlife Park 2. It probably is the next best zoo management game after Zoo Tycoon series. So, despite the negative reviews, I gave this one a shot. I thought that WP2 has negative reviews as well but that is a damn fine game. Maybe it's the same with WP3. Played it for a while, doing some campaigns to get the basics of WP3 and then started playing freemode. Here is my overall impression -
+ Runs on Windows 10. At least it worked for me.
+ Much better-looking than WP2. The animal textures, terrain, trees etc. everything looks really good.
+ You don't just buy workers. You hire them. They all have Stars to indicate their performance. Hence, workers don't require their own building like in WP2. Work area has a larger radius and can be increased where in WP2 workers already has the max radius set which is not that big, you could only decrease it and then increase it again if needed in WP2. This is not the case with this game.
+ Everything is sorted in different categories, unlike WP2 where there was no sorting option.
+ Realistic AI.
+/- UI isn't very good. Things are sorted into different categories, yes. But the texts on tooltip have weird colors. WP2 has a simple UI, but it will take a bit time to get used to this one if you have played WP2. I felt really uncomfortable with the overall UI at first.
+/- Saving system is a bit confusing at first. I thought I lost my campaign progress after I started playing freeplay mode.
- Performance is REALLY bad. Worse than WP2. Even with a high performance PC the FPS goes down really hard after you start expanding the zoo or during different weather effect animation.. In case of WP2, it's kinda okay because it's very old. But WP3 was released not very long ago compared to WP2. To be honest, WP2 run BETTER than WP3. Funny thing is, devs decided to release a DLC, but ignoring to fix the performance issue which is mentioned several times in the community discussion. Even I have posted about it and got no reply. This is the third game of this franchise, yet the worst compared to the previous games of this series.
- Limited animal variety. This might not be a con for you though.
- Poor tutorial system. It does not clearly say what you will need to do next. It does explain why you need to do this and that, but fails to show you how.
- Every map feels really smalls after you put a few enclosures. You will have trouble regarding space. Visitors want to see more animals, yet there ain't enough space to add more.
- Every time I want to see the detailed information of something, another preview window opens and I have to close it every time. This might not be a problem for you, but in WP2 it was really simple to check information so I find this system in WP3 very annoying.
- Music is just annoying and repetitive. I had to turn it off.
- The whole game just doesn't feel fun. If you have played WP2 and loved that, then you might not like the gameplay on this one, except for few people maybe.
I really wanted to love this game but it just fails on so many levels. It has it's charm but very little and it gets boring very fast. If you want to play this series, then just get the previous titles.
