If you haven't played Dragon's Lair 2, or any of the Don Bluth games in general, imagine a cartoon animation fused with Geometry Dash. Highly difficult, fast reactions, trial and error, and memory. Dragon's Lair 2 is a challenging full motion video game where you must push the arrow keys and space bar at the right moment.
The story continues from the first Dragon's Lair. After the protagonist Dirk the Daring freed Princess Daphnie from the dark magic of the Dragon's Lair, she gets kidnapped by the evil wizard Mordoc, and must use a time machine, which is oddly the nicer brother of Mordoc and talks. He must travel through different time zones and worlds to save Daphnie once again.
In gameplay, your mission is to push a button according to where a yellow flashing light appears. You have less than a second to react. The button depends on which direction it is from Dirk, the player character, or if Dirk's sword is flashing. If so, use the space bar. For experience, I too found the game pretty challenging. One death and you start over a level. Major levels are about a minute long each, the first level has two checkpoints, and the last two are pretty short. I ALWAYS play without a move guide for the most thrilling game experience. Just like what Nostalgia Critic stated in his review of Dragon's Lair, it's cheating! Without the guide, reaction times are quite slim. However, if you replay some levels and get used to the moves, it shouldn't be that stressful, especially if you are forced to replay the whole game if it tells you you missed a special "Treasure", which brings us to the next feature. Each level has at least one treasure item that flashes with the next move. Collect them all to enter the level were you fight Mordoc. There are also two modes called "Original" and "Director's Cut". In Original, you HAVE to collect all treasures to proceed to the Mordoc fight. In Director's Cut, the treasures are not required, but grants an alternate, easier Mordoc fight when they are all collected. One last thing about level gameplay, most of the levels have a chance to be mirrored, making it harder and disorienting if you played the level before.
For presentation, Don Bluth directed and animated the FMV for this game. Bluth was the legendary animator for some of our favorite nostalgic movies like Land Before Time and An American Tail, and he was called down to do a series of games by Digital Leisure, like this one! The level concepts are really clever and creative. Seeing how Dirk travels through different time zones, there are typical eras like the Prehistoric Times fighting flying creatures. There are even crazier-looking levels like the one where Dirk slides "Through the Looking Glass" into Wonderland! This is one of the most innovative video games I have played, and love it. This is why I like replaying  this game. I'm not only watching an animation, I'm playing it!
To conclude, the game is okay. The appearance is outstanding and really takes me back to when I saw "All Dogs Go to Heaven" and "Bartok the Magnificent" as a kid, which were other movies he did by the way. But I do think it should be longer, or the price lower, speaking of price, I purchased this on sale and so should you, my opinion. Bluth is also trying to get back to animation and developing a Dragon's Lair movie. I sure hope he does it!
I rate this game 8/10. To summarize: Great animation, innovative gameplay, creative concepts, but a bit too high for price and a bit too short for length.

First off - you should definitely buy this game. For most people, this is a classic "Wait for the Steam sale" game. But, if you care about video games, you care about ♥♥♥♥♥♥ DLC practices, you care about AAA games rehashing the same♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over - this might be something you want to purchase full price. Please tell Ninja Theory they did something cool, and they deserve praise for it.
This game does everything we are always talking about needing more of: story-rich game, dark/mature plotline, NO gameplay handholding, interesting take on combat, etc. In fact, combat IMO is the best part of this game. It's "heavier" than pretty much any other action RPG/fantasy game, more believable, and more *stressful*. You actually have to think about what you're doing and taking on a few enemies at once can be cumbersome.
The story and the gameplay unfold beautifully without even telling you. Probably my favorite moment playing this game was when I *accidentally* parried an enemy. I didn't even know parrying was possible in this game, and I was rewarded for it with a display of totally different attack animations from Senua. This concept only evolves, and becomes more impressive over time. Bravo, Ninja Theory.
I could go on forever about Hellblade. My only qualms with the game (the fact that there are only 2 says A LOT) are the a) Rune puzzle system and b) the ending. The Rune puzzle system just... I don't know half of the time it works and gets you to explore an area and sometimes it just feels like padding time. At first it seems unneccessary, and then I think it really works when you're in new and breathtaking environments. Oh yeah, the graphics are top-notch. I constantly found myself saying "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; every hour or so just on the landscape.
A lot of people are saying "Oh yeah, it's a SHORTER game - especially given the price tag". Yeah well, hate to break it to you but how many AAA games are done in 8-10 hours? Metal Gear Rising (great game, though), The Order: 1886, the Last of Us (great game as well), Bioshock Infinite? WE get the better end of the deal here, no question. Isn't that how it should be in vidya?
***SPOILERS***
The ending... is a bit of a let down, unfortunately. The dev team did such a phenomenal job leading you to believe you were desending into Norse hell/madness/underworld, only to have an ending where you're left saying - "Oh, I guess... it was all in her head...". That's weak, IMO. But, honestly I truly don't know how you end this plot otherwise. The silver lining here is that obviously Ninja Theory intends to make another game, and honestly I hope it's a full-fledged $60 game this time.

Remember Me is memorable and interesting but I am going to have to side with the critics on this one. There's a reason why this game "failed" and it's pretty simple: The combat is one huge cluster of a hot mess.
It sounds great in theory. A semi-deep combo system and a visceral beat-em up concept in which fists act like fists and you don't blaze through enemies like a magical witch. Which can work and other games have done this "realism" successfully and satisfyingly. But this game does not and there's the crux. It's not very fun to play and in the end her fists would be bloody stumps after episode 2 so why bother making combat resemble any sort of realism?
The levels are beautiful and the music complements what is going on very well. It's understated but well done. The bad thing is that exploring these worlds, if you can call it that, is a cinematic affair. The camera is practically up the protagonist's butt and the game guides you where to go because, well, if it didn't you'd have no idea what to do. There's no good level design from a game perspective. So, in the end, it's like a giant QTE cinema. Go climb here, go open that door, go to this battle sequence with a clunky battle system that feels like QTEs bunched together. Rinse/repeat. There's a lot of ledges to climb but unlike uncharted which did this well, this game just feels too guided and without any degree of freedom, it's not satisfying or fun to go through the motions like Uncharted was with its guided ledge climbing.
So that leaves the story. Seems great at first glance but almost nothing is explored. No memorable characters because not a single character, including the protagonist, have a proper arc. As soon as you almost get to know them they're gone. Done. You get to see their past but it never truly explains their present. The story is so incredibly undeveloped it's actually surprising they managed to make a game out of what they did and the way it's directed just seems wasted potential.
I don't know, it's a weird game that I can't find any merits in justifying the combat system, when no matter what, it could have been made more fun to play and developed a hell of a lot more story in the process. It just feels broken, unfinished.
The game ultimately feels like a prototype. Both gameplay and story. It's a shame but I think people liked where this game was going, wanted more of it, but failed to remember that this game didn't do anything well in the process. I guess that's why they want a sequel, to finish the job this game started.

The gameplay is a bit tedious. Combat is centered around an Arkhem-like crowd-control systems where multiple baddies surround you while only attacking one at a time, with occasional special enemies to alter the flow of combat. However, unlike Arkhem, the combat feels awkward, and the game's gimmick, the custom combination system, isn't really that noteworthy because the combos themselves are predetermined, there is only a limited amount of moves to do, and you only put one move into one combo at a time, effective meaning that you will have to use most if not all moves, so if you wanted to build your own fighting style (like I did,) you're out of luck. Battles are also rather sparse, making the world feel kind of empty. Between the battles, there are a lot of freeclimbing puzzles, which aren't especially interesting since you're told where to go anyway, and there not much map to explore on your own.
The story and universe feel rather familiar, and are told through cutscenes that are not very interesting, the worst offender being the player character's internal monologue scenes at the beginning of each chapter. The kicker? YOU CAN'T SKIP CUTSCENES. If you quit the game at the beginning of a chapter, you're forced to sit through the cutscenes again. All you can do is pause them.
I did like the memory-remixing game mechanic, but I only got to do it once, and the rest of the game has unmotivated me from continuing.

My inital response was 'err, this isn't what I thought it would be', so I dove into the game to actually try it properly (instead of the constant 0.3hr reviews you see).
At first, it took a short while to get going, tutorials for the moment are limited to the short in game help screens. There is a Help channel and a world channel, where 99% of all questions I've seen asked have been answered within 30 seconds by someone.
After getting the basics out of the way, I started to explore the world, the dungeons, my BOO etc.
Your character is represented by a non-animated figurine on a stand (think old-style Dungeons & Dragons tabletop miniatures), with a fair bit of customisation available from the start. There are currently 4 different character classes and 5 or 6 different races (each race has a bonus to one starting stat). Starting stats even out around level 6-7, so the main choice is in no way game breaking, and your best bet is to choose based on role-play or fun purposes.
The world (currently) consists of the main town, the Overworld, your BOO (Base of Operations - which is your stash / stall / and crafting area), and 2 dungeon types - world dungeons which are open to anyone, and private dungeons which are solo dungeons. The dungeons are also level set to a range (eg 1-3, 3-9, 5-10) which you can change from your party settings (even if solo), so you can fight easier or harder mobs as you wish.
Combat is turn-based, with actions done in order (various spells can change the orders / stop creatures acting). You can move and fight, or, move and cast, in a single round, and you can also harvest corpses (or resource nodes which sometimes show up)  provided you have the correct tools equipped.
Xp, loot, and sometimes triads (basic currency) are awarded at the end of a successful combat, with loot being anything really - recipes, crafting mats, weapons, armour etc.
The gameplay overall is very slow paced, so don't come in expecting COD/CS:S/<insert other fast game here> speeds, but this works nicely as you need to spend time to upgrade your Base, your stash, your stall and your harvesting and crafting skills (if you want to craft that is).
One thing I noticed while playing: there are VERY active Devs who sit in the game world, answer questions, help players, listen to suggestions etc, which I found very refreshing, and very nice to see.
Devs have also mentioned changes to various systems they have coming after listening to player responses to the game so far - again, very nice to see.
Overall, a bit of a bumpy start to a new game release (stupid ddos'ing script kiddies), but I highly recommend you give the game more than 20 minutes of your time if you like this type of game - you won't be disappointed.

I honestly had to come back to the store page just to see if it was in Early Access because I'm quite surprised this was released as a complete game. Stash is a neat concept on paper, but the execution of the game is horrible. The game will frequently lag, whether it be from the game itself, or spammers making everyone have a good time. The movement feels very clunky and unresponsive, as does the combat. It's not complicated by any means, but it just doesn't feel as solid and responsive as it should, though it is admittedly a bit better once you start using the hotkeys.
There are also a number of bugs as well, such as fights not ending sometimes when you finish off the enemies, so you have ot take a move, end your turn, rinse and repeat until you make it to the treasure chest. The XP bar is also, as of writing, useless and doesn't tell you a single thing. You have to manually type in /xp to get this stat. I'm not sure how an XP bar can be messed up like that, but I imagine it's not exactly a hard bug to fix.
The gameplay design is also a bit wonky in other aspects as well. You get a chance to pick a skill to go into, be it cooking, enchancing, smithing, etc. HOWEVER, to actually do things with it, you need a special item you put in your BOO (Base of Operations), and a tool to gather resources. The former you cannot actually use until you upgrade your BOO, which is not explained. So why bother giving me the ability to try and learn a skill if you're also not going to actually let me use it? The resources you need to upgrade your BOO aren't something you'll just grab along in a dungeon or something, I'm honestly still not sure. But I've uninstalled, as this game's design is just too terrible for me to try and keep going on. The description intrigued me, but until this gets patched (probably multiple times) to fix some of the more glaring issues, I can't say I'd recommend this to anyone.

Assassin's Creed is possibly one of the greatest games released in 2007. It's a sandbox nature game with remarkable visuals, sound effects and story, which is based on historical events and people. There are two overlaping stories in this game: Desmond Miles and Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad, through machine called Animus. Within the Animus, Altaïr's memories reveal that he was attempting to stop Robert de Sablé from taking an artifact from a Solomons temple, but broke all three of the assassin brotherhood's tenets in the process. The brotherhood leader, Al Mualim, demotes Altaïr to the rank of novice, and assigns him the task of assassinating nine people, all of whom are Templars, to regain his former status. As Altaïr assassinate them one by one he realises something is wrong about this assignment and that these people somehow are connected. Overall pretty good story,
The gameplay consist out a series of assassinations ordered by Al Mualim. To achieve this goal, you must travel from the Brotherhood's headquarters in Masyaf, across the terrain of the Holy Land known as the Kingdom to one of three cities Jerusalem, Acre, or Damascus to find the Brotherhood agent in that city. There, the agent, in addition to providing a safe house, gives the player minimal knowledge about the target, and requires them to perform additional "recon" missions before attempting the assassination. After completing each set of assassinations, the player is returned to the Brotherhood and rewarded with a better weapon and then given another set of targets, with the player free to select the order of certain targets.
Overall it‘s pretty good game, worth your attention but it does have downsides. The bad: It‘s repetitive and does not provide much graphic options for high end pc, combat is clunky and sometimes feels awkward. The Good: Fun parkour mechanics, great story, huge sandbox world that feels alive, great soundtrack, many little details. 7/10

I have issues when it comes to games, I feel like I need to play through entire series to get the storyline even if people say the original ones suck.
Everyone told me that the original assassin's creed was one of those games, just to avoid it and move onto 2 but I couldn't do it.. I had to play it.
It's a really pretty game, even by current 2014 standards.. but aside from that there's not much else in the way of redeeming features. You'll be doing a couple of things in this game, running around exploring, fighting and doing side quests.
All the side quests are the same, there's a million 'save a citizen' quests that just involve fighting some guards and then getting one of three canned replies from the person you rescued.. there's no variation in conversation.. by the end of the game you'll have heard a million other people say the same lines whenever you start to climb anything or knock anything over.
Climbing / freerunning is the other big thing, but it feels a bit gimmicky in the game, there's very little reason to use it other than the game forcing you to use it to explore areas by getting to vantage points.By the end of the game I was using it for that purpose and just to get places quite far away quickly, everything else was easier to just stay on the ground in my opinion.
Combat itself isn't fluid and locks away most of your combat moves until you progress the game, which makes combat start out clumsy and boring and ends up the same way as every combat move you get is defensive in nature, the entire combat system boils down to defending and counterattacking.. there's never any storming in and killing everyone like a badass.. there's storming and and defending yourself until everyone dies which just does not have the same feeling at all.

The entire game is repititous and feels extremely grindy, by the end I was putting it on for an hour and then turning it off because it just felt like work.. unless you have the same issue as me and need to see the game yourself for the storyline before moving onto the next, then honestly skip this game. And so that's how the awesome Assassin's Creed franchise begins!
Having played this game on its release time frame back in 2008 on the PS3, I now felt compelled to replay the game on PC and I have to say, the game do look much better on PC! As for the controls, I managed to play with the Xbox 360 gamepad so they weren't as clunky as mentioned with Keyboard+Mouse. Although, since this game is the first of this annual release franchise, there was many aspects that was clunky and boring. I'll get to that down below!
The game itself is linear and repetetive, but the amazing art style(which makes the game feel kinda "dusty"), freerunning mechanic and combat made the game a revolutionary success!
PROS:
+Intriguing story that keeps you guessing until the very end (both the animus and real reality),
+Interesting visuals and especially the artstyle (Impressive graphics even to this day).
+Amazing soundtrack (Jesper Kyd really truly rocks! It's great that he's back with AC2, AC: Brotherhood and AC: Revalations. Sadly, Ubisoft discarded this great composer for AC3 and AC4).
+Freerunning gameplay adds some exploration to the game.
+Escaping "your assassination" pumps your adrenaline! Sad this feature was removed on the other AC games as you actually feel like an assassin there.
CONS:
-Experienced a few game crashes and freezes so maybe it can be attributed to Windows 8.1 although, I haven't left any game progress!
-Audio stuttering.
-No subtitles (closed captions).
-Repetitive submissions, tasks.
-Can't swim!
-Eagle Eye vision mode cannot be use while moving.
-Annoying NPC that hinder your progress during freerunning (namely the beggars, drunks, etc).
-HUGE amount of collectibles that serves no real purpose besides collecting (Flags).
-Last missions requires you to SOLO fight multiple enemies at once and that repeats a few times. If you haven't mastered the controls by then, you'll be restarting quite often!
RECOMMENDATION:
Yes, I really recommend this game if by some chance, you haven't played THE GAME that spawned a big successful franchise. You may become bored though once you finished the game so for the replayability factor, it can be either low or high, if you really liked it. In my case, since I haven't played it since 2008, it was worth a revisit as I was due to catch up my Assassin's Creed craving.
RATING:
8.0 / 10

Assassin's Creed is something of a classic, the beginning of one of the biggest series of all time. While the original AC had was a very fun game, it definitely had some flaws. It was a transitional game, trying to move the parkour of Prince of Persia into a world of stealth like Tenchu or Splinter Cell, and was definitely still growing through its awkward phase. The game feels very slow at times and pickpocketing missions are tedious to say the least. Some missions feel forced or don't make sense, and some of the stealth/alert mechanics really didn't work. It's definitely worth playing for its gripping story and the combination of stealth and parkour action. It's a masterpiece in spite of its shortcomings. While the sequels have been getting progressively better, this is where it all started and is definitely worth a play through for fans of the series.

I was one of the ones who stayed on the sidelines while this game was being developed, then when it was released to mixed or negative reviews. I don't know how bad it was before, but I can say it's quite a bit of fun now. There's a steady sense of progression from the very first moment. As you make your way around your starting planet, then to other planets, then to other systems and space stations, the game places objectives before you to help lead you towards more and more self-reliance. Maybe this game gets bad after x number of hours, but after 4.5 hours it's still nice and intriguing. There's a mystery to solve, ancient structures to explore, and as you do so you continue to unlock more technology to help along the way.
Technically the game is fine. I'm running on Win7 x64 with an i7-6700k, 32MB RAM, and GTX 980 video card. I get a solid 60FPS everywhere, but I'm never super aggressive on graphics settings. Give me high res textures with anisotropic filtering and I'm happy. This game has pretty extensive quality settings, so you're sure to be able to tune it to your system with no problems.
I only have two minor complaints so far about the gameplay. First, the inventory is very limited, and the stack sizes are relatively small compared to how much material you'll need for your journey. For this reason you end up spending quite a bit of time gathering resources and juggling inventory. This was one of the initial complaints and it's still a bit annoying. There are ways to upgrade your personal inventory capacity, and you will eventually find bigger ships. You can transfer inventory directly to your ship from anywhere. After about 3-4 hours I did find a ship that was able to hold twice as much cargo, but almost all the slots are locked and require quite a few credits to unlock.
My other complaint, and this is purely a matter of personal preference, is that the universe is rather lonely. There are NPCs to interact with, but so far I haven't been forming any relationships, and they're all very alien in appearance. I like games with NPC companions, like Mass Effect and the like, but this game just has you against a mostly hostile or indifferent universe. There is an NPC that shows up for regular appearances as a matter of story, but I wouldn't call him/her a companion by any means. Being able to form a crew and having RPG options wouldn't go amiss in my book, but that can hardly be a mark against this title.
Travel times are pretty acceptable, with four different speed options - cruising, which requires you to constantly hold your thrust button down, a boost speed which is kind of like afterburners, but it lasts as long as you have fuel, a phase drive which is kind of a sublight speed, and then warp drive, which almost instantly takes you from one star system to the next. Going from space to atmosphere, then down to the surface and back is a smooth process with no hitching or jarring transitions. If your angle is too steep, you'll get a burning aurora effect around the edges of your viewable area, along with some shaking and creaking sounds, which is a cool touch. So far it appears to be visual only.
You also get a scanner, which can be upgraded. At first it will detect materials and points of interest within a certain radius. If you aim at a planet you can scan it and see what conditions to expect, and what kinds of materials are most abundant there. All planets I've found so far have the essentials - iron, carbon, and plutonium, which you need in order to maintain your various energy levels and conduct basic repairs. It's the more exotic materials you'll see as the result of a long distance scan.
In my time of playing I have never found a planet that wasn't hostile enough to drain your environmental systems while you're on foot. This system is like a hunger or thirst meter that runs down constantly. Sometimes there will be storms or something that makes it go down even faster. This means you can't venture out too far from your ship or the nearest shelter without either going back to let your bar fill back up again, or using some of the materials you've picked up to refill it out in the field. I'm sure there are M class planets around somewhere but I've yet to discover any.
Overall this is a pretty decent game. It's good enough that I can see putting 20-40+ hours into it at least. We'll just have to see beyond that. I haven't tried the new multiplayer features, but if that system is developed enough it might be a blast to do some base building with friends or family. We'll see. So far though, it's a pretty solid game, easily worth picking up on sale at least. The current sale price of $24 seems like a pretty good bargain for something like this, but I don't know if I'd go much higher than that.

The ambitious sequel to the innovative arcade game by Don Bluth and his team. The squeaky eye-candy princess Daphne has been kidnapped by the evil Mordroc, who apparently wants to marry her for some unknown reason. While the entire first game took place in the castle, in this one, you travel through 6 different timelines by using a unique flying time machine.
Another change is this game plays more like an interactive movie; inputing the correct commands to progress through the level as it goes. I am not entirely sure what the difficulty was on the first game, but this one is pretty difficult, especially when you turn off the move guides which serve as the game's training wheels. Then you have to solely rely on the yellow flashes to figure out what direction to go or when to use your sword. To make matters worse, except in the first level, if you mess up, you will restart to the beginning of the level. So you'll need good memorization skills in order to succeed, especially when turning off the move guide to get two achievements.
There are also treasures hidden in each level, which flash yellow when you're nearby. Input the correct direction to obtain the item. You have to collect all the treasures before reaching the final level or else the game will make you restart at the level(s) where you missed them. So overall, this game is a big step-up from the first one; the animation is improved in glorious Don Bluth style, the levels are distinctive to each other, and an increase in difficulty. If you played Dragon's Lair or any laser disc arcade game before, or you are a fan of Don Bluth movies (like me), or you just want a challange, I highly recommend this game.

I'd just like to say that this is totally an "act II" sort of game. It bridges the events of The New Order to the last installment not even announced yet. If you didn't realize this about the story before you forked out the cash, then you're a bit of a naïf.
Now to my objective review: In The New Order, it felt like you were an action hero meant to fight a stealth game. This time around they realized that in their designs, given the option for stealth or guns blazing, one has to have the ability to choose given the same arenas and corridors no matter the style of play. This game gives you more options, without the need to be a stealth master gamer to succeed at stealth, or likewise the embodiment of death himself to succeed at carnage.
But don't get me wrong, the game will punish you for your mistakes. Because of this, I wish the save/load was a bit more streamlined. An example of this (spoilers skip to next paragraph to avoid butt-hurt) is at the train depot under Roswell on the campaign play through. My first time through playing the game I must have reloaded this level 20 times. It was the first real test of stealth tactics, and boy was it unforgiving. I praise the creators to have the balls to do this though. Take Crysis for example: You ♥♥♥♥ up you can just go and hide, and everything dies down. Even if you miss a head shot they won't come after you despite hitting them. Here they set the alarms off. They don't forgive and let you hide. Naturally, due to the ease of the stealth in the prior installment, I never got the chance to see if Alarms were destructible. They are here, and you may need to take advantage of this.
Just to close, I want to reiterate that I feel this is a classic "Act II" story. It raises the stakes but there is no pay off in the end, because the rising tensions cannot be resolved until the last act.
It's fun, it's absurd, and full to the brim of things to keep the completion-ists very happy. But as far as story goes, they kept the formula from the New Order, but I'd say they didn't flesh it out as much as they could have.

Overall, I think it is a good game and is worth picking up, but waiting until it's complete and on sale is a good idea, as well as understanding that in comparison to other entries in the franchise this title seems quite disappointing.
Also, the politics is something to watch out for; it's superficial and could've benefitted from being a little more elaborate in my honest opinion. You have to move through the house between reality and nightmarish elements, solving puzzles and you will find various mini games along the way.
While you play you will have to interpret the story yourself. You need to do certain tasks as feeding the cat or mow the lawn, however the tasks are not as simple as you might think and there are creepy elements in the house that are after you. Like the big freaky ghost type thing that literally made me shout out loud (I do scare easily).
You only have 6 inventory slots and you need to pick up items for the tasks and puzzles. However you can pick up just about anything, even really useless items, making it a big difficult to know what items you actually need or not. If you liked Mirrors Edge or the chase scene of Casino Royale, I recommend trying out the Vector Demo on Steam.
The premise is that you're a worker drone in a future, dystopian, totalitarian society.  One day you snap and make a run for it.  And you run.  And run.  and run.  :)
So, basically it's a 2D side scroller where your character is running away from one of the policeman (who will taze you if they catch up to you).  The cool part is that you are basically running an obstacle course, as you make your getaway with some Parkour-ish flair.
The levels are achievement-based -- your score is based on time, bonuses (which are objects you pick up as you run), and stunts performed (these are cue'd at certain points in each level and make it easier for you to pick up bonus objects or time the upcoming obstacle).  You also pickup coins, which you use to unlock additional tricks.
A valid criticism is that this really isn't "free" running.  That is correct.  It's much more of a timed and scripted obstacle course.  You have to figure out the proper (or workable) timing to get all the items, coins, and trick cues.  This is interesting because it means that until you unlock all the tricks used in a level, you're never going to get the full score on the first try.  On the other hand, each level so far has been challenging enough that I've had to run through it multiple times to get the perfect 3-star score.  During that time, I usually pick up enough coins to unlock the needed tricks, usually around the time that I've gotten familiar enough with the level to understand how the tricks will help me with certain obstacles.
For an indie game, it's quite well done and surprisingly tense.  The policeman is never far behind you.  He's quite good, and a mistake on your part can easily have him almost within arm reach as you scramble to get back up to speed.
Even the failures can be amusing.  I, at least, find it amusing when, after sliding, jumping, and flipping my way over the scenery like a badas, I suddenly run off an edge and fall to my death.  Or just flat out slam into a wall.  Or faceplant on the ground.  I don't know why I find it funny, but I do.  :)  It takes the edge off of having to restart the level.  The novelty does wear off, though, and some of the levels are just crazy difficult.  Having to restart a complicated level after each failure does get frustrating after a while.
Having said all that, even though I normally hate platformers, I don't regret picking up Vector.

I am a late-joiner to the Assassin's Creed series and as of writing this review, this first installment is the only Assassin's Creed game I have played.
The game is quite obviously built upon the mechanic of climbing things, be it a castle, a barn or a horsecart. Pretty much everything is climbable. The implementation is not perfect and will sometimes frustrate you, but it is for the most part solid and works well. Without doubt, the satisfaction of scaling buildings and jumping across rooftops lasts the duration of the game.
Visually, the game is stunning for its time. In particular the draw distance is very impressive. Standing at the top of a tower in one of the game's cities and being able to see past the city gates and to the rolling hills beyond is a lovely eye-candy experience. This is definitely a strong point of the game.
I must, however, point out that the game is very poorly optimised - something I believe is largely endemic to the Assassin's Creed series on the PC. Aside from the frame rate being hard-capped at 60fps, I very rarely found myself hitting this number and instead would hover somewhere between 30-40fps.
This will turn a lot of people off and sadly there is no good reason or excuse for it. Obviously, this will annoy some people more than others. If you can "tolerate" a console-level refresh rate then you have nothing to worry about. For those used exclusively to frame rates of 60fps and above, however, you might as well give it a miss if you aren't willing to compromise on this aspect.
Another major criticism I would level at the game is its lack of variety and its reptitiveness. After I progressed past the initial levels and into the game proper, I often felt like I was playing an extended tech demo. It's clear that the title was built upon the climbing mechanic and that the plot and design came second.
This wouldn't necessarily be a bad thing were it not for the fact that you pretty much do find yourself doing the same few tasks over and over throughout the course of the game, with random spatterings of narrative here and there.
As someone who likes to complete all side objectives and acquire every collectable in my games, I found Assassin's Creed distinctly unrewarding in this regard. There are an (infamous) number of collectables in this game, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. What makes it is problem, however, are the literally non-existant rewards for actually finding all of them. The game also provides no tools to assist in your collectable hunt, instead simply relying on you meticulously combing every single inch of the maps in search of them. I disagree with this model simply because it takes up too much time unnecessarily. At any particular moment there are thousands of good games worth your attention - can you really justify spending an hour or two poking around a map looking for that one last pickup?
Personally, I say no - especially when the game doesn't reward you for it.
Despite this, I would say Assassin's Creed is worth most people's time, if only to set yourself up for the other installments in the series. One thing I have been told repeatedly is "Don't play later Assassin's Creed games before playing the first" and I can imagine why this makes sense. The game is novel provided you haven't played similar titles or other games in the series, and the meta aspect of the plot can be compelling, although you ultimately learn very little by the end of the game.
For this reason, I recommend Assassin's Creed, if only to set yourself up to play the later installments in the series.

The key is to run it in Windows Compatability Mode to get it to work.  Let me dump one way (I use a different method to make Steam do it) of easily doing it:
Launching the game:
1.Right-click game in Steam Library.
2.Click Properties, then in new window click on the local files tab.
3.Click 'Browse Local Files'.
4.Windows explorer should pop up with the game files. Right click on Antanta.exe (shown as Antanta).
5.Click properties again, then in new window navigate to compatibility tab.
6.Tick the box where it's description is: Run this game in compatibility mode for.....
7.Select Windows XP Service Pack 3.
8.Click apply, then launch Antanta.exe or play through Steam.
9.Your game should boot properly with minor graphical bugs (which go away and are only in the levels).

I was one of the ones who stayed on the sidelines while this game was being developed, then when it was released to mixed or negative reviews. I don't know how bad it was before, but I can say it's quite a bit of fun now. There's a steady sense of progression from the very first moment. As you make your way around your starting planet, then to other planets, then to other systems and space stations, the game places objectives before you to help lead you towards more and more self-reliance. Maybe this game gets bad after x number of hours, but after 4.5 hours it's still nice and intriguing. There's a mystery to solve, ancient structures to explore, and as you do so you continue to unlock more technology to help along the way.
Technically the game is fine. I'm running on Win7 x64 with an i7-6700k, 32MB RAM, and GTX 980 video card. I get a solid 60FPS everywhere, but I'm never super aggressive on graphics settings. Give me high res textures with anisotropic filtering and I'm happy. This game has pretty extensive quality settings, so you're sure to be able to tune it to your system with no problems.
I only have two minor complaints so far about the gameplay. First, the inventory is very limited, and the stack sizes are relatively small compared to how much material you'll need for your journey. For this reason you end up spending quite a bit of time gathering resources and juggling inventory. This was one of the initial complaints and it's still a bit annoying. There are ways to upgrade your personal inventory capacity, and you will eventually find bigger ships. You can transfer inventory directly to your ship from anywhere. After about 3-4 hours I did find a ship that was able to hold twice as much cargo, but almost all the slots are locked and require quite a few credits to unlock.
My other complaint, and this is purely a matter of personal preference, is that the universe is rather lonely. There are NPCs to interact with, but so far I haven't been forming any relationships, and they're all very alien in appearance. I like games with NPC companions, like Mass Effect and the like, but this game just has you against a mostly hostile or indifferent universe. There is an NPC that shows up for regular appearances as a matter of story, but I wouldn't call him/her a companion by any means. Being able to form a crew and having RPG options wouldn't go amiss in my book, but that can hardly be a mark against this title.
Travel times are pretty acceptable, with four different speed options - cruising, which requires you to constantly hold your thrust button down, a boost speed which is kind of like afterburners, but it lasts as long as you have fuel, a phase drive which is kind of a sublight speed, and then warp drive, which almost instantly takes you from one star system to the next. Going from space to atmosphere, then down to the surface and back is a smooth process with no hitching or jarring transitions. If your angle is too steep, you'll get a burning aurora effect around the edges of your viewable area, along with some shaking and creaking sounds, which is a cool touch. So far it appears to be visual only.
You also get a scanner, which can be upgraded. At first it will detect materials and points of interest within a certain radius. If you aim at a planet you can scan it and see what conditions to expect, and what kinds of materials are most abundant there. All planets I've found so far have the essentials - iron, carbon, and plutonium, which you need in order to maintain your various energy levels and conduct basic repairs. It's the more exotic materials you'll see as the result of a long distance scan.
In my time of playing I have never found a planet that wasn't hostile enough to drain your environmental systems while you're on foot. This system is like a hunger or thirst meter that runs down constantly. Sometimes there will be storms or something that makes it go down even faster. This means you can't venture out too far from your ship or the nearest shelter without either going back to let your bar fill back up again, or using some of the materials you've picked up to refill it out in the field. I'm sure there are M class planets around somewhere but I've yet to discover any.
Overall this is a pretty decent game. It's good enough that I can see putting 20-40+ hours into it at least. We'll just have to see beyond that. I haven't tried the new multiplayer features, but if that system is developed enough it might be a blast to do some base building with friends or family. We'll see. So far though, it's a pretty solid game, easily worth picking up on sale at least. The current sale price of $24 seems like a pretty good bargain for something like this, but I don't know if I'd go much higher than that.

Words do not properly describe this game, but I will try:
For me, my life was divided into two parts: before I played this game, and after. If you aren't completely heartless/unfeeling, this game will make you feel emotions you didn't know existed. You WILL cry. You WILL laugh. You WILL cry a lot more.
If any one game in my Steam collection could be used as evidence of the whole "games are art" argument, it would have to be this one. The visuals are as meticulously and lovingly created as you will find in a retro, pixel-art style, and are downright beautiful in places. The characters are amazingly written, easily likable, and easy to get attached to.
The kicker for this game though, is it's splendid use of sound and music. Kan Gao has a way of playing just the right chord progression to make the emotions of the story more impactful; the heavy moments wouldn't hit as hard if it weren't for the fantastic soundtrack. As a fellow musician, I am in awe of his work. Then, there is Laura Shigihara's song. What a beautiful piece of music played at just the right time. The music makes this game what it is: a masterpiece.
Bottom line is this:
If you buy this game at full price, it will sent you back ten bucks. Tissues will be another dollar. I can not think of a better way to spend eleven dollars. If you haven't bought and played this, stop what you are doing, and do it NOW!

Set in the late 21st century, after a corporation known as Memorize has turned Paris into a dystopian metropolis living off positive memories and forgetting the negative ones, you play as Nilin; a memory hunter with the ability to alter specific events in peoples lives or make them forget altogether the truth.
The game itself is pretty basic. You run, you platform and you fight. There's a "gun" you get early in the game called the Spammer, that lets you shoot at and stun, or sometimes kill, enemies. But for the most part, it's a fighting game and a pretty alright one at that. There's not much to say aside from that. The gameplay is standard without anything revolutionary.
The setting, however, is interesting, and Memorize is an impressive antagonist. You get to see a lot of Neo-Paris, too. From the dirty slums, to the sewers, to the tallest penthouses and the Memorize headquarters. And there's a great variety in the environments. The richer areas of the city are clearly rather sterile and have robots working to take care of people. The poorer areas are dirty and cluttered with decals and small objects, giving you a sense of the attention the developers put into them.
All in all? Pretty fun game. Worth a fiver or a tenner if you're in doubt.

If you are looking for a game to play while MvC4 is being made, then this is probably not going to whet your appetite.
Most of the online battles here are going to be one sided combo training for the guy who manages to hit first, and a brutally sad smackdown for the guy who whiffs on his first punch. Yes, this game could be tournament worthy, but the online community is so small and anemic that you have 1000 guys ready to bust out the 96 hit combo he's been practicing in Practice Mode for 3 hours before he hopped on, and maybe 50 other guys like you who are just starting the game and want to spar to get better. Online in general is a cr@pshoot, so maybe if you and your friend has less than 10 hours in the game too, then make a lobby with him and open it up to a few other people to join, so that you can see what the people who have 100 hours in this game do. That's my personal suggestion though, if you want to run up the brick wall that is random online matches, go ahead. I will say though, if your opponent isn't using a lagswitch, the net code is pretty dang good, Mike Z did his due diligence to make sure online matches weren't buggy.
Speaking of Mike Z, here's a short paragraph on the controversy with Lab Zero taking out panty shots in game. When a large part of the fans of your game buy your game for the fanservice, and you take out said fanservice, it can♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot of people, and turn them off from funding or buying any of your other projects, as they don't know whether things in game will be changed for any political, social, or artistic reason that appeals to the director. It's not too hard a concept to grasp, but apparently arguing it, makes you a mysogynist/entitled/mansplainer, etc. You could solve this problem by allowing the player to decide what assets patch they want to play with, but that's just my two cents.
Speaking of graphics, this is where the game really shines. SkullGirls is animated in 60FPS, which was what brought so many people to it in the first place. Beyond that, these animations are done very fluidly, (surprisingly, they didn't outsource the animation to some Korean team), they took their time crafting each frame, so it almost makes sense that a large part of the fanbase were miffed at the edits. Not much to complain about here, Aside from the unpleasantness in the previous paragraph, so I tip my hat to the animation team, you did very well.
Which reminds me of the story mode, another bright spot in this game. Multiplayer isn't the only mode you have to play (
), the team recognized this usual brown note in fighting games, and fully fleshed out story modes for each character, except for Fukua, but it's understandable there. Every story mode has beautifully done illustrations and dialogue that pulls you into the SG world. Even minor characters manage to pop, which was why the character voting for this game's initial release, with all of them vying for a place on the roster.
There are 13 characters on the roster, which for some leaves a lot to be desired, but for those who delve deep into each's strategies, will not be disappointed. Want a cheesy wrestler who grandstands to build power? Beowulf. Want a spritely Olive Oyl with the powers of Looney Tunes at her command? Peacock. My waifu is Eva Braun? Parasoul. The roster isn't huge, but almost everyone is going to find a character they like enough to main. Interestingly enough, you do t have to pick 1 person to main like your average fighting game. MvC fans will delight that they have the choice to play as either 1 powerful character, a team of two regular characters, or three weak characters with tons of assists.
this game can tickle your fancy, or withdraw your money from a kickstarter. Fun with friends, but beware of tortureful online brutes. Wait for the DLC to be free. Shaky thumbs up here, but good luck Lab Zero, I hope Indivisible works out.

I really like this game. I can't really analyse why the fighting is good because I really don't know about that sort of thing. What I can say is that I found combos challenging but satisfying, and the characters all feel distinct but are not hard to get a handle on. (One thing I found rather interesting is that some of the characters have their own distinct gait). I'm sure somebody much more knowledgable than I could tell you a lot more.
Now onto what I can confidently talk about: art direction, music, and story. All three are cocking great. Let's talk art first. The game has a nice art style which is applied to some fantastically imaginative designs, from the jazz cyborg Big Band to the really genuinely unpleasent eldritch abomination that is Double. The soundtrack is a bouncy mix of jazz tracks that perfectly match the 1940s America on acid setting. The basis for the plot is a standard magical endgame mcguffin type thing, but it's the world it takes place in that sets it apart. The world of Skullgirls is really nasty and grim, but only by beating the story with every character can you build up a full picture of how ♥♥♥♥ed up it really is. (This is a world in which a man who has converted children into living weapons is arguably the goodest good guy) Every playthrough will answer some of your questions, but raise more, as the relationships between the characters and the truth behind their motives are hinted at and revealed.

The point of any running game is to get used to the pace in order to know when to perform a move. In Bit Trip Runner for example, I knew exactly when to press a button, but there's always an uncertainty in Vector no matter how many times I execute the same moves.

Stash is a charming MMO with turn-based, tactical combat. The art style of the game is reminiscent of playing with tabletop miniatures, as all the characters and mobs are presented as statues on pegs. The similarity continues as you move along in the world on a grid.
So far, combat seems fairly simple. The maps are open, providing you with a lot of room to maneuver. However, I am only level 3 as of writing this review. I suspect that things will become more complex as I level and face stronger opponents. Perhaps there will be obstacles and traps that will challenge me to keep from being flanked and pinned. I don't know, yet, but I plan on continuing to play so that I can find out!
I like the fact that you get a base of operations from the very beginning of the game, where you can stash items, set up crafting, and decorate. It's nice to have your own, little space in the world! However, you do need to level your base up as you play in order to fit more and more stuff. But, I like that. It's another way of having a feeling of making progress in the game.
During my time playing, there was a DDoS attack. It brought everything to a grinding halt, for me. So, if you were caught in that and didn't realize what was happening, I can completely understand any frustration that you might have. However, the devs were online and jumped into action to get the DDoS stopped and the server stable, again. They posted in world chat about the status, as well as invited folks  to their Discord where they could keep an eye on progress made in bringing the server back up for everyone. It took a little while to  get things straight, but not excessively long. I was back in and playing, lag free, within a couple of hours.
The fact that the devs are so attentive is a great plus, in my book. Every time I have logged in, at least one dev has been online, patiently answering questions for those new to the game. That's worth its weight in gold, to me.
Great game and very enjoyable despite the DDOS attack that ruined a few players perception of the game. It is worth a download if you enjoy pen and paper rpg's or turn based combat.

I did play the first AC after I had finished AC3. I do not necessarily recommend it to people who have played the later installments. Anyone who hasn't played any AC game yet will do better with it's sequels because this original AC still lacked much. I did play it because I was curious to see how the series, Altaïr's story and the story about "Those Who Came Before" started and was fairly disappointed.
The cities and rural areas are fairly nice to look at and ride through. However they all look and feel sort of the same, both weather and the daytime are static (the whole game plays at sunny daytime). Perhaps one can see more in it if he knows Damascus, Israel and the other cities you visit in this game, though I assume they have changed a lot over the centuries. Monumental places and buildings are not "commented" by the Animus system whatsoever, which makes it hard for people who don't know these cities to connect to them and to their history. You do not buy places, build your own "home" or interact with the cities in any bigger scale either (there isn't any money or economy to begin with). There is some awe-inspiring feeling to the whole of Maysaf being the center of the Assassin order, and both Altaïr and his mentor have a feeling of serious- and meaningfulness you may miss within the later installments. But even then their outlines are fairly weak; after having finished this game I could hardly understand what the fuss about Altaïr was about for people to apparently miss him so much when Ezio became the new protagonist in AC2. Altaïr didn't feel as special as I had believed he was, hell you will probably dislike him because he is an arrogant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ throughout most parts of the game.
The true letdown is the gameplay. The combat is underdeveloped compared to the sequels (you cannot strike down enemies  with assassination streaks as they were introduced with Brotherhood, you don't have as many weapons - it didn't feel as enjoyable) and the progression throughout the game is pretty repetitive. This original game is probably most faithful to the idea of being an assassin as you are constantly tasked to kill some templars hiding in the cities, often wealthy or well-protected people you need to "locate" first by doing minor tasks that in the later installments would pass for "side activities" at best: Eavesdrop one some guys, beat up/question another, pickpocket some intel from someone else and the likes. There are about 5 of these tasks to do per kill target, you choose which to do and need to finish about 3 of them to be able to "locate", approach and strike your kill target (which thankfully have some background, and are approached in a bit more interesting way than your previous tasks). After that you go back to Maysaf, speak to your mentor and go for a new target. Rinse and repeat. And that's already about it mostly. There are activities having the nature of "collectibles", like killing templars hiding in specific locations in the cities and rural areas, or saving citiziens from repressive soldiers, but those activites are very repetitive too. They didn't really motivate me much to roam about more than I had to. There are some unique story/plot moments, but they are rare.
Also, this game had an usability issue: It doesn't have subtitles. It may seem stupid, but apparently it wasn't self-evident back then. For a game trying to take serious steps in storytelling and bringing some past time to life it would help to understand all the people. I think they all speak English in this game (in the later games the citizens partly speak in their native language), but I still can't understand them all because English isn't my main tongue. There are some whisperings of story-relevant characters in parts of the game - don't expect me to get any of their lines too well either.

I'd just like to say that this is totally an "act II" sort of game. It bridges the events of The New Order to the last installment not even announced yet. If you didn't realize this about the story before you forked out the cash, then you're a bit of a naïf.
Now to my objective review: In The New Order, it felt like you were an action hero meant to fight a stealth game. This time around they realized that in their designs, given the option for stealth or guns blazing, one has to have the ability to choose given the same arenas and corridors no matter the style of play. This game gives you more options, without the need to be a stealth master gamer to succeed at stealth, or likewise the embodiment of death himself to succeed at carnage.
But don't get me wrong, the game will punish you for your mistakes. Because of this, I wish the save/load was a bit more streamlined. An example of this (spoilers skip to next paragraph to avoid butt-hurt) is at the train depot under Roswell on the campaign play through. My first time through playing the game I must have reloaded this level 20 times. It was the first real test of stealth tactics, and boy was it unforgiving. I praise the creators to have the balls to do this though. Take Crysis for example: You ♥♥♥♥ up you can just go and hide, and everything dies down. Even if you miss a head shot they won't come after you despite hitting them. Here they set the alarms off. They don't forgive and let you hide. Naturally, due to the ease of the stealth in the prior installment, I never got the chance to see if Alarms were destructible. They are here, and you may need to take advantage of this.
Just to close, I want to reiterate that I feel this is a classic "Act II" story. It raises the stakes but there is no pay off in the end, because the rising tensions cannot be resolved until the last act.
It's fun, it's absurd, and full to the brim of things to keep the completion-ists very happy. But as far as story goes, they kept the formula from the New Order, but I'd say they didn't flesh it out as much as they could have.

Short, weak ancillary character motivations, uninspired weapon design, encounter variation is limited, clunky dual-wielding system, messy game balance, AI is a little too noticably artificial (flawed,) and the existence of DLC seems like we were locked out of precious story bits that seemed sorely lacking in the base game.
Despite all that, the gunplay is phenomenal (if you stick to one gun,) BJ Blazkowicz's personal story is very interesting and I hope the franchise returns to discuss more about his past, there are plenty of great moments spent with the other characters even if they seem archetypical and show very little reason to behave as cohesively as they do, the soundtrack is fantastic though it does seem to stick out at certain times, sound design is, too, quite fantastic, world-building collectibles are interesting, and the environments and graphics technologies at play are rather aweinspiring.
Overall, I think it is a good game and is worth picking up, but waiting until it's complete and on sale is a good idea, as well as understanding that in comparison to other entries in the franchise this title seems quite disappointing.
Also, the politics is something to watch out for; it's superficial and could've benefitted from being a little more elaborate in my honest opinion. It's such a rich idea that it feels they are too scared to tread (understandably,) but if it's something you're not into than it's not too terribly in your face and certainly doesn't expose the player to anything dangerously sanctimonious/sacrilegious just don't be shocked to hear the villains, and a protagonist or two, say morally reprehensible things given the theming of the game.

It's difficult to give the game a thumbs up or down because it all depends upon what you are looking for in this sort of game I think. If I could give it a neutral rating, I would. But because I expect more out of my Steam games (than mere mobile ports and because seemingly, there is little to no developer attention given to this game any more, I have to give it a negative review).  Don't let that dissuade from the game if you just want a quick little casual game to pass the time with however.
The game
to be a silly, casual, pc port of the not so well received mobile version (the mobile version is riddled with negative ratings due to stability, bug, and lack of developer attention on issues).
On with the nitty gritty....
It's important to understand that this is not a business sim. It isn't intended to be one. It would be like saying that the mobile app Airport Controller
is intended to be an air traffic controler simulator. No...Hospital Manager is an arcade game with the backdrop of a hospital.  It's all "finger placement" and "finger tap" but with a mouse for the PC version.
This might be more fun on a tablet, but then you'd probably be buying the seemingly abandoned mobile version of the game.
If you want a casual, arcade game with a hospital as the backdrop, and don't mind the low fps at times when things get hectic, go for it. If you are expecting something more sophisticated like an actual simulator or even something with more options/features/customization such as Theme Hospital, then you probably will be disappointed and should stay away.

I knew I shouldn't've, but gave this game the benefit of the doubt because Theme Hospital was one of my favourite games of all time and thought this could do alright. It's basically a mobile game adapted to PC - definitely not worth the $3, which sounds a bit harsh, but... there's just no gameplay. Sure, there's a tiny bit of management re: building rooms and elevating mood, but with all the clicking patients to make them happy, etc. it screams mobile. The music is repetitive, the levels are fairly boring. You can't draw your own room boundaries, it's nowhere near complex and yeah. Just not for me.
If you like not being challenged, buy it. If you're looking for something like Theme Hospital, turn around and keep walkin'.

Words do not properly describe this game, but I will try:
For me, my life was divided into two parts: before I played this game, and after. If you aren't completely heartless/unfeeling, this game will make you feel emotions you didn't know existed. You WILL cry. You WILL laugh. You WILL cry a lot more.
If any one game in my Steam collection could be used as evidence of the whole "games are art" argument, it would have to be this one. The visuals are as meticulously and lovingly created as you will find in a retro, pixel-art style, and are downright beautiful in places. The characters are amazingly written, easily likable, and easy to get attached to.
The kicker for this game though, is it's splendid use of sound and music. Kan Gao has a way of playing just the right chord progression to make the emotions of the story more impactful; the heavy moments wouldn't hit as hard if it weren't for the fantastic soundtrack. As a fellow musician, I am in awe of his work. Then, there is Laura Shigihara's song. What a beautiful piece of music played at just the right time. The music makes this game what it is: a masterpiece.
Bottom line is this:
If you buy this game at full price, it will sent you back ten bucks. Tissues will be another dollar. I can not think of a better way to spend eleven dollars. If you haven't bought and played this, stop what you are doing, and do it NOW!

The stylish Remember Me will take you on a heavily guided tour of the striking cyberpunk city of Neo-Paris.
Remember Me is not an open world game in spite of how tempted you will be to explore the highly detailed world of Neo-Paris.  Your journey from the slums and sewers to the corporate megaplexes of Neo-Paris will be strongly guided by little yellow chevrons that highlight what path to take and to which ledges to navigate.  Deviating from the recommended path will yield rewards of health and Focus (mana) increases, but the immediate dead ends will soon guide you back to the prescribed path.  While this seems like more of a deliberate design decision than a shortcoming of the game, I think it is important to know what to expect from Neo-Paris.  What you see will be beautifully detailed, but it will be exactly what the designers want you to see.
The combat is based on a combo system and while you cannot alter the sequence of punches or kicks, you can choose with which boons to imbue them.  As your character progresses you will be able to unlock punches and kicks that replenish health, deal extra damage, shorten cooldowns of your special abilities, or amplify the effect of the previous
attack.  Although you will frequently be outnumbered by foes that interrupt your combos, their attacks are broadcasted in such a way that you can dodge them to hopefully continue your combo on the baddie you have singled out.  Successfully completing a long combo will yield extra PMP (XP used to unlock Pressens, the perks you use to enhance
your punches and kicks) and finish off enemies faster.  Bosses will often be surrounded by these lesser mobs and defeating them helps build the Focus you will need to execute your S-Pressens (special attacks) to overcome the bosses' immunities and ultimately defeat them.  After depleting a boss's health, you'll enter a sequence in which you stylishly deal the finishing blows to your enemy, but you'll have to satisfy QTE prompts to dispatch him.  Failing any prompt will kick you back to the regular combat where you will have to whittle down the last fraction of the boss's health again before attempting the QTEs.  While people may not appreciate QTEs, I enjoyed the cinematic flare with which they allowed me to finish off a boss.
The S-Pressens mentioned earlier are unlocked at specific points in the story and it is up to you to figure out which ones are best used against specific enemies to exploit their weaknesses or overcome their immunities.
Also at specific to points in the plot are the memory remixes wherein the player is tasked with reviewing an NPC's memory and changing details of it to alter how an event is remembered.  Rotating the thumbstick of the controller to rewind or fast-forward through memories was a satisfyingly tactile experience (microfilm, anyone?) and although reaching the desired outcome of any memory remix is mostly an exercise in trial and error, the solutions are not as random or obscure as many puzzles of the point-and-click genre.  There are only four of these remixes throughout the game, but they are a welcome improvement on the passive cut scenes they might have otherwise been.
Neo-Paris is a fitting backdrop for uncovering a plot whose theme centers around memories.  In a world where the technology allows for the storage, transfer, and manipulation of memories you will be tasked with recovering your wiped memories and thwarting a plot to use this technology to topple the utpoian Neo-Paris.  If doing so in a richly detailed cyberpunk world with some stylish fight sequences and light puzzle and platforming sequences sounds good to you, consider picking up Remember Me.

Between Me and The Night is an adventure game about a boy with his game. There isn't much text in the story so you need to interpret the story by yourself.
The game is using a simple yet beautiful 2D graphics. Some cutscenes have graphics that look like 3D. There are usually some animation of people in the events and those looks great.
I hardly hear any music in the game but whenever i hear one, it sounds relaxing. The sfx also works well with the bgm. All in all, the music is pleasant to hear.
As i said before, there isn't much text in the story. You'll have to interpret the story by yourself from the events and cutscenes. However, some cutscenes are very laggy (i even didn't see all of the final cutscenes because the cutscene stuck which makes me have to skip it). I don't know whether it's just me or not, but i hardly understand the story
.
The game will start with a simple tutorial for the controls and then moved to the main story. In the main story itself, you are placed in your bedroom without any idea of what to do, except by following the "flashy lights" or exploring all rooms for hints. This happened all the way until the game ends which can make it hard if you don't really pay attention to the details. You can take almost all items in the game (up to 6 items at once). You also might take any useless items that way.
You might think that you'd rather to explore all rooms for hints to make it easier. However, in the very first level, the developer added a nasty ghost enemy which will kill you whenever you are close to it. This also can happen if you have a bad luck and encountering it in the place where you came out. You'll return to your bedroom if you got "hit" by them (keeping all of your items).
There are also some "boss" that you have to fight or avoid. It's usually requires a simple task such as running away and it shouldn't pose much problem (unless if you're that unlucky). These nasty enemies can only be encountered at the first level, which makes the first level to be the hardest level out there (while the last level is the easiest).
There are also some minigames throughout the game (and some are mandatory). These mini games have a very bad control that can make you spend more time than needed in order to get the achievements. The worse thing is, you have to beat one minigame which has a very slow walking speed in order to beat the game.
Lastly, there is no manual save. The game will automatically save for each level and you can load any level after you finished the game from the main menu.
Pros:
- Beautiful graphics
- Mini games
Cons:
- Bad mini game controls
- "Laggy" cutscenes
- No manual save
This is an adventure game where you have to interpret the story yourself. The story requires you to play minigames with bad controls.

I don't think people have really considered how difficult it is to make a successful surrealist game. The intended purpose of such a game, going by the definition of the surrealist movement, would be to bridge the gap between dream and reality into a unified existence... which is what a lot of games do just by the nature of their systems. It's a bold fight to pick for Between Me and The Night, especially as grounded in conventional adventure logic as it is. It would probably also help if it weren't so bogged down with bugs, but we're getting ahead of ourselves here.
Between Me and The Night puts you in the shoes of a young boy alone in his home. The nature of the house itself soon proves to be supernaturally hostile, leaving you to pick your way through bits of his reality while dodging elements of nightmare. Innocuous tasks like feeding the cat and mowing the lawn take on new depth when the cat is a hulking beast, the lawn lies on the edge of oblivion, and strange creatures roam the halls in between. As you progress through the game you'll progress through the boy's life and his long-standing and familiar love of video games.
Functionally, this plays just like any other side-scrolling adventure. You walk the boy left or right, push boxes and chairs around, climb up onto things to reach high items, and collect things to use on things to open the path to more things. The interface is a little different, hiding the mouse until you click and allowing you to grab virtually anything in the game and carry up to six potentially useless doodads. Items are used to open doors and complete tasks like the aforementioned cat feeding, or to fulfill hidden side objectives like collecting action figures or listening to cassettes.
The adventure takes you through the boy's home, school, and eventual apartment, granting glimpses of the past and hints at his present. Between these realms are interludes in a video game world where you take up sword and shield to venture through snowy mountains to scale a tower. There's combat in these bits, a sort of low-rent 2D Dark Souls thing with slow attacks and blocks and dodges. It only APPEARS Soulsish, mind you, because it's easy enough to run up to the two kinds of enemies and just clickspam them to death. There's no platforming in these bits, but there is in a few little side games you can play that emulate old NES and GameBoy games on a very limited (like, single-level) scale.
Considering how simple the tasks are and how small the areas are, that doesn't leave a whole lot to see or do even if you're going for the side achievements. This is where the monsters come in, in awkward, unwelcome fashion no less. After a short time in each area, a twisted nightmare creature will appear to slowly and loudly patrol the halls. These critters will bee-line for you if they see you, devouring you and instantly sending you back to the start of the area with no progress lost. That's right, you pretty much just get teleported away for messing up, which is good because the game gives you no way to fight or flee or distract or circumvent these things. If there's a monster somewhere, you can't do anything about it. Well, besides feed yourself to it for no penalty so it jumps to another part of the level.
I would be more gracious to the thin gameplay and annoying enemies if the rest of the game were mechanically sound, but... I had to use a walkthrough to beat it. That's not unusual for me, a lot of point-and-clicks have puzzles I get stuck on. But I had to use a walkthrough from start to finish because it is infuriatingly easy to make the game unwinnable. Seriously, in the house area, if you do any of the major tasks out of order (which you easily can since everything is open) it will break the scripting and make it impossible to progress. I had to do the house chapter FIVE TIMES because triggers kept breaking and, in one case, a monster ate me while I was solving a puzzle which made the key item to solving it disappear forever.
This is already plenty of strikes against the game, but I haven't forgotten about its claim to surrealism. At this point it should be clear that Between Me and The Night is hardly more surreal than a standard indie adventure that takes place in the character's mind. Honestly titles like Neverending Nightmares and Fran Bow have far, FAR greater claims to surrealism than this. But what really galls me is how this artistic direction gives the game the excuse to not explain anything about itself. Video games and common childhood anxieties are featured heavily but no real lines are drawn between them, and the story never really resolves with any sort of statement about the boy. For God's sake, the achievement for beating the game is called "I don't get it" which is either taunting folks who bother to divine any meaning from it, or a tacit admission that there really is no meaning to divine. And either way, it doesn't speak well to your intentions as a storyteller.
Between Me and The Night simply purports to be something it isn't. It clearly wants to be a deep and meaningful exploration of trauma and escapism, played out in a world which allows the psyche to intrude on reality. What it ends up being is a pretty standard side-scrolling point-and-click with a substandard story, purposefully removed to give the illusion of complex symbolism. I would like to have seen far more done with the sharp art style and unusual interface, but it's all in service of a game that's too short and plain to do its themes justice.

This is a quite challenging but still fun game in the old "Command and Conquer" RTS vein, but with the level of historic detail it should be compared to the "Cossacks 2" series. The interface is fairly simple as are the graphics, but the visuals maintain the game's historic accuracy (the differences between national uniform). It can't be compared to the "Blitzkrieg" series for graphics, and it's somewhat behind the "Battle of Empires" mod for "Company of Heroes", but for the price there's quite literally hours (if not weeks or even months in the campaigns) of game play with thankfully little frustration for the junior leader or even the veteran RTS player. A well-trained AI is built into the game to manage your civil or military war effort for you so you need do very little, unless you really want a challenge. Then you should fully expect General War in all his aspects! Finally and thankfully the game doesn't just park itself in trench warfare-you should expect what really happened in 1914; the dawn of twentieth-century warfare with all the associated horrors.
